The Promise of the Kurdish Peace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

August brought some truly transformative good news for Turkey, the Kurds, and Turkey’s immediate neighborhood in the Middle East. On Aug. 10, the Turkish Parliament passed a law establishing a legal framework for the dissolution of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), the Kurdish militant group, and creating a phased pathway for reintegration of its members into society.
For more than four decades, the Kurdish issue has run like an electrified barbed wire through conversations in Turkey. The armed conflict between the PKK and the Turkish government has killed around 40,000 militants, soldiers, and civilians, and cost Turkey losses estimated to be around $2 trillion since 1984. Following peace talks, in July 2025, the PKK held a symbolic weapon-burning ceremony, starting a process of disarmament and moving toward ending the armed conflict.
The law offers legal protections to former PKK militants who have not committed specific crimes and helps suspend prison sentences for some members of the group. Thousands of sympathizers, activists affiliated with the PKK, and Kurdish politicians have been living in exile in Europe and elsewhere to escape legal prosecution. The law opens a path for them to return to Turkey. And the passage of this law in the Turkish parliament with broad support is a transformative step toward lasting peace and the creation of a new social contract between Turkey and the Kurds, domestically and regionally.
How to make peace
In the past decade, Turkey established clear military dominance in the fight against the PKK. Changes in military technology, intelligence, and surveillance systems, especially the rise of Turkish drones, strengthened the country’s counter-insurgency efforts. Yet Turkey’s military capacity to suppress an insurgency was not the sole factor in persuading the PKK to give up arms. Turkey did suppress waves of Kurdish rebellions in the past without creating space for Kurdish aspirations, and each suppression was followed by a more formidable and more violent rebellion.
Turkey’s embrace of a political process—instead of simply pursuing a decisive military path—to end the conflict made it more acceptable to the PKK leadership and the Kurdish movement. Abdullah Ocalan, the leader of the PKK, had to persuade his comrades to dissolve their organization, abandon the armed struggle, and choose political struggle. Unfavorable broader regional trends against armed militancy may have helped convince Ocalan and his comrades to make that consequential choice.
The legitimacy of the political solution, in the eyes of the Kurds, determines its sustainability and transformative impact. The current peace process seeks to end the insurgency and transform the struggle for Kurdish rights and aspirations into a nonviolent political one. It could transform Turkey’s relations with its own Kurdish community and the Kurdish communities in Iraq, Syria, and Iran. Leaders of the Kurdish movement believe that they can achieve more through politics than through armed struggle, and that it isn’t only they who are transforming, but that the state, political, and legal systems in Turkey can also change. The promise of the future, rather than being beholden to the grievances of the past, is the way forward.
The Turks and the Kurds managed it without relying on foreign peacemakers or mediation. The disarmament and demobilization process for the PKK was designed, executed, and monitored domestically, without involving any foreign mediators. The talks were held between Turkey’s National Intelligence Organization, Ocalan, and several other leaders of his group based in the Qandil Mountains in Iraqi Kurdistan and across Europe. The process involved the Turkish parliament and political parties through a Parliamentary Committee, formed in Aug. 2025 to work on legal and political dimensions of the PKK’s dissolution, which helped garner broad support for the peace process across political divides in Turkey.
Turkey and the Kurds have entered a new phase that demands greater buy-in for the peace process from politicians, lawmakers, ordinary people, and from the institutions that will implement the new law. To ensure the peace process has broader societal support, the political class will need to make clear why it matters and what it promises. The stakes of getting that right are high for Turkey and extend beyond its borders.
Seeing like a state
The nation-state in the 20th century largely adopted a conception of nationhood based on a single identity and was intolerant, assimilationist, or exclusionary toward other identities. The effect was to politicize and mobilize the very groups it sought to submerge. This was true of Turkey as well. The Turkish Republic was based on a single identity and an overly centralized state with its own insecurities, largely stemming from the traumatic experience during the collapse of the Ottoman Empire.
Today, Turkey needs a new conception of the nation-state that is inclusive of different identity groups, and a new idea of a strong state that is premised on broader societal legitimacy. Centralization coupled with exclusion is a recipe for societal discontent, which weakens, rather than strengthens, the state. Turkey’s real challenge is building an inclusive national identity that recognizes distinct identity groups without losing the thread of what binds them together. The task of the ongoing Kurdish peace process, and the Kurdish politics that will follow it, will be to achieve exactly this: an inclusive notion of national identity capacious enough to accommodate Kurdish identity and aspirations.
The current political mood in the Middle East and elsewhere is not one of militant groups and insurgencies. The broader trend runs toward their integration into state structures or their disarmament and demobilization. How these processes of demobilization and integration are carried out will be highly consequential. If they rely solely on coercion, rather than embracing persuasion and the prospect of mutual transformation, disarmament risks being a prelude to the next cycle of violence, waged under new names and banners.
Demobilization of insurgent groups succeeds when it rests on the prospect of mutual transformation. The armed groups dissolve themselves and remake themselves as political actors, who cease to be adversaries of the state and work as agents of its transformation.
The state and the polity, in turn, must transform alongside them, arriving at a more inclusive conception of national and geopolitical identity. In Turkey, it would mean embracing Kurdishness and honoring Kurdish political, democratic, and cultural rights, and regarding the Kurds outside of Turkey’s borders not as threats but as allies.
The PKK’s demobilization will reshape Turkey’s threat perception, and with it, Turkey’s approach to Kurds in Iraq, Syria, Iran and their countries. Already, in step with the pace of the PKK disarmament, the language used by Turkish officials and Kurdish actors across the region towards each other has improved significantly.
Fruits of peace
Turkey and its neighborhood have already benefited from the peace process and the demobilization of the PKK. That process faced two formidable tests in Syria and Iran and passed both. Turkey treated the PKK’s demobilization at home and the integration of Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF)—led by a Kurdish militia with close ties to the PKK—into the Syrian state as parts of a single process.
After the fall of the Assad regime, reuniting a fractured Syria became one of the most formidable tasks for the new government. The SDF controlled almost a quarter of Syrian territory. Limited fighting and military pressure earlier in the year helped shift the balance, stripping the SDF of a large portion of the land it had held.
What helped make the SDF’s integration into the Syrian state relatively smooth was the peace process already underway in Turkey, given the SDF’s close ties to the PKK. August brought two momentous developments: Turkey’s parliament passed the landmark legislation providing for the disbanding of the PKK, the reintegration of its fighters and the dismissal of charges against thousands of its sympathizers and prisoners; and the SDF announced its own dissolution.
A parallel drama played out during the Iran War. There were fears that the Iranian Kurdish militant group known as the Party for Free Life in Kurdistan, or the PJAK, might join the American war against Iran. Given its close ties to the PKK, such a move could have weakened the PKK’s commitment to disarmament and risked a new phase of conflict among Turkey, the PKK, and the PJAK. Despite pressure from the Trump Administration and Israeli plans to draw them into the conflict, Iranian Kurdish groups stayed out of the war. The peace process in Turkey was a major factor in persuading them to remain on the sidelines.
Together, the Syrian and Iranian cases reveal the power of political imagination and legitimacy in advancing national security. In both instances, Turkey has achieved more through political engagement than through military force. Any national security doctrine devoid of political imagination or legitimacy remains incomplete. The tests posed by Syria and Iran have demonstrated the PKK’s commitment to demobilization, confirmed that its decision is strategic rather than merely tactical, and helped build trust between Turkey and the PKK.
This process will also have considerable implications for Turkey’s relations with major powers. No issue has bedeviled Turkish-American relations more than the Syrian civil war did before the collapse of the Assad regime. At its core, that crisis reflected the conflicting American and Turkish approaches to the Syrian Kurds, specifically the People’s Protection Units (YPG), a PKK affiliate that, with American military advice and support, was later rebranded as the SDF.
By enabling the SDF’s integration into the Syrian state, the PKK’s demobilization has removed the most formidable sticking point in Turkish-American relations, clearing the way for closer cooperation between the two countries in Syria and beyond. Ocalan framed the recently passed Turkish law as the first step of a 1000 kilometer journey. The Turkish model, and the peace it promises, are still a story in the making. Despite the milestones already reached, formidable challenges remain, demanding persistence and commitment.
No two conflicts or two peace processes are alike. Yet the central message is universal: peace is possible and leadership matters. Long-running conflicts around identity are not fates to be endured but political questions to be settled. In a world still defined by war and insecurity, the story of peacemaking is, inherently, a global one.

Taiwan’s ASE targets 57% renewable energy use by 2035
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:58:18 UTC
18:58:18 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — ASE Technology Holding said Wednesday it plans to increase the share of renewable energy in its electricity use to 57% by 2035.
The semiconductor packaging and testing company said renewable energy and certificates accounted for 22.99% of its total electricity consumption last year, per CNA. ASE said its strategy includes generating solar power, signing corporate power purchase agreements, and buying renewable energy certificates.
By the end of last year, about 89% of ASE’s manufacturing sites worldwide were using renewable energy or certificates, with 10 sites reaching 100% coverage. Approximately 86% had also adopted the ISO 50001 energy management system, while the company completed 1,422 energy-saving and carbon-reduction projects.
The company said it is also using AI and digital technologies to improve production efficiency and support innovation. Smart factories accounted for 45% of ASE’s manufacturing sites as of last year.
ASE reported consolidated revenue of NT$82.24 billion (US$2.61 billion) in August, up 11.47% from the previous month and 45.66% from a year earlier, per Liberty Times.

Taiwan museum partners with UK center to train translators
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:58:02 UTC
18:58:02 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The National Museum of Taiwan Literature and the UK’s National Centre for Writing have signed an agreement to train translators of Taiwanese literature into English, CNA reported Wednesday.
Economic Daily News reported that Culture Minister Li Yuan (李遠) witnessed the signing in Norwich, England’s first UNESCO City of Literature. The agreement creates a “Literature from Taiwan” category in the National Centre for Writing’s mentorship program for emerging translators.
The program accepts applicants worldwide who are interested in translating Taiwanese literature into English. Participants will receive mentoring and professional training to improve their translation skills and deepen their understanding of Taiwan’s literary works.
Li said Taiwan and the UK have a long history of cultural cooperation. He said the partnership could strengthen those ties and introduce more Taiwanese writers and books to British readers.
National Centre for Writing Chair Alan Waters said the organization had already been promoting Taiwanese literature before the agreement was signed. In 2024, it hosted two translators of Taiwanese literature and worked with The Strangers Press to publish five booklets featuring translated works from Taiwan.
Waters said the 2026-27 mentorship program received 16 applications. He said the number reflected strong international interest in translating Taiwanese literature.
The two organizations plan to expand their cooperation in 2027. Waters said they expect to develop a translator residency program and hold a Taiwanese literature festival in Norwich in spring 2027.
A UNESCO City of Literature is a city recognized for its literary heritage and support for books, writers, and reading. There are 63 worldwide, including six in the UK: Edinburgh, Norwich, Nottingham, Manchester, Exeter, and Aberystwyth.

====================================================================================================

Ceuta President urges the EU to take firm action against Morocco, as the city is 'on the brink of collapse'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:57:39 UTC
18:57:39 KST

Juan Jesús Vivas accused Rabat of pursuing a “harassment policy” aimed at suffocating the exclave, while the Spanish government and the EU continue to regard Morocco as a trusted partner in addressing irregular migration.
Ceuta’s president, Juan Jesús Vivas, has accused Morocco of a “policy of harassment” towards the city and urged the EU to take a tougher stance and fund border security after some 80,000 migrants entered the exclave on 30 July, distancing himself from Spain’s cooperative approach to Rabat.
Vivas met three EU commissioners and several lawmakers in Brussels on Tuesday, urging help to return irregular migrants and restore normality in the exclave, where thousands of third-country nationals, including unaccompanied minors, remain. "Ceuta is on the brink of collapse," he said.
The Ceuta leader broke with the national government, accusing Pedro Sánchez’s administration of failing to respond adequately before, during and after the July incident, which left more than 150 people dead at sea.
“The EU should tell Morocco that any fruitful and mutually beneficial cooperation begins by respecting our borders,” he said at a press conference at the European Parliament, where center-right EPP lawmakers and staff greeted him with applause.
Spain has not blamed Morocco for the Ceuta incident, despite calling it a violation of its territorial integrity.
Instead, Madrid has pointed to false claims on social media and human traffickers as the main drivers of the mass influx, while continuing to describe Rabat as a “trusted partner” in tackling irregular migration — a position echoed by the European Commission.
“The government should explain why it refuses to hold Morocco responsible, whether directly or through inaction, for the invasion,” Vivas said, after being asked about a leaked police report suggesting Moroccan forces played a role in the crisis.
He claimed that Rabat maintains a “policy of harassment” towards the city and that his fellow citizens now live in fear that a sudden major influx could happen again.
Vivas stopped short of calling for the suspension of EU funds to Morocco, a request made in recent days by Spain’s far-right party Vox. The EU is currently financing Rabat’s migration management strategy with €160 million until 2027.
In his talks with the Commissioners, he also asked for financial support to build border infrastructure and manage the humanitarian crisis that erupted after the mass influx.
According to Vivas, EU Commissioners Andrius Kubilius, Magnus Brunner, and Dubravka Šuica expressed support for Ceuta, but the Commission made no specific commitments.
Brussels is now set to send a technical mission to Ceuta this week to "assess the situation", a Commission spokesperson said on Tuesday.
As Europe’s only land border with Africa, Ceuta, along with Melilla, should have a “special status," within the EU and migration rules adapted to their circumstances, Vivas said.
Another request is for a “permanent presence” in Ceuta of the EU asylum agency (EUAA) and Frontex, the agency responsible for the bloc’s external borders.
“The situation is untenable. We need EU support to restore normality. If Ceuta falls, Europe falls,” Vivas said.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — New Taipei City Government has clashed with the central government over NT$5.41 billion in cuts to subsidies for MRT-related projects in the 2026 fiscal year.
New Taipei City Government’s Department of Rapid Transit Systems said Sunday that although the Ministry of Transportation and Communications (MOTC) increased its overall subsidies for MRT systems to NT$45.3 billion (US$1.44 billion), New Taipei City saw NT$5.41 billion in cuts, per UDN.
The department said funding for the Keelung Line was reduced by NT$4.7 billion, while the Danhai Line light rail system received no subsidies for the 2027 fiscal year.
New Taipei Mayor Hou Yu-ih (侯友宜) said Tuesday that the city’s MRT projects have long been recognized for staying on schedule and within budget, per Liberty Times. He noted that Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) had previously praised the Sanying Line for not requiring additional subsidies from the central government.
Hou said New Taipei had pushed forward with the projects at its own expense, but called on the central government to restore NT$14.41 billion in subsidies cut from the 2026 and 2027 fiscal-year budgets.
The city government also highlighted its budget implementation rate. It said MRT projects achieved a 95.87% implementation rate, compared with the 80% average cited by the MOTC, per Liberty Times.
Both the Keelung Line and Sanying Line achieved a 100% budget implementation rate in 2025, according to the city government. However, the MOTC approved 49.71% of the requested subsidies for the Keelung Line and 83% for the Sanying Line.
The city government also said the Danhai Line would have achieved a 100% budget implementation rate in 2025 had the central government provided subsidies.
New Taipei said it had applied for NT$21.79 billion in subsidies for the 2026 fiscal year but received NT$5.41 billion less than requested. The MOTC disputed the figure, saying it had approved 85.5% of the NT$18.72 billion in subsidies requested for MRT lines located within New Taipei City, per China Times. The approval rate ranked second only to Taipei, the ministry said.
Keelung Mayor Hsieh Kuo-liang (謝國樑) also called on the central government to restore the reduced subsidies, warning that further reductions could affect the Keelung Line’s construction schedule, per Liberty Times. He said Keelung’s budget was already under considerable pressure from its share of the project’s costs.
The dispute over MRT subsidies has become an issue in the November local elections.
The KMT legislative caucus said New Taipei had submitted its subsidy application for Phase 2 of the Danhai Line 13 times and had been rejected on each occasion, per ETtoday. DPP New Taipei City councilors, on the other hand, called on the city government to submit more comprehensive proposals to the central government instead of blaming it for delays, per NOWNews.
KMT New Taipei mayoral candidate Lee Shu-chuan (李四川) said the Sanying Line, which faces subsidy reductions, serves residents in the electoral district of DPP candidate Su Chiao-hui (蘇巧慧), per ETtoday. He called on Su to address the funding issue.
Su responded Wednesday, saying she would ensure that no further reductions are made to the subsidies, per SETN.

Which countries banned goods from settlements but trade with Israel?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:52:50 UTC
18:52:50 KST

Which countries banned goods from settlements but trade with Israel?
More European countries are calling to ban products from illegal Israeli settlements, despite sizable overall trade with Israel.
The United Kingdom has announced a ban on the import of all goods produced in illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said in Parliament on Tuesday.
It comes in response to an intensifying wave of Israeli settler pogroms and settlement expansions in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem.
The ban, set to come into effect within six to nine months, would target settlement exports such as dates, olive oil and agricultural products, with Miliband saying he did not believe “the British people want us supporting the occupation by accepting products from settlements in our shops”.
The International Court of Justice in July 2024 called Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory “unlawful”. Months later, the United Nations passed a resolution calling for an end to the Israeli occupation within a year.
Israel’s response was furious, as it announced four “counter-measures”, including banning 12 British MPs from entering Israel and closing the British consulate in Jerusalem.
After Miliband’s speech, 11 more countries: Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden, shared a joint statement supporting the so-called two-state solution and announcing their own intentions to impose restrictions on trade with illegal Israeli settlements.
Spain and Ireland had already announced their own national bans earlier this year, alongside the Netherlands and Belgium.
How much do these countries trade with Israel?
Aside from Canada and the UK, the rest of the countries considering or already banning settlement goods are European Union members.
The EU is Israel’s largest trading partner, accounting for 31.7 percent of Israel’s total trade in goods in 2025 (43.3 billion euros, or $50.4bn), according to the European Commission. The EU supplied 33.1 percent of Israel’s imports (28 billion euros, or $32.6bn) and received 29.4 percent of Israel’s exports (15.3 billion euros or $17.8bn).
Israel is the EU’s 27th largest trade partner, with Ireland, the Netherlands and Germany being its biggest individual trade partners.
According to a 2026 report by Global Echo Litigation Center, a Palestinian rights legal advocacy group, roughly 5,900 shipments from Israel were headed to Europe, with more than 17 percent containing products originating from settlements.
While no specific figures for settlement trade alone are known, it is understood to be a tiny fraction of total EU-Israel trade, meaning the ban’s impact is much more symbolic than economic.
The table below shows each country’s total trade with Israel for the European countries that have banned, or are introducing bans on, illegal Israeli settlement goods.
The top five European trading partners with Israel either enforcing or set to introduce settlement bans are Ireland, the Netherlands, the UK, France and Spain.
Ireland
Ireland-Israel bilateral trade totalled $5.36bn in 2025. Ireland is Israel’s second-largest export market for goods after the United States, driven largely by tech, particularly semiconductors and integrated circuits.
The Netherlands
Netherlands-Israel bilateral trade totalled roughly $4.8bn in 2025. The Netherlands is also Israel’s largest single foreign investor, accounting for roughly two-thirds of all EU investment in the country.
United Kingdom
According to UN Comtrade, UK-Israel bilateral trade totalled $3.73bn in 2025. An Al Jazeera investigation found at least 17 companies linked to illegal Israeli settlements hold more than 2.1 billion pounds ($2.85bn) in UK public-sector contracts.
France
France-Israel bilateral trade totalled $3.62bn in 2025. A large part of France’s trade with Israel constitutes export licences for surveillance and military technologies.
Spain
Spain-Israel bilateral trade totalled $2.79bn in 2025. In September that year, Spain banned the import of goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory, as well as the trade of arms.
What are Israeli settlements?
Israeli settlements are Jewish-only communities built illegally on Palestinian land.
Settlements are illegal under international law as they violate the Fourth Geneva Convention, which bans an occupying power from transferring its population to the area it occupies.
Illegal Israeli settlements continue to grow, decades after the 1993 Oslo Accords, which established limited Palestinian self-rule and were meant to lead to a permanent peace settlement.
At the time, about 270,000 settlers lived across the occupied territory. Today, that figure has more than doubled to between 600,000 and 750,000 people, about 10 percent of Israel’s Jewish population, living across some 250 illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem.

Search and rescue efforts are underway for eight people, including five journalists, who went missing after traveling to the area around Indonesia’s Anak Krakatau island to cover a volcanic eruption, authorities said.
Al Amrad, head of the Search and Rescue Office in Indonesia’s Banten province, said in a statement that contact had been lost with a speedboat carrying five photojournalists, two crew members and a guide.

Meanwhile, although the intense eruptions at Anak Krakatau have subsided, volcanic activity on the island continues.
Volcanic eruption disrupted air traffic
An eruption occurred at Indonesia’s Anak Krakatau volcano on Sept. 6, sending volcanic ash up to 6,000 meters (19,685 feet) over Java and as high as 15,000 meters (49,213 feet) over Sumatra.
Flights were canceled at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport in the capital Jakarta after volcanic ash spread across western parts of the country.
More than 2,300 domestic and international flights were canceled nationwide following the eruption, leaving around 340,000 passengers stranded at seven airports.
Authorities later determined that conditions were safe for aviation, and Soekarno-Hatta International Airport and Halim Perdanakusuma Airport, along with three other airports where flights had been suspended following the eruption, resumed operations.

Lebanon: New media law makes progress but leaves serious free expression gaps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:51:55 UTC
18:51:55 KST

Following years of advocacy by civil society organisations, journalists and activists, Lebanon has passed a new media law that introduces important human rights-based reforms, but falls short of bringing all the changes needed to ensure that the right to freedom of expression is respected, protected and fulfilled in the country, Amnesty International said today.
The Lebanese Parliament adopted a long-awaited Media Law on 11 August 2026 replacing outdated legislation from 1962 and 1994. The law published in the official gazette on 3 September, introduces several long-overdue safeguards for journalists, media workers and people exercising their right to freedom of expression online, including decriminalizing insults and defamation in some instances, introducing stronger protections for sources, prohibiting pretrial detention in media-related cases, restricting military court jurisdiction for such cases, and expanding protections for online expression.
However, parliament missed an opportunity to address other threats to the right to freedom of expression, including by retaining provisions in the Penal Code that carry prison sentences for protected speech such as “insulting” or defaming foreign states, and it also introduces new criminal offence for “false or harmful news”.
“After years of efforts by Amnesty International and other rights groups advocating legislative reform to protect expression in Lebanon, the new media law takes multiple steps forward, including by removing criminal penalties for certain insult and defamation offences and expanding protections for online speech. However, long-standing provisions in Lebanese law that criminalize protected expression remain on the books and could end up undermining progress towards decriminalization that parliament spent nearly years negotiating,” said Reina Wehbi, Lebanon campaigner for Amnesty International.
“In recent years, people in Lebanon that have published or written on controversial topics or criticized powerful actors have been summoned to face criminal investigation or brought to court for peacefully exercising their right to freedom of expression based on vague insult and defamation articles. The Lebanese parliament must not look away from the legal provisions that could still be used to prosecute and intimidate people for peacefully expressing their views and should complete the reform process by repealing the offence of ‘false and harmful news’ which is not a recognizable offence under international law and fully decriminalizing defamation, as well as repealing insult offences.”
As the new law governs expression disseminated through media outlets, publications, websites, online platforms and other electronic means, the protections and exemptions it establishes do not necessarily apply in other contexts in which freedom of expression could be exercised.
New safeguards introduced
One of the positive aspects of the new media law is that it introduces safeguards to reduce the risk that criminal law, military institutions, or investigative powers will be used to suppress criticism or journalism.
Article 114 prohibits pre-trial detention for offences committed through the media and electronic means governed by the law, regardless of the status or profession of the accused. By expressly extending this protection to online expression, the provision resolves a long-standing ambiguity under the previous framework, under which journalists, content creators and other individuals posting online could be prosecuted under the Penal Code and denied the procedural safeguards available in publishing-related cases.
The law improves on existing provisions in Lebanese law concerning “incitement of sectarian conflict, or violence against individuals or groups on the basis of, or because of, their actual or perceived racial, religious, sectarian, ethnic affiliation, color, or sex” by requiring courts to consider factors such as context, intent, influence, dissemination and likelihood of harm when assessing whether speech amounts to unlawful incitement, in line with international human rights standards. These safeguards help distinguish genuine incitement from protected expression, although concerns remain regarding the undefined concept of “sectarian conflict”.
Article 113 strips military courts of jurisdiction over all media and expression cases governed by the law. This addresses a long-standing concern of Amnesty International, which has highlighted cases in which civilians such as journalists faced military prosecution for speech-related offences.
Articles 115 and 116 establish explicit guarantees for editorial independence, protect journalists from interference, intimidation and retaliation aimed at influencing their work, safeguard their right to organize, and provide strong protections for confidential sources by restricting disclosure, surveillance, search and seizure measures capable of revealing a source’s identity except in narrowly defined circumstances subject to judicial oversight.
Additionally, the law modernizes Lebanon’s media framework by expressly recognizing digital media and establishing a clear notification-based registration system for media websites and platforms, which are not subject to prior authorization or licensing. It also removes prior authorization requirements for periodical publications, repeals restrictions on the number of political periodicals, removes the distinction between political and non-political publications, allows internet and satellite-based media outlets to operate through a notification process rather than a licensing regime, and abolishes prior censorship over the printing, publication and distribution of non-periodical publications.
Article 98 gives significant legal weight to the public interest, explicitly protecting reporting that exposes corruption, scrutinizes public officials, or addresses other matters of legitimate public concern. 
 
“These new safeguards represent years-long, diligent and dedicated work by activists, advocates and journalists to improve the environment for free expression in Lebanon. It is now on the state to ensure these safeguards are rigorously adhered to in the days and months ahead,” said Wehbi. 
Serious free expression gaps remain
While the positive developments are significant, there are also a number of gaps that the law did not address retaining problematic provisions on the books that violate freedom of expression.
The new law takes a step backward by criminalizing disinformation, without clearly defining it. Article 104(b) of the new law creates a new offence criminalizing the “intentional fabrication of falsehoods and the dissemination of false or harmful news”, which is punished with up to three years’ imprisonment.
The provision is problematic because it is open to abuse since vague, undefined terms like “harmful news”, create a high risk of arbitrary summons, investigations and prosecutions of journalists, media workers and others.
“Disinformation has a detrimental impact on human rights and it is important for states to take steps to prevent, identify and counter it, however criminalization is not an effective way of addressing it. Given that the scope of this offence will often be unclear, the provision risks becoming a new tool for going after people exercising their right to freedom of expression,” said Reina Wehbi.
After years of debate, this law should mark a decisive shift away from criminal penalties for speech, not create new tools for censorship and prosecution.
Reina Wehbi, Amnesty International
“Parliament should urgently amend the law to ensure that any provisions addressing false news are narrowly defined, and fully consistent with international standards on freedom of expression. After years of debate, this law should mark a decisive shift away from criminal penalties for speech, not create new tools for censorship and prosecution.”
Lebanon’s Penal Code and Military Justice Code include a number of crimes for speech-related offences which have been used to restrict criticism of public officials, state institutions and other powerful actors.
In a step forward, the new media law repeals offences against religious or national sentiment and shifts the framework for addressing a number of speech-related offences relating to insult, libel and slander from a criminal to a civil liability framework for means of expression governed by the law. The law also expands protections for criticism of public officials and public figures by allowing defendants to rely on evidence, indications of truth, and public-interest considerations in their defence.
However, the new media law falls short by excluding a number of speech-related criminal offences from this shift. For example, Article 292 of the Penal Code, which criminalizes insults and defamation directed at foreign states, their heads or their political representatives in Lebanon, remains in force.
Further, ambiguity remains regarding whether cases of libel and slander directed at public authorities and officials have shifted from a criminal to a civil liability framework for means of expression governed by the law.
Articles 107 and 108, which concern the new civil liability framework, include libel and slander for cases involving public officials and public figures. But, in its list of speech-related offences for which criminal penalties had been repealed, Article 105 did not explicitly reference Articles 385 to 387 of the Penal Code, which criminalize libel and slander against public officials, judges, public institutions, the army and the President. Legal experts consulted by Amnesty International said, in their assessment, the legislature likely intended to shift these offences into the new civil framework, but that the absence of an explicit reference leaves room for judicial authorities to continue to apply them.
Amnesty International continues to call for the repeal of laws criminalizing insults directed at heads of state, public officials or other public figures. Public figures are legitimately subject to criticism and political opposition and should tolerate more criticism than private individuals.
Background
Amnesty International has repeatedly documented how Lebanon’s criminal defamation, insult, and other speech-related laws have been weaponized by authorities to investigate, prosecute, and harass journalists, activists, and government critics. In 2023, the organization launched its #MyOpinionIsNotaCrime campaign, demanding the decriminalization of defamation offences, an end to military court jurisdiction over civilian expression, and full compliance with international legal standards.
The reform process of laws governing the media began in 2010 with a draft law presented by former MP Ghassan Moukheiber and the Maharat Foundation to replace the 1962 Publications Law. Over 16 years, the draft underwent extensive revisions across parliamentary subcommittees before final adoption on 11 August 2026. Throughout this process, Amnesty International and its partners in the Coalition for Freedom of Expression in Lebanon have continuously campaigned to ensure that Lebanese legislation protects, rather than suppresses, peaceful debate and media freedom.

S. Korea's school violence hits record high on digital isolation, post-pandemic aggression
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
17:51:03 CST
18:51:03 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's school violence hit a record high, driven by the deepening digital isolation and the post-COVID-19 pandemic aggression, education ministry data showed Wednesday.
According to a school violence survey of 3.9 million students ranging from fourth grade through high school senior year, the overall victim rate stood at 2.9 percent in 2026, up 0.4 percentage points from a year earlier.
It marked the highest since the Ministry of Education began tracking the data in 2013, indicating that almost three out of every 100 elementary, middle and high school students experienced school violence.
The online survey, conducted at least twice a year, saw a participation rate of 81.9 percent, or 3.19 million students, in this year's first round, down 0.3 percentage points from last year.
The survey tracked school violence experiences from the second semester of 2025 through May 2026.
The historic peak underscored an alarming trend as school violence soared relentlessly every single year throughout the 2020s following the post-pandemic school normalization.
The victim rate, which stood at 1.6 percent in 2019, plummeted to 0.9 percent in 2020 due to remote learning during the pandemic, but then climbed to 1.1 percent in 2021, 1.7 percent in 2022, 1.9 percent in 2023, 2.1 percent in 2024, and 2.5 percent in 2025.
Experts warned that the figures revealed a disturbing, longstanding scar from the pandemic era, which caused years of social isolation, alongside heavier reliance on digital devices that hindered the conflict resolution skills of students and led to heightened aggression in classrooms.
"Amid the growing daily use of digital devices, teenagers lack experience in forming direct, face-to-face relationships with others, and their capacity for empathy is also worsening," said Sung Yun-sook, a senior research fellow at the National Youth Policy Institute who conducted and analyzed the survey.
The victim rate rose across all tiers, with elementary schools hitting 5.7 percent, middle schools at 2.3 percent and high schools at 0.8 percent.
By type, verbal violence remained the most prevalent at 37.8 percent, followed by group bullying with 17.1 percent, physical violence with 15.7 percent and cyberbullying with 7 percent.
While verbal violence and cyberbullying decreased by 1.2 percentage points and 0.8 percentage points, respectively, physical violence and group bullying increased by 1.1 percentage points and 0.7 percentage points each.
The overall offender rate reached 0.8 percent this year, down 0.3 percentage points from last year.
The witness rate, however, advanced 0.6 percentage points to 6.7 percent, indicating that while fewer students admit to instigating violence, a larger portion of students is exposed to a hostile school environment. ■

Turkish defense manufacturer MKE enters Egyptian market, sets up company for joint production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:50:03 UTC
18:50:03 KST

Utku Simsek and Fatma Zehra Solmaz
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
- MKE focusing on Egypt not merely as a 'market' but as a country with which it can 'do joint business,' says MKE's General Manager Keles
- 'Egypt has capability to produce military vehicles. We are ... integrating Egypt’s capabilities with our turret and command-and-control systems'
Turkish defense manufacturer Machinery and Chemical Industry (MKE) General Manager Ilhami Keles said the company has established a wholly owned subsidiary in Cairo under Egyptian law, named “Zafer (Victory),” to conduct commercial activities and facilitate joint production projects in Egypt.
Keles spoke to Anadolu at the El Alamein International Airshow in Egypt’s coastal city of El Alamein.
Emphasizing the valuable ties between Egypt and Türkiye as friends and allies, Keles said Egypt is a country with shared historical and religious ties with Türkiye and with which Ankara has close political relations.
“Therefore, doing something with Egypt is very valuable for us,” he said.
Keles said MKE is focusing on Egypt not merely as a “market” but as a country with which it can “do joint business.”
He noted that MKE signed its first contract at the inaugural defense industry exhibition in Sarajevo shortly before arriving in Egypt.
‘We signed a contract with Egypt’
Keles said MKE signed a memorandum of understanding with Egypt’s Ministry of Military Production.
“We signed a contract with Egypt for the joint production of energetic materials and explosives, as well as the joint production of various ammunition equipment.”
Keles said interest in MKE’s TOLGA system has increased, particularly amid the diversification of asymmetric threats.
TOLGA is MKE’s counter-drone system designed to detect and neutralize aerial threats.
“Egypt is also interested in this, and we have sold TOLGA to Egypt,” he said.
He described the initial sale as a symbolic one aimed at introducing TOLGA into Egypt’s inventory, adding that MKE plans to use the joint venture it will establish in Egypt as a platform to market the system across Africa and eventually the Gulf.
“Egypt has the capability to produce military vehicles. We are moving forward with joint production integrating Egypt’s capabilities with our turret and command-and-control systems, as well as our hard-kill and soft-kill solutions,” he said.
Keles added that MKE’s local partner had also requested TOLGA systems at the exhibition.
Technology transfer becoming more important
Keles said MKE’s accumulated know-how, developed through its long-standing capabilities in ammunition and weapons production, has become increasingly valuable.
“All countries are now striving to carry out this kind of production in their own countries. As a result, the ability to transfer technology has begun to take precedence over product exports,” he said.
Keles said MKE is in talks with several countries not only on exports but also on mechanisms for joint production.
“We are establishing joint ventures in Canada, and those processes are continuing. Immediately after here, we will travel to the United States, where we will discuss a number of investments,” he said.
He added that infrastructure for potential cooperation is also developing in countries in Southeast Asia, including Malaysia and Indonesia.
“We entered a tender in Malaysia. Localization is also part of the tender we entered. Therefore, we will also be undertaking something in terms of localization,” he said.
Keles said MKE is continuing contacts with other countries as it seeks to expand its production network, partnerships and markets worldwide.
“We are trying to expand both our production network, our network of contacts and our market around the world with these capabilities. The current international environment is also very conducive to this, and we intend to make use of it,” he said.
‘Zafer’ to manage MKE’s activities in Egypt
Keles said MKE established the Zafer company in Cairo under Egyptian law as part of its agreement on joint production with Egypt.
“We established a company called ‘Zafer’ entirely under Egyptian law, with all of its shares owned by MKE,” he said.
The company will manage MKE’s commercial activities in Egypt and serve as the vehicle through which joint production facilities established with local partners will operate, he added.
“Thus, MKE now has a company here capable of operating under Egyptian law. Just as in Azerbaijan, MKE will continue to have a presence in Egypt through its own legal entity,” he said.
He said the Cairo-based Zafer company will establish partnerships with other companies and local firms in Egypt.
“In other words, Zafer will be a partner in those companies. We established this company in Cairo to contribute to our commercial operations in Egypt, as well as our commercial activities in Africa and the Gulf region,” he said.

The Origins of Wrongful Death Law: How a Victorian Railway Disaster Changed Legal History  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:49:32 UTC
18:49:32 KST

Before 1846, English common law contained a striking gap: a person injured through another’s wrongdoing could generally pursue a civil claim, but a claim did not survive the person’s death. The result was a legal system in which the death of an injured person could eliminate the civil action that might otherwise have been available.
That rule had consequences far beyond the courtroom. As industrialization brought factories, mines, and railways into increasingly widespread use, fatal accidents became a growing social and political concern. The eventual response helped establish the statutory wrongful-death framework that would later influence legal systems in the United States.
The Centuries-Long Blind Spot in Common Law
English common law was traditionally based on the idea that the person who suffered the injury was the person entitled to bring the action. That principle created an obvious problem when the injury was fatal: the injured person could no longer bring a lawsuit.
The 1808 English case Baker v. Bolton became an important statement of this rule. The decision reflected the common-law position that a civil claim for personal injury did not continue simply because the injury resulted in death.
The practical consequences could be severe for surviving relatives. A worker who survived an accident might have a personal claim for injuries, while a family could face a very different legal position if the same accident proved fatal.
As Britain industrialized, this distinction became increasingly difficult to ignore. Railway expansion, mining, and factory work exposed large numbers of people to industrial hazards, while fatal accidents attracted growing public attention.
The Fatal Accidents Act and Lord Campbell’s Role
Pressure for legislative change increased during Britain’s railway boom in the 1840s. Public concern over fatal accidents contributed to calls for a statutory remedy for families who lost relatives through another person’s wrongful conduct.
Parliament responded in 1846 with the Fatal Accidents Act 1846, commonly known as Lord Campbell’s Act. The legislation created a statutory right for specified relatives of a person whose death was caused by a wrongful act, neglect, or default to seek damages.
The Act represented a major departure from the common-law position. Instead of leaving surviving relatives without a civil remedy simply because the injured person had died, Parliament created a specific statutory cause of action.
The original legislation was considerably narrower than many modern wrongful-death statutes. Recovery was structured around the financial consequences of the death, and eligibility was limited to particular categories of relatives.
Even so, the basic legislative idea proved influential: a wrongful death could create a legally recognizable loss for surviving family members, rather than ending the possibility of civil recovery altogether.
How the Idea Crossed the Atlantic
The United States inherited the English common-law tradition, including the general rule that there was no common-law wrongful-death action. As American industrialization accelerated, however, states increasingly confronted the same practical problem that Britain had faced.
New York became the first U.S. state to enact a wrongful-death statute, drawing on the approach established by Lord Campbell’s Act. Other states subsequently enacted their own statutes, although the details differed substantially from state to state. (American Bar Association)
This history helps explain an important feature of modern American wrongful-death law: there is no single nationwide statute governing every claim. Instead, each state has developed its own rules concerning who may sue, what damages may be recovered, and how long a claimant has to bring an action.
For example, a denver wrongful death attorney handling a Colorado claim works within Colorado’s particular statutory framework rather than a single federal wrongful-death code.
That state-by-state development has produced significant differences. Some jurisdictions recognize various forms of noneconomic loss, while others place greater emphasis on financial damages. Rules governing eligible claimants, damages, limitation periods, and punitive damages can also differ.
The Scale of the Problem the Law Addresses Today
Wrongful-death law originated in an era of industrial accidents, but fatal injuries remain a major issue in the United States.
These statistics describe different categories of unintentional injury and do not, by themselves, establish that a particular death was legally wrongful. Whether a surviving family has a wrongful-death claim depends on the facts of the case and the applicable state law.
What Changed—and What Families Still Debate Today
Modern wrongful-death statutes are substantially broader than the original 1846 legislation. Depending on the jurisdiction and circumstances, damages may include losses associated with the deceased person’s earnings, services, companionship, or other legally recognized interests.
The rules are not uniform across the United States. States differ in how they define eligible claimants, calculate damages, apply damages limitations, and establish filing deadlines.
That variation is one of the most important legacies of the history of wrongful-death law. The basic principle may be shared across the country, but the legal remedy is largely shaped by state legislation.
For families, these differences can have practical consequences. The identity of the person entitled to file a claim, the categories of damages available, and the applicable deadline may all depend on the state in which the claim arises.
A Quick Reference: Key Milestones in Wrongful Death Law
● 1808: Baker v. Bolton reinforces the English common-law rule concerning civil claims following death.
● 1846: Parliament passes the Fatal Accidents Act, commonly known as Lord Campbell’s Act, creating a statutory wrongful-death remedy in England.
● Late 1840s onward: U.S. states begin adopting their own wrongful-death statutes, with New York becoming the first.
● 20th century: State wrongful-death laws develop further, including broader approaches to damages and eligible claimants.
● Today: Wrongful-death law remains primarily state-based in the United States, with substantial differences among jurisdictions.
Why This History Still Matters
Wrongful-death law is the product of a fundamental legal change: the recognition that a fatal injury can create legally compensable consequences for the people left behind.
The transition did not happen overnight. It emerged from centuries of common-law doctrine, growing industrialization, public concern over fatal accidents, and legislative efforts to provide families with a civil remedy.
The 1846 Fatal Accidents Act was an important turning point. Its approach helped influence the development of wrongful-death statutes in the United States, where individual states eventually built their own versions of the remedy. (American Bar Association)
Today, the underlying question remains familiar even though the legal rules are much more developed: when someone’s wrongful conduct causes a death, what legal remedy should be available to the people who depended on or were connected to that person?
The answer varies by jurisdiction, but the history explains why wrongful-death claims exist at all—and why their rules continue to evolve.

Skibitsky said Russia’s broader plans also included attempts to blockade the Black Sea and draw Belarus into the war against Ukraine alongside hybrid operations targeting NATO.
However, Ukrainian intelligence has not detected signs that Belarus is currently preparing offensive military formations on its territory, he said.
“At present, we do not see real indicators of preparations for strike groups on Belarusian territory, but we remember January and February 2022,” Skibitsky said.
He identified domestic political risks, limited military capabilities and possible economic problems as the primary factors discouraging Belarus from directly entering the war.
However, HUR considers it likely that Belarus will continue supporting Russian hybrid activities, including allowing its territory to be used to increase pressure along NATO’s borders and to intensify information and psychological operations.
Skibitsky said Russia remained a threat to both Ukraine and Europe. He thanked partner countries for their support and again called for stronger sanctions to deprive Moscow of foreign components used in weapons targeting Ukraine.

Mohammed Sameai and Sahin Demir
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthi group continued across four provinces Wednesday, leaving several people dead, including civilians, amid the country’s widest military escalation since 2022.
Clashes and attacks were reported in the western provinces of Taiz, Al-Bayda, Al-Dhale and Al-Hudaydah, while government reinforcements were sent to the strategic western coastal city of Mokha near the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
The government-aligned Giants Brigades said in a statement that its forces carried out “precise strikes” against gatherings of Houthi fighters on the western coast.
The forces released footage showing vehicles and fighters being targeted but did not specify the location of the strikes.
In a separate statement, the Giants Brigades said its forces targeted a Houthi vehicle in the central Al-Bayda province, killing everyone inside.

Separately, Maj. Gen. Abdulrahman al-Lahji, commander of the government-aligned Nation’s Shield Forces, arrived in Mokha at the head of reinforcements for active fronts, according to the military media of the government-aligned National Resistance Forces.
The latest fighting is part of the widest escalation between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis since 2022, when a UN-brokered truce largely halted major hostilities. The truce later expired, with military confrontations resuming in July this year.
Fighting intensifies
Fighting has intensified in recent days on several fronts, particularly in Taiz, Al-Jawf and Al-Bayda, alongside airstrikes targeting Houthi positions.
The escalation has also spilled into neighboring Saudi Arabia. Riyadh said Tuesday that Houthi attacks targeting civilian and economic sites in the southwestern cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran injured 73 civilians, including women and children.
The Houthis, accused of receiving Iranian support, claimed that they targeted facilities belonging to Saudi energy company Aramco and an air base with dozens of ballistic missiles and drones.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014. A Saudi-led Arab coalition intervened in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.

A Seoul court on Wednesday ordered South Korean video game tycoon Kwon Hyuk-bin to pay more than $1.5 billion (two trillion won) in a divorce settlement, marking the largest asset division ever awarded in the country.
The amount surpasses the $666 million (944 billion won) awarded in the divorce settlement between SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won, whose conglomerate owns chipmaker SK hynix, and his former wife Roh Soh-yeong.
Kwon founded Smilegate in 2002 and built it into one of South Korea’s most successful gaming companies.
The Seoul Family Court granted the divorce and ordered Kwon to transfer a 35 percent stake in Smilegate, worth about $1.9 billion (2.5 trillion won), and pay $48.8 million (65 billion won) in cash, the court said.

Lee argued that she had contributed to the company’s founding and early management, as well as indirectly through domestic work, and was therefore entitled to half of Kwon’s stake.
A court spokesperson said the marriage had “broken down beyond repair” after the court considered the circumstances behind the couple’s prolonged conflict and the prospects for reconciliation.
The court found that “both sides bore equal responsibility for the breakdown of the marriage” and granted the divorce but rejected Lee’s claim for damages.
Kwon reportedly opposed the divorce and argued that Lee was neither a co-founder nor involved in the company’s management.
The court valued Kwon’s assets at as much as eight trillion won, according to local media.
The ruling comes after Chey appealed a court decision in August ordering him to pay $666 million to his former wife Roh.
The Seoul High Court ruled in July that Roh was entitled to a cash payout worth about one-third of the couple’s marital assets, including Chey’s shares in SK, citing her role in the family and support for SK Group’s activities.
Chey’s appeal sent the case to the Supreme Court.
Analysts say the appeal could prolong a closely watched legal battle that has drawn attention to Chey’s control of SK Group as the artificial intelligence boom boosts the value of its chip assets.

France 'will reject extremism' and Le Pen in presidential election, Haddad says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:45:47 UTC
18:45:47 KST

Polls suggest far-right veteran Marine Le Pen is on course to become France’s next president, though the race remains in its early stages. But EU minister Haddad says voters will reject her.
French minister for European Affairs, Benjamin Haddad, told Euronews he's "quite confident" the French electorate will reject extremism and won't elect a far-right candidate to replace President Emmanuel Macron in next year's election.
His comments come days after an Elabe poll for BFMTV/La Tribune Dimanche showed Le Pen dwarfing all other candidates, predicting her to win between 34% and 35.5% of first-round votes.
Le Pen was cleared to stand in July despite an appeals court upholding an embezzlement conviction against her.
"We still have a long way to go before the election, but I'm quite confident that the French, like they've done so many, many times, will refuse extremism," Haddad said on Euronews' interview programme 12 Minutes With.
"The French people have repeatedly said no to extremism, to euroscepticism, and populism," he said.
He said next spring's 2027 election will be "a tough one, like every election," but added that he "never trusts the polls," arguing that they have been wrong in the past.
"When I personally started supporting Emmanuel Macron in 2016, he was far, far behind in the polls," said Haddad, who belongs to Macron's party, Renaissance (formerly La République En Marche!).
Ahead of the 2017 elections, Macron rose from third position in the polls after he declared his candidacy in November 2016, to briefly poll ahead of Le Pen weeks ahead of the elections.
He gained 24% of the vote in the first round in April 2017, then won the presidency in the second round with 66% of the vote, in contrast with Le Pen's 34%. This margin narrowed significantly in the second round of the 2022 elections, when Macron beat Le Pen with 59% of the vote to her 41%.
French are 'deeply European'
Haddad said the French are "deeply European" and will ultimately reject Le Pen.
"The French are proud of the role that their country is playing on the European stage," he said.
"Marine Le Pen, for a long time, has been the candidate of 'Frexit'," he said, referring to the demand by some on the fringes of French politics, who called for France to leave the EU and the eurozone.
The prospect of France leaving the EU was a strong component in Le Pen's 2012 and 2017 manifestos. At present, she still maintains a staunchly eurosceptic stance, pledging to cut back on Europe's contributions to the bloc and calling for the scrapping of norms, but no longer explicitly advocates for a referendum on France's membership of the EU.
"She's been the candidate [standing for] leaving the eurozone. She was the candidate of the alliance with Vladimir Putin," Haddad said.
"She's trying to make people forget about all of this and sometimes even says that it never happened, even though we know her stance on the European Union for a long time."
Despite his conviction that the French public will vote against Le Pen, Haddad warned politicians from other parties should approach the rise of the far-right and populism "with a lot of humility."
"Our first responsibility is to continue to deliver on results. All the issues that we're discussing, from migration and security, from competitiveness, prosperity, from defending the security of Europeans against foreign threats, we have to continue to deliver on this, Haddad explained.
He went on to say that continuing to "campaign, to meet the French, to listen to voters, and to respond" is also central in this mission.
Uniting around one candidate?
The linchpin to his proposal to beat the far-right will perhaps be the most challenging of all to attain, given the fragmented nature of the race with eight months to go until the first round of elections.
"We need to unify around a candidate, because right now we have a lot of talent in the centre, but we have a fragmented political offer," Haddad said.
Around 30 figures have already expressed their ambition to run. Two of those considered likely candidates are Macron’s former prime ministers: centrist Gabriel Attal (Renaissance) and centre-right figure Édouard Philippe (Horizons), while conservative candidate Bruno Retailleau (Les Républicains) is one of the president's former ministers.
On the hard-left, Jean-Luc Mélenchon (La France Insoumise) is vying to be president, while other candidates running on the left include Marine Tondelier (the Greens) and MEP Raphaël Glucksmann (Place Publique).
"I think by the end of the year we will have one candidate that can rally the centre and the centre-right and then we will make a case." Some candidates have suggested they would consider partaking in a primary.
Extremism 'not the answer to uncertainties'
Still, Le Pen remains the front-runner in the polls. In 2024, her party won the European Parliamentary elections in France with more than twice the number of votes of Macron’s party, pushing the president to call a snap election at the time.
Haddad conceded that global uncertainties fuel populism's popularity, pointing to the fact that many of the certainties people had before "are crumbling."
"Trade is being weaponised as a tool of pressure. You see China's subsidised overcapacities coming to our markets and destabilising our industries. Our traditional alliances are being questioned; there's the war of Russian aggression on our continent," he explained.
"When you have these uncertainties, and the pillars on which we built our European Union and our transatlantic alliance are questioned, this very often paves the way for radical answers," Haddad added, noting that he doesn't believe those answers are right,
"I don't think that in a world where you have the pressure from China, from the US, the threat coming from Russia, we would be stronger going it alone. I don't think we'd be stronger looking inwards."
The first round of the French presidential election will take place on 18 April 2027, while the second will be held on 2 May 2027 if no candidate wins a majority of votes.

Conspiracy theories can provide answers, but not peace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:45:00 UTC
18:45:00 KST

Conspiracy theories can provide answers, but not peace
September 9, 2026
Psychology is not an exact science. That may irk a few researchers in the field. But it is important to mention upfront: Researching the psychology of conspiracy theories — why people are drawn to believing them and the effect they have on those people — is a complicated field of research, and conclusions are difficult to derive.
That is due, in part, to one of the basic problems with psychology, whether it's in treatment or in research, and that is that it relies on people's self-awareness.
If we take the example of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, some people continue to maintain it was "inside job", orchestrated by a secretive and powerful club of evil doers in the US government, intent on controlling citizens' lives by fear. And that may be true. But it may also be true that you, as a believer in such a theory, have always felt powerful people — your parents or teachers — have controlled and curtailed your agency in life. You may even have a false memory of how the terrorist attacks evolved on that day in 2001. Then, if someone asked you, "What really happened?", could you really say it for sure? I couldn't.
Self-report data is an issue in conspiracy research
Whether as patients or participants in a study, we may be asked to "self-report" — to look inside ourselves and express how we feel and why.
Self-reporting is an established way of measuring conspiracies, said Neil Dagnall, a professor of psychology at Manchester Metropolitan University, in an interview with DW.
But self-report data are "not perfect," he added.
They can be difficult data to handle because each judgment a person makes about themselves is relative, inherently subjective, and open to outside influence and bias. People's answers can change from day-to-day, especially when they involve emotions or feelings about mental state, depending on a multitude of events and experiences in our lives. In addition, there is no common scale.
Say, for example, you and a friend were asked, "Are you happy?" You may both say "yes," but your reasons for doing so may be completely different and be subject to different variables. The same goes for a question like, "Do you believe in conspiracy theories?"
"The judgment I'm making is a relative one. What's my norm? Am I comparing it to my friends who don't believe in conspiracies or am I in a group of people who do believe in conspiracies? We're always making relative judgments about our psychological propensities," said Dagnall. 
Which suggests we're unlikely to ever get a definitive answer. Self-report data suggest correlations, not causation.
In a study on conspiratorial beliefs and well-being, which Dagnall co-authored and published in May 2026, "self-report data" was specifically highlighted as a limitation.
This makes it very difficult to assess whether "conspiracy belief" or "conspiracy ideation" is good or bad for people and their sense of well-being. Especially as people who seek and believe in conspiracy theories often start out with a skewed view of reality.
Observing behavior can offer clues
There are ways of "triangulating" self-report data, as the authors of the study put it, to get a more reliable, objective reading of a person's emotional, or psychological, state.
For example, psychologists use behavioral observations, like measuring heart rate variability, or Galvanic Skin Responses such as the electrical conductance of a person's skin, which is affected by sweating under stress. You can also retest participants' self-reported data, and therefore its reliability, by asking the same questions at different points in time.
But there is another factor that complicates research into the psychology of conspiracy theories, and that is that they, and people who believe in them, are more common than we like to think or admit (even when we believe them ourselves).
"The idea that people who believe in conspiracies in general populations are remarkable or different is not true," said Dagnall.
The truth: 'conspiracies theories are common'
Most of us, at some point in our lives, are bound to see something strange or stressful in society and question whether we, as individuals or as a member of a group, accept the accepted truth of how that thing or event came about. It can be a healthy sign of a questioning mind.
There are positive examples of conspiracy theories that happened to kickstart investigations that then revealed the horrible truth of government corruption.
Take Partygate during the COVID pandemic in the UK or — the mother of all conspiracies — Watergate during the Nixon Administration in the US.
And there are other conspiracy theories, such as the one that nobody has ever landed on the moon, which you can either take seriously or laugh about.
It all comes down to "the degree to which we engage in conspiracies generally, and the extent to which they interfere and disrupt our everyday lives," said Dagnall.
For Dagnall, who doesn't believe in the 1969 moon landing, it doesn't seem to disrupt his daily life — at least, that is what he self-reported to DW.
But for some people, conspiracy theories are disruptive and can lead to a sustained sense of dissatisfaction.
"Ample studies suggest that exposure to conspiracy theories or belief in them might lead to more negative emotions, heightened anxiety, or even paranoid thoughts," said Zuzanna Molenda, a researcher at the Polish Academy of Sciences and lead-author of a 2023 study on emotion dysregulation and belief in conspiracy theories.
Some people may be primed to more readily believe in conspiracy theories because they generally struggle to deal with psychological threat and distress. When they then seek answers in conspiracy theories, their pre-existing negative psychology may be enhanced.
"If anything, the available evidence suggests that rather than help people manage difficult emotions, conspiracy beliefs may be accompanied by or contribute to further distress," wrote Molenda in an email to DW.
No long-term benefit from conspiracy belief
There may be some psychological benefit to conspiracy theories, said Molenda, but only in the short term.
"Conspiracy beliefs can provide people with a sense of explanation and understanding when events feel uncertain or difficult to make sense of. For some people, they might also be a source of entertainment and fun. For others, they can provide a sense of belonging and connection with others who share the same beliefs, and they can be an important part of social identity," Molenda said.
But these potential benefits do not necessarily translate into better well-being in the longer term, said Molenda.
In the end, we're all searching for meaning and purpose in life. If we find a satisfactory answer, it gives us, what psychologists call presense — a direction in life, and that is good.
But if your search only leads to more uncertainty, more anxiety, and more doubt in your purpose in life, then that's bad. "And people who believe in conspiracies are asking questions but not getting answers," said Dagnall.
Edited by: Kristie Pladson

Police step up campaign to stop illegal fireworks at New Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:44:57 UTC
18:44:57 KST

Police step up campaign to stop illegal fireworks at New Year
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Dutch police say they will take a “zero tolerance” approach to illegal New Year fireworks in the first year after a ban was imposed on most types of rockets and firecrackers.
A nationwide crackdown was launched after the ban came into force on August 1, including monitoring border crossings and checking vehicles that have been used in the past to import illegal firerworks.
“One of the conditions for introducing the fireworks ban was an extensive enforcement plan,” Ko Minderhoud, national fireworks co-ordinator for the Dutch police force, told the Telegraaf.
“We have a larger team than ever ready to go and we are starting earlier.”
MPs voted to ban all fireworks apart from the lightest category, F1, which includes sparklers and Roman candles, last year following a long campaign by doctors and emergency service workers.
The annual fireworks bonanza on December 31 is the busiest night of the year for police, ambulance and fire services.
Attacks on first responders in recent years prompted centre-right parties such as VVD and CDA to change their position and accept the need for a ban, even though many voters see New Year fireworks as a national tradition.
30% have fireworks stashed
The task facing the police is a daunting one. A survey by RTL found that nearly 30% of people who regularly set off fireworks said they still have some left over from before the ban, but just 4% are willing to hand them in.
View this post on Instagram
Just seven people turned up on the first day of an amnesty in Terneuzen on September 1 to take advantage of an offer to dispose of their fireworks anonymously without risking a fine.
The amnesty runs until October 9, with police buses touring the country to collect fireworks that are no longer permitted such as rockets and fountains.
Minderhoud said the illegal fireworks trade has been taken over in recent years by criminal gangs and increasingly resembles the drugs trade. “It’s become a sideline for classic organised criminals, because there’s a lot of money to be made,” he said.
“We see armed men transporting container loads. It was a different story a few years ago.”
He urged consumers to play their part by not buying illegal fireworks at New Year. “Set a good example and abide by the law,” he said.
“It’s also very dangerous. Look at the recent incidents at football matches. If you buy fireworks despite the ban, you’re getting involved in a murky world with very dangerous stuff.”
