Iran-backed fighters in Yemen, Iraq unite to threaten the Gulf
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:34:01 UTC
17:34:01 KST

Breadcrumb
Iran-backed fighters in Yemen and Iraq are joining forces to threaten the Gulf, officials say
In July, Saudi Arabia and the United States bombed Iran-backed militias in Iraq after blaming them for drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities that had been claimed by Yemen's Houthi rebels, another Iranian ally.
Now, regional officials tell The Associated Press that the Houthis helped the Iraqi militias plan and execute the two-day swarm attack, showing a new level of coordination.
Iran spent decades building up armed groups on Israel's frontiers that suffered major losses in the wars following Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
Regional officials and experts say Iran is now using the Iraqi militias and the Houthis to threaten Saudi Arabia and other American allies in the Gulf in order to drive up the costs of the war launched by the US and Israel in February.
It is a risky strategy. A wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi oil facilities on Tuesday threatened to reignite full-scale war with the kingdom. Iraq has ordered militias to disarm by the end of this month, though powerful Iran-backed groups have refused to do so. A new American effort to economically isolate Iran could spark further escalation.
A pincer movement 
The Houthi involvement in the Iraqi drone attack was confirmed by two Saudi officials, citing intelligence, and a senior Iraqi security official. They said Houthi emissaries worked in an operations room run by Iraqi militias.
Saudi Arabia and the US responded with joint airstrikes that killed at least 20 Iraqi fighters, six Iranian advisers and at least one Houthi official. The death of the Houthi, not previously reported, was confirmed by a Houthi official and an Iraqi militia member.
A US military official said Houthis had been killed in previous strikes in Iraq. The US is concerned about the Houthi presence there and their ability to launch attacks on other countries, including Saudi Arabia, the official said.
Two officials with the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), an umbrella group of militias that is officially part of Iraq's security forces, denied involvement in the attack on Saudi Arabia and denied that the Houthis were operating under its auspices. The PMF includes powerful militias backed by Iran that sometimes act independently.
All the officials and the militia member spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to media. The Houthis did not respond to a request for comment.
Cooperation grew during the war on Gaza 
Cooperation between the Iraqi militias and the better organised Houthis had grown throughout the war in Gaza, when they coordinated attacks on Israel, according to the Houthi and regional officials. At the height of the war, Houthi leader Abdel-Malek al-Houthi spoke of a joint operations room.
After the US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February, Iran and its allies began firing on Gulf nations to broaden the conflict and inflict pain on major oil producers hosting US forces.
"Iran has a hybrid strategy in the current war. We are not fighting on one front and we are not using one tool," Mahdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran's parliament speaker, wrote on social media in June.
"The Houthis' growing prominence during the Gaza war opened up a new horizon in Iraq. Many groups there became eager to support the Houthis, and in return, the Houthis started sharing their military expertise with Iraqi militias," said Ahmed Nagi, senior Yemen analyst at the Crisis Group, an international think tank.
Now they are "squeezing Saudi like with pliers," Nagi said.
A week before the drone swarm attack, the Houthis declared a blockade against Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, threatening another critical trade route as the wartime disruption of the Strait of Hormuz has jolted the world economy.
Since late July, the Houthis have carried out over a dozen attacks against Saudi oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea, according to the war monitor group ACLED.
On Tuesday, they launched a wave of attacks on oil and other facilities in southern Saudi Arabia, wounding more than 70 people, including women and children, Saudi authorities said.
The Houthi blockade has forced Saudi Arabia to adopt a “dark” transit policy that includes turning off tracking signals on oil tankers in the Red Sea, according to ACLED.
Saudi oil exports in the crosshairs 
Saudi Arabia had diverted much of its oil to the Red Sea after Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz. When the Houthis began attacking, the kingdom started shipping more oil north to the Suez Canal and Egypt's SUMED pipeline, whose flows have risen from 650,000 barrels a day in June to over 1.9 million in August, according to global shipping monitor Kpler.
Last month, the Houthis showed they can target that route as well, striking a Saudi tanker in the northern Red Sea with a missile. The tanker had reportedly traveled from the Saudi port of Yanbu to the Suez Canal, some 1,000 kilometers (700 miles) from Houthi territory.
The Houthis "are willing to weather some shorter term pain for what they feel will be longer term gains," such as extending their reach along the Red Sea coast, said Adam Baron, a Yemen expert at the New America think tank in Washington.
"The train to a return to full scale war has left the station, and it's unclear if anyone is going to jump in to stop it," he said, citing the US focus on Iran and the Saudis' reluctance to intervene in Yemen again.
The rebels seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in 2014. The following year, the Saudis joined with Yemen’s internationally recognized government in a counteroffensive, likely fearing that the kingdom could end up with a Hezbollah-like group on its doorstep.
The civil war has killed at least 150,000 people, according to UN estimates, and at times pushed Yemen to the brink of famine. A ceasefire that had mostly held since 2022 is now in tatters.
For years, a Saudi-led blockade has raised pressure on the Houthis while exacting a heavy toll on ordinary people in rebel-held parts of Yemen.
The Houthis have often responded by escalating hostilities, and renewed fighting could allow them to gain control of energy-rich areas of eastern Yemen, said Elisabeth Kendall, a Yemen expert at Cambridge University's Girton College.
The Houthis, who control northern and central Yemen, have been smuggling in advanced weapons for years, circumventing the blockade and a UN arms embargo. Iran denies arming the rebels, but Iranian-made weaponry has been found on the battlefield and in intercepted shipments.
The rebels have an array of cruise and ballistic missiles, drones and unmanned submarines.
Saudi-backed forces in Yemen are fighting back on a number of fronts, including the crucial port city of Hodeida and the province of Taiz along Yemen's west coast. The Houthis have attacked Mokha, the main Red Sea port still held by the government.
Saudi Arabia appears reluctant to directly target the Houthis again, but if the rebels continue to escalate, "it will have to act decisively once and for all," Kendall said.

The Trump show: Republicans put president centre stage in unprecdented US midterms convention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:33:21 UTC
17:33:21 KST

Trump delivers Wednesday's keynote and returns for Thursday's finale after Vice President JD Vance speaks. Cabinet members and candidates in closely watched House and Senate races are also on the programme.
US Republicans open an extraordinary midterm convention in Dallas later on Wednesday betting that putting Donald Trump at the centre of their campaign can rescue a party facing grim election forecasts, despite the president's deeply negative approval ratings.
The two-day gathering, dubbed "Trumpapalooza," is designed to persuade the Republican leader's supporters that he is effectively on the ballot on 3 November, when Republicans risk losing the House of Representatives and face a fierce fight to retain the Senate.
"So what I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot," Trump said recently at a rally in South Carolina. "Just come and vote. It's so important."
Decision Desk HQ projects Democrats to win the House 230-205 and the Senate to finish 51-49 in their favour, revising its 50-50 prediction as the outlook continues to worsen for Republicans.
Trump, whose approval rating stood at just 33% in recent polling, will speak on both convention nights at the American Airlines Centre.
His challenge is to mobilise voters personally loyal to him without further alienating independents already souring on his presidency amid inflation woes, gasoline prices topping $4 (€3.40) a gallon and the continuing war with Iran.
"Many Trump supporters only vote when he's on the ballot," Matthew Green, a politics professor at the Catholic University of America, told the AFP news agency.
"They're not diehard Republican voters; they're diehard Trump voters. So, in that respect, it makes some sense to feature Trump in the hopes of getting those folks to turn out in November."
But Green was sceptical that asking those supporters to imagine Trump on their ballots could overcome his broader weakness.
"When you're in the low- to mid-30s, that's traditionally associated with a very bad midterm for your party," he said of the 80-year-old's approval ratings.
Trump show
The gathering is the first Republican national convention held specifically for a midterm election, although Democrats experimented with similar meetings in the 1970s and 1980s.
No candidates will be nominated and no formal party business is planned.
Instead, organisers have constructed what amounts to a two-night television rally touting Trump's record and Republican candidates.
More than 100 House members and candidates are expected, with over 50 speakers or presentations scheduled each night.
Trump delivers Wednesday's keynote and returns for Thursday's finale after Vice President JD Vance speaks. Cabinet members, congressional leaders and candidates in closely watched House and Senate races are also on the programme.
Republicans plan to highlight tax cuts, immigration enforcement, manufacturing and prescription drug prices, while depicting Democrats as dangerously far to the left.
Some Republicans, however, are privately hoping Trump sticks to that script rather than the personal grievances and off-message subjects that regularly dominate his appearances.
Staying home
Not everyone is coming. Numerous lawmakers in competitive races have decided that, less than two months from Election Day, their time is better spent campaigning at home.
Green said vulnerable Republicans have two reasons to keep their distance: Trump's unpopularity and the cost of losing precious days in their districts.
"If you are a Republican running in a swing district, you probably want to get as much distance from Trump as possible," he said.
House Speaker Mike Johnson has acknowledged the dilemma, saying some members need to remain home because it is a "critical time" immediately before early voting accelerates nationwide.
Republicans who do attend have also been asked to contribute at least $25,000 (€21,000) for tickets and lodging.
The event doubles as a huge fundraising opportunity, with a Trump roundtable priced at $250,000 (€214,000) per person and photographs with the president offered for $88,600 (€76,126).
And even Trump's promised national television showcase faces an unusually formidable rival: both convention nights coincide with the opening games of the NFL season.
"Spending three or four days away from your district to go to a convention is not a good way to spend your time if you're facing a tight re-election," Green added.

41 injured as torrential rain lashes Japan’s Nagoya city
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:32:56 UTC
17:32:56 KST

Faisal Mahmud
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
At least 41 people sustained minor injuries after record rainfall battered Nagoya in central Japan, prompting the city to announce emergency relief measures Wednesday, local media reported.
A linear rainband pounded the Tokai region Tuesday, inundating roads and railway tracks and paralyzing transportation across Nagoya, according to Kyodo News.
Around 1,600 people had sought refuge at evacuation centers as of Tuesday evening, while at least 200 vehicles had been damaged by early Wednesday, local authorities said.
The downpour left many commuters and students stranded overnight as train and subway services were disrupted.
The Japan Meteorological Agency issued its highest Level 5 emergency flood warning on Tuesday for the Shonai River, which flows through Aichi and neighboring Gifu prefecture, as water levels rose following the intense rainfall.
NHK reported that rain clouds developed over the Tokai and Shikoku regions, producing extreme downpours in some areas.
The weather agency on Wednesday warned that heavy rain could continue across large parts of Japan through Thursday as an active front stretches along the Pacific coast.
Up to 200 millimeters (7.9 inches) of rain is forecast in the Tokai and Kinki regions in the 24 hours through Thursday morning, with 150 mm expected in Shikoku and up to 120 mm in Kanto-Koshin, including Tokyo.
Authorities warned that even relatively small amounts of additional rainfall could trigger landslides or flooding in areas where the ground is already saturated.

Hungary expels ten Russian diplomats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:32:35 UTC
17:32:35 KST

Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán has announced that in order to protect the country’s security and sovereignty, an order has been issued to expel ten Russian diplomats, writes Politico.
The decision comes several months after the Russian investigative journalism publication Agenstvo reported that almost a third of the 47 employees of the Russian embassy in Budapest are connected to Russian intelligence services.
Orbán (the minister is not related to the former Hungarian prime minister) indicated that Russian diplomats in Hungary had taken actions that, according to the Vienna Convention, are unacceptable. The Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations is an international agreement that sets out the basic principles of diplomatic relations.
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said that the Russian diplomats had taken unacceptable actions, although neither he nor Orbán specified what exactly they had done. The Hungarian Foreign Ministry also declined to comment further. Orbán only added that the expulsions did not indicate a break in diplomatic ties with Russia.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Moscow’s response would be “harsh and painful.”
The Hungarian leader has sought to sever ties with Moscow since taking office in May, replacing Viktor Orbán, in sharp contrast to the previous prime minister’s friendly and comfortable relations with the Kremlin. In July, Hungarian authorities opened an investigation into former foreign minister Péter Szijjártó over allegations that Szijjártó had passed sensitive information to Russian officials.
In August, the Hungarian government, briefing its delegation to the UN General Assembly, declared that Russia was a threat to Hungary, Europe and the international order.

Iran fires at US warship as destroyed tankers deepen Hormuz crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:32:00 UTC
17:32:00 KST

Iran carried out fresh attacks on U.S. targets in the Middle East Wednesday in retaliation for American strikes on Iranian oil tankers, deepening the conflict between the two foes.
Tehran's powerful Revolutionary Guards said Wednesday they attacked 20 U.S. vessels trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for the world's oil and gas that Iran has largely controlled since the war erupted.
The United States and Iran are locked in a stalemate six months into the war, with Iran maintaining a stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz and Washington pushing a campaign to choke Iran's ports and economy.
The Guards said Wednesday they pummeled a U.S. military base in Jordan in response to U.S. forces destroying five Iranian oil tankers the day before.
The U.S. military said it acted after Iran targeted an American warship, the second such attack in less than a week.
Oil prices climbed to $100 a barrel as the flare-up threatened to further choke supply from the crude-rich Middle East.
The Islamic republic also said it would target oil tankers off U.S.-allied Kuwait and Bahrain in retaliation for the U.S. strikes on its tankers.
Minutes later, Iran's Revolutionary Guards – the most powerful arm of the Iranian military – said they had struck the U.S. air base of al-Azraq in Jordan with missiles, state media reported.
The "punitive operation" damaged maintenance and repair facilities, deployment locations and shelters for fighter jets, according to IRNA.
Jordan's army said it shot down 18 missiles from Iran targeting the kingdom.
The strikes came after Tehran urged crews on oil tankers off Kuwait and Bahrain to leave their vessels, warning they "will be targeted", the Guards said in a statement posted on IRNA.
The latest round of fighting was triggered after U.S. forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers, with the U.S. military saying it "directed the crews to abandon ship" before hitting the vessels.
"Iran continues to try to hit U.S. naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers, and I think you'll see that again today," U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on Tuesday on a visit to Colombia.
Iranian media reported Tuesday that a U.S. missile struck a tanker off the coast of Kharg Island, adding that there were no casualties.
The chief of staff of Iran's army Ali Abdollahi had warned the Islamic republic would hit U.S. bases in the region if Iranian oil tankers were hit.
Iran has asserted control of the Strait of Hormuz -- which normally carries around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas -- since the start of the war in February, with traffic through the waterway virtually paralysed.
Tehran requires vessels to obtain permission and pay transit fees before using the strait.
Iran's Guards also said on Tuesday they seized "one of the most modern, unmanned" American submarine drone in the Strait of Hormuz.
The U.S. military said that the drone had "malfunctioned", insisting it was an "older model" that did not carry any sensitive data.
Iranian state TV also said the Guards had attacked two U.S. destroyers with ballistic missiles.
The U.S. military did not immediately comment on the report.

India: 5 baby orangutans rescued, smuggling suspected

India: 5 baby orangutans rescued, smuggling suspected
Published September 9, 2026last updated September 9, 2026
What you need to know
- Forest officials have rescued five baby orangutans thousands of kilometers from their native habitat
- Indian officials say they have nothing to do with the BAPS-Eiffel Tower controversy
- Preparation for the BRICS summit is in full swing, but staying at a luxury hotel could burn a serious hole in your pocket
Below is a roundup of the top headlines from India from Wednesday, September 9.
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
India distances itself from Eiffel Tower row over Hindu group's visit
India's Ministry of External Affairs on Tuesday distanced itself from the controversy arising from Hindu group Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha's (BAPS) visit to the Eiffel Tower.
BAPS had earlier apologized after the Eiffel Tower closed Monday when staff went on strike over allegations that female workers were sidelined during a visit by roughly 100 members of the organization.
"As to the particular issue pertaining to the Tower, this is a matter purely between the entities concerned," MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said during a press briefing, confirming India was aware of the controversy following BAPS's inauguration of France's first traditional Hindu temple near Paris on Sunday.
Jaiswal also addressed Prime Minister Narendra Modi's virtual address at the temple's opening, calling it standard practice for the government to convey "good wishes" on such occasions and saying there was "no cause for any comment" on the matter, local media reported.
BAPS said the visit had been pre-coordinated with the tower's operators and that, to its knowledge, no one was denied access, though it apologized to anyone "hurt or inconvenienced."
Tower operator SETE acknowledged accepting a request to limit "interactions with women," calling it a mistake it should not have agreed to.
Eiffel Tower staff, in their own statement, condemned what they called instructions that left female employees "sidelined, replaced, and rendered invisible based on their gender," saying some were told to leave their posts or avoid certain areas while the delegation was present.
Read more about the controversy here.
Baby orangutans rescued, sparking international smuggling probe
Indian forest officials rescued five baby orangutans in the eastern state of Odisha on Tuesday, with authorities suspecting the great apes were smuggled into the country from Southeast Asia.
The animals, not native to India, were found in a forest in the Balasore district. Local legislator Goutam Buddha Das told The Telegraph newspaper that villagers first spotted the orangutans dangling from a tree and initially mistook them for monkeys, before alerting forest officials that their appearance didn't match.
He said the area's coastal location suggested the animals could have arrived by sea from Indonesia.
"I demand a high-level inquiry to find out who is involved in the racket," Das said.
Balasore forest officer Pratik Prakash Indalkar said the three male and two female orangutans were examined by veterinarians, found to be in good health, and given food and oral rehydration solution before being transferred to Nandan Kanan Zoo in Bhubaneswar for quarantine.
Odisha Environment Minister Ram Singh Khuntia said the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau is now investigating how the animals reached India.
"We suspect that an international racket might be involved in this," he told the IANS news agency. Authorities are also examining whether the animals were destined for sale to buyers in Kolkata.
Orangutans are native only to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra. Only about 104,000 remain in the wild, according to the World Wildlife Fund, down from more than 230,000 a century ago.
The Tapanuli orangutan is critically endangered, with fewer than 800 animals thought to be left.

US-Israeli attack on Iran cannot destroy nuclear capabilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:30:05 UTC
17:30:05 KST

An Iranian delegation attending the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Board of Governors meeting in Vienna made the remarks in a statement released on Tuesday, saying Iran’s nuclear “capabilities are not confined to buildings or machines.”
The statement said US-Israeli aggression against Iran in 2025 and 2026 “might have damaged our peaceful nuclear facilities [and] affected our access to nuclear technology in some vital areas. But Iran’s nuclear capabilities are rooted in knowledge, determination, and human resources of a proud nation.”
“Facilities may be attacked and scientists may be assassinated, but once science takes root in the people, it survives, promotes and passes from one generation to the next. This is the reality of Iran, and no amount of force can change it,” the statement added.
According to the delegation, Iran’s achievements in nuclear science and technology were the result of sustained investment, accumulated knowledge, specialized human resources, and the development of indigenous equipment and infrastructure.
“These achievements have resulted in a mature and sustainable scientific and technological capacity that meets a significant share of the country’s needs,” it added.
The statement highlighted the peaceful applications of nuclear technology in Iran, including agriculture, environmental protection, crop improvement, pest and disease control, food preservation, and the efficient use of water and fertilizers, according to Press TV.
It said the country had also developed capabilities in the production and application of radioisotopes, irradiation and sterilization, as well as radiation-based technologies in medicine and industry.
“These activities are supported by capabilities in radiation protection, monitoring, measurement, and detection,” the statement noted.
MNA

OpenAI says its models solved one of math's hardest problems as researchers cry foul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:29:13 UTC
17:29:13 KST

OpenAI says its models solved one of math's hardest problems as researchers cry foul
US tech giant OpenAI on Tuesday said it had solved one of the hardest problems in mathematics with an unreleased artificial intelligence model after just 88 hours – and millions of dollars' worth of computing power. But a US mathematician and a researcher at rival Anthropic allege that OpenAI only took up the problem after it had gotten wind of their own AI-assisted efforts to crack the challenge which had demanded months to craft a radically distinctive approach.
OpenAI said Tuesday that one of its unreleased artificial intelligence models had solved a mathematical puzzle that has eluded mathematicians for generations, in a claim which also drew a fight with rival researchers over credit.
Researchers at OpenAI said it took just days – and millions of dollars in computing power – to crack what is known as the Navier-Stokes problem.
Navier-Stokes is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, a list of the hardest open questions in mathematics drawn up by the Clay Mathematics Institute.
It concerns the equations describing how fluids such as air and water move, which are used in aircraft design, weather forecasting and the study of blood flow.
OpenAI said its work showed that these equations are fatally flawed, answering the question as set out by the Millennium Prize.
"This is a significant milestone for AI research, and its promise for the world is that even more of our hardest questions would become possible to answer," Mark Chen, OpenAI's chief research officer, told reporters.
In a blog post describing the breakthrough, OpenAI said it began training a new model in late August, more capable than anything it had released publicly.
Read moreOpenAI begins rollout of GPT-6 amid growing scrutiny over safety
Days later, seeing online rumours that a competitor had solved Millennium problems, OpenAI turned the system loose on all six that remain open.
Work on Navier-Stokes showed unexpected promise, and the company poured its computing power into it.
Competing claims
By the final stage, OpenAI researcher Sebastien Bubeck said, 10,000 AI agents – programs that operate on their own – were working on the problem at once, passing messages back and forth.
Chen said the computing costs ran "emphatically in the millions of dollars", with Bubeck adding this was roughly 1,000 times what the company spent on earlier mathematical results.
According to OpenAI's account, the agents reached a solution Saturday, about 88 hours after launching the project.
The claim arrived hours after Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University, and Levent Alpoge, who works at OpenAI competitor Anthropic, released their own AI-assisted work on three related equations.
In a statement published alongside his papers, Buckmaster said OpenAI had taken up the problem only after word of his research spread, and pursued the same unusual approach he and Alpoge had spent months developing.
Watch moreArtificial intelligence in Europe: Does advanced AI have a glass ceiling?
OpenAI's researchers denied having had any access to the rival team's work and said they proposed sharing credit before realising that Buckmaster and Alpoge had fallen short of solving the problem.
"To be clear, we did not use their prompts or proofs to prompt our models or direct our agents," Bubeck said.
However, in a later post on X, OpenAI said "while unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models."
Each Millennium Prize Problem carries a $1 million reward, and only one has been solved since the list was published in 2000. OpenAI says it will not claim money if its finding is confirmed.
According to the prize rules, a solution has to be published in a peer-reviewed journal and survive two years after gaining acceptance in the mathematical community before the institute will even convene a committee to consider the work.
"The process of evaluation is deliberately unhurried, and we shall ensure that it is absolutely rigorous," Professor Martin Bridson, President of the Clay Mathematics Institute, told AFP.
ChatGPT-style AI is revolutionising the world of high-level math by quickly solving famous, long-unsolved problems that stumped experts for decades.
But it has also sparked debate over whether machine-generated answers truly count as real human understanding.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

The case against 10 Russian servicemen over drone attacks on civilians in the Kherson region has been sent to court
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:28:50 EEST
17:28:50 KST

The case against 10 Russian servicemen over drone attacks on civilians in the Kherson region has been sent to court
Kyiv • UNN
The accused attacked civilians, medics, and rescuers with drones in 2025. They are charged with violating the laws and customs of war.
The Kherson Regional Prosecutor’s Office has submitted to the court an indictment against 10 Russian military personnel involved in drone attacks on civilians in the Kherson region. This is reported by the Office of the Prosecutor General, according to UNN.
Details
The case concerns servicemen of the 404th Motorized Rifle Regiment of the Territorial Troops of the "Dnieper" military grouping of the Russian armed forces. According to the investigation, throughout 2025 they were stationed in the temporarily occupied left bank of the Kherson region and launched drones from there toward the right-bank part of the region.
The operators monitored people in real time through UAV cameras, selected targets, and carried out strikes. They used drones capable of dropping munitions and kamikaze FPV drones, including ones controlled via fiber optics. High-explosive fragmentation warheads, improvised explosive devices, and incendiary devices were used. Among the documented episodes were attacks on a man and a woman on one of the central streets of Kherson, the dropping of an explosive device on a man who was walking his dogs, as well as attacks on civilian vehicles
In addition, according to the available information, medics and rescuers were repeatedly targeted. In particular, one of the servicemen attacked State Emergency Service rescuers twice as they arrived to deal with the aftermath of previous shelling.
The dropping of a munition near a city clinical hospital and ambulances bearing appropriate medical markings was also recorded. The attacks injured drivers, pedestrians, medical workers, and rescuers. They suffered burns, barotrauma, fractures, and shrapnel wounds, including injuries that posed an immediate threat to life. The actions of the defendants were classified under Part 1 of Article 438 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — violation of the laws and customs of war
To remind you
Law enforcement officers identified 10 Russian military personnel who, resorting to drone terror and real-time killings, attacked the civilian population of the Kherson region.

Russia Wants Postwar Ukraine Turned Into ‘Buffer Zone,’ Lavrov Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:27:19 UTC
17:27:19 KST

Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov has called for Ukraine to be turned into a giant “buffer zone” after the fighting ends, as Moscow continues to signal demands that could undermine renewed US-led efforts to revive peace talks.
Speaking on Russian state television on Tuesday, Sept. 8, Lavrov said Ukraine should become the buffer Moscow claims it needs to prevent future threats from its western neighbor.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Everyone argues that Russia needs a ‘buffer zone.’ Let Ukraine become this buffer,” Lavrov said, according to Russia’s foreign ministry.
In July, Bloomberg reported that the Kremlin no longer planned to return any occupied Ukrainian territory as part of a future peace deal.
Instead, Russian President Vladimir Putin intended to keep occupied areas of the Sumy and Kharkiv regions as permanent buffer zones while continuing his push to seize all of the Donetsk region, according to three people familiar with the Kremlin’s thinking.
That would mark a significant shift from earlier informal proposals in which Russia was reportedly prepared to return occupied parts of Sumy and Kharkiv in exchange for Ukraine ceding the remainder of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions.
Lavrov was asked how Moscow could guarantee that the war would not resume in 25 years. He responded by arguing that Ukraine could not be allowed to retain what he called a “Russophobic, aggressive, neo-Nazi regime” that threatens Russia.
Ukraine Unveils New Air Defense Missile to Replace Soviet Osa-AKM Stocks
The remarks came as US special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday before traveling to Kyiv on Sunday, but the diplomatic effort failed to produce significant progress.
Lavrov also said Russia would not accept an outcome in which the “regime ruling in Kyiv” remained in power after the war. He claimed such a government would continue violating “human rights, language rights, and the right to choose one’s religion.”
The Kremlin has pushed the idea of a “buffer zone” along Ukraine’s border with Russia for years. Russian President Vladimir Putin first publicly raised the concept in 2023 and has since repeatedly claimed that Russian forces need to expand such a zone to protect Russian border regions.
The comments also echo broader Russian territorial ambitions. Sources close to the Kremlin told The Moscow Times in March 2025 that Moscow was considering seizing additional Ukrainian territory, including parts of the Dnipropetrovsk or Sumy regions, before potentially offering it in an exchange for Ukrainian-held parts of the Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions.
Lavrov has meanwhile rejected the idea that Russia is currently engaged in meaningful peace negotiations.
In a separate interview on Tuesday, Sept. 8, he said Moscow would continue fighting until the West makes concessions, accusing Ukraine’s Western supporters of repeatedly preventing a peace deal.
He also dismissed new Western proposals on Ukraine, saying Western countries should not “fuss” over their “new ideas.”
The comments underscore the gap between Washington’s push to restart diplomacy and Moscow’s continued demands for a postwar Ukraine constrained by Russian security and political conditions.

Trafficked into fraud: An African crisis situation in Cambodia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:27:00 UTC
17:27:00 KST

Trafficked into fraud: An African crisis in Cambodia
September 9, 2026
Southeast Asia has long emerged as a major hub of highly organized online fraud operations, targeting people all around the world.
According to the United Nations, these operations generate tens of billions of dollars annually, having long surpassed the illegal drug trade as the most profitable activity for criminal networks, as reported by the United States Institute of Peace.
However, those who fall prey to scams and other fraudulent activities aren't the only victims of these criminal rings; alone in Southeast Asia, the scam industry is powered by at least 300,000 trafficked workers from 66 countries. They are routinely subjected to torture, sexual abuse and forced labor, according to a recent UN Human Rights report.
African nationals now form the largest group of those trafficked to and stranded in countries like Myanmar and Cambodia, without any viable pathway to go back home, says the NGO Freedom Collaborative.
In Cambodia, one of the main obstacles to helping stranded Africans return home is that many countries on the continent, such as Uganda, Liberia, Ghana and Nigeria, lack consular representation.
But there are other reasons.
"Some countries have zero interest," says Montse Ferrer, co-regional director of Amnesty International, who also blames the home countries for their inaction.
"They're not even picking up the phone, let alone providing the paperwork for the money for them to go back."
Cambodia's reluctant crackdown on scam operators
Ferrer believes that the Cambodian government also has an interest in keeping scam trafficking victims in the country. This is because many of the victims now have overstay fines for their visas against their names in Cambodia, reaching thousands of dollars in many instances.
"They don't allow NGOs to provide the support these people need, and instead they have resorted to arresting and threatening them," Ferrer told DW.
Following great pressure from the international community — including threats of financial sanctions by the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and the European Union — Cambodia did eventually agree to launch a crackdown on the scamming industry earlier this year.
According to the Cambodian Ministry of Information, the initiative resulted in many arrests and triggered a mass exodus of dubious operatives from scamming industry.
But the crackdown also created a secondary crisis: Thousands of trafficked foreign workers remain stranded in the country without documentation nor legal status; now, they also lack shelter and money in many instances, NGOs say.
Many who have sought in Cambodia help have reportedly been placed in immigration detention, while others have to sleep rough and beg for food.
Instead of being given protection, trafficking victimes often face stigmatization and abuse on the street of the capital Phnom Penh and elsewhere.
Lured to Cambodia under false pretenses
Emmanuel David is one of those stuck in Cambodia. The 28-year-old Liberian national arrived there in 2025 after a treacherous irregular journey originating in Vietnam.
"My friend told me there was work in Cambodia, but he did not explain that it was scamming work," David explained.
The scamming company had offered him a lucrative deal of making around $800 (€700) per month, which is more than double the average wage for qualified individuals in Liberia.
The reality hit quite differently: Once there, David was forced to work 14 hours a day to deceive women on various dating apps to part with their money.
But David was initially unable — and later unwilling — to meet the set target quota of scams per day.
In response, the criminal group he worked for started billing him for food and accommodation through his wages and later even confiscated his belongings, including his passport.
David says he also faced substantial physical violence, including beatings, for four months.
Eventually, he left "with no documents and no money," and is now hoping to find a way back to Liberia.
His story is far from unique.
'Hundreds' of Africans trafficked to criminal compounds
Another survivor, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of retaliation, also recounted how he was "beaten and [subjected to] electric shocks."
The abuse resulted in him having to be hospitalized for three weeks, and is now unable to pay his medical bills.
Pia Oberoi, chief of the Right to Development Section at UN Human Rights, told DW that "despite the promise of a good salary, most come out in debt."
She also confirmed that a growing number of trafficking victims in Southeast Asia come from African countries, "because there is clearly a recruitment industry that's built around Africa, targeting African nationals."
Other victims have corroborated this development, describing hundreds of Africans packed into heavily fortified compounds.
"Once you're inside there's no way out," an informant, who also chose to remain anonymous, told DW.
He said the compounds have their own laws, and that sexual abuse and psychological violence are an integral part of how they operate.
The police, he says, just turn a blind eye.
No government assistance from any direction
Amnesty International speaks of an unfolding humanitarian crisis, warning that escapees are widely being treated as criminals rather than as trafficking victims, a sentiment the UN shares.
"They shouldn't be punished for crimes they were forced to commit," the UN's Oberoi highlights.
Several of the victims contacted by DW said their governments were "slow" to help with their repatriation.
DW attempted to contact several African foreign ministries for comment but has yet to receive a response.
A statement issued by the Cambodian government meanwhile said that more than 700 compounds run chiefly by Chinese nationals had been raided, with 58,266 foreign nationals deported and nearly 30,000 suspects arrested over the past year.
However, the Cambodian government did not reply to DW's direct request for further information.
The UN's International Organization for Migration (IOM) meanwhile said it's trying its utmost to help the trafficking victims; but in the face of severe budgetary constraints, it can only provide "limited, prioritized support."
Fear, guilt and stigma
Humanitarian groups also warn of a high risk of victims being re-trafficked. This is a danger even for those who have managed to return to their countries of origin.
In some instances, those who come back home are stigmatized as a failure — "a situation that is really unbearable," says Ferrer.
Emmanuel David is a prime example: He feels obliged to to apologize to his family for not returning a success.
When asked about his little daughter, he says "Daddy can't go home without money."

Lubinets: Russia systematically attacks Ukrainian education, over 4,650 institutions damaged, 423 destroyed
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:26:55 EEST
17:26:55 KST

In Ukraine, since the start of the full-scale Russian invasion, more than 4,650 educational institutions have been damaged, and another 423 have been completely destroyed, reported Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets.
"A school should not be a target. A child should not be afraid to go to class. A teacher should not hold lessons to the sound of explosions," Lubinets wrote on social media.
According to him, Russia is systematically attacking Ukrainian education, including schools, kindergartens, universities, and vocational education institutions.
Lubinets emphasized that attacks on civilian targets and the deliberate destruction of educational infrastructure are incompatible with the norms of international humanitarian law.
Separately, he noted that in the temporarily occupied territories, Russia imposes the Russian education system, propaganda, and distorted history on children, depriving them of the opportunity to study according to Ukrainian standards.
"Russia must be held accountable for every destroyed educational opportunity of a Ukrainian child," Lubinets stressed.

French Navy gets new Falcon Albatros surveillance aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:26:33 UTC
17:26:33 KST

- France's DGA delivered the first two Falcon 2000 LXS Albatros maritime surveillance aircraft to the French Navy's Flottille 24F squadron.
- The AVSIMAR program will field 12 Albatros aircraft total, replacing eight Falcon 50M and five Falcon 200 Gardian planes.
France’s defense procurement agency has delivered the first two Falcon 2000 LXS Albatros maritime surveillance aircraft to the French Navy, the agency said in a social media post.
The Direction générale de l’armement, or DGA, said the aircraft are headed to Flottille 24F, a French Navy air squadron based at Lann-Bihoué in Brittany. The delivery is the first hardware handover under the AVSIMAR program, which will eventually field 12 Albatros aircraft built by Dassault Aviation for maritime patrol and rescue work.
The Albatros is built on Dassault’s Falcon 2000LXS business jet, a twin-engine aircraft with a range of roughly 7,400 km (4,000 nautical miles) and low-speed handling that lets it operate from smaller airfields. For the Navy version, Dassault fitted a radar under the fuselage, a high-performance optronic turret for visual tracking, observation windows for crew members to scan the water below, and a system for dropping search-and-rescue kits to people or vessels in distress.
The sensor package draws on several French suppliers. Thales provides the SearchMaster surveillance radar, the TopAXYZ inertial navigation system, the TopStar 100-2 military GPS receiver and the TopShield anti-jamming antenna system. Safran Electronics & Defense supplies the Euroflir 410 electro-optical and infrared camera turret. Dassault developed the aircraft with Naval Group and Safran as program partners.
The Navy expects the Albatros to handle three main jobs: patrolling French waters, gathering electromagnetic intelligence and identifying threats, and hunting submarines. France controls roughly 11 million square km of exclusive economic zone, the world’s second-largest maritime area after the United States, which the Navy says requires an aircraft capable of sustained, wide-area surveillance.
The 12 Albatros aircraft will replace eight Falcon 50M and five Falcon 200 Gardian aircraft that have flown maritime patrol missions for French naval aviation for decades. The Falcon 50Ms fly out of Lann-Bihoué in western France’s Morbihan region, while the Falcon 200 Gardians are based in the Pacific, supporting French territories there. Retirement of the older aircraft began in 2025 as the newer jets came closer to entering service.
France ordered the first seven Albatros aircraft in December 2020, under a contract that also commits Dassault to a 10-year guaranteed availability clause for maintenance support. The DGA placed a second order for five more aircraft in September 2025, completing the planned 12-aircraft buy.
The first Albatros made its maiden flight from Bordeaux-Mérignac in January 2025, and the type has since been going through testing at the DGA’s flight test center in Istres, in southern France.
The French Navy has previously said it expects the Albatros fleet to reach initial operational capability by the end of 2026, though a full delivery schedule for the remaining 10 aircraft has not been made public.

Maritime trade faces fragmentation due to geopolitical strife
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:23:58 UTC
17:23:58 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Global maritime trade is facing the threat of fragmentation amid a structural shift provoked by geopolitical turmoil, reports said Wednesday.
The warning came from the Consultative Shipping Group, a cooperation framework between the maritime authorities of 18 shipping nations, including the UK, Canada, Japan, South Korea, and Singapore. The group said that 80% of global trade is conducted by sea, with disruptions threatening to cut off supply chains and paralyze the global economy, per Liberty Times.
The COVID-19 pandemic, the war in Ukraine, drought in the Panama Canal, and Middle East conflicts have raised uncertainty and affected supply chains, the group said in a statement. Discriminatory trade measures and the fragmentation of rules and markets are signs of a structural shift.
The group also noted the emergence of a parallel system, with hundreds of ships circumventing sanctions and operating outside regular safety, environmental, and insurance standards. The two-tier system features one side following the rules and the other governed by opacity, but ultimately weakening both sides, the group said.
The statement ended with a call for improving the alignment of existing international rules. All maritime nations should support basic principles including freedom of navigation, the group said. Closure of the Strait of Hormuz demonstrates that when shipping supply chains fragment, the global economy fragments with it.

Taichung mayor urges Taiwan Power to honor coal-reduction pledge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:23:57 UTC
17:23:57 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕) on Tuesday called on Taiwan Power Company (Taipower) to honor its pledge to dismantle coal-fired generators at the Taichung Power Plant as new gas-fired units come online.
Lu made the remarks during a visit to the plant, where she warned that adding gas-fired capacity without removing coal-fired units could increase total power-generation emissions and undermine efforts to improve air quality in central Taiwan.
“If gas-fired units are added without dismantling coal-fired units, the resulting carbon emissions from power generation could cause greater harm to citizens and the environment,” per CNA.
She said the central government had pledged to dismantle one coal unit for every gas unit added. Lu said Taichung had issued operating permits for the new gas-fired units based upon the understanding that existing coal-fired units would be dismantled.
Lu added that with two new gas-fired units, the number of generators at the central Taiwan power complex would exceed 14, while the number of chimneys would increase from five to seven. Taipower rejected the suggestion that it was simply adding gas-fired generation without reducing coal use.
The state-owned utility said the new gas-fired units are part of a broader transition away from coal, adding that it will begin dismantling the existing coal-fired units one and two in October. The utility said it remains committed to achieving coal-free power generation at the Taichung plant by the end of 2034, per MOEA press release.
Taipower said demand for electricity in Taichung has increased as industrial and urban development has expanded. The city has had the nation's highest electricity consumption for seven consecutive years. Furthermore, existing generating units at the plant have been unable to meet local demand since 2019, requiring electricity to be supplied from other parts of Taiwan, per CNA.
The first unit of Taipower's new gas-fired project is expected to enter commercial operation by the end of September. The second unit is undergoing testing, with commercial operation expected in March 2027.
The government's longer-term plan calls for additional gas-fired capacity to come online from 2031. The utility said it will then progressively dismantle coal-fired units three and four and convert units five through 10 into emergency backup units, with the goal of eliminating routine coal-fired generation at the plant by the end of 2034, per Cabinet press release.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) reiterated the government's commitment during a Sept. 4 inspection of the plant, saying the old chimneys associated with coal-fired units one and two would be dismantled according to schedule. Chou reiterated the government’s aim to achieve coal-free generation at the plant by the end of 2034.

rom Trenches to Catwalk: Ukraine’s Amputee Soldiers Hit the Runway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:23:57 UTC
17:23:57 KST

In the corner of a vast brick hall, models slipped silently and elegantly into linen dresses, as the chink of a metal prosthetic limb pierced the quiet.
Ukrainian veteran Yaroslav Sharkiy, who lost his leg fighting at the front, was preparing to take to the catwalk at Kyiv Fashion Week.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He is one of anywhere from 50,000 to 100,000 Ukrainian soldiers to have lost a limb fighting to fend off the Russian invasion, according to non-governmental organisations.
“I’ve got one leg in the Donbas, the other on the Fashion Week runway,” joked the former combat medic, barely in his thirties.
“It’s a bit unusual but I’ve learnt to switch between these realities.”
Far from the explosions, he now battles a touch of stage fright and teasing from his former comrades.
On the catwalk, he sported the latest line of clothes created specifically by Ukrainian designer Igor Sidletskiy for people with prosthetic limbs.
With four other veterans, he slid his metal leg into a wide pair of black shorts.
Amputated below the knee, Sharkiy usually has to remove his trousers completely to adjust the device, which makes him feel “uneasy” in public.
“I can see that people around me are sometimes uncomfortable too,” he told AFP.
But Sidletskiy’s designs are loose and easy to put on.
“It’s comfortable, while still being stylish,” Sharkiy said confidently.
As the designer’s voice cut the silence -- “Be ready in 10 minutes” -- he tuned his collar up and added some black sunglasses.
Ukraine Unveils New Air Defense Missile to Replace Soviet Osa-AKM Stocks
“Loud and clear,” Sharkiy barked back in an army-style call-and-response.
- Destruction and creation -
In the forest of endless slender legs, Mykola Kovalyov’s metal limbs moved briskly around the changing room.
The young man put on a flowy shirt, brushed his long black hair back and struck a few playful poses, laughing.
“I’m not an actor, I’m not a star, I’m not a dancer. But we’re trying,” he insisted.
The former soldier lost both his legs in a fight in the northeastern Sumy region -- four years after he enlisted to join the Ukrainian army right after Russia invaded.
Since then, the 22-year-old has felt lost.
“I still don’t know who I am or what I want to do,” he said.
He did not hesitate when the opportunity arose to present inclusive fashion on the catwalk.
“It’s art -- something that can give us a resource, while war has taken that away from us,” he said.
“Over there, we had to destroy. Here we create.”
After some final adjustments, he frantically searched for his sunglasses -- nerves before his first-ever show.
Behind him, a murmur rose as the first guests took their seats.
Under dresses and trousers, a few prosthetic limbs could also be spotted in the audience.
Then laughter erupted, extravagant outfits were ready, there was a burst of flashes. The show had begun.
- ‘With style’ -
Before the usual parading, there was a solemn minute of silence commemorating the hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian soldiers killed since Russia invaded in 2022.
To a few piano notes, the first models then started to step forward.
Between the cascades of painstakingly curled hair, the shaven head of a broad-shouldered soldier stood out.
A wave of applause erupted as he took to the stage.
At the end of the runway he instinctively snapped his heels together -- a routine from the army parade training ground -- then pivoted and walked back.
Behind him, Kovalyov and Sharkiy strode forward confidently.
The white-and-beige fabrics contrasted with the chrome glean from their prosthetic limbs.
As the last model struck their pose, the hall rose in a thunder of applause.
Designer Sidletskiy, 27, rushed on stage, grinning from ear to ear.
Backstage, 30-year-old model Olga Dolga was struggling to hold back her tears.
The only civilian in the show, she lost her leg when Russia bombed a shop in her hometown of Dobropillya, heavily targeted by Moscow’s troops.
“Now, more than ever, we need to highlight the issue of inclusivity, because so many boys and girls have lost limbs,” she told AFP.
That same battle drives Sharkiy, who plans to launch his own clothing brand “so that amputees no longer have to wonder where to find comfortable trousers”.
“But the main thing is style,” he said. “Because for me, style is important.”

Scholar warns Taiwan political gridlock straining democratic institutions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:23:55 UTC
17:23:55 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Flaws in the government have begun to undermine the nation’s democracy, Dr. Kharis Templeman, a research fellow at Stanford University’s Hoover Institution, said on Wednesday.
He pointed to the constitutional court crisis, in which the KMT-majority Legislative Yuan blocked President Lai Ching-te’s (賴清德) seven constitutional court justice nominees in December 2024 and last July.
“I think Taiwan is on the edge of the point where healthy, political competition and pluralism are starting to damage the institutions of democracy,” Templeman told Taiwan News.
Because of these vacancies, the court did not meet the 10-justice quorum requirement and was therefore unable to hear or rule on major cases. “When your constitutional court is no longer functioning, that is a pretty serious situation,” Templeman said.
In December 2025, the court repealed the law that required 10 justices to hear and decide cases and at least nine justices to agree on rejecting a law. However, it remains understaffed and politically constrained.
Templeman also expressed concern about Premier Cho Jung-tai’s (卓榮泰) refusal to sign legislation passed by the Legislative Yuan, “basically creating a power that no previous premier had ever claimed they had.”
Cho said that signing amendments to the Radio and Television Act, the Cable Radio and Television Act, and the Satellite Broadcasting Act, would allow political parties, the government, and the military to acquire shares in media corporations and thereby exert influence.
The premier defended his decision on Tuesday, saying that not countersigning the bills was the Cabinet’s duty to history and his personal responsibility.
Despite the political deadlock, the scholar said the three major political parties still pass much legislation, including a special defense budget. “A lot of legislation actually still passes by cross-party consensus,” he said.
Regarding Chinese infiltration, Templeman said Beijing follows a dual-track strategy. The first is a hard track, which uses threats to try to prevent Taiwan from moving towards independence. The soft track includes people-to-people engagement and other methods to influence public opinion.
Templeman said that generally speaking, China has not succeeded in directly shaping Taiwan’s politics. “They have certainly kept moves towards independence limited, but they have not changed hearts and minds,” he said.
He argued this is because Taiwanese are politically engaged, highlighting their close attention to politics, high voter turnouts, and frequent protests.
“Large parts of Taiwan society are hyper aware, hyper sensitive to (Chinese) influence,” he said, “so it's actually very easy for people to identify the more overt forms of (Chinese) interference in Taiwan's democracy.”
Templeman said he was optimistic about the nation’s democratic future. “There's a democratic DNA in civil society, in the engagement of ordinary people with politics, and over the long run, I think that will carry on forward.”
He added that despite past and present political infighting, he was confident the country will overcome it and end up with a stronger democracy.
“Presuming that the (Chinese) threat is held at bay, I think Taiwan's democracy will be in a better place in 10 or 15 years,” Templeman said.

17:23:43 KST

Britain is bringing forward plans to give the RAF’s Protector drone a maritime capability, with a review of the programme now under way and revised milestones expected by December 2026.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard disclosed the move in response to a written parliamentary question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked what progress had been made towards integrating Protector with P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft and Type 26 frigates.
Pollard said: “The Defence Investment Plan directed Maritime capabilities for the PROTECTOR RG Mk1 be brought forward, and a review of PROTECTOR is therefore currently underway. Rebaselined milestones are expected by December 2026, with a Review Note to follow.”
He added: “In the interim the Capability Sponsor, Cyber and Specialist Operations Command, is progressing capability development activity.”
The 2025 Strategic Defence Review recommended exploring a maritime surveillance capability for Protector, integrated with the RAF’s P-8 Poseidon fleet and the Royal Navy’s new Type 26 anti-submarine warfare frigates.
The review said Protector should be enhanced with maritime surveillance equipment and improved connectivity to give the long-endurance remotely piloted aircraft wider utility. It also placed Protector within the planned evolution of Britain’s anti-submarine warfare force under Atlantic Bastion, envisaging underwater, surface and airborne drones operating alongside Type 26 frigates, P-8 maritime patrol aircraft and nuclear-powered attack submarines.
The concept would use Protector’s endurance to provide persistent surveillance over large maritime areas while connecting its sensor picture with crewed aircraft and warships. The aircraft can remain airborne for more than 30 hours, providing a potentially useful means of maintaining coverage without continuously committing a P-8 to the same task.
The concept is not entirely new to British forces, of course. In 2021, a maritime-configured MQ-9B SeaGuardian, the maritime variant of the aircraft family on which Protector is based, took part in a series of demonstrations in the UK.
During Exercise Joint Warrior, SeaGuardian operated with an RAF P-8 in a manned-unmanned teaming demonstration supporting anti-submarine warfare activity, including the tracking, monitoring and reporting of sonobuoys.
The maritime MQ-9B configuration demonstrated at the time included a maritime surface-search radar, Automatic Identification System receiver and electro-optical and infrared sensors. General Atomics has also developed an anti-submarine warfare mission kit capable of working with sonobuoys.
Those capabilities should not be taken as confirmation of the final equipment fit for British Protector aircraft, which has yet to be disclosed or properly evaluated.
Defence had already begun examining a wider maritime role before publication of the Strategic Defence Review. In January 2025, ministers said Britain was working with the NATO Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance Force to scope options for using Protector in the North Atlantic and Arctic.
After the Strategic Defence Review, however, the Government stopped short of giving a timetable. Asked in October 2025 when Protector would be integrated with P-8 Poseidon and Type 26, Pollard said the maritime capability was being considered through the forthcoming Defence Investment Plan.
The published Investment Plan subsequently allocated £590 million to Protector over the four years to 2029-30, but did not explicitly describe the maritime surveillance programme. It separately committed £260 million to upgrade the RAF’s P-8 Poseidon aircraft and equip them with the UK-built Sting Ray torpedo.
The latest answer now confirms that the Investment Plan actually resulted in a direction to bring Protector’s maritime capabilities forward, with detailed programme milestones being reconsidered as part of the wider Protector review.
That review comes as the overall aircraft programme works through a number of outstanding issues. The latest government major-projects assessment rated Protector Red, citing its pending programme rebaseline alongside trained crew numbers, Full Motion Video metadata dissemination and delays to weapons testing.
Some of those issues have since moved forward. Protector is already being employed operationally, Paveway IV has been operationally available since March 2026 and Brimstone 3 testing has progressed to analysis ahead of operational clearance.
By December, Defence now expects to have rebaselined the milestones governing the programme, including the work intended to turn Protector from a predominantly land-focused persistent surveillance and strike aircraft into another sensor within Britain’s increasingly integrated North Atlantic maritime force.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) defended the government’s new registration requirement for group travel to China on Wednesday, calling it a “necessary precaution” for people traveling to risky areas.
The Mainland Affairs Council had previously warned that new Chinese travel rules — including restrictions on leaving China on national security or other grounds — that are set to take effect Tuesday could increase risks for Taiwanese traveling to China, per Storm Media. In response, the Ministry of Transportation and Communications required travel agencies to assist customers with registering through the MAC’s reporting system for travelers going to China.
Agencies that fail to comply could face fines ranging from NT$10,000 (US$317) to NT$50,000. MAC Deputy Minister Liang Wen-chieh (梁文傑) clarified Thursday that the registration requirement was introduced to address a new form of group travel to China that emerged after the government banned travel agencies from organizing tours, per Storm Media.
Under the new arrangement, travel agencies assist customers in organizing trips but do not directly operate the tours. Liang said travel agencies would not be penalized if individual participants declined to register.
The policy drew criticism from the tourism industry. Taiwan Strait Cross-Strait Tourism Development Association Chair Hsiao Po-jen (蕭博仁) said members of the public are not required to report their overseas travel to the government and argued that the new requirement was intended to discourage travel to China, per UDN.
Hsiao said travel agencies would sue the Tourism Administration if it imposed fines under the new rules. He also suggested that any penalties should be imposed on travelers rather than travel agencies.
Facing strong opposition, the Tourism Administration delayed enforcement of the requirement and gave travel agencies a grace period to adapt to the new rules. KMT Legislator Lee Yen-hsiu (李彥秀) said that if the government intends to turn the registration requirement from discretionary to mandatory, it should apply the same standard to other destinations classified as Level 3 under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ travel advisory system, per ETtoday.
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office Spokesperson Chen Binhua (陳斌華) also criticized the measure, saying that the new rule was a tactic by the DPP administration to discourage cross-strait exchanges, per UDN. He added that Taiwanese in China are afforded equal protection under the law and can seek assistance from tourism authorities or local Taiwan Affairs Office branches.
Chuang defended the registration requirement, saying it is the government’s responsibility to obtain information that could be used to assist citizens in an emergency, per CNA. Given the travel advisory and the risks associated with traveling to China, he said it was reasonable for the government to take precautionary measures.
Chung also urged the government to improve communication with travel agencies and called on the industry not to misconstrue the measure’s intentions as surveillance. He argued that with the opposition controlling the legislature, the government does not have the time to “surveil its people.”

‘Totally reliant on Mother Nature’: UK drought raises water security fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:19:45 UTC
17:19:45 KST

‘Totally reliant on Mother Nature’: UK drought raises water security fears
Record heatwaves have troubled British farmers, raising concerns over reservoir levels and food supply.
London, United Kingdom – In a wheat field near High Wycombe in the rolling English countryside, Alex Nelms watched the harvest on his farm die in a matter of days.
His crop had looked strong until the first heatwave came in May, when temperatures surpassed 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit) just as his milling wheat entered its grain-fill phase, the critical weeks when the plant fattens its kernels.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Sudan’s date palm trees under threat from drought and wildfires
- list 2 of 4How wildfires are scorching France’s wine industry
- list 3 of 4El Nino: A phenomenon supercharged by climate change
- list 4 of 4Dead fish fill vanishing river as drought grips Indonesia
“It just killed everything stone dead,” he told Al Jazeera. “Everything was finished really early, and when we were sort of full of optimism and hope, it was scuppered almost overnight.”
Nelms farms just over 2,000 acres (809 hectares) of arable land in south Buckinghamshire, on a business his grandparents founded in 1955. His uncle, who has worked the farm for more than 40 years, has just suffered the worst harvest of his career.
Last month, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said almost three-quarters of England, 71.3 percent, remained in drought. Rainfall in August reached just 34 percent of what would normally be expected by that point in the month, Defra said, and reservoir levels were 18.2 percentage points below where they should be for the time of year.
“We’re totally reliant on Mother Nature,” Nelms said, and nature did not deliver this year.
After a historically dry spring and a run of summer heatwaves, the farm is down roughly 1,000 tonnes on its average harvest, a shortfall of some $270,000 in revenue.
The farm, tucked in the Chiltern Hills, a steep, long ridge of white limestone rock, has no irrigation and never will.
“That has serious knock-on effects on our cash flow,” he said. A third consecutive difficult year would mean hard conversations with his bank and landlord, and farming to minimise risk rather than maximise output, “consequently, probably producing less food”.
‘Financial crisis point’
The National Farmers’ Union (NFU) says farmers are at a “financial crisis point” after the worst drought in 50 years, with historically low harvests, stunted grass growth, rising fuel and fertiliser costs, and a severe outbreak of bluetongue disease in livestock.
The union puts the gross production value loss of wheat at approximately $499m and the cost of replacing a shortfall in forage at roughly $45m.
NFU president Tom Bradshaw has said farmers now lack “breathing space” and are “increasingly exposed to geopolitical shocks, as well as repeated weather extremes, animal disease and global wars”.
He believes action is needed now to ensure the future of British farming “and enable the next generation to keep producing the nation’s food”.
To manage the risk, Nelms is diversifying, planting oilseed rape again on about 350 acres (142 hectares) for the first time in 20 years. He says that the crop’s usual insecticide protection, neonicotinoid seed treatments, is now banned, leaving it exposed to cabbage stem flea beetle and to game birds that can “absolutely nibble, eat, and destroy a crop”.
Growing it also means breaking a continuous wheat rotation that has kept a soil-borne disease called “Take-all”.
Tax allowances would make investing in grain storage and diversified income worthwhile, he said, as well as government-backed bridging loans, modelled on COVID-era support, to survive a bad year without permanent damage.
It is the kind of relief the NFU is pressing the government to provide nationally.
The union wants an interest-free “Keep Britain Growing” loan tied to drought losses, help covering the cost of disposing of livestock lost to bluetongue, faster planning permission for on-farm reservoirs, and clearer rules letting farmers access water as soon as levels allow, echoing Nelms’s case for storage on his farm.
“Drought conditions will continue to worsen until we receive sustained rainfall across the country and we still all have a role to play in conserving precious water supplies,” according to Philip Duffy, the Environment Agency’s chief executive, in a statement shared by Defra.
The Environment Agency has applied for a drought order to restrict abstraction from the River Severn, and 10 water companies, serving 30 million customers, now have restrictions in place.
“A few days or even weeks of wetter weather cannot reverse the impacts of several months of exceptionally dry conditions,” added Duffy.
Defra noted that the first meaningful rains since June have fallen but they have been patchy, so reservoirs and groundwater are still declining even as a handful of rivers see brief upticks in flow.
Despite the losses, Nelms is hopeful about farmers pulling together – sharing labour, machinery and market routes. He points to the Central Chiltern Farmer Cluster, where growers meet to talk through their problems and find solutions together.
“We’re working together, not competing with each other,” he said.
For a farm like Nelms’s, with no irrigation and no water in reserve, that patchiness is the problem. Soil parched from months without rain needs to absorb sustained rainfall before groundwater can even begin to recharge, let alone refill the reservoirs a future harvest might depend on.
“Our climate has changed,” Water Minister Emma Hardy, who chairs the National Drought Group, said late last month, “and we will continue to take all action necessary.”

Addressing fellow researchers across commercial labs, Coxon urged workers to "call for different conditions" and noted that slowing the competitive race may require drastic measures, including pacing agreements between labs or a temporary ban on capability advancements.

AI generated
TBILISI - Amid the debris six metres beneath Tbilisi's main thoroughfare, roadworks that have frustrated residents have yielded an archaeological prize: a cache of 10th-century pottery among the oldest mediaeval works ever found in the Georgian capital.
Work on Rustaveli Avenue, the city's stately central boulevard, began this summer to add pedestrian crossings, improve signage and make other upgrades.
The project has brought traffic chaos and drawn complaints from residents, who must now navigate gaping holes and crushed brick on their daily walks, but it has also given archaeologists a rare glimpse into Tbilisi's past.
The discovery of the ceramic workshop came as little surprise to David Lordkipanidze, director of the National Museum, located just a stone's throw from the dig site.
"Tbilisi is very rich with archaeological material...so it's very logical to find workshops of different periods," he said.
Medieval Georgian chronicles date Tbilisi's founding to the 4th century, when Vakhtang I ruled over the kingdom of Kartli in what is now eastern Georgia.
Preliminary studies of the pottery's ornamentation suggest the fragments date from sometime between the 10th and 11th centuries, when Tbilisi was under Arab rule and an important stop along the Silk Road. The archaeological findings will be brought to the National Museum for 3D scanning and proper review, Lordkipanidze said.
Tbilisi blossomed in the medieval period, during which time the city changed hands between the Umayyad caliphate of Damascus, Baghdad's Abbasid caliphate and the formidable Seljuk Empire, among others.
"Tbilisi was always multicultural," Lordkipanidze said, and "a real centre for the region, particularly an economic centre."
Successive waves of conquest by the Mongols, Persians and Russians have influenced the look of the city, where crumbling, 19th-century houses cling to hillsides above the Kura river, which flows from the Caucasus mountains to the Caspian Sea.
Tbilisi's name - which means "a warm place" in Georgian - refers to the hot, sulphurous waters that pour forth from the mountains ringing the city and form creeks that trickle below its streets. Some are now on full display due to the renovation works along Rustaveli Avenue.
Tbilisi's mayor has pledged a "well-organised and modern" result and workers are labouring through the night to meet a November deadline. The city hall is under pressure to investigate claims that asbestos was dug up from the bowels of the avenue. REUTERS

Two bear cubs killed in Tartu County after repeated human contact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:17:00 UTC
17:17:00 KST

Two bear cubs killed in Tartu County after repeated human contact
Two bear cubs were culled in Tartu County on Sunday after repeatedly returning to residential homes despite being relocated, the Environmental Board (Keskkonnaamet) said.
The board said the bears had lost their species‑typical behavior, damaging yards and entering outbuildings, and attempts to return them to the wild proved impossible.
While in the past there was a bear culling season in the fall, brown bears can now only be culled via a special license, for instance issued if they are judged to be a nuisance. In this case the state Environmental Board said the bear cubs were treated as animals in a helpless state were no longer capable of surviving independently in the wild, in the understanding of the Animal Protection Act.
Tanel Türna, head of the Environmental Board's hunting and aquatic wildlife department, said so far as is known the young bears first came to a settlement in early June in Kõnnu village, Kastre municipality, and at the time they numbered four.
"The loss of their fear of humans was probably caused by people themselves feeding wild animals. Hopefully, two of them have since returned to a normal life as bears.," Türna said, noting these had not been seen again. "Unfortunately, the two bears fitted with ear tags and GPS tracking devices did not" return to to normal lives, he went on.
At the same time, the bears in question in any case also damaged beehives near a residential home and repeatedly entered outbuildings, and attempts to return them to the wild by the home owner themselves did not work out.
Türna said their had been multiple such incidents, which indicated an "unnatural" pattern of behavior had developed with the bears, mostly relating to a lack of fear of humans, resulting from members of the public feeding them.
"As a result, a difficult decision had to be made last Sunday and, as a last resort, the bears were killed," Türna said, noting zoos and wildlife parks had been contacted but none had spare capacity to house the cubs.
Bear cubs need to keep a healthy fear of humans and be capable of independently foraging for food in the wild, rather than continually returning to human settlements, he added.
"We ask people not to seek contact with wild animals and under no circumstances to feed them. It must be kept in mind that bears that are currently young and still relatively small will be large by next year and, if they seek proximity to people, could pose a very serious danger," Türna stressed.
There are an estimated 1,100 Eurasian brown bears in Estonia at present.
What to do if you encounter a bear in the wild
In most encounters, bears are not looking for a fight — they want to move away from a perceived threat. What looks like a charge is often a bluff, intended to warn rather than attack.
A brown bear will often rear up on its hind legs and growl before a potential attack. If you spot one, back away slowly, speak calmly, avoid eye contact, and never run. If attacked, lie flat on the ground, protect your head and neck, and play dead.
Prevention is the best protection. Make noise while walking in the forest — talk, clap, or step on dry branches so bears can avoid you. Don't walk alone in known bear habitats, stay clear of cubs, and never approach animal carcasses, which bears may defend. If a bear enters your yard, scare it off with loud noises rather than stopping to take photos.
Bears are most active at dusk and at night, but they can also be seen during summer berry season and in autumn near oat fields.

Paul Fogel, chief engineer, and his team met with over a dozen defense tech companies in several special events, including a demo day held in the Gaza border communities.
