“Ninety‑seven percent of our work is classified, but the remaining three percent gives you a glimpse into the complexity and advanced capabilities our teams are developing,” she added.

Oil surges past $100 a barrel again as US-Iran clashes intensify
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:16:34 UTC
17:16:34 KST

Brent crude has shot up to above $100 a barrel after US forces destroyed five Iranian tankers and Tehran responded with missile strikes on Jordan, the latest escalation in the conflict that has kept the Strait of Hormuz largely shut since February.
The front month contract on Brent crude, the international standard for oil prices, crossed $100 per barrel again on Wednesday morning while the US standard, WTI, hovered around $95.
Prices have risen almost 20% since the middle of last week as fighting around the world's most important oil chokepoint has once again intensified.
It is also the first time since 23 July that oil has hit the $100 mark.
US Central Command said its forces destroyed five Iranian tankers carrying crude oil on 8 September after Iran's Revolutionary Guard fired ballistic missiles at a US Navy warship twice within two days. The command did not identify the ship, but said it was not hit and continued patrolling regional waters.
It followed a similar strike on 5 September, when Iranian forces fired ballistic missiles at a US aircraft carrier and a destroyer, both of which evaded the attack. The command responded by disabling or destroying three Iranian tankers.
Tehran retaliated by firing missiles at a US military base in Jordan, where air defences intercepted most of them, and renewed threats to target tankers in Kuwaiti and Bahraini waters.
Iran has also repeatedly warned vessels against using unauthorised routes through the Strait of Hormuz.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said Tehran would soon declare an exclusion zone outside the strait, warning that any vessel entering without Iranian coordination would be added to a sanctions list.
Saudi Arabia has been drawn in too, with Aramco facilities at Jazan attacked again on Monday, though damage was reported as limited.
Roughly 7 million barrels a day are still moving through the Strait of Hormuz, against about 20 million before the war began on 28 February.
No end in sight
The military escalation is running alongside a financial one.
Washington launched Operation Economic Outcast in late August, an effort to sever Iran from the global financial system by targeting its access to digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping.
The US Treasury designated close to 60 companies, individuals and vessels at the outset and has signalled fresh measures weekly, with the European Union endorsing the campaign this month.
Rhetoric on both sides has hardened.
US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said the country "will destroy [and sink]" Iranian oil tankers if Iran fires on American vessels while the Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf replied by stating "strike our assets and you get struck".
US President Donald Trump has continued to insist the waterway is functioning, posting on Truth Social last week that "Hormuz volumes are BACK" and claiming 18 million barrels a day were flowing.
However, the US Energy Secretary Chris Wright put Monday's figure at 17 million barrels of crude and products combined, while acknowledging the multi-day rolling average is considerably lower.
During last week's White House press conference, US Vice President JD Vance also declined to categorise the ongoing conflict as a war and stated that "the only reason we do not have a worldwide energy crisis is because of the leadership of the President."
Faced with the latest developments, analysts are adjusting upward.
Goldman Sachs raised its Brent and WTI forecasts by $5 on Monday to $85 and $80, respectively, for December and warned prices could exceed $120 next year should Gulf output remain 4 million barrels a day below pre-war levels, though the bank does not treat that as its base case.

1,000 Patriot missiles arrive too late for this winter, so Ukraine asked the Ramstein arms coalition to open its warehouses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:14:59 UTC
17:14:59 KST

Ukraine is contracting about 1,000 missiles for its American-made Patriot air defense systems, but most arrive only in later years, so at the Ramstein meeting of its allies it asked for interceptors out of their existing stocks before winter, the Defense Ministry said. Nine governments announced new contributions there, and Germany was the only one to commit interceptors from its own stocks. The Ramstein format meeting is the Ukraine Defense Contact Group, a coalition of roughly 50 countries that coordinates weapons for Ukraine, named after the US air base in Germany where it first met in 2022.
Ukraine contracts for later, asks for stock now
Ukraine's Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara told partners the country is signing for roughly 1,000 Patriot missiles, whose PAC-3 version is the only round in its arsenal that reliably stops Russian ballistic missiles, paid for with partner support and the European Union's credit line. Those deliveries take time. So Ukraine asked allies to release missiles from their warehouses now and take the improved contracted rounds later. It made the same case for air-to-air missiles and shoulder-fired launchers, which crews use against cruise missiles and, as a stopgap, against the jet-powered Shahed attack drones, the Iranian-designed weapons Russia now flies at Ukrainian cities by day.
The European Commission cleared the loan money for interceptors days earlier. How many rounds it buys depends on the price Washington sets.
What partners pledged
The ministry listed the results by country.
- 
Germany promised interceptors for Patriot systems and for F-16 fighter jets, plus drone purchases.
- 
The United Kingdom put up £100 million ($135 million) through PURL, short for the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, the NATO mechanism that lets allied and partner governments buy US-made arms for Ukraine. London added another 95,000 drones by the end of the year and tens of thousands of extended-range artillery shells financed by other countries.
- 
The Netherlands pledged $300 million for the Drone Line, Ukraine's program that holds a drone-strike zone over the front, and 300 counter-drone missiles.
- 
Estonia committed to keep its support at at least 0.25% of its economic output in 2027.
- 
Norway confirmed a previously announced $200 million for Patriot missiles.
- 
Spain gave €2 million ($2.3 million) for fuel through NATO's procurement agency, plus air-defense missiles and artillery ammunition.
- 
Lithuania put $10 million into PURL.
- 
Poland prepared a €50 million ($58 million) package including air-defense equipment.
- 
Sweden pledged $28 million, half of it to PURL.
It was the coalition's 36th session, co-chaired online by Germany and the United Kingdom according to the German Defense Ministry's invitation, and the first for Khmara and for Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi, the general who took over Ukraine's army in July.
Brussels cleared Ukraine to spend EU loan money on American Patriot missiles for the coming winter of Russian attacks
Germany opens its own warehouse
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said he decided, alongside the NATO summit, to give Ukraine urgently needed PAC-2 interceptors, an older Patriot round, from the stocks of the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces, before winter. Russia has announced it will attack Ukraine's energy system. He told the others to check their reserves and do the same.
Germany will also step up deliveries of AIM-9 air-to-air missiles from the same stocks, the US-made rounds fighter jets fire at incoming drones and missiles, and keep delivering IRIS-T air defense systems, including serially produced guided missiles for them. Ukraine intends to order several thousand more IRIS-T rounds using the EU loan.
The money and the deadline
Allies allocated more than $10 billion over the past year for American weapons through PURL and the US foreign military sales program, $3.5 billion of it under the EU loan, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said. Khmara said partners promised €70 billion ($81 billion) this year, while Ukraine sees €62 billion, and the missing €8 billion is needed to meet that pledge, with the total defense deficit at €23 billion ($27 billion), according to the ministry's readout. He asked for those decisions by November. A day earlier, Ukraine handed the alliance a list of priority air- and missile-defense needs, the Defense Ministry reported.
Two timelines at the table
Elbridge Colby, the US under secretary of war for policy and the Pentagon's top policy official, told the group his department cannot predict when the war ends, that Russia is rebuilding its forces and defense industry, and that Ukraine's needs will persist for months and years. Europeans already lead on conventional defense and provide most of the support, he said.
Russia is expanding its manpower too, and by Ukraine's estimate plans to mobilize about 300,000 more soldiers this year and the same in 2027, Khmara said, Radio Svoboda reported. He presented the war plan Ukrainian forces now operate under, and said their drone kill zone stops Russian advances and kills more than 30,000 Russian soldiers a month, by the military's own count.

Ukraine, Russia trade drone strikes, killing 6

Three people were wounded in the strike on the Starokozace border crossing, around 500 kilometres (310 miles) south of Kyiv, Ukraine's State Border Guard Service said.
The strikes forced the checkpoint to close temporarily, Kiper said, adding that multiple fires broke out as a result of the attack.
Ukrainian emergency officials also said the capital, Kyiv was attacked overnight. While some fires were started, there were no casualties.
What is the latest in US-brokered peace talks?
Russia on Tuesday resumed its near-daily airstrikes on Kyiv after a brief pause while US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow for talks.
At least five people were killed in Kyiv on Tuesday, officials said.

Ukraine has suggested talks that could take place in September, but Russian officials have said it is "too early" to discuss specifics such as a venue or dates for the talks.
Despite US pressure, talks between Moscow and Kyiv have yielded no results beyond sporadic prisoner swaps.

Republicans put Trump center stage in US midterms gamble
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:13:22 UTC
17:13:22 KST

Breadcrumb
Republicans put Trump center stage in US midterm convention in Dallas
US Republicans open an extraordinary midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday betting that putting Donald Trump at the center of their campaign can rescue a party facing grim election forecasts—despite the president's deeply negative approval ratings.
The two-day gathering, dubbed "Trumpapalooza," is designed to persuade the Republican leader's supporters that he is effectively on the ballot on 3 November, when Republicans risk losing the House of Representatives and face a fierce fight to retain the Senate.
"So what I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot," Trump said recently at a rally in South Carolina. "Just come and vote. It's so important."
Decision Desk HQ projects Democrats to win the House 230-205 and the Senate to finish 51-49 in their favor—revising its 50-50 prediction as the outlook continues to worsen for Republicans.
Trump, whose approval rating stood at just 33 percent in recent polling, will speak on both convention nights at the American Airlines Center.
His challenge is to mobilize voters personally loyal to him without further alienating independents already souring on his presidency amid inflation woes, gasoline prices topping $4 a gallon and the continuing war with Iran.
"Many Trump supporters only vote when he's on the ballot," Matthew Green, a politics professor at the Catholic University of America, told AFP. "They're not diehard Republican voters; they're diehard Trump voters. So, in that respect, it makes some sense to feature Trump in the hopes of getting those folks to turn out in November."
But Green was skeptical that asking those supporters to imagine Trump on their ballots could overcome his broader weakness.
"When you're in the low- to mid-30s, that's traditionally associated with a very bad midterm for your party," he said of the 80-year-old's approval ratings.
Trump show
The gathering is the first Republican national convention held specifically for a midterm election, although Democrats experimented with similar meetings in the 1970s and 1980s.
No candidates will be nominated and no formal party business is planned.
Instead, organisers have constructed what amounts to a two-night television rally touting Trump's record and Republican candidates.
More than 100 House members and candidates are expected, with over 50 speakers or presentations scheduled each night.
Trump delivers Wednesday's keynote and returns for Thursday's finale after Vice President JD Vance speaks. Cabinet members, congressional leaders and candidates in closely watched House and Senate races are also on the program.
Republicans plan to highlight tax cuts, immigration enforcement, manufacturing and prescription drug prices, while depicting Democrats as dangerously far to the left.
Some Republicans, however, are privately hoping Trump sticks to that script rather than the personal grievances and off-message subjects that regularly dominate his appearances.
Staying home
Not everyone is coming.
Numerous lawmakers in competitive races have decided that, less than two months from Election Day, their time is better spent campaigning at home.
Green said vulnerable Republicans have two reasons to keep their distance: Trump's unpopularity and the cost of losing precious days in their districts.
"If you are a Republican running in a swing district, you probably want to get as much distance from Trump as possible," he said.
House Speaker Mike Johnson has acknowledged the dilemma, saying some members need to remain home because it is a "critical time" immediately before early voting accelerates nationwide.
Republicans who do attend have also been asked to contribute at least $25,000 for tickets and lodging.
The event doubles as a huge fundraising opportunity, with a Trump roundtable priced at $250,000 per person and photographs with the president offered for $88,600.
And even Trump's promised national television showcase faces an unusually formidable rival: both convention nights coincide with the opening games of the NFL season.
"Spending three or four days away from your district to go to a convention is not a good way to spend your time if you're facing a tight re-election," Green added.

UK keeps door open to more E-7 Wedgetails
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:13:19 BST
17:13:19 KST

Britain remains open to buying additional E-7 Wedgetail airborne early warning aircraft, but any further procurement will depend on available funding, Defence Minister Luke Pollard has said.
The update came in response to a written parliamentary question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked what progress had been made on Recommendation 47 of the 2025 Strategic Defence Review, including maintaining the aircraft and exploring further procurement through cost-sharing arrangements with NATO allies.
Pollard confirmed that Defence will take responsibility for maintaining the UK’s E-7 fleet once the aircraft have formally entered service.
He said: “The MOD will assume responsibility for maintaining the E-7 Wedgetail aircraft once they are accepted into service.”
Preparations for that transition are already under way, with personnel being trained to support the aircraft ahead of Initial Operating Capability.
Pollard said: “In preparation, training of maintenance personnel is already underway as part of wider efforts to establish and sustain the UK E-7 enterprise ahead of Initial Operating Capability.”
The E-7 Wedgetail is intended to provide the RAF with airborne early warning and control capability, using its radar and mission systems to detect and track aircraft and other threats while helping coordinate friendly forces across a wide area.
The UK programme has attracted significant amount of scrutiny over the size of the planned fleet, particularly after the number of aircraft was reduced from the original order. Recommendation 47 of the Strategic Defence Review called for the existing E-7 capability to be maintained while exploring options to procure additional aircraft, including through cost-sharing arrangements with NATO allies.
On further procurement, however, Pollard of course stopped short of announcing a new order or confirming that a NATO cost-sharing arrangement had been agreed.
He said: “The UK remains open to exploring all opportunities for future E-7 Wedgetail procurement, subject to the availability of funding.”
The wording leaves open the possibility of expanding the fleet in future, but makes clear that no additional purchase has yet been committed.
For the immediate programme, the focus remains on bringing the existing aircraft into service and establishing the personnel, maintenance and support structure needed to sustain them.

- The result has increased pressure on Merz, who is being blamed by some in his conservative Christian Democratic Union for the party's poor performance
Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, September 9, 2026:

Germany weighs risks to national intelligence amid far-right gains
German federal and state officials are discussing how to guard against potential security risks posed by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) following its election victory in Saxony-Anhalt.
Security officials are particularly concerned about how sensitive intelligence could be protected if the AfD were to lead a state government, including the risk that information could be passed to Russia.
The heads of Germany's federal domestic intelligence agency and its 16 state counterparts are expected to discuss the AfD during a regular meeting in Stuttgart.
Security sources rejected reports that the three-day meeting had been specially convened because of the Saxony-Anhalt election. However, officials are expected to consider ways of preventing sensitive information from being improperly disclosed.
The AfD won 43.8% of the vote in Sunday's election, narrowly missing an absolute majority.
Officials do not intend to cut a possible AfD-led government off from intelligence entirely, the Reuters news agency reported, citing security sources.
Information would still need to be shared, for example, if authorities received warnings of a planned attack in Saxony-Anhalt or if the state obtained intelligence about threats elsewhere.
However, officials could restrict the sharing of some information on right-wing extremists because the AfD itself has been classified as a confirmed right-wing extremist organization in several German states.
There are also concerns that intelligence services in allied countries could become more reluctant to share sensitive information with Germany if AfD officials had access to it.
North Rhine-Westphalia state Premier Hendrik Wüst, of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), called for a joint federal-state working group involving domestic intelligence officials, constitutional law experts and other specialists to examine how authorities should deal with the AfD.
Wüst cautioned against rushing into an attempt to ban the party, saying any review should remain open-ended and consider other possible legal measures.
Banning a political party should be the last resort for protecting the constitution, he said.
AfD demands its candidate lead Saxony-Anhalt under any coalition deal
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt says it would only cooperate with other parties if its lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund is elected state premier in the first round of voting.
The stance puts particular focus on the left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), whose support could give the AfD the seats it needsafter the far-right party fell just short of an absolute majority in Sunday's state election.
"That is the condition for cooperation, regardless of which party it is, and therefore of course also with the BSW," deputy AfD state leader Hans-Thomas Tillschneider told The Pioneer news platform.
The AfD emerged as the strongest party in Sunday's state election with 43.8% of the vote but fell short of an absolute majority.
The BSW won just over 5% of the vote and entered the state parliament.
BSW representatives have said they are prepared to hold talks with all parties, including the AfD, but have so far ruled out a formal coalition.
A few days before the vote, Wagenknecht spoke on TV broadcaster ntv about overlapping policy preferences of BSW and AfD voters: "These are people who have similar concerns: They want controlled migration, they do not want this uncontrolled migration and they want above all that politics is again conducted in their interests, that their lives are the focus."
Tillschneider also said cooperation with the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) could be possible if the party abandoned its "firewall" against working with the AfD.
Under the firewall, other German political parties have pledged not to cooperate with the far right AfD.
"A CDU that gives up its firewall against the AfD and opens itself up to cooperation could be a partner," he said.
He argued, however, that the CDU was currently moving in the opposite direction.
Attempted Leipzig airport drone attack planned in Russia, Merz says
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Wednesday that an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport had been prepared in Russia over a period of months and that a major disaster had only narrowly been avoided.
"This attack was planned in Russia for months and was specifically targeted at Germany, and only by pure chance was major material damage and harm to people prevented," Merz told the Bundestag.
The alleged attack has become part of a broader debate in Germany over Russian hybrid threats and the country's ability to protect critical infrastructure.
Merz made the remarks days after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won the Saxony-Anhalt state election. The party has repeatedly called for closer relations with Moscow.
Russia has denied involvement in the Leipzig incident. Its foreign minister has described Germany's accusations as "the start of a real war."
Merz blasts AfD's 'remigration' policy
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz sharply attacked the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) over its migration policy during Wednesday's Bundestag debate.
He described the party's concept of "remigration" as "nothing other than ethnic cleansing based on skin color and origin."
Merz said such a policy would also have severe consequences for Germany's labor market, where many people with migrant backgrounds are employed.
"If things were to happen the way the AfD wants, the skilled trades in Germany could no longer function, not a single care home would be able to operate, not a single hospital would be able to operate, and not a single restaurant could be run," Merz said.
"That would be the result of your remigration policy," he told AfD lawmakers.
Merz said there was agreement within his governing coalition that many people without a right to remain permanently in Germany should be deported.
"But we distinguish carefully between those who work in Germany, who contribute to our prosperity, who are welcome in Germany, and those who do not have a permanent right to remain and who must leave our country again," he said.
The government made that distinction carefully "in contrast" to the AfD, Merz added.
Merz hits back at AfD after Saxony-Anhalt vote
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in the German parliament, the Bundestag, gave a barbed response to opening remarks from the far-right Alternative for Germany's (AfD) co-leader Alice Weider, who lambasted Germany's ruling coalition as a "failure."
The Bundestag debate comes days after the AfD's after its strong showing in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, warning the party against assuming it was on course for broader majorities.
"Ms Weidel, today you can barely contain yourself," Merz told AfD co-leader Alice Weidel during the Bundestag's general debate on Wednesday. "But you do not have an absolute majority, and you will not achieve one in Germany."
"Nowhere in Germany will you win majorities with this politics," Merz said. "You are, and you remain a destructive force."
Merz acknowledged that the AfD had achieved "a remarkable election result in every respect" in Saxony-Anhalt.
"The voters spoke pretty clearly. They also sent us, and me personally, a clear message," he said.
However, he stressed that the AfD had failed to achieve its stated goal of securing an absolute majority in the state parliament in Magdeburg.
Merz accused the AfD of showing "contempt for our democratic institutions" and of repeatedly denigrating representatives of the state.
"You are and will remain a destructive force," Merz said.
He said there was a "deep divide" between the AfD and the other parties in foreign, European, social and peace policy.
Merz also accused the AfD of damaging German interests through its friendly stance towards Russia.
"The only thing that really threatens Russia and Putin is the appeal of democracy," he said. "And yet you are obviously still standing on Russia's side."
"You are part of the problem we have in Germany — and we will resist that with everything at our disposal."
AfD's Weidel says Merz coalition is 'over' after state vote
Alice Weidel, co-leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), said Chancellor Friedrich Merz's governing coalition had been rejected by voters after the AfD's victory in Saxony-Anhalt.
Speaking in the Bundestag's general debate in her first direct encounter with Merz since Sunday's state election, Weidel said voters wanted a change of political direction rather than "more of the same."
"The voters in Saxony-Anhalt have made it absolutely clear to you, in the language of democratic choice: black-red is over," Weidel said, referring to the traditional party colors of the conservative CDU/CSU and center-left Social Democrats within the governing coalition.
Weidel also attacked the government's fiscal policy, accusing Merz of pursuing unprecedented levels of borrowing.
She said Germany's public finances had been "shattered" and accused the chancellor of leaving behind "scorched earth."
"You are driving Germany towards national bankruptcy in record time," Weidel said.
She described the government's draft budget as a "declaration of surrender" by the coalition and claimed it was unconstitutional.

Second Reform minister resigns in a week as Andres Sutt steps down

Second Reform minister resigns in a week as Andres Sutt steps down
Andres Sutt has announced his resignation as Minister of Energy and Environment, the second Reform Party government minister to leave office in the space of a week.
Sutt said he made the decision ahead of the March 2027 Riigikogu election, which he said he will not be running in.
Sutt said he had thoroughly considered his situation over a lengthy period of time, making his final decision in mid‑summer.
"During an election autumn, people always ask who will be running. This time around too, and me too. This time, my answer is no," Sutt noted on social media.
Sutt noted it is customary for a minister to run in elections, meaning now was the time for him to step down. "Consequently, it is only right to make room for the next person who will run in the elections and for me to return to the Riigikogu. At the Riigikogu I will help see through to the finish line both the energy and environmental bills which are halfway there. I will certainly be having my say on financial and fiscal matters. Naturally, I will also support the party and the next minister with advice," he continued.
The outgoing minister added he would remain active in national politics until the end of his Riigikogu mandate – up to the 2027 elections. "I will remain a member of the Reform Party and I am not going anywhere as far as Estonia is concerned," Sutt added.
He also expressed a desire to return to his professional field after eight years in politics, adding two parliamentary terms is the right time to move on after.
Sutt, 58, joined Reform in 2018 following a lengthy career at the Bank of Estonia (Eesti Pank), where he was vice governor from 2001 to 2009. He was made energy and environment minister in March 2025 at the start of the current Reform‑Eesti 200 administration, having already served as minister of enterprise and information technology in Kaja Kallas' first cabinet, from January 2021 to July 2022.
This is the second minister from the Reform Party to have resigned in the past week: Hanno Pevkur stepped down as defense minister after four years in the post, following controversy over a defense procurement deal. His replacement is due to be announced today, Wednesday.
Government ministers do not sit at the Riigikogu, but it is standard practice for them to run in elections as "vote magnets." Following an election and the formation of a new administration, those elected as MPs who are made ministers vacate their Riigikogu seats, which are usually given to the next highest‑polling candidate not to have secured a seat and from the same party's numerically ordered electoral list. Conversely, when they step down as a minister and return to the Riigikogu, as in Sutt's case, that alternate MP must vacate the seat for them.

AI generated
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump gave his executive assistant Natalie Harp a US$45,000 (S$57,000) cash gift, US media reported Sept 8.
Two other White House employees, Margo Martin and Chamberlain Harris, received similar amounts, according to The Washington Post.
The three women described the payments as “cash gift for holidays”, The Post reported, citing financial disclosure forms.
Harp has been a near-constant presence at Trump’s side in his second term, sometimes typing out social media posts for him and printing out information, a role that has seen her dubbed the “human printer”.
She earns US$150,000 a year in her role as the special assistant and executive assistant to the President, according to an annual report to Congress.
A White House spokesperson defended the gifts, citing Trump’s “longstanding practice of giving Christmas gifts to people in his orbit, including at times employees and aides”.
They said the gifts were unrelated to any of the individuals’ duties, making them “entirely permissible under relevant legal and ethical standards”. AFP

Archaeologists uncover 38 skeletons at ancient Peru citadel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:09:30 UTC
17:09:30 KST

Archaeologists have uncovered a collective tomb containing the remains of 38 people at Chan Chan, a vast pre-Hispanic adobe citadel in northern Peru. Aerial footage shows teams working among the remains and excavating the site.
The tomb was discovered a few weeks ago at the archaeological complex near Trujillo, around 500 kilometres north of Lima. The remains were found alongside copper and gold objects, adding to the evidence being studied at the ancient complex.
Chan Chan was the capital of the Chimú civilisation, which flourished along Peru's northern coast before the Inca conquest. Archaeologists continue to investigate the tomb and its contents as they seek to learn more about the people buried there.
The complex covers a large area, with the excavation work and archaeological remains visible from above.

Türkiye leads OECD in PISA 2025 score gains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:09:23 UTC
17:09:23 KST

Türkiye has recorded the largest score increases among the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries in all three areas assessed by the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2025, according to results released by the OECD.
The assessment covered 91 countries and economies and evaluated the skills of 15-year-old students in science, reading and mathematics.
Türkiye has participated in PISA since 2003.
The 2025 assessment was conducted digitally between April 14 and May 16 across 203 schools in 56 Turkish provinces, involving 7,702 students from 12 regions.
Türkiye posts gains across all three subjects
Türkiye's scores increased in every field compared with 2022. Its overall ranking among participating countries rose by 15 places in science, 18 in reading and 11 in mathematics.
Türkiye scored 494 in science, 472 in reading and 462 in mathematics in PISA 2025.
Compared with its first participation in 2003, Türkiye improved its science score by 60 points, reading by 31 points and mathematics by 39 points.
While average education performance has declined in both the OECD and globally since 2003, Türkiye's scores have moved in the opposite direction.
Türkiye climbs OECD rankings
Among the 38 OECD members, Türkiye ranked 14th in science, 13th in reading and 23rd in mathematics.
The Ministry of National Education said Türkiye was the only OECD country to increase its scores in all three areas over the past decade. It also recorded the largest score increases among OECD members in science, reading and mathematics compared with 2022.
Because the number of participating countries has more than doubled since 2003 — from 41 to 91 — Türkiye's long-term progress was also assessed using percentile rankings.
From 2003 to 2025, Türkiye improved its relative position by 64 percent in science, 60 percent in reading and 52 percent in mathematics.
The results were published simultaneously worldwide, with separate reports issued by Türkiye's Ministry of National Education and the OECD.
Türkiye’s PISA gains follow years of investment in school infrastructure, digital education, and programmes aimed at strengthening basic skills and reducing learning gaps.
In 2024, the education ministry launched the Türkiye Century Education Model that seeks to focus on STEM education by training teachers.
Türkiye has also increased its focus on reading, literacy and mathematics through supplementary materials and targeted support, while free textbooks and expanded preschool access have aimed to strengthen foundational skills.

Athens cracks down on e-scooters as Europe sounds safety alarm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:08:28 UTC
17:08:28 KST

In the first eight months of 2026, a total of 6,127 checks were carried out on electric scooter users across the Attica region and 3,700 offences were recorded.
Greek traffic police service in the Attica region have launched a new round of intensive checks on electric scooters, after two serious accidents on Tinos and Glyka Nera, in which a 14-year-old girl and a 16-year-old boy were badly injured.
The checks focus mainly on the use of electric scooters by minors, as well as on general compliance with the Highway Code, while businesses that sell, supply or rent out these vehicles are also coming under scrutiny.
Particular emphasis is being placed on the centre of the capital Athens, where the use of electric scooters is especially widespread. At the same time, according to traffic police, there have been several complaints about scooters being abandoned on pavements, reducing available space for pedestrians.
3,700 offences in more than 6,000 checks
Data from the Attica Traffic Directorate illustrate the scale of the problem.
In the first eight months of 2026, a total of 6,127 checks were carried out on electric scooter users and 3,700 offences were recorded.
Of these, 1,844 concerned rental scooters while around 1,800 cases concerned privately owned ones.
The vast majority of offenders were adults: 3,544 people. However, 156 underage offenders were also recorded, 20 of them aged between 12 and 15 and 136 older than 15.
The most frequent offences relate to riding without a protective helmet and excessive speed. There are also cases of electric scooters being used on high-speed roads and running red lights.
56 road accidents in eight months
The figures on accidents are even more worrying. In the first eight months of the year, 56 road accidents involving an electric scooter were recorded in Attica.
Three people were seriously injured and a further 53 suffered minor injuries.
The two recent incidents involving minors have brought the issue of enforcing the rules, especially age limits for users, back to the fore.
Greek legislation has already been tightened. The use of electric scooters is prohibited for people under 17, an insurance requirement has been introduced and stricter penalties are provided for riding them on roads where the speed limit exceeds 50 kilometres per hour.
Fines are also foreseen for businesses that sell, rent or supply electric scooters to people under 17.
Despite the stricter framework, however, the situation on the streets suggests that enforcing it remains a challenge.
Europe sets limits on electric scooters
The debate is not confined to Greece. The spread of electric scooters as a means of micromobility has forced many European countries to seek a balance between alternative forms of transport, road safety and the protection of pedestrians.
The most radical example is Paris. Since September 2023, the French capital has banned dockless rental electric scooters, following a vote in which 89% of participants backed their abolition. The three companies operating in the city at the time were ordered to remove their vehicles.
Restrictions in Paris became even stricter in August 2026. Wearing a helmet and reflective equipment is now compulsory for anyone using an electric scooter on the city's public roads and the fine for not wearing a helmet is €135. The minimum age is 14 and the maximum permitted speed is 25 kilometres per hour.
Madrid has taken a similar path. In 2024 the city council revoked the licences of the three electric scooter rental firms operating in the Spanish capital and stated that it would not issue new ones.
Among the reasons it cited were gaps in insurance cover and the failure to implement technology that would prevent the vehicles from being used or parked in prohibited areas.
In Brussels, the regional government decided on a complete ban on shared electric scooters from 1 January 2027. The licences of the existing companies expire at the end of 2026 and will not be renewed.
The decision was taken after a significant rise in accidents: in 2025, 666 injuries were recorded in incidents involving electric scooters in the Brussels Region, an increase of 26% compared with the previous year.
Authorities also point to the problems abandoned scooters cause for pedestrians, as well as their use in criminal activities.
Helmets, insurance and age limits
Italy has chosen a different approach, tightening the rules for the vehicles themselves and their riders.
Italian law now requires helmets to be worn, a specific identification mark for each electric scooter and compulsory third-party liability insurance. The insurance requirements came into force in 2026.
In Finland, since June 2025 there has been a minimum age of 15 for using most electric scooters. It is also forbidden to hand such a vehicle to a child under 15. At the same time, an alcohol limit of 0.5% was introduced and the police were given the power to carry out breathalyser tests and checks for narcotic substances on users.
In Hungary, compulsory insurance has already been extended to certain categories of electric scooters, depending on their weight and maximum speed.
In Germany, the new framework tightens the liability of electric scooter rental companies, such as Lime and Bolt, in the event of an accident.
The aim is to make it easier to compensate victims even when the rider cannot be identified, while companies may also be held liable for accidents caused by abandoned scooters left on pavements.
The figures are telling: rental scooters made up around 20% of insured electric scooters in 2023, but were linked to about 40% of related compensation claims.
A stricter framework is also being promoted in Cyprus, where the minimum age for using an electric scooter has been raised from 14 to 17.
At the same time, a decree is out for public consultation that would allow electric scooters to be impounded for 30 to 90 days in the case of serious offences, such as riding by people under 17, using them on roads where they are banned or exceeding the limit of 25 kilometres per hour.
The common denominator is the attempt to address problems that have emerged alongside the rapid spread of micromobility: road accidents, use by children, riding on unsuitable roads and pavements and the uncontrolled parking of rental vehicles.

Australians question US commitment to Aukus submarine deal in crowdfunded inquiry
Under the Australia-UK-US security pact, Canberra will get eight nuclear-powered submarines at an estimated cost of up to US$266 billion
At an Aukus public inquiry in Canberra last week, one of Australia’s leading submarine experts, retired Rear Admiral Peter Briggs, called the plan “flawed and undeliverable”.
Australia scrapped an agreement for France to supply Attack-class submarines in favour of the Aukus sale in 2021. Briggs said the French deal was the better option, arguing that US shipyards, already struggling to meet the domestic demands, could not deliver the promised nuclear-powered submarines on time.
At the same inquiry, former civil servants dealing with national security Michael Keating and Jon Stanford said joining Aukus meant Australia was significantly more likely to be dragged into a conflict with China and potentially targeted with nuclear weapons. Australia had “sacrificed considerable sovereignty” to the US while leaving the country vulnerable without a guaranteed security safety net, they said.

EU faces complaint over plan to simplify more environmental laws
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:07:20 UTC
17:07:20 KST

EU faces complaint over plan to simplify more environmental laws
BRUSSELS, Sept 8 - Environmental campaign groups lodged a complaint against the European Commission on Tuesday, accusing the EU executive of moving ahead with an overhaul of water protection and management laws without enough evidence.
The complaint is the latest by environmental groups over the European Union's efforts to simplify and scale back policies, a strategy known as the EU "omnibus", which responds to complaints from industries who say burdensome laws hurt their competitiveness with global rivals like the U.S. and China.
The complaint concerns a Commission plan to revise the EU's main water legislation this year, in part in response to concerns by mining and metals companies that say the law's environmental safeguards are delaying permits for new critical raw materials mines and other industrial projects.
In a complaint filed with the European Ombudsman — the EU's independent watchdog — the World Wildlife Fund, the European Environmental Bureau and three other groups said the Commission had failed to sufficiently gather evidence and consult stakeholders before announcing the planned revision.
This failure amounted to maladministration, they said.
"Their cumulative effect amounts to a flagrant deviation from established due process, one that materially affects citizens' rights," the NGOs said. They argued that the EU water laws are not the reason new mines struggle to get permits, and do not need revising.
A Commission spokesperson said it had not yet been notified of the complaint, but that it would continue to engage with stakeholders as it prepares to revise the water laws.
"The Commission has been engaging in a transparent and inclusive dialogue with member states and stakeholders, and is currently assessing the input from stakeholders," the spokesperson said.
The Ombudsman will now decide whether to open an inquiry into the complaint. That process can take a few weeks, a spokesperson for the watchdog told Reuters.
The EU watchdog does not have enforcement powers, but rather makes recommendations that can affect future EU lawmaking, and increases scrutiny of the Commission.
Last year, the Ombudsman obliged the Commission to publicly explain why it had fast-tracked other proposals to curb sustainability laws, and not assessed whether the changes complied with Europe's climate change commitments. REUTERS

Three others injured as passengers and vehicle traffic temporarily halted after attack causes large fire, Ukrainian officials say.
Russian drones have struck a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova in the southern Odesa region, killing at least two people, and also targeted the capital, Kyiv, overnight, according to Ukrainian authorities.
Two civilians were killed and three others were injured in the attack near the Starokozache crossing, Governor Oleh Kiper said on Wednesday in a post on Telegram.

Passenger and vehicle traffic were temporarily halted across the border after the attack, which caused a fire, officials said.
Russia also attacked Kyiv overnight, causing fires but no casualties, emergency services said in a Telegram post.
The Russian defence ministry said its forces had struck a Ukrainian cargo vessel carrying military equipment in the Black Sea en route to the port of Odesa, as well as a warehouse in Kyiv, belonging allegedly to a company manufacturing drones, Russian news agencies reported.

Moscow resumed its near-constant air attacks on Kyiv on Tuesday after a brief halt during the visit of US peace negotiators. Officials said five people were killed in the capital.
Meanwhile, Russian forces shot down 596 Ukrainian drones during the night, the defence ministry said Wednesday.
The attacks left four dead in Novorossiysk in the southern Krasnodar region, governor Veniamin Kondratyev said on Telegram.
Mayor Andrei Kravchenko said drone debris fell on the premises of a number of businesses and close to an inhabited building in Novorossiysk late on Tuesday.
Ukrainian authorities confirmed attacks in the area, saying that military vessels at a naval base in Novorossiysk were hit overnight, the commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, Robert Brovdi, said.
Brovdi said missile carriers were among the vessels “lost” at the base, but did not say how many vessels had been struck.
Novorossiysk, a frequent target of Ukrainian drone strikes, is a major outlet for Russian oil, oil products and grain exports, among other commodities.

U.S. Supreme Court rejects Missouri's push to use new congressional map
China

2026-09-09
16:02:48 CST
17:02:48 KST

WASHINGTON, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday rejected an emergency appeal by Missouri officials seeking to use a new congressional map in the November midterm elections, a decision that initially left the state set to revert to its previous district boundaries.
The nation's highest court declined Missouri's request to suspend a ruling by the Missouri Supreme Court last week that blocked the use of the new congressional map drawn by Republican state lawmakers. The state Supreme Court ruled that Missouri must use the congressional district map drawn after the most recent census.
The Missouri Supreme Court also ordered that the new congressional map be put before voters in November, when they cast ballots in the midterm elections, to determine whether it can take effect in subsequent elections.
President Donald Trump and Missouri Republicans opposed the state Supreme Court's ruling. On Friday, Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway filed an emergency appeal with the U.S. Supreme Court, asking it to reinstate the new map for the November elections. The Supreme Court rejected the request on Tuesday.
U.S. states typically redraw their congressional districts based on the results of the decennial census. In 2025, however, Texas Republicans broke with that tradition and pursued another round of redistricting roughly five years after the previous nationwide redistricting cycle. The move triggered a series of battles between Republicans and Democrats over congressional district maps.
As part of a nationwide Republican effort to gain more seats in Congress, Republican lawmakers in Missouri redrew the state's congressional districts last year.
U.S. media outlets reported that the Supreme Court's decision marked a setback for Republican efforts to use mid-decade redistricting to strengthen their position ahead of the November midterm elections. ■

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: China's inflation edges up, signaling sustained recovery in domestic demand
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:02:25 CST
17:02:25 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- China's price levels continued their moderate recovery in August, reflecting sustained improvement in domestic demand under supportive policy measures.
Data released by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) on Wednesday showed the consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.4 percent month on month in August, reversing three consecutive months of decline, while the year-on-year gain accelerated from 0.5 percent to 0.8 percent.
NBS statistician Dong Lijuan attributed the uptick to several factors: rising energy prices, seasonal increases in food prices, continued gains in travel services during the summer holiday period, and higher prices for smartphones and computers driven by the surging demand for computing power.
Core CPI, which strips out food and energy prices, edged up to 1 percent year on year from 0.9 percent the previous month.
Factory-gate prices also sent encouraging signals. The producer price index (PPI) rose 0.4 percent month on month in August, swinging from a 0.7 percent decline the previous month, while the year-on-year gain widened to 3.8 percent.
The NBS cited the pass-through effect of rising global commodity prices and stronger demand in some sectors driven by domestic industrial upgrading.
Wednesday's price data is consistent with the broad pickup in consumer activity seen across China this summer.
Railway passenger trips totaled 954 million in July and August combined, and summer box office receipts reached 12.5 billion yuan (1.84 billion U.S. dollars). To channel consumer enthusiasm, more than 30,000 events centered on summer leisure, study tours and night economy were held nationwide, while over 450 million yuan in consumption subsidies were distributed by local governments.
Expanding domestic demand remains high on China's economic agenda. At a high-level meeting in late July, policymakers called for effectively expanding domestic demand, broadening quality supply to meet the needs of different consumer groups, and tapping the potential of service consumption. The Ministry of Commerce recently issued a set of guidelines to accelerate the release of demand for personalized consumption.
Experts believe more efforts should be made to smooth the flow of consumption and lift income expectations of individuals.
Chasing Securities predicts the policy measures to continue driving a moderate recovery in price levels. Wang Qing, chief macro analyst at Golden Credit Rating, forecasts that CPI will continue to edge up year on year in September, with price levels expected to remain moderate.
The role of consumption as a primary engine of economic growth is set to strengthen. Official data showed final consumption expenditure contributed 2.1 percentage points to GDP growth in the first half of the year, continuing to lead all growth drivers.
For the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), China has released a dedicated consumption expansion plan setting out 28 priority measures, with efforts to cultivate new consumption models and scenarios, raise household spending capacity, and optimize the consumer environment.
A strong domestic demand helps ensure a stable economy. With expanding domestic demand as a strategic anchor, China's pro-consumption policies will inject sustained internal growth momentum into the broader economy, experts said. ■

Saudi Arabia lifts alert in southern city a day after Houthi strikes
Sept 9 - Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense lifted an alert it had announced in the southern city of Khamis Mushait on Wednesday, a day after Houthi attacks there and in three other nearby cities wounded 73 people and set oil installations ablaze.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis struck an airbase in Khamis Mushait and oil infrastructure in the nearby cities on Tuesday in one of the biggest attacks in Saudi Arabia since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran in February.
Saudi authorities did not provide details for the reasons behind Wednesday's alert in Khamis Mushait.
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has escalated in recent months, raising fears of a return to broader conflict after a U.N.-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted years of war.
Saudi Arabia leads an Arab coalition that backs a government based in Yemen's south, which was driven from the capital Sanaa by the Houthis 12 years ago. The conflict has become a theatre in the wider regional war, with the Houthis close allies of Iran and Saudi Arabia an ally of the United States.
The Houthis declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea in July, prompting the Saudi-led coalition to strike what it said were Houthi military facilities in Yemen.
In recent days, Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces have launched a multi-pronged offensive on Houthi-held areas after the group attempted to advance on government positions. The government says it aims to recapture all Houthi-held territory.
Houthi-run Al Masirah TV, citing the group's health ministry, said at least 21 people had been killed in Saudi strikes on Yemen's Al Jawf over the past two days. Saudi Arabia has not announced or confirmed carrying out strikes there.
Saudi Arabia has described the Houthi attacks as a dangerous escalation, while the Saudi-led coalition has said it would take measures to deter further attacks. The Houthis say their strikes are in response to Saudi escalation in Yemen. REUTERS

EU firms remain bullish on ASEAN: survey
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:02:06 CST
17:02:06 KST

SINGAPORE, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- ASEAN remains the top growth market for European Union (EU) companies, with 78 percent of surveyed business representatives expecting trade and investment in the region to increase over the next five years, the Singapore-based EU-ASEAN Business Council said on Tuesday.
The proportion rose from 71 percent in 2025, while ASEAN remained the region offering the strongest economic opportunities for a fourth consecutive year, according to the council's 12th Business Sentiment Survey.
About 78 percent of respondents plan to expand operations in at least one ASEAN market, with Vietnam and Indonesia remaining the top two destinations.
However, uncertainty over U.S. tariff policies remains a key concern, with 81 percent saying it has weakened business confidence in ASEAN.
Among companies recalibrating supply chains amid trade uncertainty, 67 percent are considering ASEAN as an alternative or additional base.
Non-tariff barriers and regulatory fragmentation continue to constrain trade and investment in ASEAN, with 73 percent of respondents citing excessive barriers to efficient supply-chain operations.
"The region has strong fundamentals that make it an attractive supply-chain hub -- market heft, a strategic location, and regional connectivity. Addressing regulatory and cross-border frictions will strengthen market integration, allowing businesses to derive greater value from ASEAN's combined scale and encouraging more commercial activity," said Chris Humphrey, the council's executive director. ■

US firm used AI to hijack WeChat account, spurring call for cyber cooperation with China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:01:12 UTC
17:01:12 KST

US firm used AI to hijack WeChat account, spurring call for cyber cooperation with China
The flaw allowed for remote account takeovers without user interaction, prompting Tencent to patch the problem after Calif cybersecurity team flagged it
US cybersecurity researchers have demonstrated how artificial intelligence could help hijack WeChat accounts via unanswered voice calls, intensifying concerns about AI-driven cyber threats and prompting renewed calls for bilateral cooperation between the United States and China.
US security firm Calif said on Tuesday that its AI system identified a critical flaw in Tencent Holdings’ widely used messaging and payments app in July. In just a little over a week, researchers developed WeWorm – an experimental exploit that could allow an attacker to take full control of a target’s WeChat account via a simple voice call, without the victim ever picking up the phone.
Tencent patched the bug in late August, according to Calif, which alerted the Chinese tech giant.
A Tencent spokesperson confirmed on Wednesday that a server-side fix was deployed, requiring no user action, and noted there was no evidence that the vulnerability was ever exploited in the wild. Tencent added that it was “grateful to the researchers for bringing this to our attention and working with us”.
The experiment underscores the speed at which AI is accelerating cyber threats. A worm of this complexity previously required months of work from larger engineering teams, but Calif researchers noted that “AI can already do most of the work here”.
The findings left some analysts alarmed.

Alonnisos, Liepāja and Dalsland: The lesser-known destinations to put on your radar for 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:00:25 UTC
17:00:25 KST

Intrepid Travel’s annual ‘Not Hot List’ highlights under-the-radar spots where your tourism spending could really make a difference.
Overtourism is a major problem for residents living in some of the world’s most popular destinations.
Visiting in off-season, or opting to avoid the busiest neighbourhoods and sights, can help, but the best thing you can do is to just not visit these cities in the first place.
That’s not to say you shouldn’t travel at all – on the contrary, you just need to choose your holiday spots wisely.
Which is where Intrepid Travel’s annual “Not Hot List” comes in. First launched in 2018, the list puts the spotlight on under-the-radar alternatives and lesser-visited spots where your tourism money will have a positive impact on locals.
“If we want tourism to continue to be a force for good, we need to constantly rethink how and where we travel,” Erica Kritikides, general manager of experiences at Intrepid Travel, said.
“The Not Hot List isn’t just about surfacing lesser-known places, it aims to shift the conversation and help travellers to discover new destinations where their visit can make a meaningful contribution to local communities and economies.”
Each of the spots on the list must have the infrastructure and capacity to support more tourists, and the 10 were selected because of new initiatives, improved connectivity or major events that mean 2027 is the year to visit.
At the top of this year’s list is Kenya’s Samburu National Reserve, having been chosen as an alternative to East Africa’s busiest national parks, like Serengeti in Tanzania or Maasai Mara in Kenya.
Under-the-radar spots in Europe to visit next year
Certain Greek islands are among the most overtouristed spots in the world, with the summer months seeing tourists far exceeding the number of residents.
Those who want all the charm of the islands (read: great food, picturesque towns and some of the best beaches in Europe) without the crowds should take a look at Alonnisos.
Located in the Northern Sporades archipelago, and only accessible by ferry or private yacht, Alonnisos saw just 70,000 visitors in 2024.
Tourists make the effort to visit here for its underwater delights, with the National Marine Park of Alonnisos and Northern Sporades being Europe’s largest marine protected area. The island is also home to Greece’s first-ever underwater museum, the Peristera shipwreck.
Even those who don’t scuba dive will find plenty to love about the island, like the picture-perfect old town Chora.
Liepāja in Latvia also made it onto the list, having been named a European Capital of Culture for 2027.
The year will see more than 500 cultural events taking place, but it’s also a great coolcation alternative to the Mediterranean thanks to its eight kilometre beach.
Rounding out the top 10 is Sweden’s Dalsland.
Known as Sweden’s Lake District, Dalsland is massively underexplored, but it won’t stay that way for long thanks to the launch of a new rail link between Malmo and Oslo in June this year.
There are more than 2,000 lakes for you to explore, and Dalsland is also known for its gravel biking, with 850 km of roads.
According to Intrepid, “the drawcard isn’t so much a specific sight, destination or highlight – it’s the opportunity to travel slowly and the type of freedom that is hard to come by in the modern age”. Sounds good to us.
The top 10 destinations on Intrepid’s ‘Not Hot List’
- Samburu National Reserve, Kenya
- Mestia, Georgia
- Northern Highlands, Jordan
- Whitehorse, Yukon, Canada
- Alonnisos, Greece
- Dili, Timor-Leste
- Pekoe Trail, Sri Lanka
- Liepāja, Latvia
- Carretera Austral, Chile
- Dalsland, Sweden
