Indians trust the classroom, see better opportunities abroad: Global survey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
03:07:46 UTC
12:07:46 KST

Phir Bhi Dil Hai Hindustani. Not because the Ipsos Education Monitor survey mirrors the plot of the Shah Rukh Khan-Juhi Chawla film, but because the title neatly captures the contradiction in its India findings. Indians may believe better opportunities for growth and prosperity lie offshore, yet they remain remarkably bullish about their education system, their degrees and, above all, the future of their youth.More than half of Indian respondents rate the country’s education system as good. Three-fourths believe youth will have a better life than their parents. Nearly two-thirds think even young people from lesser privileged backgrounds have a bright future. And Indians remain strikingly convinced that a university degree still has value. However, ironically, 76% of Indian respondents say young people would have better opportunities by moving abroad.For some parameters, TOI looked at the subset of India’s position among the 16 individual G20 member countries included in the 31-country Ipsos survey. China, Russia and Saudi Arabia were not surveyed. The survey covered 23,537 online adults across the 31 countries between June and July 2026, with about 1,000 respondents in India.
Ipsos in its methodology has cautioned that its India sample is more urban, educated and/or affluent than the general population and should be interpreted as reflecting the views of the country’s more “connected” segment.The 31-country average is an unweighted average of country results; it is not adjusted for the population size of each country.
The robust belief in education, with a rider
The first question was straightforward. How do people rate the overall quality of their country’s education system? In India, 51% called it good. Among the G20 countries covered by the survey, only Australia was higher, at 53%. The 31-country average was 33%. But that 51% is a number in retreat. India was at 65% in 2025, 69% in 2024 and 55% in 2023. The 14-point fall from 2025 is the steepest year-on-year decline among countries with comparable 2025 data.
Education confidence chart
The contrast with several richer economies is sharp. Britain was at 43%, the US and Brazil at 32%, Italy at 29%, Japan at 24%, while France and Germany were both at 17%. That does not mean India has a better-performing education system than advanced economies. This is a matter of perception. And on that measure, Indians appear unusually confident. Just less than before.
Optimism about Yuva Shakti
The gap becomes even more striking when the question shifts from institutions to the people coming out of them. Asked whether young people in their country have a bright future, 72% of Indian respondents agreed. That was not merely the highest figure among the G20 countries covered. It was the highest among all 31 countries surveyed. The 31-country average was 45%.
Highest youth optimism score
Within the surveyed G20 set, Australia and South Africa were next at 54%, followed by Mexico at 52% and Canada at 50%. France was at 22%. It is perhaps one of the strongest votes of confidence in the survey. Indians appear to have placed enormous hope in their youth to put the country on the right track and take it forward.
The Indian dream remains intergenerational
One of the hallmarks of an aspirational society like India is the belief in accumulating wealth and opportunity across generations. People believe that the hard work of one generation will make the lives of those that follow smoother. That belief gets backed in this survey. Three-fourths of Indian respondents, 75%, believe young people today will have a better life than their parents. The 31-country average is 48%.
India's faith on future
Indians are also optimistic about people escaping the poverty trap. 64% believe young people from poorer backgrounds have a bright future, compared with a 31-country average of 40%. India is the highest among the G20 countries covered on both measures. And 69% of Indian respondents believe the education system contributes to reducing social inequalities, again the highest among the surveyed G20 countries. That figure is also below earlier readings, 72% in 2024 and 79% in 2023.Together, these numbers suggest that Indian respondents continue to see education as a vehicle for upward social mobility. That belief becomes even clearer when the survey turns to higher education.
In India, the college degree has not lost its promise
NITI Aayog’s recent Reimagining Skilling for Viksit Bharat@2047report also points to the continuing pull of degree programmes, noting that vocational pathways are often not seen as credible, growth-oriented alternatives and that degrees can become the safer choice amid limited counselling, social bias and low trust in existing skill systems. The Ipsos survey, albeit with a more urban and connected Indian sample, points in a similar direction. 75% of Indian respondents say a college or university degree is very important to succeed in life. 78% believe it helps people go further in their careers. And 70% say degrees in their country offer good value for money.
Bullish on college degree
On the first measure, India is the highest among the G20 countries surveyed. On both the other measures, it ranks second. The contrast with several advanced economies is large. On whether a degree is good value for money, India’s 70% compares with 38% in the US, 41% in Germany, 30% in Japan and 28% in Britain. Ipsos itself finds a strong positive relationship across countries between believing that a degree helps a career and believing that it offers value for money.
India trusts the curriculum, yet worries about the jobs connection
Here again, the Ipsos study broadly aligns with a concern flagged in NITI Aayog’s skilling report that education and credentials do not automatically translate into the skills and pathways that the labour market demands. The Ipsos survey shows a deep-seated faith in formal education and yet a growing realisation that job-market demands are at times different from what is being taught in the classroom.Asked whether the school curriculum adequately prepares students for future careers, 67% of Indians agree, the highest share among the G20 countries covered by the survey. Even here, the direction has been downward: 74% agreed in 2024, 72% in 2025 and 67% now.
Education-Jobs paradox
Yet in another question on the greatest challenges facing young people, 36% of Indian respondents select “education and training systems not matching labour market demands”. That too is the highest among the G20 countries in the survey.
A bright future. Somewhere else?
India again falls on one extreme of a scatter plot for its two seemingly contradictory sets of beliefs. On one hand, 72% say young people have a bright future. On the other hand, 76% say young people would have better opportunities by moving abroad. The 31-country average on that question is 62%.Indonesia and South Africa are even more likely to say opportunities are better overseas, at 87% and 80% respectively. Italy is at 79%. Romania matches India at 76%. But none combines that level of outward-looking aspiration with India’s exceptional optimism about the future of its young.
Hope at home, opportunity abroad
This is perhaps the central finding of the entire report for India. Respondents may be optimistic about India’s young people precisely because they believe those young people possess education and skills that give them more options, including the option of leaving. The optimism may be about the people. The doubt may be about the location of opportunity.
Social media? Restrict it. AI? Not necessarily
The dichotomy in the approach of Indians extends to technology too. 78% support banning social media for children under 14, both inside and outside school. The 31-country average is 73%.Support has climbed 10 points in a year. India was at 68% in 2025 and 73% in 2024.On smartphones, 57% of Indian respondents favour a ban in schools, exactly matching the 31-country average. That is up from 50% last year and 52% in 2024. But attitudes to AI are different.
On use of AI
Only 26% of Indian respondents say AI, including ChatGPT, should be banned in schools, compared with 39% across the 31 countries. Indian opinion on AI has moved sharply over the four editions of the survey. 39% wanted AI banned in schools in both 2025 and 2024, compared with just 16% in 2023. The 13-point drop from 2025 to 2026 is the largest year-on-year fall among countries with comparable 2025 data.
Britain, the US and Poland moved in the other direction, rising to 52%, 56% and 46%, respectively.To sum up, India’s ‘connected’ population has not lost faith in education. Quite the opposite. It remains unusually convinced that education matters, degrees pay, children can surpass their parents and those from poorer homes can climb. What appears less certain is where that promise will ultimately be realised.Karmabhoomi and janmabhoomi may finally be different. That is the sobering realisation one can derive from this survey.

Both sides have been attempting to assert control over the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway through which roughly one-fifth of the world's traded oil passed before the war began.

The US and Colombia signed two strategic memorandums of understanding Tuesday during a ceremony in the Colombian coastal city of Barranquilla attended by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella and Foreign Minister Omar Bula Escobar.
The first memorandum establishes a framework between the US and Colombian governments to secure supply chains in the mining and processing of critical minerals and rare earths, while the second concerns strategic civil nuclear cooperation between the two countries.
Speaking after the signing, Rubio praised De La Espriella as a leader of "energy, strength, vision and courage," noting that the new administration inherited severe challenges, including the aftermath of a recent earthquake and an "institutional" crisis from prior governance that had frayed bilateral relations.

I have proposed to Mr. Secretary that we consolidate a bilateral prosperity dialogue featuring concrete projects, responsibility, financing and schedules, the work on which our teams will continue in Washington. Asked whether Colombia's request for the US to lift tariffs had come up in his talks, Rubio said the US Supreme Court's ruling striking down the tariff mechanism that President Donald Trump had originally used meant the administration had to reinstitute it through the Section 301 process, which requires a bilateral agreement.
"The president of the United States has a desire to reach an agreement with Colombia as soon as possible. Ambassador (Jamieson) Greer has been working with Colombian authorities on that negotiation. I think it's going very well, and I hope to have good news soon in regards to that once such an agreement can be reached," Rubio told reporters.
"I think there's been two rounds of that discussion, and good progress is being made, but obviously no announcement today," he added.

Colombia’s State Council says gov’t has not sought legal opinions on potential joint military operations with US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
03:00:28 UTC
12:00:28 KST

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Colombia’s State Council said Tuesday that it has not received any formal requests from the government to issue legal opinions on potential joint military operations with the US or the presence of foreign troops in the country.
It issued the clarification in response to a petition filed by Alejandro Lanz Sanchez and Sebastian Lanz Sanchez, co-directors of Temblores ONG, a prominent progressive, grassroots human rights non-governmental organization (NGO) based in Bogota.
The organization submitted 27 questions seeking to establish whether the executive branch had requested official authorization for foreign military deployments.
Following a review of its official records and institutional inbox, the General Secretariat reported that no requests regarding the entry, transit or participation of US forces were filed between Aug. 7 and the date of response.
The query came amid heightened public scrutiny regarding Washington's security role in Latin America and the legal boundaries governing foreign defense forces in Colombia.
The court referenced key legal precedents, including an April 1999 ruling on troop transit and a November 2020 decision concerning the deployment of the US Security Force Assistance Brigade (SFAB).
Under Article 237 of the Colombian Constitution, prior review by the State Council is mandatory for the transit of foreign troops or the stationing of foreign warships and military aircraft in national territory.
However, the tribunal clarified that international cooperation activities such as technical assistance, capacity building, training or advising without direct participation in combat operations or the carrying of weapons do not legally constitute troop transit.
The council also emphasized that while its consultative role is legally required in applicable scenarios, its final advisory opinions are non-binding, leaving the president with the legal authority to adopt or reject its findings.

US, China trials suggest a single nanodrug shot might stop bad cholesterol forever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
03:00:09 UTC
12:00:09 KST

US, China trials suggest a single nanodrug shot might stop bad cholesterol forever
Separate trials using CRISPR and base editing to silence lipid genes show drastic drops in LDL-C without daily medication
Imagine swapping your daily cholesterol pill for a single injection that keeps “bad” cholesterol under control for a year, a decade – or even a lifetime.
Two clinical trials, one in the United States and another in China, suggest that this one-and-done approach could become a reality.
Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), better known as “bad” cholesterol, is a major driver of heart disease – the leading cause of death worldwide. Triglycerides, another type of blood fat, add to the risk.
For millions of people, the standard fix is a daily statin pill.
Research led by the Cleveland Clinic in the US and carried out in Australia, New Zealand and Britain, tested a gene-editing nanodrug called CTX310 on 15 volunteers.
The therapy uses tiny particles to carry a CRISPR gene-editing tool straight into liver cells. Its target is a gene named ANGPTL3, which helps control how much fat circulates in the blood.
Some people are born with a natural mutation that inhibits ANGPTL3. They have extremely low cholesterol and triglycerides, and they rarely develop heart disease.
CTX310 is designed to mimic that genetic switch.

He reiterated New Zealand’s support for a two-state solution, calling it “the best hope” for Israelis and Palestinians to live in peace and security.
Earlier Tuesday, the UK, France, Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden announced steps to restrict trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories.

====================================================================================================

China Focus: Chinese students find growing appeal in research-oriented universities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:48:09 CST
11:48:09 KST

HANGZHOU, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- In China, a high score in the annual national college entrance examination, or gaokao, has traditionally opened the door to the country's established elite universities. However, this September, as universities across the country welcome new students, some high achievers are taking a different path.
Shen Chenlin, from the eastern province of Zhejiang, ranked around 750th among over 400,000 local gaokao candidates with a score of 688 -- enough to meet the application cutoffs of over 30 universities in the country's elite group of 39.
Yet, Shen chose the Eastern Institute of Technology, Ningbo (EIT) in Zhejiang, a fledgling institution now welcoming only its second cohort of undergraduates.
As he begins university life, Shen is excited about EIT's freedom to explore different fields before settling on a major, an approach not typically offered at most Chinese universities.
"We'll take general education courses in our first year and choose a major in the second," Shen told Xinhua. "That gives me time to explore different fields and find what I really like."
Particularly interested in engineering software and simulation design, he hopes to find his future career direction at EIT, whose academic programs span science, engineering, information technology and business, with a particular focus on frontier fields such as AI, integrated circuits and unmanned technologies.
Another draw is EIT's faculty. The university has 16 academicians from various countries and more than 100 faculty members across different majors who will teach Shen and the other 129 undergraduate students in his cohort.
"Having top scholars work directly with undergraduates means we can access high-quality academic resources from the start, which will be a great help when I pursue research in the future," Shen said.
A NEW CHOICE
Many students who scored highly in this year's gaokao made choices similar to Shen's, turning to a new generation of research-oriented universities, a small part of China's higher education landscape numbering only around 10 among more than 1,300 institutions offering undergraduate programs nationwide.
Their choices have put relatively young institutions such as Westlake University in Zhejiang, Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech), Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology (SUAT) and Great Bay University (GBU) in the southern province of Guangdong, and Fuyao University of Science and Technology in east China's Fujian Province in the spotlight this summer.
Although these research universities still have small undergraduate enrollment -- typically just a few hundred students per cohort -- some expanded their intake this year while keeping admission scores on par with many of China's top universities.
Observers say the growing appeal of these universities reflects a shift in how Chinese students assess their college options, as more look beyond university prestige to consider their academic interests, learning experience and future career prospects.
Research institutions typically focus on science and engineering, with programs concentrated in fields aligned with the country's strategic priorities. Designed to offer a different model of higher education in institutional management, academic disciplines and talent development, their rise comes as China seeks new ways to cultivate talent and pursue original research amid rapid advances in science, technology and industry.
Tian Gang, founding president of GBU, said research universities are facing an unprecedented opportunity. Frontier fields that China urgently needs to develop, including AI, advanced materials and new energy, offer ample room for these relatively young institutions to leverage their flexibility, focus resources and pursue breakthroughs.
The country's education roadmap released in June envisions establishing several more such universities between 2026 and 2030, while provinces like Shandong, Zhejiang, Jiangsu and Hainan have pledged support for their development in local government work reports or 2026-2030 plans.
DIFFERENT STRENGTHS
According to Chen Xianzhe, an education professor at South China Normal University, the strengths of research-oriented universities lie in their focused academic programs, strong emphasis on research and innovation, and close links with industry.
SUAT, for example, has an unusually compact academic portfolio. Established in 2024 in the global innovation hub of Shenzhen, the university currently offers just nine undergraduate programs, all focusing on emerging areas such as semiconductors, AI, new energy, biomedicine and synthetic biology.
Westlake University, established in 2018 in Hangzhou, exemplifies a research-intensive model with an international outlook. Supported by both public and private funding, it has enrolled over 3,200 students to date, including more than 420 undergraduates and nearly 2,800 doctoral students. Its academic community of over 2,200 faculty and staff members comes from more than 30 countries and regions.
EIT in Ningbo, meanwhile, places greater emphasis on linking education and research with industry. It has partnered with 33 technology companies to co-train undergraduates. Established in 2025, EIT has already secured 786 research projects and incubated 21 technology companies.
"We aim to cultivate undergraduates into scientists with an entrepreneurial spirit and entrepreneurs with a strong grounding in science," said Zhang Dongxiao, EIT executive vice president.
Chu Zhaohui, a researcher at the China National Institute of Education Sciences, said these institutions can adapt more quickly to changing needs than some established comprehensive universities.
That responsiveness is strengthened by the ecosystems surrounding many of these universities. Often based in cities with strong technology and industrial bases, they have close ties to companies, research institutions, and emerging industries, which opens up diverse opportunities for students in both academic research and their future careers.
At the Shenzhen-based SUSTech, a pioneering research-oriented university established in 2012, more than 100 university-industry joint laboratories support collaboration in frontier fields including new energy, quantum technology and energy storage, with each partnership worth at least 5 million yuan (737,000 U.S. dollars).
The latest data show that the university has transferred 723 research achievements to industry, with technology transfer contracts totaling more than 1.51 billion yuan.
SUSTech has also ranked among the top 10 universities on the Chinese mainland in the Global Employability University Ranking and Survey for five consecutive years, underscoring its graduates' strong career prospects.
This shift in students' choices, however, does not mean that higher education should move in just one direction.
The growing appeal of these science- and engineering-focused institutions reflects the demands of a changing economy, but less popular fields remain important to broader social development, said Zhu Xi, a professor at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen. "A strong higher-education system should allow different talents to find their place."
The same diversity is needed among universities. The rise of research universities does not diminish the value of established institutions. Rather than replacing one another, the two models can complement each other, bringing different strengths to China's higher education, said Ming Liang, a senior researcher at the think tank China Development Institute. ■

Gambian leader pledges halt to rolling blackouts as protests turn violent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Gambian leader pledges halt to rolling blackouts as protests turn violent
Barrow pledges new power infrastructure, including a 24-megawatt plant, to tackle The Gambia’s worsening electricity crisis.
Gambian President Adama Barrow has said the country will boost energy supplies by next month, hoping to quell violent protests over prolonged power outages as the premier stands for re-election.
Protesters burned tyres and built barricades blocking traffic, demanding that Barrow resign, in The Gambia’s capital, Banjul, and nearby cities on Monday and Tuesday.
Police used tear gas to disperse crowds who gathered in multiple locations, including near Barrow’s residence and the National Water and Electricity Corporation (NAWEC) headquarters, which supplies the country’s electricity.
Barrow declared the outages an emergency and a “national security issue” during a visit to a NAWEC power station. In a national address, he announced that the government would install a 24-megawatt generation machine by the end of October.
“I know that the fans have stopped turning, children work in the dark, mothers throw away stale food, and the heat is unbearable by day and by night,” Barrow said.
The rolling blackouts are taking place during the West African country’s hot season and have lasted up to 48 hours in some places.
The Gambian president also announced an additional 50-megawatt solar power plant that would begin construction soon.
NAWEC Managing Director Gallo said the prolonged electricity cuts were in part due to climate change and the US-Israel war on Iran. The electricity provider, in a statement released in August, also claimed that it was experiencing an “unforeseen surge” in demand due to high temperatures.
The blackouts come just months ahead of the December presidential election, in which Barrow is running for a third term.

British retailers targeting 100,000 jobs for young people by 2029
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:47:47 CST
11:47:47 KST

LONDON, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Leading retailers in Britain are working with the government to offer work opportunities to young people, aiming to create up to 100,000 jobs by the end of Parliament in 2029, a government statement said Tuesday.
A new work experience program will provide 18- to 24-year-olds who are not in education, employment or training (NEET) with two to four weeks of hands-on experience, at 16 to 35 hours per week, as part of more than 11,000 placements with Britain's biggest retailers, complete with dedicated workplace support and interview experience, according to the statement from the government's official website.
The program aims to give young people the skills and experience they need to get their first job. Participants could be offered a permanent role if one is available, placed in the retailer's talent bank, or directed towards apprenticeships and other opportunities.
Since too many young people are trapped in a "no-experience, no-job doom loop," high-quality work experience is essential to fix this problem, said Helen Dickinson, chief executive at the British Retail Consortium.
"Retail is uniquely placed to make a difference on the NEETs crisis, given the industry's scale and reach touching every corner of the country," she said, noting that work experience is a first step and, with the right conditions for businesses to invest and create new entry-level jobs, employers across the economy can help tackle the NEET crisis.
In the second quarter of this year, 981,000 young people aged 16-24 were NEETs, accounting for 13 percent of the age group, earlier data from the Office for National Statistics showed.
The government has launched a range of youth employment support, including the Jobs Guarantee scheme, which has been backed by over 400 employers and offers a direct route into work for eligible young people. More than 90,000 young people will be supported into work by the scheme in the next three years, according to the statement. ■

====================================================================================================

S. Korea's employment growth hits 5-month high in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:47:43 CST
11:47:43 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's employment growth hit a five-month high last month, indicating a steady recovery trend despite prolonged downturns in manufacturing, construction and the youth labor market, statistical ministry data showed Wednesday.
The number of employed people aged 15 and older gained 184,000, or 0.6 percent, from a year earlier to 29,151,000 in August, marking the largest on-year job growth since March, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics.
After maintaining a steady expansion of 100,000 to 200,000 jobs in the first quarter, the job growth slowed sharply to 74,000 in April. The number of jobs shrank by 40,000 in May before rebounding in June with a growth of 63,000 and 108,000 in July.
The overall employment rate for those aged 15 and older remained flat at 63.3 percent in August from a year ago, while the OECD-standard hiring rate for those aged 15-64 rose 0.5 percentage points to 70.4 percent.
Employment among manufacturers fell 38,000 in August from a year earlier, posting its 26th consecutive month of decline. It was slower than a contraction of 68,000 in the previous month.
Jobs lost in the construction industry reached 32,000 in August, extending the streak of losses to 28 straight months, though the falling pace moderated compared to a reduction of 57,000 in July.
The accommodation and food services sector saw a drop of 61,000 jobs last month, its sharpest fall in 13 months.
The losses were offset by strong hiring in the health and social welfare service, the arts, sports and leisure service, and the business facility management industries, which recorded a job increase of 186,000, 73,000 and 45,000 each.
The cold spell for youth labor was prolonged. The number of employed people aged 15-29 plummeted 143,000 in August on a yearly basis, continuing to go down for 46 successive months.
The youth employment rate tumbled 1.0 percentage point to 44.1 percent, falling for 28 months in a row.
The elderly population compensated for the slack in youth hiring. The number of jobs for those aged 60 and older surged 191,000, while the figures for those in their 30s and 50s swelled 91,000 and 62,000 each.
Among wage earners, the number of regular workers mounted 180,000, while the readings for irregular employees and daily laborers shrank 50,000 and 17,000 each.
Among non-wage workers, the number of the self-employed with employees swelled by 47,000, and the figure for the self-employed without employees increased by 62,000.
The number of unemployed people totaled 588,000 in August, down 4,000 from a year earlier. The unemployment rate was unchanged at 2.0 percent.
The expanded jobless rate dipped 0.6 percentage points to 7.6 percent in the cited month, while the corresponding rate for those aged 15-29 added 0.1 percentage points to 15.4 percent.
The official unemployment rate gauges those who are immediately available for work but have failed to get a job for the past four weeks despite efforts to seek a job actively.
The expanded jobless rate, called the labor underutilization indicator, adds those who are discouraged from searching for a job, those who work part-time against their will to work full-time, and those who prepare to get a job after college graduation, to the official unemployment rate.
The economically inactive population, who had no willingness to seek a job and remained unemployed, rose 77,000 from a year earlier to 16,297,000 in August.
The reading for discouraged jobseekers dwindled by 42,000 to 367,000 last month.
The number of the "take-a-rest" group, who replied that they took a rest during a job survey period, reduced by 89,000 to 2,551,000 in the same month.
The take-a-rest group is considered important as it can include those who are too discouraged to seek a job for an extended period. ■

FBI involved in locating bodies of Jake and Callum Robinson in Mexico, court hears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
02:42:25 UTC
11:42:25 KST

FBI involved in locating bodies of Jake and Callum Robinson in Mexico, court hears
In short:
The bodies of two Australian men and their American friend who were shot dead while on a surfing trip in Mexico in 2024 were found through the United States FBI, a murder trial has been told.
Three men are on trial on a number of charges for the alleged killing of Jake and Callum Robinson.
What's next?
The judge-only trial is expected to run for more than four weeks.
The bodies of two Australian men and their American friend, who were shot dead while on a surfing trip in Mexico in 2024, were found by the United States FBI, a murder trial has been told.
A Mexican court has also heard that a group of friends went looking for the men when they first went missing and were the first to find the camp where they were last seen.
On day two of the trial into the murders of Perth brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and American Carter Rhoad, a colleague of one of the brothers revealed for the first time that the FBI had been "cooperating with Mexican authorities" on the case.
The involvement of the American intelligence agency has not been made public before.
The three men were believed to have been camping at a remote coastal area when they were attacked and shot dead in April 2024. Their bodies were later found dumped in a well.
Jesús Gerardo, also known as "El Kekas", Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús are currently on trial in a small court in Ensenada, on Mexico's Pacific Coast.
They have each been charged with aggravated homicide, aggravated robbery, violent robbery and grand theft auto.
A colleague and friend of Carter and Callum, who asked not to be identified, told the trial that he had travelled with the two Australian brothers and the American on their surf trip to Mexico.
The man said he returned home to San Diego early for work and became concerned when he texted Callum and Carter on April 28 and did not receive a reply.
He then contacted the Airbnb where the men were supposed to be staying and was told by the hosts they had not heard from them.
He told the court he rang Natalie Weirtz, the wife of Carter Rhoad, to inform her he was going to file a missing person's report.
The man told the court that Ms Weirtz was able to locate where Carter's phone had last pinged to a neighbourhood near Ensenada.
The unnamed man told the court he and a group of seven other friends took it upon themselves to track down their friends.
They drove to the neighbourhood where Carter's phone was last located. But the man claimed that when the group arrived, they believed it did not look like a neighbourhood where someone could safely knock on strangers' doors.
They instead decided to drive to Punta San Jose, which is where the man believed Jake, Callum and Carter were planning to camp on April 27.
It was there that he spotted what he described as the "black footprint" of what looked like a burnt-out tent along the bluff.
The man said he immediately recognised a mug that belonged to Callum. Other items included a Birkenstock buckle and a glasses case that belonged to Carter Rhoad.
The group also found what they assumed to be blood and a shell casing. Mexican authorities identified it as a crime scene.
The man said he was told in the following days that the bodies of his missing friends had been found.
The ABC asked local Mexican authorities to confirm the involvement of the FBI, and they refused to comment.
Parents don't hold 'animosity' towards killers
The Robinson parents have travelled from Perth to Mexico to attend the trial in person.
In testimony lasting more than an hour, Martin Robinson told the court about the timeline of his sons' disappearance and the discovery of their bodies.
"I'm here because my two sons were murdered," he told the court.
He recalled receiving a phone call on May 1 from an American phone number that he had initially assumed belonged to Callum because it was his birthday. It turned out to be a friend of his son telling him the brothers were missing.
Mr Robinson said he and his wife, Debra, left Perth to fly to America two days later. When they arrived in Tijuana, they met with the attorney-general and were asked to identify their sons' bodies.
Martin Robinson identified Callum by his tattoos and Jake by photos of his face. He then provided DNA and blood samples, birth certificates, and a registration certificate for Callum's pickup truck in order for them to match the bodies.
"We don't hold any animosity against the people who did this, but what we don't understand is how they could rob the world of two beautiful men who had such bright futures," he told the court during his testimony.
"We miss them every day, and our lives are never going to be the same again."
As he got up from the stand, his wife, who had been quietly crying in court as he spoke, whispered some words of encouragement before they embraced.
Ms Robinson was called to the stand yesterday but only identified herself before the prosecution said her testimony was not necessary.
Carter's mother says killing looked like 'an execution'
The mother of Carter Rhoad, Page Rhoad, also gave testimony at the trial, appearing via videolink in court from her home in the United States.
She testified that she had been told her son and the two Australian men had been shot "three times". The autopsy for the three men has not yet been revealed in court.
In a similar account to the one given by the unidentified friend of Carter and Callum, Ms Rhoad also discussed how a search party was assembled to go to Mexico to look for the missing men.
She said the group of eight, which included one of her sons, gathered at Ms Weirtz's house in the south of San Diego, before they got into two separate cars and crossed the border.
Ms Rhoad said she and one of her daughters then decided they would travel to San Diego. On May 3, they met with the FBI and were told bodies had been found in a well. The next day, she was told those bodies were believed to be Carter, Jake and Callum.
Ms Rhoad said she travelled to Mexico to help identify her son's remains. When she looked at photos of the body, she said she recognised her son straight away.
"I'm not an expert, but to me it looked like an execution," she said of seeing the bodies.
She went on to describe Carter as an "amazing son" who was looking forward to holding a public ceremony with his wife, whom he had secretly married in December 2023.
The case against the accused
The prosecution has outlined a case consistent with previous public comments about a robbery gone wrong, although defence teams have claimed in court there is not sufficient evidence to prove the theory.
On the first day of the trial, a judge ordered the removal of the three defendants from the courtroom after the prosecution said two witnesses had been intimidated by people connected to the accused.
The three men were returned to the courtroom for today's session.
Yesterday, the court heard from two witnesses: one was the former girlfriend of El Kakas, and the other was her adult son. They are both in witness protection.
The man, whose name was withheld, provided an account of what took place on the day the Australian brothers were murdered, while his mother testified about her relationship with El Kakas and his alleged domestic violence.
Ari Gisell, another ex-girlfriend of one of the men now on trial, was sentenced to 20 years in jail last year for her role in connection with the murders.
The prosecutor had argued Gisell was the instigator of the attack on the tourists because she had expressed interest in the tyres of the car they were driving and their phones.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said on Tuesday it had captured a US uncrewed submarine at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, offering a rare glimpse into how underwater drones are being used in military operations.
Iranian state media said the vessel was a Dive-LD, a large autonomous underwater vehicle built by California defense firm Anduril. The 19-foot (5.8-meter) submersible can carry out missions including mine countermeasures, seabed mapping, intelligence gathering, and the inspection of underwater infrastructure such as cables and pipelines, the company has said.
"We trapped one of the most modern, intelligent, and unmanned submarines of the terrorist American army at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz. This submersible is equipped with the latest technologies," the IRGC Navy said in a statement carried by Iranian state media.
In response, a Pentagon spokesperson said an underwater drone had "malfunctioned more than a day ago."
"It was surveying regional waters in support of ongoing operations. The defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment," the spokesperson said.
Reuters could not independently verify Iran's claims and the Pentagon did not address them in its statement.
Anduril confirmed the loss of one of its vessels, but downplayed the significance of the incident.
"Dive-LD is an attritable autonomous system, meaning it is designed from the outset to operate in dangerous environments where loss of the vehicle is an expected possibility," a company spokesperson said.
US military investing in unmanned naval systems
The US military is investing heavily in unmanned naval systems, including underwater and surface vessels, as it seeks cheaper ways to monitor vast areas of ocean, gather intelligence and track adversary ships and submarines without putting sailors at risk.
According to Anduril's website, Dive-LD can operate for up to 10 days without returning to base and is designed to dive to depths of up to 6,000 meters (19,700 feet). Dive-LD units cost about $2.5 million each, US military news site DefenseScoop reported in 2024.

Huawei heads to trial in US over its business dealings in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
02:39:12 UTC
11:39:12 KST

Eight years after US prosecutors secretly charged China's Huawei Technologies with defrauding HSBC and other banks over its business with Iran, the case is finally heading for trial.
Huawei also faces charges of conspiring to steal trade secrets from five US technology companies, and is accused of lying about its dealings in North Korea and supplying surveillance equipment to Iran to track protesters during 2009 anti-government demonstrations in Tehran. Jury selection began on Tuesday in federal court in Brooklyn, New York.
The trial will bring to a close one of the US government's earliest and most closely watched battles against a Chinese company. The case will play out as tech competition heats up between the two countries and Washington seeks to prevent American technology from aiding Beijing's military. The US-China tech war has now spread across multiple technology sectors, including artificial intelligence.
The saga began in 2018 with the arrest of Huawei Chief Financial Officer Meng Wanzhou in Vancouver, which sparked a diplomatic crisis involving the United States, China and Canada.
Convictions on the Iran-related charges would bolster Washington's case for having placed Huawei, one of China's leading technology companies, on a US trade blacklist in 2019, citing alleged criminal conduct that threatened national security.
The trial before US District Judge Ann Donnelly in Brooklyn, New York, is expected to last about three months and overlap with Chinese President Xi Jinping's September 24 meeting with President Donald Trump in Washington. Potential jurors have filled out 27-page questionnaires, including about their views on China's and Iran's governments.
Other charges include violating US sanctions against Iran, money laundering, racketeering, wire fraud and obstruction. Huawei has pleaded not guilty to all charges and denied any wrongdoing.
The criminal case is based in part on Reuters reporting in 2012 and 2013 about close ties between Huawei and Skycom, a firm that operated in Iran.
Reuters reported that Skycom had offered to sell at least €1.3 million ($1.5 million) worth of embargoed Hewlett-Packard computer equipment to Iran's largest mobile-phone operator in 2010. Reuters also reported that Meng had served on Skycom's board of directors between February 2008 and April 2009.
Beijing says case aims to undermine Chinese tech
Beijing has long criticized the case, saying it was part of a bigger campaign against China's technological rise. A Huawei spokesperson said in a statement on Saturday, "The government's overarching narrative is demonstrably false."
Today Huawei is a centerpiece of China's AI chip ambitions, and has diversified beyond network gear and smartphones. It has described the criminal case as an effort to undermine its competitiveness and the theft accusations as a repackaging of long-resolved commercial disputes.
If Huawei is convicted, prosecutors will seek the forfeiture of property or proceeds obtained from its illegal activity. Should the company be found guilty on all counts, experts said it could face a significant financial penalty.
“The penalty is going to be determined by the benefit to the company and then multiplied by how serious the wrongdoing is — and that could range from hundreds of millions to billions of dollars,” said Todd Haugh, a professor of business law at Indiana University Kelley School of Business.
If there's a guilty verdict, he added, “a big fight is going to be proving how much Huawei benefited from their criminal behavior.”
The case against the company was brought during the first Trump administration, which also took actions to curb the use of Huawei equipment in the US and pressed other countries to drop Huawei from their telecommunications networks, saying China could use its equipment for espionage.
The indictment covers alleged wrongdoing between about 1999 and 2020.
It accuses Huawei of using Skycom to obtain embargoed US goods, technology and services for Huawei's Iran-based business, and to move money out of that country through the international banking system.
The US said one bank, which was not named in the indictment but which sources and documents reviewed by Reuters identified as HSBC, cleared more than $100 million worth of US-dollar transactions related to Skycom.
Prosecutors accused Meng of misrepresenting Huawei's ownership and control of Skycom in a presentation to an HSBC executive. She later admitted the statements were false, as part of an agreement with prosecutors to drop the charges against her.

US reading scores hit near-25-year low in latest global assessment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
02:36:44 UTC
11:36:44 KST

US reading scores hit near-25-year low in latest global assessment
Scores among US 15-year-olds dropped 14 points from 2022, as the Trump administration pushes for ‘school choice’.
Reading scores among 15-year-olds in the United States have fallen to the lowest level in about 25 years, according to an international education assessment.
On Tuesday, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) released findings from the 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), a global metric for educational achievement.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3NYC’s AI ban through grade 8 sets stage for rest of US, experts say
- list 2 of 3Advocates decry US House vote to defund universities that boycott Israel
- list 3 of 3US adds 162,000 jobs in August, raising Fed rate hike expectations
The results showed that US reading scores fell 14 points from 2022, the last time PISA results were released.
The decline was part of a broader international trend, with an OECD average from 23 countries also dropping 16 points.
But the US stood out for the size of its performance gap. Some 25.7 percent of US students were ranked as low performers in reading, while 13.3 percent were flagged as top performers.
“Looking across all 90 participating countries, there was not a single country with significantly wider inequality in reading scores than the US,” Michael Kieffer, a professor of literacy education at New York University, told Al Jazeera. “What is clear is that we are under-serving many students.”
The PISA results come as the administration of US President Donald Trump seeks to reshape the federal government’s role in education.
In March 2025, Trump issued an executive order calling on Education Secretary Linda McMahon to begin the process of dismantling the Department of Education, a federal agency that tracks student achievement, distributes federal education funds and enforces civil rights in schools.
The Education Department, however, does not establish school curriculums or academic standards. That responsibility has traditionally fallen to state and local authorities.
Still, Trump pointed to slipping test scores as a reason to shutter the department. He has also denounced the department for its “entrenched bureaucracy” and called for its responsibilities to be redistributed to the states.
In response to a request for comment on Tuesday, McMahon sent a statement to Al Jazeera echoing Trump’s push.
“The United States of America is a nation built to lead the world, yet our one-size-fits-all federal education bureaucracy has shortchanged our children and stifled our future,” McMahon wrote.
The White House has argued that federal education spending is excessive and has failed to translate into higher standardised test scores.
Since the Education Department was founded in 1979, it has spent more than $3 trillion, according to the White House.
“This moment is a stress test for our nation’s future,” McMahon said in her statement to Al Jazeera. “To pass it, we must enact a hard reset that stops protecting a failed status quo and instead builds a system that empowers state leaders and embraces innovative learning options through school choice.”
“School choice” has been a rallying cry for many US conservatives. The term refers to the practice of diverting taxpayer money away from public education to help parents finance alternative choices for their child’s schooling, like charter schools, homeschooling or private institutions.
The practice is controversial. Critics have accused the “school choice” system of weakening public education in favour of less regulated school systems that receive money with little oversight.
But since returning to office in 2025, Trump has embraced “school choice” as a form of “educational freedom”.
Last year, the Education Department announced $500m for its Charter School Program, touting the funds as the “largest investment” the initiative has ever received.
The money was earmarked to allow states to expand their charter school systems and fund new charter-school developers.
In July 2025, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act – Trump’s signature piece of legislation – also created the first federal tax credit for donations to organisations that provide scholarships for primary and secondary school students, including for private-school tuition and tutoring.
Last month, Trump hosted a “school choice”-themed event at the White House to kick off the start of the new school year.
But critics warn that greater investment in education is needed across the board to reverse diminishing test scores.
“PISA 2025 shows that reversing declines in student performance is urgent,” OECD Secretary-General Mathias Cormann said in a statement.
“The most successful education systems focus on fewer areas in greater depth, invest in teachers, engage parents and provide targeted support for the students and schools that need it the most.”

US bans Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and dairy products as trade spat escalates
The US and Canada escalated a bitter trade dispute on Tuesday, with Washington imposing new import bans on Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and dairy products as Ottawa's retaliatory tariffs on US goods took effect.
The United States banned a broad swath of Canadian alcoholic beverages, motorcycles and dairy products from import on Tuesday, sharply escalating an already acrimonious trade spat.
The import bans, which go into effect on September 29 and were published on the White House's website, came after Canada's own retaliatory tariffs on US goods took effect after midnight on Tuesday.
Those Canadian levies themselves followed 50 percent tariffs that the United States imposed on some $20 billion of Canadian goods last month, after several rounds of negotiations collapsed.
The breakdown has widened a rift between the longtime allies, who have blamed each other for the failed talks, spurred Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to urge a further shift away from Canada's biggest trading partner, and cast doubt on the viability of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement.
"We have everything we need to pivot and prosper," Carney said on Tuesday in a video posted on YouTube.

"That pivot will come at a cost. There's always a cost to action. But it doesn't come close to the cost of standing still," he said.
The US bans appeared to cover most alcohol products, including beer and various types of wine, whisky, bourbon, rum, vodka, vermouth, tequila, mezcal, and brandy. The dairy ban covers whey protein, invert molasses, cane molasses and non-alcoholic beer, per notices on the White House's website.
In addition to the import bans, various cheese products were added to a list of products subject to a 50 percent tariff, but not banned outright. Some paper, aluminium, wood, furniture, lighting and other products were also added to the list.
A US official said President Donald Trump's pre-existing threat to increase tariffs on Canadian autos from 25 to 50 percent on January 1 remained in effect. The official added that US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer had spoken with Dominic LeBlanc, Canada's minister responsible for bilateral US trade, over the past couple of days, and the pair were expected to speak again in the coming days to see if there was an alternative path for the two countries.

In a social media post on Tuesday night, LeBlanc criticised the latest US measures and said he was in contact with Greer regarding a path forward.
"As has been the case for the last 18 months, our first priority remains on protecting and supporting Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses from these unjustified actions," he wrote.
Ottawa strikes back
Ottawa's retaliatory measures, which in turn provoked Washington's move on Tuesday night, were designed to put economic and political pressure on Washington, Canadian government officials said.
Those counter-tariffs cover some $20 billion of US goods, with duties ranging from 15 to 50 percent across products from steel and furniture to clothing and electronics, and are expected to hit sectors in some competitive states such as Michigan and Ohio, ahead of US midterm elections in November.
While the tariffs affect a small amount of exports compared with total trade between the US and Canada, some analysts worry the standoff could destabilise the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, the free-trade pact that succeeded NAFTA. Together they have underpinned commerce across North America for decades.

California Gov. Newsom, a presidential hopeful, slams Netanyahu and AIPAC in PBS interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
02:31:24 UTC
11:31:24 KST

California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a 2028 presidential hopeful, ventured farther than ever in his criticisms of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in a weekend interview that delved into the Democratic Party’s relationship with Israel.
“I think it’s overwhelmingly opposed to the current regime in Israel,” Newsom said of the party, in a PBS NewsHour interview with Amna Nawaz.
Pressed by Nawaz on divisions among his colleagues on Israel, Newsom denied that the subject is “even controversial anymore,” stressing that “the condemnation of what Bibi Netanyahu’s doing is almost universal.” The governor slammed the Israeli military’s conduct in Gaza and condemned the settler violence that has expanded in the West Bank.
“We want a democratic and secure Israel, and we want a secure and democratic Palestinian state as well right next door,” Newsom said, adding that Netanyahu has proved counterproductive to achieving a two-state solution.
Though he repeatedly maintained that Democrats are not divided on Israel, the governor acknowledged that “some of the language” by fellow Democrats “has been weaponized.” Certain “aspects of rhetoric” from individual candidates, he added, are on “the spectrum of concern,” Newsom said.
A number of candidates from the party’s far left place most if not all of the blame on Israel for a war in Gaza that has resulted in tens of thousands of Palestinian deaths. and downplay the role of Hamas in launching the war with the Oct. 7, 2023 raid inside Israel in which 1,200 people were killed and more than 250 were abducted.
Newsom’s rhetoric is in step with party moderates who are critical of the Israeli government but who call for a secure Israel, reject Hamas, and resist pressure from the left to call Israel’s actions “genocide.”
Newsome nonetheless insisted that the party is unified on the issue. “But I think universally, everyone agrees, even if you don’t think it’s genocide, that it’s been a moral catastrophe,” he said of the war in Gaza. “The vast majority of us also agree about the atrocities on Oct. 7th and how horrific and unacceptable it was, and the terrorism that was perpetrated by Hamas.”
Newsom among many US politicians to visit Israel
Newsom was among the many US politicians to visit Israel in October 2023, meeting with survivors and families impacted by the attacks.
During a March book tour, Newsom sparked a backlash when he said that some people were referring to Israel “appropriately as sort of an apartheid state.” He quickly walked back these remarks, telling Politico that he had used the term “in the context of the direction that Bibi is going.”
“I revere the state of Israel,” he declared at the time.
The governor warned, however, that if Netanyahu proceeds in the direction of West Bank annexation, apartheid could become “a word you may hear others use.”
In addition to amplifying his condemnation of Netanyahu this weekend, Newsom also addressed the fact that fewer Democrats are accepting funds from political action committees affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the pro-Israel lobbying group.
As for Newsom himself, Track AIPAC, an organization that compiles Federal Election Commission data to flag pro-Israel campaign contributions, did not log any such donations to the likely presidential candidate. But the group did flag him as “pro-Israel.”
“It’s a minority of Democrats that are accepting AIPAC,” the governor said, noting a “dramatic change” over the last couple of years.
“The vast majority of Democrats I talk to, even Democrats in the past that have in the past have taken AIPAC money, are pledging not to now,” Newsom added. “That’s more of a mainstream position, interestingly, within the Democratic Party.”

Ko Wen-je appears in Taiwan High Court appeal over political donations

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Former Taipei Mayor and TPP founder Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) appeared before the High Court on Tuesday as his appeal against a 17-year prison sentence entered its second stage, with the court initially focusing on alleged misuse of political donations.
Ko denied wrongdoing and maintained his not-guilty plea. Prosecutors, meanwhile, argued that the sentence imposed in the first trial was too lenient and asked the High Court to overturn parts of the ruling and impose heavier penalties, per CNA.
The High Court divided the case into three parts to prepare the appeal. Tuesday's hearing focused on the political-donation allegations involving Ko, former campaign officials Lee Wen-tsung (李文宗) and Lee Wen-chuan (李文娟), and Muko Co.
Prosecutors alleged that Ko and Lee Wen-tsung used NT$1 million (US$31,760) in political donations to invest in a commercial media venture associated with producer Chiu Fu-sheng (邱復生). They argued that political donations cannot legally be used for commercial investment and that the district court was wrong to acquit the defendants on this part of the case, per PTS.
Prosecutors also challenged the first-instance findings concerning money transferred through Muko. According to the Taipei District Court's March judgment, Ko, Lee Wen-tsung, and Lee Wen-chuan jointly misappropriated NT$62 million from the political-donation account.
The court found that NT$15 million was transferred to Muko under the guise of payments for the authorization of Ko's image rights, after which NT$4.5 million was transferred from Muko to Ko's personal account as image-rights fees.
Ko's lawyer Cheng Shen-yuan (鄭深元) asked the High Court to livestream the proceedings, arguing that the court's evidence examination and legal arguments should be publicly broadcast.
Prosecutors submitted 428 pages of statements and other evidence in support of their appeal. The court said the first phase would involve determining the scope of the appeals and reviewing the evidence before moving into substantive arguments.
Lee Wen-tsung denied the charges, including allegations that money from the Chung Wang Foundation was improperly used to pay campaign-office employees. He argued that the campaign organization had to employ staff and pay their salaries. Lee Wen-chuan also denied the charges, per TVBS.
Tuanmu Cheng (端木正), who was accused of falsifying accounting documents, changed his plea to guilty in the second instance. He asked the court for leniency, including a sentence that could be commuted to a fine or suspended, and said he was willing to contribute his professional expertise through community service, per NewTalk.
Muko also appealed the first-instance order to confiscate more than NT$56.84 million in alleged illicit gains. Its lawyer argued that the company itself had not been indicted but had nevertheless been ordered to forfeit the money.
The High Court scheduled further hearings for Lee Wen-tsung and Lee Wen-chuan on Oct. 19, Duan on Nov. 5, and Ko on Nov. 16.
TPP Chair Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌), speaking to reporters after the hearing, said there was no substantive debate as the prosecutor outlined the scope of the appeal and the evidence they will provide. He said preparations for this part of the criminal proceedings will likely be conducted three times, per PTS.
Ko's March 26 first-instance sentence totaled 17 years in prison and six years of civil rights deprivation. The Taipei District Court sentenced him to 13 years for accepting a bribe in connection with the Core Pacific City case, as well as additional prison terms for misappropriation of public funds and breach of trust. The sentences were to be served concurrently.

Among the index’s most heavily weighted stocks, TSMC was the only gainer. The chipmaker ended up 0.41% at NT$2,470.
MediaTek fell 1.05% to NT$4,710, while Foxconn declined 1.76% to NT$251.50. Delta Electronics dropped 2.43% to NT$1,805, and ASE fell 0.48% to NT$618, according to Anue.
Robot and automation stocks, which had posted strong gains in recent weeks on interest surrounding the Taiwan Automation Intelligence and Robot Show, faced profit-taking as their share prices had already reflected positive factors. Solomon Technology lost 4.58%, Hiwin Technologies declined 3.98%, and Airtac International Group fell 2.55%, according to Sinotrade.
Passive component stocks also faced selling pressure despite strong fundamentals and record-high August revenue reported by industry leader Yageo. Yageo fell 3.74%, Holy Stone Enterprise declined 3.11%, and Walsin Technology lost 1.39%.
Probe card makers were among the few sectors to buck the broader market’s decline. WinWay Technology rose to its daily limit-up of NT$7,700.
Mpi gained 5.56%, while Chunghwa Precision Test Technology rose 4.32%. A probe card tests individual chips on a wafer before packaging, allowing manufacturers to identify defective chips and reduce production waste and costs, according to Business Next.
Semiconductor intellectual property stocks were relatively resilient, benefiting from accelerated orders from major cloud service providers for their own chip designs. The trend is expected to continue, with revenue from IP licensing and chip development services being recognized ahead of schedule. M31 rose 6.57%, while Global Unichip gained 0.42%.
Memory chip manufacturers gained, with Winbond Electronics rising 4.44%, Nanya Technology advancing 2.71%, and Macronix International climbing 1.2%. The sector continues to benefit from strong AI server demand, which has led major memory chipmakers to shift production capacity toward high-end DDR5 and high-bandwidth memory. This has tightened supply and driven higher contract prices for standard DRAM and NAND flash.
Biomedical stocks attracted attention as companies released strong August revenue figures. Energenesis Biomedical, Handa Pharmaceuticals, and NaviFus hit their daily limits, while InnoCare Optoelectronics, PharmaEssentia, VizionFocus, and Obi Pharma moved higher.
Investors also turned to financial stocks, which are often viewed as more stable during periods of market volatility. E Sun Financial Holding rose 4.59%, TS Financial Holding gained 4.14%, and CTBC Financial Holding added 1.19%.
E Sun High Tech Fund manager Lin Che-yu (林哲宇) said investors will be watching companies’ August revenue figures as they are released throughout the week. He said the monthly and quarterly moving averages should provide support if the market enters a period of consolidation, as both are trending upward and could encourage buying when the market pulls back, according to CTEE.
Lin recommended taking profits in sectors that have gained significantly in the short term while buying on dips in sectors with stronger earnings prospects. He favored optical communications, advanced substrates, and mature semiconductor processes, where valuations have pulled back.

China’s factory-gate price growth picks up in August as Iran war fuels energy volatility
Producer price index rises 3.8 per cent, beating economists’ projections amid war-driven oil surge and weak domestic demand
China’s factory-gate price growth accelerated in August, while consumer inflation picked up again, amid volatile energy and commodity costs linked to the US-Israel war on Iran.
The producer price index rose 3.8 per cent year on year last month, up from 3.5 per cent in July, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) on Wednesday.
The reading beat a 3.6 per cent projection from economists polled by financial data provider Wind.
Meanwhile, the consumer price index (CPI), a crucial gauge of inflation, rose 0.8 per cent year on year, rebounding after two months of slower growth. That figure improved upon July’s 0.5 per cent rate and was broadly in line with Wind’s projection of a 0.78 per cent rise.
“Rising international prices for crude oil and non-ferrous metals drove up prices in related domestic sectors,” said Dong Lijuan, a senior NBS statistician.
Dong noted that coal mining prices surged 26.6 per cent year on year in August, while non-ferrous metal processing rose 20.8 per cent. Prices in the oil and gas extraction industry climbed 10.5 per cent.

Anduril confirmed the loss of one of its vessels, but played down the significance of the incident.

US judge dismisses suit by British anti-disinformation activist against deporting him
WASHINGTON, Sept 8 - A federal judge in New York dismissed a lawsuit by British anti-disinformation campaigner Imran Ahmed that challenged the Trump administration's ability to detain and deport him.
U.S. District Judge Loretta Preska in Manhattan said on Tuesday that while Ahmed "very well may have valid causes of action," she was required to conclude under a recent appellate court ruling that she lacked jurisdiction to hear his free speech and due process claims under the U.S. Constitution.
Preska's ruling opens the door to Ahmed's detention, but the judge said she would leave the earlier restraining order in effect for five business days to allow Ahmed time to pursue an appeal.
President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown and his administration's use of visa and green card revocations have faced legal challenges that have divided U.S. courts.
Late last year, a U.S. judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration from detaining Ahmed, after the U.S. permanent resident sued officials over an entry ban for his role in what Washington alleges is online censorship.
Washington had imposed visa bans last year on Ahmed and four Europeans, accusing them of working to censor freedom of speech or unfairly target U.S. tech giants with burdensome regulation.
Ahmed, the 47-year-old CEO of the U.S.-based Center for Countering Digital Hate, lives in Washington. He says his wife and child are both U.S. citizens. He did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
A federal judge in July blocked the Trump administration from enforcing the policy that targeted foreign nationals who study disinformation and hate speech on social media for visa denials and deportation.
Legal permanent residents, known as green card holders, do not need a visa to remain in the U.S., but the Trump administration has attempted to deport some over their political views, such as participation in pro-Palestinian protests against U.S. ally Israel's war in Gaza.
Trump has cast such voices as "anti-American" and as foreign policy threats. Advocates have raised free speech and due process concerns and said the Trump administration is punishing such people for criticism of the U.S. government.
The Trump administration has also initiated probes against some activists and rights advocates and sanctioned some international judges. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Revisiting Chopper Read reveals a time when the manosphere was on TV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
02:25:59 UTC
11:25:59 KST

analysis
Most of us remember Chopper Read as a loveable bogan, but revisiting his story is eye-opening
To say that we're currently living through an era of backlash seems bleedingly obvious.
The cigar-smoking, private-jet flaunting, women-hating influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate were arrested in Miami in July on British charges of rape, trafficking for sexual exploitation and offences related to indecent images of a child.
Pauline Hanson called domestic violence a "two-way street" and referred to family violence leave as "holiday leave". And an education report found that female school teachers are being subjected to intimidation and sexual harassment from male students in a culture some described as "toxic masculinity".
In the aftermath of #metoo — a time that witnessed a global outpouring of women's stories of sexual violence as well as popular and political discussion on its causes and remedies — regressive gender norms are again having a renaissance.
And who better represents this than the Tate brothers with their fantasies of masculine physical prowess, financial affluence, emotional repression and garden-variety misogyny?
Andrew tells us that women should be men's domestic or sexual servants and the reporting by journalist Heidi Blake in The New Yorker into the most recent sexual allegations argues that this is not mere rhetoric. Date night with Andrew involved strangulation, being beaten unconscious and rape. He denies this and claims he "loves women".
While it's hard to disagree with the idea that there's been an almighty swing against feminism by men of a younger generation, the problem with framing our current moment as simply "backlash" is that it limits our collective memory to 2017 when #metoo went global.
The manosphere was once bigger
If we go back a few decades earlier to the 1990s and early 2000s we find something much worse than the manosphere: the manosphere writ large as national culture.
This is conservative, Howard-era Australia.
Rather than the Andrew Tates of the world ferreting away in a dark and grubby corner of the internet preying on pimply teenaged boys, they're on our national television giving public service announcements on domestic violence and drink driving, they're ambling into the offices of the ABC where they're adored as great Australian raconteurs, they have advice columns in national newspapers, they write best-selling autobiographies and audiences rush to their comedy shows to hear unfiltered racism, sexism and homophobia, normalised as larrikin culture.
What's my evidence for this? Research I recently did for ABC history podcast The Dead Can't Sue into Chopper Read, a man who transformed from criminal into beloved folk legend and who was elevated to the pantheon of national heroes in the period following his prison release in the 1990s until his death in 2013.
Today most of us remember Chopper as that laughable boganical figure with a handlebar moustache, an inky gallery of tattoos on his hulking, mutilated body, Miami Vice-style glasses and a penchant for tossing enemies into cement mixers — at least this was what he claimed in a notorious interview with Elle McFeast.
But revisiting his writing and his life-story today is like rewatching a beloved childhood film only to find that Aladdin is an Orientalist hellscape and Molly Ringwald ended up with a sex-pest in Sixteen Candles.
Leaving aside the fact that Chopper stole almost all of his stories of being a fearsome stand-over man from other prisoners in Pentridge, the model of masculinity that he represented, and that Australians lapped up at the time, bears a lot in common with the Tate brothers.
A similar brand of masculinity
Firstly, they both grew up in the bleached atmospheres of dread that permeate a physically and psychologically abusive family.
Like the Tate brothers who believe that their father's physical beatings made men of them, Chopper too claims in his autobiography that he loved his dad and "he belted the hell out of me as a child right up until I fought him back at the age of 15".
Being a man meant emotional repression and physical aggression, which, like the Tate brothers, led Chopper to bare-knuckle fighting.
Both Chopper and the Tate bros promote a model of masculinity based on physical power which sees its most benign forms in gym culture — all share a commitment to working out to maintain a muscular, indomitable masculine physique — and its most terrifying forms in intimate violence.
The Tates are currently facing 59 offences in the UK related to sexual violence.
Chopper was never charged but his first wife Mary-Ann Hodge has written of the nightmare of living with a domestically abusive man.
"He'd get wild with me about something, hold me down on the floor and hogtie my arms behind my back. Then he'd bash me around the head," she told journalist Rochelle Jackson.
More publicly, Chopper was shamelessly racist, much like the Tates.
In his autobiography he says that he grew up hating "all Asians", but claims that this is not "real racism, just part of the rough as guts Australian sense of humour, part of the Aussie culture and attitude".
And he was right, at least for a large part of Australian society in the 1990s and early 2000s. People flocked to his shows, his autobiography remains one of Australia's best-selling books, he released a rap album and the media adored him. And yes, he was asked to do Public Service Announcements on domestic violence and drink driving.
We don't often think of the 1990s and early 2000s as an historical era. But like any moment in time, it was crosscut with intimations of the future and residues of the past.
In the life of Chopper we see both: he was born of a culture that has long elevated toxic forms of masculinity to a proud national tradition and a future that draws on this tradition to create its new masculinist monsters.
Perhaps the most uplifting part of this story is that today we have a rich vocabulary to understand and call out the behaviour of today's Choppers, to confine them to grubby corners of the internet or prison, if they're found guilty.

UN General Assembly's 81st opens with call to restore trust in multilateralism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
02:24:51 UTC
11:24:51 KST

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has warned that restoring confidence in the global system is “the defining challenge of our time”, as the 81st session of the UN General Assembly opens with newly installed President Khalilur Rahman calling for renewed international cooperation and trust in multilateralism.
Addressing the Assembly, Secretary-General Antonio Guterres pledged full support to Rahman, affirming that restoring confidence in the multilateral architecture represents the essential priority for member states.
Guterres highlighted ongoing armed conflicts, nuclear escalation risks, deep poverty, climate disruption, and unregulated artificial intelligence as severe forces straining international bodies, including the Security Council and global financial institutions.
He concluded with an appeal for diplomatic engagement: "Through diplomacy, dialogue, and collaboration, this Assembly can rebuild the trust and good faith that is missing from our geopolitics today and ensure the people of the world inherit a better, healthier and more peaceful future."
Avoiding global catastrophe
Rahman observed that the organisation's endurance over eight decades reflects its foundational mission, noting: "For more than eight decades, our organisation has helped the world avoid plunging into a third world war, arguably the very reason for its existence."
"A widening trust deficit is testing confidence in international institutions and collective action, a deficit that we must close by working together through dialogue, renewed cooperation, and delivery," Rahman said, pledging to work tirelessly throughout the session to revive faith in the institution.
The 81st session is convening under the theme: "Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All."

What Ramstein Revealed: 300 Patriots, a $27 Billion Gap and Russia’s Longer War

Ukraine urged allies on Tuesday to immediately release 300 Patriot interceptor missiles from existing stockpiles, warning that Russia is exploiting gaps in Kyiv’s ballistic missile defenses as it prepares for renewed winter attacks on Ukrainian cities.
The urgent request was part of a broader list presented at the 36th Ukraine Defense Contact Group meeting, which also included 500 air-to-air missiles capable of countering cruise missiles, additional MANPADS and $2 billion for drones.
