Force Regeneration through the Veteran ID Card and Defence Gateway
A low-cost route to force regeneration: actively manage the Veterans ID card and Defence Gateway to build a dynamic, trained virtual reserve from those who have served.
Events in Ukraine over the past five years have marked the conclusion of the European Peace Dividend of the early 1990s, and the return of European Great Power Rivalry. The pace of the radical transformation in the technical character of non-nuclear warfare has left politicians and conventional military thinkers struggling to keep up, and to adapt decades old mantras and systems to the new realities of conflict. An overwhelming conventional strike on civilian ports, airfields, transport and communication hubs, food distribution warehouses, refineries, utilities infrastructure and healthcare nodes across the UK would lead to massive dislocation of an unprepared civilian population of ~70 million people.
We are now in a historical period which may be equated to the pre-war and phoney war conditions of the two world wars of the 20th century. However, any reliance on historical parallels to the effect that ‘we managed then, so we will manage again’, might be fatefully misplaced, given the speed and scale at which events can now evolve.
The Demands of Regeneration of Human Resources for a Future War
As in past major conflicts, a future major European war will require the full mobilisation of the nation’s human and material resources to endure and outlast the threat. Much work remains to be done (Mooney and Crackett 2018, Brazier 2022, Mundell 2025, Reynolds and O’Neill 2026). The reliable and trained human resource needs may be broadly classified as follows:
1. Combat power in four-dimensional warfare on land, at sea, in the sky and in space, with a new set of skills for survival and success in the age of drone and electromagnetic warfare.
2. Sufficient personnel for territorial defence and for the maintenance of public discipline and order in the face of chaotic conditions, to pre-empt the breakdown of social cohesion.
3. Adaptive training of the civilian emergency, life and infrastructure preserving services.
4. Engineering, construction and repair to optimise survivability and societal resilience.
And so the list goes on. We are now charged to rebuild a ‘Citizen’s Militia’ at scale and at the speed of relevance to demonstrate credible national resolve against the ill winds from the East. However, we know that we cannot hope to solve the manpower deficit by throwing money at it, and the topic of mobilisation is still politically very sensitive.
The recently launched HM Armed Forces Veterans ID card now provides a simple and cost effective framework for the regeneration of a virtual reserve force across all defence services
Throughout the 20th century, the Territorial units and their nationwide infrastructure provided the framework for force regeneration in 1914 and 1939, through the Cold War and in the Gulf (1990-1991), Iraq (2003 – 2009) and Helmand (2003-2013), prior to their disbandment a decade or so ago. They also infused intellectual and operational originality into the regular armed forces at war, as in the creation of the UK Special and Commando Forces during the Second World War.
Towards Strategic Force Regeneration with Austere Resources
The UK Armed Forces are steeped in a tradition and history of innovation and imagination to maximise strategic impact with limited resources. In the pressing mission of force regeneration at the human level, we have a number of factors in our favour, including:
- A strong tradition of volunteerism and public service in all communities. In 2012 we saw the rapid mobilisation of volunteer support to make the Olympic Games a success. It has also been evident in the formation of UK volunteer support networks for Ukraine since 2022.
- A modern digital framework for communication and organisation, both in the public sector around Gov.UK and its subsystems; in commercial computing and in evolving machine learning and artificial intelligence tools.
- An intellectual framework of rapid and cost-effective informatics development which is founded in the systems design principles of the Government Digital Service (GDS). These methods distil to the time-honoured military order of ‘load, test and adjust’.
The Veteran’s Card and Agile Iterative Experimentation in Force Regeneration
The starting point in the assembly of a new coalition of willing citizens should logically be among those former service personnel, whether Regular or Volunteer Reserve. The state has already invested substantial resources in their training, expertise, ethos and discipline, and they now live their diverse and productive lives within civilian communities across the UK and abroad. The adaptable skills and loyalties of past service life are more valuable than specific experience on outdated weapon systems and dated doctrines.
Importantly, courageous Ukrainians of both sexes have shown us that age and biology are no barrier to effective voluntary contributions to their war effort through intelligent re-employment and in societal and community leadership.
The practical technical mechanism to set this process in motion is now established in the national digital infrastructure, and it is at the fingertips and/or on the desktops of every digitally connected citizen.
The recently launched HM Armed Forces Veterans ID card now provides a simple and cost effective framework for the regeneration of a virtual reserve force across all defence services. It has the potential to keep track of individuals and their skills after release from Reserve or Regular Service, and to mitigate the potential for local chaos, such as that I well-recall from the rapid medical mobilisations of 1991 and 2003.
My proposed entry level solution to force regeneration lies in experimentation with the active management of the Veterans ID (VetID) Card (www.gov.uk/veteran-card) and its supporting data systems. The VetID is ripe for further promotion and exploitation, in that:
- Registration for the card is currently voluntary.
- It is issued on a one–off basis on request.
- It offers limited benefits which are poorly promoted.
I therefore propose that it should now be provided to every individual on the termination of service and distributed to all who have served and can be traced, including those who are in receipt of a military pension through those record systems.
The real benefit would flow from a design which obliged regular updating of the data set behind an individual’s VetID card with contemporary information, as to the recipient’s past military service, current whereabouts and contact details, state of health, current employment status, skills (computers, IT communications), hobbies (drone and model aircraft flying?), availability for renewed service or other contributions and in what circumstances.
Thereafter, the regular invitation and continuous facility to update a personal linked record through changing circumstances would produce a rich source of anticipatory human resource planning information. Much of this process could be automated, as could the analysis of the data returns with AI tools. This will keep administrative costs to a minimum, and make best use of nudge tools to maintain contact with the volunteer.
The Defence Gateway and the Virtual Training and Education Environment
Once the willing volunteer is enrolled in the system, the challenge arises as to how best to keep him or her engaged and informed on technical, operational and other matters which are relevant to their possible military roles.
In its early days, a decade ago, the Defence Gateway website provided a rich resource of interesting and educational content. This could have evolved into a gateway to a powerful, suitably adapted, continuously evolving, trade-specific Virtual Learning Environment for Veterans. Defence Gateway still needs a lot of work to realise this potential, but it offers a valuable development opportunity for an established framework system.
Many other public, institutional and commercial organisations could adopt similar methodologies to engage with their former employees or alumni to support civic needs.
In Summary
There is no simple solution to force regeneration at pace and scale. However, the intelligent use of informatics tools which already exist provides the framework for intelligent experimentation with the addressable post-service community.
There will be many questions to answer and trips, falls and adjustments on the way. However, the evolved result should be a dynamic, adaptable voluntary national service database, communications and virtual training system with wide potential.
This will give civil and defence planners much better tools to secure core force regeneration at the speed of relevance as national circumstances change, at very modest set up and maintenance costs.

Episode 128: The Future of War: How Autonomous Systems Are Reshaping Conflic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

Episode 128: The Future of War: How Autonomous Systems Are Reshaping Conflict
General David Petraeus discusses autonomous warfare, drone technology and the military transformation driven by Ukraine.
Ukraine offers the clearest evidence that warfare is changing in revolutionary ways. Unmanned systems now account for nearly 90% of Russia’s killed and wounded on the front line, with around eight million drones produced by Ukraine every year. Software is updated weekly and hardware every few weeks, a pace no Western procurement system matches.
Traditional armoured manoeuvre has effectively stopped, replaced by a dense zone of surveillance and strike drones along the front. For Gen. Petraeus, Senior Vice President of RUSI, this demands a complete institutional overhaul, covering doctrine, force structure, training, procurement and personnel, on a scale far beyond the changes he oversaw during the Iraq surge.
He argues the UK is unusually well placed to lead this shift, given its visibility into the Ukrainian battlefield, political continuity across governments, and a parliamentary system that can move fast, though entrenched interests in legacy platforms will resist the change required.
Key themes discussed:
- The rise of drones and unmanned systems in Ukraine.
- Ukraine as a laboratory for the future of warfare.
- Why militaries need to rethink force structures and procurement.
- The shift from remotely piloted to autonomous systems.
- How artificial intelligence could transform military decision-making.
- Changes needed to training, education and personnel.
- Institutional and political resistance to replacing legacy systems.
- Why the UK is particularly well placed to lead military transformation.
Gen. David Petraeus is Senior Vice President of RUSI, former Commander of US Central Command, former Commander of the Multi-National Force in Iraq, and former Director of the CIA.

Sri Lanka a close friend, India stands by it: Rajnath Singh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Sri Lanka a close friend, India stands by it: Rajnath Singh
Defence minister Rajnath Singh said in Colombo Tuesday that India and Sri Lanka are close friends and India will always stand firmly with Sri Lanka whenever the island nation faces a crisis.Singh, who is on a three-day visit to Sri Lanka, has become the first Indian defence minister to visit the island nation for defence-level talks after nearly 40 years. KC Pant was the defence minister to visit the island for such talks in 1988. "The relationship between India and Sri Lanka is based on shared history, culture, and faith. We stand with Sri Lanka through thick and thin and are committed to the peace, prosperity, and development of both countries," said Singh as he began his visit with an interaction with the Indian diaspora.
Singh said both nations share close cultural and civilisational ties which have provided a strong foundation for the growth of bilateral relationship. "I am experiencing a sense of belonging after coming here," he said while emphasising the importance of robust regional alliances. He highlighted India's expanding global influence and economic strength, and appreciated the work done by the diaspora.Before leaving for Colombo, Rajnath posted on X, "Besides our longstanding partnership as well as deep historical and civilisational ties, Sri Lanka is one of our most important partners under the 'Neighbourhood First' and 'MAHASAGAR' initiatives."
Addressing the diaspora, Rajnath highlighted India's rapid economic transformation, stating that the country is among the fastest-growing major economies in the world and contributes more than 16% to global growth.He said that India's economy, which stood at $2 trillion in 2014, has doubled to approximately $4 trillion over the last decade.
The defence minister added that amid global economic challenges, the country's economy grew at 7.8% in the first quarter of financial year 2026-27. Singh also underlined the improvement in macroeconomic stability, saying that average inflation over the last 12 years has been approximately 4.7%, compared to 10-11% during the earlier period.The minister said India has concluded trade deals with 38 countries over the last 12 years, including free trade agreements with eight major nations, compared to just four before 2014.Referring to the India-EU FTA as the 'Mother of all deals', he said the agreement opens access to the massive EU market and reflects India's growing diplomatic and economic capabilities.

US forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday after Tehran twice attempted to strike an American warship with ballistic missiles in recent days, marking a renewed escalation in the conflict between Washington and Tehran.
US Central Command said the tanker crews were ordered to leave the vessels before American forces attacked them.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“American forces directed the crews to abandon ship before the vessels were struck and rendered inoperable,” CENTCOM said, according to AFP, describing the operation as retaliation for Iran’s latest failed attacks.
The five vessels were identified as the Kivik, Charminar, Horizon 1, Riesco, and Derya. They were struck in the Gulf of Oman and near Kharg Island, the center of much of Iran’s oil export infrastructure.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington intended to continue hitting Iranian tankers if Tehran persisted in targeting US naval forces.
Speaking during a visit to Colombia on Tuesday, Rubio said each new Iranian attempt to attack US ships would bring further consequences for Tehran’s tanker fleet.
The latest US strikes quickly triggered a threat of retaliation from Iran.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy warned crews aboard oil tankers at or near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to abandon their vessels immediately, saying the ships could become targets.
Russian Generals Simulate War With NATO for Years
The IRGC accused Kuwait and Bahrain of facilitating US military operations because both countries host American forces. Iranian state media said tankers at anchor or docked in the two Gulf states could be targeted.
The threats raised fresh concerns over commercial shipping in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important oil transit routes.
Tuesday’s strikes came after the US military hit three Iranian oil tankers over the weekend following earlier Iranian ballistic missile attacks on US Navy ships. Washington had warned that it was prepared to further target Iran’s oil fleet if attacks on American forces continued.
Oil prices climbed toward $100 a barrel Tuesday as renewed US-Iran fighting and threats to Gulf shipping intensified fears of further disruption to global energy supplies.

Ukraine Unveils RK-2PZ Surface-to-Air Missile Based on Barrier Anti-Tank Missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:28:21 UTC
19:28:21 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Ukraine Unveils RK-2PZ Surface-to-Air Missile Based on Barrier Anti-Tank Missile
Ukraine’s state defense conglomerate Ukroboronprom has unveiled a new anti-aircraft missile designed for upgraded Strela-10 surface-to-air missile systems and the new Desna air defense system, Militarnyi reported from the MSPO defense exhibition in Poland on September 8.
The new RK-2PZ surface-to-air missile was developed on the basis of the Barrier anti-tank guided missile, itself a modification of the R-2 missile family.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The RK-2PZ has a caliber of 130 mm and carries a 6.1-kilogram warhead. The missile itself weighs 28.9 kilograms, while its total weight in the launch container reaches 47 kilograms.
After receiving target designation, the operator selects a target for automatic tracking using a control panel and either the television or thermal imaging channel of the system’s optical targeting station.
Once launched from its container, the missile is guided toward the target using a laser guidance system. As it approaches, a proximity sensor is activated to initiate the high-explosive fragmentation warhead. In the event of a direct hit, a contact sensor triggers the warhead.
The RK-2PZ is intended for use with upgraded Strela-10 air defense systems, also known as Ryf. The modernized system retains the original Strela-10’s MT-LB tracked chassis, launcher rotation mechanism, and operator station.
The Ryf underwent its first live-fire tests in December 2021.
The missile is also intended for the new Desna air defense system. Unlike the upgraded Strela-10 platform, Desna is a newly developed launcher module for RK-2PZ missiles that will be mounted on a chassis that has not yet been publicly demonstrated.
According to Militarnyi, detailed performance specifications for both the RK-2PZ missile and the Desna air defense system have not been publicly disclosed.
During the exhibition, Ukraine has also revealed the launcher for its Koral surface-to-air missile for the first time, showcasing an upgraded system intended to engage both conventional aerial threats and ballistic targets.

Russian Defense Ministry Colonel Andrei Krestyansky Killed in War Against Ukraine
Russia has confirmed the death of a senior Defense Ministry colonel who took part in the war against Ukraine, according to the OSINT project Killed in Ukraine (KIU) on September 8, which tracks Russian officer losses.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Colonel Andrei Vladimirovich Krestyansky served as a senior instructor and inspector at the Inspection of the Training Center for Command Personnel of Russian Defense Ministry formations, KIU reported.
According to Militarnyi, his death was also confirmed by authorities in the Marks municipal district of Russia’s Saratov region. An official notice stated that Krestyansky had participated in Russia’s war against Ukraine and was killed while performing military duties.
KIU noted that neither the circumstances nor the exact date of Krestyansky’s death are currently known. His funeral is scheduled for September 9, and further details may emerge afterward.
Researchers believe he may have been killed in a Ukrainian missile strike on a command post in Russian-occupied Donetsk on August 26, although this has not been confirmed.
Krestyansky’s reported death follows the loss of another senior Russian officer in the Donetsk region earlier this year. Lt. Col. Oleg Rudomyotov, commander of Russia’s “Yugra” battalion, was killed in a Ukrainian drone strike.
Prior to his deployment in Russia’s war against Ukraine, Rudomyotov reportedly participated in counterterrorism operations in the North Caucasus. He was mobilized from Seversk in Russia’s Tomsk region in October 2022.

Russian Lines Give Ground Near Lyman as Ukrainian Counterattacks Bite Across Multiple Fronts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:28:19 UTC
19:28:19 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russian Lines Give Ground Near Lyman as Ukrainian Counterattacks Bite Across Multiple Fronts
Ukrainian forces have pushed back Russian troops around the Lyman-Sloviansk sector while launching successful counterattacks across several other parts of the front, with Russian sources acknowledging that Moscow no longer holds positions it previously claimed, according to the Institute for the Study of War’s (ISW) September 8 assessment.
The clearest signs of Ukrainian progress emerged east of Lyman in the Donetsk region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
A Russian military blogger acknowledged that Russian forces no longer hold positions east of Lyman, west of Ivanivka, in northwestern Zarichne and in northeastern Yampil.
ISW had either previously assessed Russian advances in those areas or recorded Russian claims that Moscow’s troops were present there.
ISW said Ukrainian forces have recently advanced or maintained positions in the Sloviansk direction, although analysts cautioned that there is still insufficient public evidence to determine the full scale of the Ukrainian counterattacks around Lyman.
Ukrainian troops have also continued rejecting Russian claims that Moscow advanced into Sviatohirsk.
Ukrainian military officials said Russian forces are concentrating additional troops and increasing assault activity around Lyman, but repeated Ukrainian strikes have prevented them from making sustained progress.
The fighting remains mixed elsewhere in the Donetsk region. Russian troops recently advanced in central Kostiantynivka and continue attempting infiltration missions around the city.
In the Dobropillia sector, however, Russian forces conducted offensive operations on September 7 and 8 without securing new gains.
Russia recorded clearer progress northwest of Pokrovsk. Geolocated footage reviewed by ISW indicates Russian forces recently seized Myrne and nearby Vasylivka.
Russian troops also carried out limited assaults in the Novopavlivka direction on September 7 and 8 but failed to advance.
Ukraine meanwhile continued counterattacking farther north. In the Sumy region, Russian forces maintained offensive operations on September 7 and 8 but made no confirmed gains as Ukrainian troops struck back.
Russian sources reported Ukrainian counterattacks around Kindrativka and Novokostiantynivka, both north of Sumy.
A similar pattern unfolded around Kupyansk and Borova in the Kharkiv region. Russian forces continued attacking in both sectors but did not achieve new confirmed advances as Ukrainian troops counterattacked.
Russian sources also reported Ukrainian counterattacks near Zapadne, north of Kupyansk. One Russian military source claimed Moscow’s command is already preparing for winter operations around Kupyansk by compiling lists of personnel expected to remain in the city.
The source assessed that the preparations suggest Russian commanders themselves do not expect the battle for Kupyansk to be resolved before the end of fall.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukrainian forces have restored control over nearly the entire Dnipropetrovsk region, with only the area around the settlement of Dachne still under Russian occupation as fighting continues.

Ukraine Revives Osa Air Defense Systems With New Domestically Made RK-19 Missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:27:56 UTC
19:27:56 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Revives Osa Air Defense Systems With New Domestically Made RK-19 Missile
Ukraine has developed a new domestically produced surface-to-air missile designed to replace Soviet 9M33-series interceptors used by the Osa-AKM short-range air defense system.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Militarnyi on September 8, the RK-19 missile was displayed at Ukraine’s defense industry stand during the MSPO defense exhibition in Poland, where its intended role and key technical specifications were disclosed publicly.
The RK-19 can engage aerial targets at ranges of up to 10 kilometers and altitudes of up to 5 kilometers. Its maximum flight speed is listed at 600 meters per second, exceeding the roughly 500-meter-per-second maximum speed of the Soviet 9M33M3 missile it is intended to replace.
Like the original Osa ammunition, the Ukrainian missile uses radio-command guidance. The RK-19 carries a 14.3-kilogram warhead, while the missile and its launch container have a combined weight of 163 kilograms. The container measures 3,255 mm in length, 320 mm in width, and 303 mm in height.
The missile was first shown publicly in April 2026 during a video address by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy marking Ukraine’s Gunsmith Day. At the time, its specific launch platform had not been officially detailed.
The latest presentation confirms that the RK-19 was developed as a replacement for the Soviet-made 9M33 family used by the Osa-AKM, potentially allowing Ukraine to keep the existing air defense systems operational without relying on dwindling stocks of Soviet missiles.
The Osa-AKM is a mobile, short-range surface-to-air missile system designed to protect troops and infrastructure from aircraft and cruise missiles. Each combat vehicle carries six 9M33M3 missiles and can engage targets at ranges of up to 10 kilometers and altitudes of up to 5 kilometers.
Ukraine has operated Osa systems extensively during Russia’s full-scale invasion, including against Russian drones and cruise missiles. However, stocks of compatible Soviet-produced interceptors have declined during the war, limiting the intensity with which the systems can be employed.
Earlier, Ukraine unveiled the launcher for its domestically developed Koral surface-to-air missile, a significantly redesigned interceptor intended to engage both conventional aerial threats and ballistic targets. The latest version weighs about 450 kilograms, carries a 36-kilogram warhead, and uses inertial navigation, radio-command correction, and an active radar seeker.

Russia Bleeds 1.5 Million Troops in Ukraine—100 Times the Soviet Toll in Afghanistan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:27:37 UTC
19:27:37 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Bleeds 1.5 Million Troops in Ukraine—100 Times the Soviet Toll in Afghanistan
Russia’s military personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine have surpassed 1.5 million killed and wounded, according to figures released by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on September 9.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The General Staff said Russian forces lost another 1,480 personnel on September 8, bringing Ukraine’s estimate of total Russian personnel losses since February 2022 to 1,500,870.
“This is the largest loss in a single war suffered by the Russian army since World War II,” the General Staff said, adding that the figure exceeds the combined losses of the Soviet and Russian armies in all wars and armed conflicts of the second half of the 20th and early 21st centuries.
“This is 100 times greater than the Soviet Union’s losses in Afghanistan over 10 years,” the General Staff said. Ukraine’s military also said the estimated losses are 125 times higher than the officially acknowledged Russian losses in the First and Second Chechen wars.
The 1.5 million figure represents cumulative battlefield personnel losses reported by Ukraine and includes both Russian troops killed and wounded. Moscow does not publish comprehensive figures that can be directly compared with Ukraine’s running estimate, and the total cannot be independently verified in real time.
Ukraine has published daily estimates of Russian personnel and equipment losses throughout the full-scale invasion, updating its figures as new battlefield information becomes available.
Meanwhile, Russia is preparing to mobilize up to 600,000 additional troops through 2027, according to Ukrainian military intelligence chief Oleh Ivashchenko. He said Moscow is currently able primarily to replace battlefield losses, while additional manpower would be needed to expand offensive operations in Ukraine.

Returning Rams superstar to miss MCG NFL clash with 49ers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
22:56:26 UTC
07:56:26 KST

LA Rams star Aaron Donald to miss NFL Melbourne game against San Francisco 49ers
In short:
Aaron Donald will miss the Los Angeles Rams' NFL season opener against the San Francisco 49ers at the MCG on Friday morning.
Donald is coming out of retirement in 2026 after leaving the game back in 2024.
What's next?
ABC Sport will have live blog coverage of the Rams-49ers game from 10:30am AEST.
Aaron Donald will not play in the Los Angeles Rams' season opener against the 49ers at the MCG, delaying the three-time defensive player of the year's return to the field after ending his retirement last month.
"I think he'll be ready to go sooner rather than later. But we're making a decision that we think is best for him and for our team," coach Sean McVay said.
The 35-year-old Donald rejoined the Rams in August after two seasons away from the team, and the eight-time-first team All-Pro has been working his way back into game shape.
But with a 16-hour flight on deck ahead of the game at 10:35am on Friday, McVay decided the prudent choice was to keep Donald at home and allow him to continue his preparations.
"He's as great a competitor as there is," McVay said.
"Wants to be out there. Wants to influence and affect positive change for us. But I think he also understands there's a necessary ramp up."
The Rams are flying in just one day before the season opener in Melbourne, while the 49ers have been in Australia for the past week.
Donald was earlier coy on his playing status after a scheduled day off from practice to focus on his cardio, saying he has been pleased with how his body is responding to his return to football.
"I'm feeling good, knocking the rust off," Donald said.
"I thought I'd be a lot more rusty than I was, but taking it day by day."
The Rams have spent the previous seasons developing their defence for a future without Donald, including drafting Kobie Turner and Braden Fiske, signing Poona Ford in free agency, and trading for reigning defensive player of the year Myles Garrett.
McVay said his trust in that group to perform at a high level factored into the call to not rush Donald back onto the field immediately.
"Every single game is so important. We want him out there. But I do think what's great for our group is (I) feel great about the guys that are going to be playing in Australia," McVay said.
"Any good defensive line I've been a part of, there's a rotation where you got to have five, six guys that play and play meaningful snaps."

Israel expands 1984 ‘state land’ declaration to include 48 acres in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
22:54:05 UTC
07:54:05 KST

Qais Abu Samra and Mohammad Sio
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Israeli authorities have redrawn the boundaries of a 42-year-old “state land” declaration in the occupied West Bank, adding nearly 194 dunams (48 acres) of Palestinian land near the villages of Jalud and Al-Mughayyir, an official Palestinian government agency said Tuesday.
The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said Israel’s “Blue Line Team” approved the inclusion of 193.93 dunams (47.9 acres) in the declaration originally issued in 1984.
The revision also removed 15.07 dunams (3.72 acres) from the previous boundaries and left 1,433.85 dunams (354 acres) unchanged, resulting in a net increase of approximately 179 dunams (44 acres), the commission said.
The measure does not automatically mean expanding the settlement's area of influence, but it makes the added land available for possible planning or allocation procedures at later stages.
Jalud is located southeast of Nablus, while Al-Mughayyir is northeast of Ramallah, in an area witnessing continuous expansion of illegal settlements and outposts, along with restrictions on the use of agricultural land and grazing areas, according to the commission.
The commission said this move is part of a broader strategy in which Israeli authorities employ various tools to control Palestinian land, including declarations of “state land” and “government property,” confiscation and expropriation orders, and modifications to settlement jurisdiction areas and the redrawing of their boundaries.
In August, the commission reported that Israeli authorities declared approximately 1,152 dunams (284 acres) of land belonging to Sinjil, Al-Lubban ash-Sharqiya and Qaryut as “government property,” with the aim of expanding the Karmei Oz settlement and strengthening the geographical contiguity between settlements and outposts in the area between northern Ramallah and southern Nablus.
Israeli settlements established in the occupied West Bank are considered illegal under international law.

Air Force EO Overhaul Lets Commanders Dismiss Some Complaints
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
22:53:53 UTC
07:53:53 KST

The Department of the Air Force’s new equal opportunity and harassment policy, rolled out to comply with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s directives, redefines key terms and empowers commanders to dismiss complaints they deem not actionable. The new rules also bar investigations based on anonymous complaints.
Unveiled 11 months after Hegseth directed changes to the Pentagon’s Equal Opportunity and Military Equal Opportunity programs, the new rules are dated July 28, but weren’t announced until late August. Hegseth called for the overhaul nearly a year ago, saying the programs had been “weaponized” by poor performers against leaders and commanders.
“No more frivolous complaints, no more anonymous complaints, no more repeat complaints, no more smearing reputations, no more endless waiting, no more legal limbo, no more side-tracking careers, no more walking on eggshells,” Hegseth said last Sept. 30 at an all-call with hundreds of generals and admirals.
The Department of the Air Force policy follows on similar updates from the Army and Navy, also announced in August.
New Definitions
Each military department’s policy includes the same new definitions of three key terms: “bullying,” “hazing,” and “harassment.”
The new definition of harassment represents the biggest change, said retired Lt. Col. Colby Volkey, a former Marine Corps Judge Advocate General. The new definition explicitly exempts standard training programs, stating “official military or governmental activities conducted in a professional manner, such as basic military training, professional military education, physical training programs, disciplinary or corrective actions, or combat readiness exercises, do not constitute harassment.”
It also states that “behavior that is rude, ignorant, abrasive, or unkind, is not necessarily indicative of harassment, but may constitute harassment depending on the totality of the circumstances.”
The revisions appear to be “an attempt to limit the types of activities that are considered harassment, Volkey said in an email.
The new definition of hazing no longer includes the phrase “any form or initiations or congratulatory acts that involves physically striking another person in any manner or threatening to do the same,” language that was included in the past in an effort to stop the practice of pounding on newly earned rank or other insignia, such as aviators’ wings.
Equal Opportunity Definition Changes
Bullying
Bullying: As described in DoDI 1020.03, while not a form of prohibited harassment under equal opportunity (EO) law but is a prohibited form of conduct, bullying is a form of harassment that includes acts of aggression by service members or DoD civilian employees, with a nexus to military service, with the intent of harming a service member either physically or psychologically, without a proper military or other governmental purpose. Bullying may involve the singling out of an individual from his or her coworkers, or unit, for ridicule because he or she is considered different or weak. It often involves an imbalance of power between the aggressor and the victim. Bullying can be conducted through the use of electronic devices or communications, and by other means including social media, as well as in person.
Bullying is evaluated by a reasonable person standard and includes, but is not limited to, the following when performed without a proper military or other governmental purpose:
- Physically striking another person in any manner or threatening to do the same.
- Intimidating, teasing, or taunting another person.
- Oral or written berating of another person with the purpose of belittling or humiliating.
- Encouraging another person to engage in illegal, harmful, demeaning, or dangerous acts.
- Playing abusive or malicious tricks.
- Branding, handcuffing, duct taping, tattooing, shaving, greasing, or painting another person.
- Subjecting another person to excessive or abusive use of water.
- Forcing another person to consume food, alcohol, drugs, or any other substance.
- Degrading or damaging another’s property or reputation.
- Soliciting, coercing, or knowingly permitting another person to solicit or coerce acts of bullying.
Bullying does not include properly directed command or organizational activities that serve a proper military or other governmental purpose, or the requisite training activities required to prepare for such activities (e.g., command-authorized physical training). Service members may be responsible for an act of bullying even if there was actual or implied consent from the victim, and regardless of the grade or rank, status, or service of the victim. Bullying is prohibited in all circumstances and environments, including off-duty or “unofficial” unit functions and settings.
Bullying (Military): A form of harassment, as described below, that involves repetitive, intentional hurtful conduct by an individual or a group, which intimidates, humiliates, torments, isolates, degrades, exploits, controls, or creates a risk of mental, physical, or emotional distress or harm.
- Inflicting or threatening to inflict physical pain or injury.
- Berating or belittling a Service member’s duty performance, professional abilities, or personal attributes.
- Threatening, teasing, or taunting a Service member.
- Destroying or confiscating a Service member’s personal property or work equipment or deliverable.
- Excluding a Service member from work-related opportunities, information, or social activities.
- Posting malicious gossip, rumors, and lies on social media, sharing humiliating photos, or sending vicious text messages
Harassment
Harassment (Military): As described in DoDI 1020.03, conduct that is unwelcome or offensive to a reasonable person, whether verbal or nonverbal, written, electronic, or physical, that creates an intimidating, hostile, or offensive environment. Harassment may include offensive jokes, epithets, ridicule or mockery, insults or put-downs, displays of offensive objects or imagery, stereotyping, intimidating acts, veiled threats of violence, threatening or provoking remarks, racial or other slurs, derogatory remarks about a person’s accent, or displays of racially offensive symbols.
Types of harassment include, but are not limited to, discriminatory harassment, sexual harassment, hazing, bullying, stalking, revenge porn, and other sexual misconduct. Stalking, Revenge Porn, Other Sexual Misconduct. Formal complaints involving conduct that may be punishable under Articles 130 (stalking); 117a (wrongful broadcast or distribution of intimate visual images); and 120c (other sexual misconduct) of the UCMJ will be referred to the appropriate military criminal investigative organization or other law enforcement organization with criminal investigators who are specially trained to conduct such investigations. Harassment can be oral, written, or physical. Harassment can occur in person, through electronic communications, including social media, and other forms of communication. Activities or actions undertaken for a proper military or governmental purpose, such as combat survival training, making work assignments, or conducting performance counseling are generally not considered harassment. For the purpose of this publication, the DAF MEO program is limited to processing complaints alleging bullying and hazing as “other forms of harassment.”
Harassment (Military): Conduct by a Service member or civilian employee, without a legitimate military or governmental purpose, that would be unwelcome or offensive to a reasonable person in the military environment, whether delivered verbally or nonverbally, including by written or electronic means, or in-person, that creates an intimidating, humiliating, or abusive environment.
Hazing
Hazing—As described in DoDI 1020.03, hazing is a form of harassment that includes conduct through which service members or DoD employees, without a proper military or other governmental purpose, but with a nexus to military service, physically or psychologically injure or create a risk of physical or psychological injury to service members for the purpose of: initiation into, admission into, affiliation with, change in status or position within, or continued membership in any military or DoD civilian organization. Hazing can be conducted through the use of electronic devices or communications, and by other means including social media, as well as in person.
Hazing is evaluated by a reasonable person standard and includes, but is not limited to, the following when performed without a proper military or other governmental purpose:
- Any form of initiation or congratulatory act that involves physically striking another person in any manner or threatening to do the same.
- Pressing any object into another person’s skin, regardless of whether it pierces the skin, such as “pinning” or “tacking on” of rank insignia, aviator wings, jump wings, diver insignia, badges, medals, or any other object.
- Oral or written berating of another person with the purpose of belittling or humiliating.
- Encouraging another person to engage in illegal, harmful, demeaning or dangerous acts.
- Playing abusive or malicious tricks.
- Branding, handcuffing, duct taping, tattooing, shaving, greasing, or painting another person.
- Subjecting another person to excessive or abusive use of water.
- Forcing another person to consume food, alcohol, drugs, or any other substance.
- Soliciting, coercing, or knowingly permitting another person to solicit or coerce acts of hazing.
Hazing does not include properly directed command or organizational activities that serve a proper military or other governmental purpose, or the requisite training activities required to prepare for such activities (e.g., administrative corrective measures, extra military instruction, or command-authorized physical training). Service members or DoD civilian employees may be responsible for an act of hazing, even if there was actual or implied consent from the victim, and regardless of the grade or rank, status, or service of the victim. Hazing is prohibited in all circumstances and environments including off-duty or “unofficial” unit functions and settings.
Hazing (Military): A form of harassment, as described below, that involves intentional or reckless conduct by an individual or group, which humiliates, degrades, or creates mental, physical, or psychological injury or harm, or reasonably perceived as such, directly related to the affected Service member’s affiliation, entry, advancement, reinstatement, change in status or position, or continued standing within a military unit, command, or DoW or military affiliated organizations regardless of whether the affected Service member consented to the activity.
- Inflicting or threatening to inflict physical violence, including striking, restraining, branding, causing body modifications, tattooing, shaving, greasing, duct taping, or engaging in any form of unwanted physical contact that causes pain or injury.
- Subjecting a Service member to abusive physical discomfort or fatigue.
- Destroying or confiscating a Service member’s personal property or work equipment or deliverables.
- Requiring financial contributions.
Dismissing Complaints
The new policy instructs installation commanders to dismiss formal equal opportunity complaints in certain circumstances, such as if:
- The complaint “does not contain sufficient or actionable information to investigate.”
- “A complainant does not respond to request for information.”
- “A complainant files duplicative or related complaints”
- If a commander or supervisor to the service member making the complaint determines “through an adverse action or UCMJ action” that the complaint was a false official statement
Under the new policy, equal opportunity directors have five days to review a formal complaint before forwarding it to an installation commander, who in turn has 30 days to consult with the “servicing legal officer’ and determine if the complaint should be dismissed. The commander then has seven days to inform the complainant, who in turn has five days to appeal.
Giving commanders the power to dismiss complaints is a radical change, said David Sheldon, a former Navy JAG who now represents military clients from every service branch as a civilian attorney. The policy leaves it up to commanders to make a legal determination over whether the complaint is “sufficient or actionable.” Indeed, Congress only recently determined that commanders were not well suited to prosecute certain serious crimes, including murder, sexual assault, and domestic violence.
“It’s kind of a step in the wrong direction in my thinking, for the very reason that you have a conflict of interest,” Sheldon said. Commanders have a built-in incentive not to be seen as having EO problems within their commands, he said.
Dismissing or resolving a case removes the holds that have sometimes delayed promotions, held key jobs opened, or resulted in foreshortened careers. Once closed, the policy states, “all favorable administrative personnel actions (e.g., awards, promotion, retirements) for an alleged offender of an [Military Equal Opportunity] complaint will be resumed or completed.”
Similarly, an individual being under investigation for an EO complaint is no longer sufficient grounds to withhold awards, promotions, retirement and other favorable actions. In the past, EO complaints have resulted in holds that could remain in place for months.
Anonymous Complaints vs. Confidential Reports
The new policy eliminates military equal opportunity complaints based on anonymous allegations, with some exceptions. Instead of filing anonymously, service members may submit “confidential reports,” revealing their identities only to equal opportunity directors and staff. But confidential reports do not constitute either informal or formal complaints, and therefore cannot trigger an investigation. Rather, they are merely a means for service members “to disclose allegations, receive information regarding available resources and reporting options, and obtain referrals to appropriate support services,” the policy states.
Commanders may choose to “look into the matter and take appropriate action in response to a referred anonymous report of prohibited discrimination or discriminatory harassment,” and a service member can choose, within time limits, to upgrade a confidential report into a complaint.
Allegations regarding sexual harassment and those concerning bullying or hazing are not covered by that limitation, however. Anonymous allegations regarding sexual harassment must be referred to the Sexual Assault Prevention and Response office. Allegations of bullying and harassment can be anonymous, but must include “sufficient information,” such as the offender’s name and rank, date of the incident, and units involved.
Shorter Timeline
The timeline for service members to file complaints is now shorter, just 60 days versus 90 days previously. But there are exceptions:
- Multiple incidents: In cases involving an alleged series of incidents or pattern of behavior, only one instance needs to have taken place within the past 60 days.
- Deployments: Service members who are deployed when an incident occurs and who lack resources at their deployed locations have 60 days to file once they return.
- Delays: Those who waited too long can submit a memo to their installation commander explaining the circumstances and seek an extension.
- Sexual harassment: By law, these complaints are exempt from the 60-day requirement.
A service member who makes a confidential complaint and then wants to formalize it, must do so within 60 days of the incident—not the report.
Sheldon suggested this makes it harder for complainants. Whether it is 45, 60, or 90 days, he said, “obviously “I would like a longer window just to give the aggrieved party an opportunity to be heard.”
Mediation
The new policy opens the door for “facilitation,” a form of mediation in which a neutral third party meets with the accused and the complainant to try to resolve the conflict. Facilitation is “a method for resolving problematic situations before they rise to the level of misconduct,” the policy states.
The confidential process can be offered for both informal and formal complaints, so long as both parties agree; commanders are instructed to consult with their legal offices before determining if it is a suitable solution for a given complaint. Commanders may also forgo facilitation if they determine it would “negatively impact good order and discipline.”

Shin Bet, Police dismantle broad West Bank Hamas network recruiting armed cells across region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

07:51:11 KST

A large Hamas-linked terrorist infrastructure that allegedly recruited cells across the West Bank to carry out attacks against Israeli civilians and security personnel was uncovered in a joint operation by the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), Israel Police and the IDF, the agencies announced on Tuesday.
More than 30 suspects from Jerusalem and the West Bank were arrested as part of the operation, according to the security agencies. Investigations into some of those detained remained ongoing.
Among those arrested were Jerusalem residents Tzabih Abu Tzabih and Rashid Rishq, whom authorities identified as members of Shabab al-Aqsa, an organization affiliated with Hamas.
Abu Tzabih is the son of Misbah Abu Tzabih, who carried out a shooting attack in Jerusalem in October 2016 that killed two Israelis. The victims in that attack were Adv.-Staff-Sgt.-Maj. Yosef Kirma, 29, a police officer, and Levana Malichi, 60, a former Knesset employee.
Abu Tzabih opened fire near Israel Police headquarters before being pursued and killed by police.
Rishq was released in 2025 as part of a hostage-release deal, according to Tuesday's statement.
Broad Hamas terror infrastructure established, armed cells recruited
Three additional Jerusalem residents, Mohammed Abu Tzabih, Mohammed Azmi Bakri and Ahmad Azmi Bakri, were also arrested on suspicion of belonging to the infrastructure.
The Shin Bet and the Jerusalem District Police's Central Unit investigation found that Rishq and Tzabih Abu Tzabih had allegedly established the broader terrorist infrastructure and recruited armed cells under their command throughout the West Bank, according to the statement.
The cells were intended to carry out attacks against Jews and Israeli security personnel, authorities said. Weapons allegedly intended for attacks, along with other combat equipment, were seized during the investigation.
Investigators also found that Ahmad Azmi Bakri and Rishq allegedly intended to advance an attack at a restaurant in Modi'in where Bakri worked.
Mohammed Bakri allegedly instructed Rishq and Mohammed Abu Tzabih on how to prepare explosive devices after the two told him that they intended to carry out terrorist activity, according to investigators.
Shooting attack planned against security personnel
Rishq and Tzabih Abu Tzabih also allegedly planned a shooting attack against security personnel in Eizariya, east of Jerusalem, the agencies said.
Following the conclusion of the Shin Bet and Jerusalem District Central Unit investigation into the five Jerusalem suspects, an indictment was filed against them on charges including managing a terrorist organization, active membership in a terrorist organization, conspiracy and preparation to commit an act of terrorism involving aggravated murder, weapons offenses, possession of property for terrorist purposes, recruiting and attempting to recruit members to a terrorist organization, and additional offenses.
Authorities said they expected to file indictments against West Bank residents suspected of involvement in the network in the coming days.

Issued on: Modified:
François Picard is pleased to welcome Anish Gawande. He sees the controversy surrounding the inauguration of the BAPS temple near Paris as more than an isolated dispute over the treatment of female staff at the Eiffel Tower. From his perspective, the incident exposes a broader and insufficiently scrutinized intersection of religion, diplomacy, political power, labor practices, and diaspora politics. At the center of his argument is an ambiguity over the boundary between private religious and state-sanctioned activity.
Gawande questions why senior Indian diplomatic representation and Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s remarks evoking India-France relations accompanied the inauguration if the ceremony was not official. He highlights Modi’s longstanding political association with BAPS, while also highlighting controversies and allegations surrounding the organization’s social, labour and political practices abroad.
Gawande challenges the notion that the new temple is solely representative of Hinduism in France, highlighting the country’s diverse Hindu traditions and Indian communities. He warns that the Eiffel Tower controversy may acquire a political life beyond BAPS itself, particularly if it becomes material for far-right narratives about immigrants, religion, and national identity in France. His central contention is therefore institutional as much as political: the controversy should prompt scrutiny of how the project was facilitated, how land was allocated, whether labour protections were respected, and where the boundaries between religious organizations and state power were drawn.

UN General Assembly's 81st session kicks off with focus on restoring trust in multilateralism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
22:43:23 UTC
07:43:23 KST

Merve Aydogan
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
The 81st session of the UN General Assembly opened on Tuesday with President Khalilur Rahman calling for renewed efforts to restore trust in multilateralism, as UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned that rebuilding confidence in the global system is "the defining challenge of our time."
Rahman said the UN's endurance over eight decades speaks to its core purpose, noting "for more than eight decades, our organization has helped the world avoid plunging into a third world war, arguably the very reason for its existence."
Highlighting the often unseen work of the UN, he said, "every day, often far from the spotlight, the United Nations and its dedicated corps of professionals work to feed millions of people, including refugees and other displaced populations around the world, support peace and security, combat chronic diseases, and help countries address complex transboundary challenges."
Rahman also acknowledged the institution has repeatedly failed to meet expectations, noting the conflicts, fragile development gains and worsening climate impacts. 
"Conflicts continue to inflict immense human suffering, development gains remain feeble and fragile, climate impacts are intensifying," he said.
Warning that these compounding crises have eroded faith in collective action, he said, "a widening trust deficit is testing confidence in international institutions and collective action, a deficit that we must close by working together through dialogue, renewed cooperation, and delivery."
"Today, our responsibility is not merely to defend this institution—there are good reasons to do that—but to strengthen it, not simply to invoke trust on which multilateralism rests, but to earn it every day," he said, adding: "My pledge for the 81st session, dear colleagues and friends, is to work tirelessly to revive trust in this institution, upon which success of our collective action ultimately depends."
The session's theme, "Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All," reflects that pledge.
Guterres, addressing the Assembly, backed Rahman's leadership, pledged his "full support to you, Mr. President, as you take on this important role."
Welcoming the session's theme, Guterres said rebuilding faith in the multilateral system is "the defining challenge of our time," citing conflicts, nuclear escalation risks, deepening poverty, climate disruption and ungoverned artificial intelligence as pressures straining global institutions, from the Security Council to the international financial system.
He closed with a call for cooperation, saying "through diplomacy, dialogue, and collaboration, this Assembly can rebuild the trust and good faith that is missing from our geopolitics today, and ensure the people of the world inherit a better, healthier and more peaceful future."

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle were "surprised" by a new letter from King Charles, clarifying their status as non-working members of the Royal Family, according to media reports on Tuesday.
The Sussexes "were a little surprised not to have been told about this in advance," a spokesperson for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex was quoted by the BBC as saying.
However, royal sources said Prince Harry and Meghan were made aware of the letter, sent on Monday afternoon, before it was made public, according to the report.
On Monday, lhe letter sent on behalf of King Charles by the lord chamberlain, a top palace official cleared that the duke and duchess of Sussex will still not be able to use titles of "His and Her Royal Highness" and will remain "private citizens."
The letter has been sent to Prince Harry's team, government departments, military officials, and lord lieutenants, who are the monarch's local representatives, and government staff often involved in royal visits and engagements, according to palace sources.
It comes after the duke and duchess – born Meghan Markle – returned to the UK with their children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, on Aug. 26 six years after stepping away from their roles as senior working members of Britain’s royal family and starting a new life in California.
The message highlighted that the position agreed in 2020 when the Sussexes left the UK, the so-called Sandringham Agreement, is still in place.
This ruled out any "half-in and half-out" status, so the couple could not continue their own commercial interests while remaining to be working royals.
"It is well known that in January 2020 the Duke and Duchess stepped down from undertaking representative duties on behalf of the Sovereign, and are no longer working members of the Royal Family," said the letter.
It added: "The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity."

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Sept 9, 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
22:36:39 UTC
07:36:39 KST

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Sept 9, 2026
US accuses Chinese AI firms of ‘malicious’ copying
The US government on Sept 8 accused Chinese artificial intelligence companies of maliciously copying technology from American AI firms, potentially complicating relations ahead of a planned meeting between leaders of the world’s two biggest economies later this month.
The Chinese companies copied US AI labs’ intellectual property through a technique known as distillation, according to a statement from US law enforcement and intelligence officials.
Distillation is the process of training smaller AI models using output from larger, more expensive ones as part of an effort to lower the costs of training a new AI tool.
US officials accused six Chinese companies, including DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and Alibaba, of tapping variants of American-made AI models to train their AI products more quickly.
Israel to close UK consulate over West Bank import ban
Israel said on Sept 8 it was closing Britain’s consulate in East Jerusalem in response to plans by the UK, France and Canada to block imports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
Britain will also no longer participate in a US-led coordination mission for Gaza and some British officials, including former Labour party leader Jeremy Corbyn, and other nationals will be banned from entering Israel, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said.
“The British move is morally distorted, and constitutes blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and its electoral process,” he said, describing comments by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband about ethnic cleansing of Palestinians by Israel as accusations that were “outrageous lies”.
Air traffic control issue disrupts flights at UK airports
Flights at major British airports were disrupted on Sept 8 by a technical fault at air traffic control provider NATS, the latest in a series of failures that renewed questions about the resilience of Britain’s aviation infrastructure.
The cancellation of hundreds of flights and delays to hundreds more renews scrutiny on NATS three years after a flight-plan processing failure caused even more widespread disruption.
As passengers waited for information in departure halls across the country on Sept 8, airlines questioned whether the country’s air traffic control system was fit for purpose.
HK’s first chief executive Tung Chee Hwa dies, aged 89
Hong Kong’s first chief executive, Tung Chee Hwa, who was China’s choice for the city’s leader but whose administration faced a number of challenges, including the Asian financial crisis, widespread protests, and the Sars outbreak, died on Sept 8, aged 89.
Tung died peacefully, surrounded by his loved ones, official Hong Kong broadcaster RTHK reported early on Sept 9.
Tung was Hong Kong’s first local leader after the city’s handover from British colonial rule to Beijing in 1997, and he governed the city until he resigned in 2005, citing health problems.
Journalists missing in Indonesia after volcano mission
Indonesian rescue teams were searching on Sept 8 for eight people including five journalists who had gone missing while travelling to cover the eruption of Mount Anak Krakatau, the national rescue agency said.
The group set out on a speedboat from an area near the capital Jakarta on the afternoon of Sept 7, but “until now they have not returned, and the boat owner has not received any information from the crew”, the agency said.
The five Indonesian journalists on board were sent to capture photos and video of the volcano’s eruption, which since Sept 5 has paralysed several airports and blanketed Jakarta and neighbouring cities in volcanic ash.

Iran says it captured US submarine drone in Strait of Hormuz
Unknown

Iran says it captured US submarine drone in Strait of Hormuz
WASHINGTON – Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Sept 8 that it had captured a US uncrewed submarine at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, offering a rare glimpse into how underwater drones are being used in military operations.
Iranian state media said the vessel was a Dive-LD, a large autonomous underwater vehicle built by California defence firm Anduril.
The 5.8m submersible can carry out missions including mine countermeasures, seabed mapping, intelligence gathering and the inspection of underwater infrastructure such as cables and pipelines, the company has said.
“We trapped one of the most modern, intelligent and unmanned submarines of the terrorist American army at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz. This submersible is equipped with the latest technologies,” the Revolutionary Guards Navy said in a statement carried by Iranian state media.
In response, a Pentagon spokesperson said an underwater drone had “malfunctioned more than a day ago”.
“It was surveying regional waters in support of ongoing operations. The defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment,” the spokesperson said.
Anduril confirmed the loss of one of its vessels, but downplayed the significance of the incident.
“Dive-LD is an attritable autonomous system, meaning it is designed from the outset to operate in dangerous environments where loss of the vehicle is an expected possibility,” a company spokesperson said.
The US military is investing heavily in unmanned naval systems, including underwater and surface vessels, as it seeks cheaper ways to monitor vast areas of ocean, gather intelligence and track adversary ships and submarines without putting sailors at risk.
According to Anduril’s website, Dive-LD can operate for up to 10 days without returning to base and is designed to dive to depths of as much as 6,000m.
Dive-LD units cost about US$2.5 million each, US military news site DefenseScoop reported in 2024. REUTERS

Russia destroys or damages 2,687 medical facilities in Ukraine
The Ministry of Health of Ukraine reported this, according to Ukrinform.
“As of September 1, 2026, information provided by healthcare departments of the regional military administrations and the Kyiv City Military Administration confirms damage to or destruction of 2,687 facilities belonging to 854 healthcare institutions. Of these, 340 facilities belonging to 127 healthcare institutions have been completely destroyed,” the ministry said.

Despite daily threats and the challenging security situation, efforts to restore medical infrastructure are continuing, the ministry said. So far, 752 facilities have been fully restored, while another 317 have been partially rebuilt. At the same time, 87 facilities that had been completely restored subsequently sustained further damage.
“Medical facilities continue to operate even under difficult conditions. Currently, services are being provided at 1,639 facilities, while another 187 are operating partially, and 241 facilities have been relocated to other sites,” the Ministry of Health said.
Information on facilities in Mariupol and other temporarily occupied territories is incomplete because it cannot be independently verified.
The ministry also reported that since the start of the full-scale invasion, 345 emergency medical vehicles have been destroyed, 225 damaged, and 80 seized by Russian forces.
As previously reported, Russian aggression has affected 2,138 cultural heritage sites and 2,640 cultural institutions across Ukraine.

Australians face 'unacceptable levels of harm' as sexual violence reaches historic high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
22:27:34 UTC
07:27:34 KST

in brief
- Sexual violence reports have reached the highest rate since recording began in 1993.
- The Domestic, Family and Sexual Violence Commissioner deemed the family law system a "site of ongoing weaponisation and harm".
This article contains references to domestic and family violence and sexual assault.
Australians are continuing to experience "unacceptable levels of harm" in the areas of sexual violence and the family law and justice systems.
The nation's Domestic, Family and Sexual Violence Commissioner, Micaela Cronin, released her third annual update to parliament on Wednesday, which found that progress made by governments and communities was not yet at the scale or pace needed to save lives.
It comes amid reports of sexual violence being at their highest level since national recording began 33 years ago.
The commission identified it as one of two "persistent" areas, alongside family law and justice systems, where people are experiencing unacceptable levels of harm.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"The scale of sexual violence in Australia demands sustained national investment and action, commensurate with the scale of the problem," Cronin said.
"Collectively, we must send a clear message that these behaviours are not acceptable, and that people who have experienced sexual violence will be heard, treated with dignity and respect, and supported through their justice and healing journey."
The report notes almost six in 10 sexual assaults recorded by police occurred outside family and intimate partner relationships.
This underlined a "distinct national problem, not simply an extension of domestic and family violence".
Meanwhile, the family law system was also a "site of ongoing weaponisation and harm".
The commission pointed to "intense public and political conversation around institutional responses to sexual violence" and "misogynistic content influencing young people" as bolstering its call for sustained, rather than episodic, national attention to both sexual violence and the family law system.
It acknowledged the commitment made by political leaders at national cabinet to address sexual violence as a priority.
Eight recommendations were handed down to help inform the national plan to end violence against women and children by 2032.
Addressing Parliament on Wednesday, Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek will point to actions already taken by the federal government, such as reforming family courts and social security, so women and children can rely on the systems.
"We have changed this country before. Now is the time to move together to change it again," she will say.
"We owe the women and children who have had their lives stolen by this violence more than our horror. We owe them action."
If you or someone you know is impacted by family and domestic violence, call 1800RESPECT on 1800 737 732, text 0458 737 732, or visit 1800RESPECT.org.au. In an emergency, call 000.
The Men’s Referral Service, operated by No to Violence, can be contacted on 1300 766 491.

BUDAPEST, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Policymakers, researchers and industry leaders gathered at AI Summit Budapest 2026 on Monday and Tuesday to discuss artificial intelligence (AI) development, governance and applications as the technology rapidly reshapes economies and societies.
The two-day summit brought together more than 300 speakers for discussions ranging from frontier AI models and digital infrastructure to governance and practical applications.
Opening the summit, Hungary's Minister for Innovation and Technology Zoltan Tanacs described AI as a technology that lies "between two extremes" -- "salvation or total catastrophe." He said governments should embrace innovation while putting appropriate safeguards in place as AI capabilities advance.
As part of its AI strategy, Hungary plans to invest 500 million euros (581.2 U.S. dollars) in AI development programs over the coming years and join the European AI Gigafactory initiative, which aims to strengthen Europe's AI computing infrastructure.
Tanacs said Hungary also plans to expand AI education and university research, attract leading AI developers and improve AI literacy among businesses and the public.
Addressing participants via video, Jin Xiaoming, president of the China Association for International Science and Technology Cooperation, warned that unequal access to AI technology and governance could widen what he called the "innovation divide."
"The gap between frontier AI creators and mere consumers keeps widening," Jin said, warning against "rules imposed by the few upon the many" and calling for AI governance based on shared responsibility, adaptive safeguards and human-centered development.
The summit also explored the growing use of AI in business and industry.
Presenting Alibaba Cloud's latest AI developments, Huang Ye, general manager of Solution and Products at Alibaba Cloud Central Europe, said AI is evolving from simply understanding users' requests to completing increasingly complex tasks and end-to-end workflows.
Huang highlighted advances in model capabilities, human-AI collaboration and multimodal AI, as well as the growing role of open-source development. He said Alibaba Cloud has open-sourced more than 400 AI models, with more derivative models based on Qwen being used in areas such as education, healthcare and manufacturing.
Huang said Alibaba Cloud was already using AI to improve customer service and assist engineers with coding and product demonstrations.
While opinions differed on how AI should develop and how it should be regulated, participants broadly agreed that closer international cooperation and wider access to AI technologies will be essential to ensuring that the technology benefits society.
The fourth edition of the summit was held across three venues with 15 parallel tracks, bringing together nearly 4,000 attendees. ■

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- The United Nations condemns the cross-border attacks by the Houthis in Yemen against multiple sites in southern Saudi Arabia, which affected civilian and energy infrastructure, said a UN spokesperson on Tuesday.
The world body also expresses deep concern over reports of civilian casualties in the attacks, said Stephane Dujarric, spokesperson for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.
The United Nations is equally concerned by the intensification of military clashes across multiple front lines within Yemen, particularly reports of possible civilian casualties resulting from the fighting, said the spokesperson.
"We call upon the parties to exercise restraint and prevent further escalation, and further urge them to uphold their obligations under international humanitarian law to refrain from directing attacks against civilians or civilian infrastructure, and to take constant care to spare the civilian population, civilians, as well as civilian objects," Dujarric said.
UN Special Envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg continues engaging directly with the parties with the aim of containing the current escalation and preserving space for dialogue. Continued military escalation risks devastating political, economic and security ramifications for Yemen. The parties should engage constructively with UN-led political efforts, said the spokesperson.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said an escalation in fighting in Yemen is devastating communities already struggling to survive after more than a decade of conflict.
More than 5,600 households have been displaced across Taiz governorate and southern Al Hodeidah governorate since the escalation in fighting on Thursday. At least 11 civilian casualties have been reported in the last week, including two children killed and nine people injured, said the office.
In Marib governorate, there are reports that shelling struck displacement sites over the weekend, resulting in the deaths of two children and injuries to 15 other people. Shelters have been destroyed and families forced to sleep in the open, it said.
Humanitarians are mobilizing to respond, said OCHA. As of Monday, partners have reached 2,340 households, mainly in Taiz, as well as Marib and Abyan, with emergency supplies. Reaching many people in need remains a major challenge.
The world body urgently needs funding to scale up the response. The humanitarian appeal for Yemen, which requires 2.2 billion U.S. dollars, remains just 20 percent funded, said OCHA.
The United Nations calls on all parties to respect international humanitarian law. They must protect civilians, including by allowing them to move to safer areas, and must facilitate unimpeded access for humanitarian relief to reach all those in dire need, said the office. ■

80th session of UN General Assembly concludes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
06:26:48 CST
07:26:48 KST

Khalilur Rahman (2nd L), president of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, takes over the gavel at the closing meeting of the 80th UN General Assembly at the UN headquarters in New York, Sept. 8, 2026. Outgoing UN General Assembly (UNGA) President Annalena Baerbock declared the 80th UNGA session closed on Tuesday, concluding a year marked by efforts to reform the United Nations, uphold the UN Charter and advance the process for selecting the next secretary-general. (Xinhua/Zhang Fengguo)
UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Outgoing UN General Assembly (UNGA) President Annalena Baerbock declared the 80th UNGA session closed on Tuesday, concluding a year marked by efforts to reform the United Nations, uphold the UN Charter and advance the process for selecting the next secretary-general.
In her speech at the closing session, Baerbock said one of the priorities of the 80th session was UN reform.
The 80th session made it clear that without deep reform, the United Nations will not last, she said. "If we are not capable of freeing this organization from overlapping structures and mandates, as well as a heavy bureaucratic mentality, it will erode over time."
However, Baerbock stressed that the UN principles must not change. Rather, reform is all about protecting the principles through better, more effective delivery, especially at a time when the world body and the very idea of multilateralism it represents has come under direct attack.
She said the other priorities of the 80th session were defending the UN Charter and promoting development, as well as the selection of a new UN secretary-general.
On the secretary-general's selection, she said the UNGA has worked to deliver on the strong call of the UN membership for transparency and inclusivity.
Baerbock said the 80th session convened 18 high-level meetings, 26 mandated intergovernmental processes, held 116 formal plenary meetings and adopted 317 resolutions, and opened a whole new chapter for the United Nations: the governance of artificial intelligence.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, in his remarks, said the 80th UNGA session took place at a moment of profound challenge for humanity.
"We have seen the destruction, death and displacement of multiplying conflicts; the inequalities, injustices, hunger and poverty that result from a system that is stacked against those who are most vulnerable; another year of record-breaking heat, as our climate shoots past the 1.5-degree limit; the possibilities and perils of world-changing technologies like artificial intelligence; and the wide financing gap that impedes progress on the Sustainable Development Goals," Guterres said.
The United Nations was created precisely for moments like this. And by wielding the timeless tools of diplomacy, debate and dialogue, the 80th session came together to develop solutions, he said.
"Eighty-one years after the organization's creation, our founding principles are needed more than ever. In these troubled times, all countries must present a common front, work hand in hand, and find solutions together," said Guterres. "As we close this session, and prepare to open the following one, let us remain true to the spirit of collaboration and the shared ideal that have guided this organization from the very beginning. And let us never doubt what we can achieve when we stand united."
Khalilur Rahman, president-elect of the 81st UNGA session, took an oath of office and was handed the gavel of the assembly.
The 81st session of the assembly opens on Tuesday afternoon. ■
