Who are the ‘extremist settlers’ sanctioned by Britain?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:37:08 UTC
04:37:08 KST

In addition to economic sanctions targeting Israeli settlements, the British government imposed measures on five Israeli citizens, several of whom are prominent figures in Israel’s far-right and settlement movements.
Britain sanctioned Bentzi Gopstein, Baruch Marzel, Meir Mordechai Ettinger, Avichai Suissa and Eliav Libi, describing them as “extremist settlers.”
The individual sanctions come as Britain and 11 other countries move toward restrictions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, part of growing international pressure over settlement expansion and violence against Palestinians.
Meanwhile, Yossi Dagan, head of the Samaria Regional Council, which represents Israeli settlements in the northern West Bank, was visiting Slovenia, where he met senior officials including newly elected Prime Minister Janez Janša, whose government is considered more supportive of Israel than its predecessor. Dagan was seeking to head off further European measures against Israel.
“The British decision to boycott products from Judea and Samaria and impose sanctions on Jews simply because they live and operate in parts of their homeland is a disgraceful antisemitic step,” Dagan said, using the biblical names commonly used in Israel for the West Bank. “It is time for Britain to wake up: The British Mandate ended almost 80 years ago.”
During Dagan’s meeting with Slovenian Deputy Prime Minister and Transportation and Energy Minister Jernej Vrtovec, the Slovenian official wore a Samaria pin.
“Thank you very much, Mr. Dagan, for your visit to Slovenia,” Vrtovec said. “Slovenia and Israel are friendly countries, and we need to strengthen that spirit under our new conservative government.”
The five Israelis targeted by Britain have differing backgrounds but are associated with far-right activism, the settlement movement or organizations operating in the West Bank.
Bentzi Gopstein is a prominent far-right activist and a follower of the late Rabbi Meir Kahane, whose Kach movement was banned in Israel over its racist ideology.
Gopstein was placed on the electoral slate of the far-right Otzma Yehudit party in two Israeli elections. Still, the Supreme Court barred him from running following petitions challenging his candidacy.
He founded Lehava, an organization that campaigns against relationships and marriages between Jews and non-Jews.
In 2024, a Magistrate’s Court convicted Gopstein of incitement to racism after he compared Arabs to cancerous growths during a memorial event for Kahane. In February 2025, a District Court accepted a prosecution appeal and also convicted him of incitement to terrorism.
Responding to the British sanctions, Gopstein said he had no intention of traveling to Europe and derided the measures.
“I wish them great success with the Arab occupation they are experiencing. We would be happy to send them the Arabs from here as well,” he said. “Down with the White Paper! We in Lehava will continue to save the daughters of Israel, and they will continue imposing sanctions.”
The reference was to Britain’s 1939 White Paper, which sharply restricted Jewish immigration to Mandatory Palestine on the eve of World War II.
Baruch Marzel is another prominent far-right activist and former follower of Kahane. He has been arrested numerous times over the years on suspicion of offenses involving public disturbances and confrontations with Israeli security forces and Palestinians.
Marzel was first convicted in the 1980s of obstructing a police officer during the evacuation of an unauthorized outpost. In 2003, he was convicted of assaulting a police officer during clashes at the Gilad Farm outpost in the West Bank and sentenced to community service.
In 2023, under a plea agreement involving reduced charges, Marzel was convicted of participating in a brawl and shoving another person following a confrontation with a left-wing activist in Hebron. He received a suspended prison sentence.
Marzel has run for the Knesset several times but has never been elected. In 2019, the Supreme Court barred him from running after reviewing statements including a filmed interview in which he said: “Arabs — an enemy must be expelled! You don’t try to educate them.”
Marzel has also spoken against employing Arabs, saying that “anyone who employs them is committing an offense.”
Meir Mordechai Ettinger, another Israeli sanctioned by Britain, is a far-right activist and grandson of Kahane. The Shin Bet domestic security agency has identified him as a prominent figure among the so-called hilltop youth, a loose movement of radical young settlers associated with unauthorized West Bank outposts.
Ettinger has been described as an ideological architect of a movement known as “The Revolt,” which seeks to dismantle Israel’s existing state institutions and replace them with a state governed according to Jewish religious law.
Following the deadly 2015 arson attack in the Palestinian village of Duma, in which three members of the Dawabsheh family were killed, Ettinger was held in administrative detention for about 10 months. He was not accused of participating directly in the attack. Israeli security authorities instead described his connection to the extremist milieu surrounding it as ideological.
Ettinger was previously convicted under a plea agreement of conspiracy to commit a crime with a racist motive. Israeli authorities have also issued dozens of administrative orders barring him from the West Bank and other areas.
The United States, Canada and Australia have previously imposed sanctions on him.
Avichai Suissa was among the founders of Hashomer Yosh, a security organization operating in West Bank settlements and agricultural outposts that takes its name and inspiration from Hashomer, an early 20th-century Jewish defense organization. Suissa previously served as the organization’s CEO.
The European Union imposed sanctions on Suissa in May, accusing him of involvement in abuses against Palestinians.
Eliav Libi is a right-wing settlement activist and one of the founders of the Farms Association, which works to formalize the status of Israeli agricultural farms in the West Bank.
He has established several outposts, some of which later developed into recognized communities, including Malachei Hashalom in the Binyamin region north of Jerusalem.
Libi currently heads the Habayta Forum, which advocates Jewish settlement in parts of the West Bank designated as Areas A and B under the Oslo Accords. Under the agreements reached between Israel and the Palestinians in the 1990s, Area A was placed under Palestinian civil and security control, while Area B was placed under Palestinian civil control with varying Israeli security authority.
The organization seeks to overturn those territorial arrangements and promotes tours for politicians and other public figures at settlement outposts. Among them is the Tel Talpiot outpost in the Binyamin region, which has been evacuated several times.
Libi’s son, David, was killed in the northern Gaza Strip on May 29, 2025, when an explosive device detonated on the bulldozer he was operating. David Libi worked as a heavy-equipment operator for a contractor carrying out infrastructure demolition work for the IDF.
Responding to the British sanctions, Eliav Libi quoted a saying associated with Israel’s founding prime minister, David Ben-Gurion: “It doesn’t matter what the gentiles say; what matters is what the Jews do.”
“I say clearly: We will not be deterred and we will not stop,” Libi said. “We will continue to struggle and fight for the people of Israel and the redemption of Israel.”
He called on the Israeli government to adopt a clear policy and provide full support to individuals and organizations targeted by international sanctions, which he described as “antisemitic persecution and a blatant violation of Israeli sovereignty.”
“We will continue to build, settle and put down roots in our ancestral homeland,” he said.
‘We will respond with more construction and communities’
Israel Ganz, head of the Binyamin Regional Council and chairman of the Yesha Council, the umbrella organization representing Israeli settlements in the West Bank, also denounced the British measures as antisemitic.
“The British decision to boycott products from Judea and Samaria and impose sanctions on Jews simply because they live and operate in parts of their homeland is a disgraceful antisemitic step,” Ganz said.
“Instead of dealing with the serious problems at home, the British government is assembling a coalition of pro-Palestinian countries for an economic war against Jews in Binyamin, Judea and Samaria. It is a moral disgrace.”
Ganz said international pressure would not stop settlement expansion.
“Our message to Britain and anyone joining the boycott is clear: You will not succeed in removing the Jews from Judea and Samaria,” he said. “For every attempt to harm the settlement enterprise, we will respond with more construction, more communities and Israeli sovereignty.”
Shai Alon, head of the Beit El Local Council, a settlement north of Jerusalem, called on the Israeli government to reconsider cooperation with Britain in response to the sanctions.
“I call on the Israeli government to examine retaliatory measures, including reducing cooperation with Britain in cyber, artificial intelligence, medicine, agriculture, water technologies and defense industries,” Alon said.
“Those who seek to benefit from Israeli innovation cannot expect a one-sided relationship,” he added. “Reciprocity and national respect are fundamental conditions in relations between countries.”

The UN human rights office also hailed the plans, saying such measures contribute to efforts to end violence and occupation in the West Bank.
"The seriousness of the situation in the West Bank calls for urgent and concrete measures," spokesperson Jeremy Laurence told Anadolu in a written statement, adding that UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk was reiterating his call on third states to take "meaningful steps toward ending the violence and occupation of the West Bank."
The office cited a July 2024 ruling by the International Court of Justice stating that states should prevent trade or investment relations that help maintain Israel's illegal presence in the occupied Palestinian territory, and a September 2024 UN General Assembly resolution calling for an end to imports of settlement products.
"The High Commissioner calls on all States to undertake rigorous, comprehensive, transparent assessments of what action they could take to ensure they are not helping to entrench Israel's unlawful presence in the territory," Laurence said.
Addressing the Human Rights Council on Monday, Turk said companies "need to end business practices that support illegal settlements."
Eleven European countries — France, the UK, Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, and Sweden — plus Canada, announced on Tuesday their intention to impose national restrictions on settlement trade and/or support European restrictions.
The countries said the situation in the occupied West Bank was "rapidly deteriorating," citing unprecedented levels of settler violence and settlement expansion, and firmly opposed "any action resulting in the annexation of Palestinian land and the forced displacement of Palestinian populations."
They further urged Israel to immediately halt the expansion of illegal settlements and civilian administrative powers, while ensuring accountability for settlers responsible for violence.
‘Much-needed beginning’
UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese welcomed the UK's new stance of imposing a trade ban on goods from illegal settlements, describing it as a "much-needed beginning."
"I welcome the stance taken by the UK government on Israel's occupation and its illegality," Albanese wrote on X. "A much-needed beginning, even if it does not yet reverse all policies undermining Palestinian self-determination. May the UK government and people hold firm. The pressure will be fierce."
Her remarks came after British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced the UK would ban imports of goods from illegal Israeli settlements, citing the "ethnic cleansing of Palestinians."
Addressing lawmakers in the House of Commons, Miliband said the announcement marked the "beginning of a new approach" towards Israel, adding that legislation would be in place within six to nine months alongside more immediate measures.
The steps, he said, were intended to send a "clear message" that Britain would not acquiesce in the destruction of the two-state solution — though the sanctions regime would target settlements, not Israel itself.
‘Victory for the Palestine solidarity movement’
Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot also welcomed the plans, calling the move an "important step."
"The decision taken today by several countries including the UK, France and Canada, to join the group of countries who, like Belgium, have taken action against the settlement policy of Israel is an important step," Prevot wrote on X, urging Israel to end its settlement expansion.
Canadians for Justice and Peace in the Middle East (CJPME) welcomed Canada's announcement, calling it a major step forward while urging Ottawa to go further by extending the policy beyond imported goods to trade in services, investment, and property.
"This is a victory for the Palestine solidarity movement and everyone who wants Canadian trade policy to uphold human rights and international law," said CJPME President Yara Shoufani, adding that the announcement "marks the first time that Israel will face material, economic consequences for its blatant violations of international law."
Approximately 750,000 illegal Israeli settlers reside in 516 illegal settlements and outposts in the occupied territory, carrying out near-daily efforts to displace Palestinians from their land.

Thomas is autistic. At 13, the AFP 'fed' his IS fixation. Years later, he was charged again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:35:05 UTC
04:35:05 KST

Watch the full documentary 'Autism, Extremism and Recruitment' on our YouTube channel.
This article contains distressing content
In many ways, Thomas Carrick (the pseudonym he was later given in court) was an extremist recruiter’s dream.
He was young, just 13 at the time, vulnerable, with autism and a cognitive disability, and like many kids his age, he was searching for acceptance.
Bullied and 'isolated'
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Court documents say he was bullied at school for his 'weird and awkward behaviour'. His parents say it began with name-calling and exclusion, before it took a turn.
"The kids started calling him a Muslim and a terrorist and Osama bin Laden," his mother said.
But Carrick knew little about the religion, or the extremist groups his classmates were talking about. His father said he went online looking for answers.
"He started searching. Who are Taliban? Who is Osama [Bin Laden]?".
Not long after, his parents say he started using extremist language to frighten the other students and protect himself.
School staff viewed him as "a sweet boy" whose behaviour was a product of his disability and special needs. His psychologist and his school staff agreed the behaviour was an attempt to get attention, shock his classmates and fit in.
But what had started as searches was becoming a fixation.
From interest to fixation
Thomas was viewing material associated with the self-proclaimed Islamic State (IS) group on school computers and had sent a female student an image of a decapitated body.
He had also taken his mother’s phone to post IS group material on TikTok. To a student who knew what he had done, he threatened: "If you tell the teacher about this I will rip your organs out," a court document read.
His parents said they looked for help, seeking the guidance of his paediatrician, and engaged a psychologist and his school, but his behaviour was escalating.
They saw him as vulnerable and feared he could be exploited. They worried his search for acceptance was taking him somewhere increasingly dangerous.
"He is very vulnerable and he can be misused. His vulnerability can be exploited to the extent that it may cause irreversible harm to him and to others," his father said.
And one day, he came home talking about how to make a bomb — the tipping point for his parents, according to the court document.
“He came back home and he says, 'Okay, mama, I know how you make a bomb.’ And he was laughing. He was telling me in a very casual way because he was a child," his mother told The Feed.
His parents went looking for help
Searching for a way forward, his parents tried something they hadn't before. They walked into a Melbourne police station and asked for help. A court document says his father told police he was "prepared to sacrifice my son for the safety of the Australian community".
"We went to the police station, not with a criminal, but with our child with disabilities who needed help," his father said.
Victoria Police agreed to manage him therapeutically, and he was referred to the Countering Violent Extremism (CVE) Unit.
There was a plan to rehabilitate Thomas; he was assigned a case worker, an imam was meant to offer him an outlet for his questions and a psychologist remained part of the picture.
A psychologist from the program who assessed Thomas said his actions need to be viewed in the context of his Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD).
She said, "One of the key diagnostic criteria for ASD is highly restricted, fixated interests that are abnormal in intensity or focus", and that it appeared to be an autistic fixation, not evidence of an ideology.
The parents gave the CVE program what a magistrate described as "unlimited access" to their lives and son.
The AFP covert operation begins
Three months after the rehabilitation began, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) entered his life with one officer acting under two covert online personas.
The family and the boy had no idea, with Thomas telling his mother he had made some friends online.
"My son, he started telling me that I just met few friends online and they are my very good friends and they understand me," his mother said.
Across 71 days, the AFP officer communicated with Thomas on 55 of them, sometimes several times a day.
"He got so engaged," his father said. "He didn't want to lose that person at any cost because that was the only person [friend]."
His parents began to notice a change in his behaviour. Eventually, they decided to look at his computer to see what was happening.
The conversations he was having with the AFP officer spoke about things that were expected for a boy his age — food, school, his family — but they were also being repeatedly returned to violent extremism.
"Started with our child telling that person, 'I'm 13-year-old. I have autism.' In the other response, he will track him back to, 'Hey, what do you think that we blow up Flinders Street?'" his father said.
During the covert operation, Thomas was encouraged to make a bomb and told he would make "a good suicide bomber or sniper", court documents would later show.
In another exchange, he asked whether the IS group had a "kid section". He was directed to reports of overseas attacks and sent information about an 11-year-old who had committed murder.
His mother has still not read all of the messages, which span 1,400 pages.
"I haven't been able to see all the chats because it's quite distressing for me," she said.
Believing their son had encountered an extremist online, his parents contacted the intervention program he was already participating in and raised the alarm.
What they didn’t know was the person they feared was recruiting their son was actually the police.
The conversations with their son continued.
Thomas later sent a photograph of himself in his school uniform, holding a knife with the word ISIS written on it.
Then came his 14th birthday. Victoria Police officers visited the family with presents and a cake, three months into his intervention.
But days later, AFP officers came to make an arrest.
"Turned out to be like in a nightmare," his mother said. "They came, they arrested him, and he was handcuffed."
Only later did the family learn that the person Thomas had come to regard as his closest online friend was an AFP officer.
"What ISIS [IS group] do is they do the thing that AFP has done in this instant," his father said. "They groom children, right? ISIS, AFP groom children."
The case reaches the Children's Court
When the case reached court, after he was charged with advocating terrorism and membership of a terrorist organisation, the magistrate was damning of the AFP’s operation and threw the case out.
She found the undercover officer had "fed" Thomas’ fixation, "groomed" him and given him new terminology and boundaries for what was a partial fantasy world.
The worst thing they have done is that they gave him a feeling of belonging. They filled his isolation.
The magistrate found Thomas’ rehabilitation was "doomed" once the undercover operation began, and that he was redirected, often back to violent extremism.
For his parents, one aspect of the relationship was particularly difficult to reconcile.
"The worst thing they have done is that they gave him a feeling of belonging. They filled his isolation."
'Played into that vulnerability'
In recent years, the AFP has identified a range of factors that can make some young people more vulnerable to radicalisation.
"These include social dislocation, peer influence, mental health challenges, neurodiversity factors, active online engagement with extremists, and triggering or traumatic events," the AFP said in a submission during a statutory review of the Online Safety Act in 2024.
Nicole Rogerson, CEO of Autism Australia, says there are characteristics associated with autism that, for some people, can create vulnerabilities online.
"Things such as an immense interest or focus on something. It can be a misinterpretation. It can be a literal interpretation," she told The Feed.
"The reality is we know that for some people with autism, they do have problems with communication. Communication is fundamentally the disorder that underpins autism spectrum disorder."
Criminal defence lawyer Nick Jane, who has represented Thomas for about five years, said the operation is an example of the AFP playing into the very vulnerabilities it has identified.
"To intervene in a way that completely plays into that vulnerability, it is incongruous with their position," Jane told The Feed.
"In the Carrick case … it was someone who recognised the vulnerability and preyed on it rather than helping him."
Jane said if public safety was the priority, the operation instead steered Thomas towards attacks.
It was someone who recognised the vulnerability and preyed on it rather than helping him.
The AFP declined multiple interview requests and did not respond to the Feed's extensive list of questions. But, when questioned about the case at a Senate inquiry in 2024, then-deputy commissioner Ian McCartney said he would authorise the operation again in the same circumstances.
"It was obviously a decision that we didn't take lightly," he said. "The decision to approve the controlled operation was due to the escalation of threat, the need to protect the community, but at the same time, taking into account the age of the individual."
A missing middle?
Peta Lowe, who spent years leading the NSW government’s Countering Violent Extremism program for young people, believes the Carrick case exposes a gap in Australia’s response.
Lowe believes Thomas' intense interest in the IS group could look remarkably similar to radicalisation, but that his age, autism and intellectual disability affected his capacity to translate that interest into a genuine threat.
She also believes the intervention from Victoria Police was not given enough time before the AFP covert operation began.
"I think he had four years of developing those behaviours and they expected an autistic, intellectually disabled young person to change them in a month," she said. "I think that shows a lack of understanding about neurodivergence and adolescent behaviour."
For Lowe, cases like Thomas' need another option between intervention and prosecution, particularly where age, disability or other vulnerabilities complicate the circumstances.
"There should be some way of diversion before prosecution when we understand that there are some extenuating vulnerabilities," she said.
The former extremist working in prevention
Mubin Shaikh knows something about the appeal of violent extremism because he once felt it himself.
As an 18-year-old, he travelled to remote areas of Pakistan, where a chance encounter with the Taliban left him, as he puts it, "enamoured" by them.
He got so deep into the pull of violent jihad when the September 11 attacks happened, he initially celebrated.
"After that attack happened, I realised that this is not right," he said. "How did I come to a place where the group that I supported, this is what they produced?"
Today, from his home in Toronto, Canada, Shaikh spends much of his time trying to pull others away from extremism.
He works with Parents for Peace, an independent organisation that intervenes with people involved in extremism and their families, drawing on former extremists such as Shaikh to help build trust.
That independence from law enforcement is important, he says, particularly for parents trying to decide where to turn when they become concerned about their child.
"Parents are obviously mortified to even consider the option of, 'do I call the police on my child?'" Shaikh told the Feed. "Because what do police do? Police come and they arrest, and then your kid's going to go to prison."
But Shaikh does not argue police should be removed from the equation. Where someone poses a risk, he says law enforcement has a role to play.
Sometimes, the prospect of prosecution can provide the "stick" needed to push someone towards intervention.
His preferred approach is a co-response model: police are there to manage risk, while an independent organisation can occupy the space between law enforcement and the family. This, he said, would get more families to reach out.
Australia has no model like this.
Shaikh says neurodivergence comes up frequently in his work, particularly among young people. In the program, he estimates about 65 per cent of cases involve some form of neurodivergence, with autism making up the majority of those cases.
Working with neurodivergent young people can require patience and repetition, he says.
Shaikh describes a pattern he calls "looping", where weeks of apparent progress can be followed by a return to radical ideas.
"I have spent weeks and weeks up to months developing this genuine relationship with this individual," he said. "And we've hit on some topics and it's going really well. And then for whatever reason, we'll come back and it was like we didn't have that conversation at all."
At first, Shaikh said, he found it frustrating but said this can be the nature of working on disengaging a young, neurodivergent person.
Counterterrorism expert Peta Lowe believes Australia needs an independent service similar to Parents for Peace and is in the process of bringing it to Australia.
Part of the problem, Lowe argues, is distinguishing between an intense fixation and an intention. Doing that with neurodivergent young people, she says, requires specialist expertise.
"[Police] are not trained to understand this stuff," she said. "They might understand autism broadly, but unless they've done specialised training, they're not going to understand how to work with neurodivergent kids."
Thomas Carrick returns to court
But the court’s decision in 2023 did not mark the end of Thomas' involvement with extremism. When he was 17, in 2025, Thomas published violent extremist material online.
The following month, he sent a threatening email to the Melbourne Hebrew Congregation under the name "Adolf Hitler".
"There will be a shooter coming in at night and shooting everyone of you," the email read and he said ISIS members would "burn and slaughter" all Jewish people.
Thomas later pleaded guilty to those offences, and he spent about a year in youth detention.
"Yes, he must be held accountable for his wrongdoings," his father said.
But his parents continue to blame the earlier AFP operation for intensifying the fixation they had originally sought help to address.
In a statement to the Feed, Victoria Police said its CVE program continues to provide early intervention for people assessed as "vulnerable to, or holding, violent extremist beliefs" and said that case management can include connecting people with mentors, psychological counselling and education or employment support.
The AFP is also examining the role neurodivergence and other vulnerabilities may play in youth radicalisation.
In an address to the National Press Club in 2025, AFP commissioner Krissy Barrett said a number of youth cases will be assessed for trends, looking at their networks and vulnerabilities, and "any prevalence of mental health issues and neurodiversity".
"This will help better understand how youth are being influenced and radicalised, and so importantly, how we can prevent it as early as possible," Barrett said.
Thomas’ mother says the family has been left in a more difficult position than when they first approached police for help.
With Thomas now back home, his parents say they are hopeful he will not offend again under their watch. But their trust in authorities has vanished.
The family is now suing the AFP, alleging age and disability discrimination, saying authorities need to better understand how to handle cases like theirs and so the same is not repeated with others.
"They just left us with a much tougher job," his mother said. "But we as parents, we will not give up and we will not lose our hope."
"What I want for my son is the same what I wanted in 2021. I want him to live a good and normal life."

The taboo wealth tax debate experts say Australia can no longer ignore
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:33:58 UTC
04:33:58 KST

in brief
- Rising intergenerational wealth transfers are widening Australia's economic divide by rewarding inherited capital over earned wages.
- Experts argue that unaddressed untaxed wealth threatens retirement security and demands urgent structural tax reform.
Australia faces a "tsunami" of retirees unable to support themselves if it doesn't address the growing issue of untaxed intergenerational wealth transfer, advocates warn.
New research from the Australian Institute of Family Studies (AIFS) released on Wednesday shows that intergenerational financial support — flowing from older, wealthy family members to younger ones — is increasingly driving inequality.
The report found that Australians receiving inheritance grew from 4.8 per cent to 7.2 per cent between 2001 and 2018 while the proportion receiving financial gifts grew from 10.5 per cent to 15. 8 per cent over the same period.
The timing of such financial aid has a major impact, the report emphasises, with earlier assistance shaping opportunities at critical life stages. Inheritance, while typically larger, often comes after decisions around housing have been made.
"Not all families have the same capacity to provide assistance," Dr Jody Hughes, head of families and society at the AIFS said.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"Understanding who can access these forms of support, and who misses out, is important for understanding broader patterns of wellbeing, financial security and inequality both between and within generations."
The new data comes as comparison site Finder revealed that 30 per cent of homeowners in Australia received financial support from family to buy their homes. Home loans expert Richard Witten noted that the "bank of mum and dad has become a major player" in the property market.
Christian charitable community services network Anglicare has been campaigning on tax reform to address inequality, with its own data finding the baby boomer generation is set to pass on roughly $5.4 trillion to their families — much of it untaxed.
Kasy Chambers, executive director of Anglicare, told SBS News that Australia's unusual lack of inheritance tax and its generous superannuation concessions allows wealth to "build and build".
"We're about to see the biggest wealth transfer ever in human history," she said. "That will concentrate wealth, which doesn't really do anybody any good because it takes it out of tax systems, it puts it in the hands of a very small amount, and it makes running any kind of government services ... very, very difficult."
Chambers noted Anglicare is seeing a rise in people using its services as precarity climbs the income ladder, driving more people to food banks.
"Normal is not enough," she notes, explaining that families on median incomes are increasingly struggling to afford the basics.
Is a death tax the answer?
In May, the government came under fire as its reforms to trusts were branded a "death tax" by the Opposition.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers introduced changes in the budget to discretionary trusts, imposing a minimum 30 per cent tax rate from 2028 and making their use by families to distribute income to beneficiaries less attractive, and denied the proposal was a death tax.
Australia abolished its inheritance tax in 1979, making it an outlier in developed nations, most of which have some form of duty owed on capital and assets transferred to family members.
Chambers supported the government's reforms to superannuation and capital gains tax but said Labor should go further.
"It's unpopular, but when you model what happens when people that have wealth simply pass all of it on, it very quickly ends up very, very concentrated," she said.
Other experts aren't so sure, with Tax and Transfer Policy Institute Director, Professor Robert Breunig, telling SBS News that such taxes could sound good in theory but fail in practice.
Upper-middle class individuals who die unexpectedly tend to shoulder the greatest burden of inheritance taxes, as "really wealthy" individuals frequently make adjustments to avoid paying them, he said.
Labor's tax reforms primarily affect income tax while largely avoiding wealth accumulation, such as the value of property and inheritance, which the AIFS report notes is the primary driver of growing inequality.
Breunig notes that such inequality is not intergenerational — ie, between baby boomers and millennials — but a growing class one between those with wealthy families and those without.
The housing safety net
Parental support is not only helping young people buy homes, it is also widening the wealth gap, as financial support is more likely to go to those who are already homeowners, the report highlights.
Miriam and her partner, both in their 30s, told SBS News that they have been saving for a house deposit since before they got married over a decade ago. Currently, the couple is in the final stages of closing on their first home in Sydney's Baulkham Hills — a $1.4 million townhouse.
"We've been making sacrifices across the board," Miriam said. "We tried to not live closer to the city, so that we wouldn't be paying so much in rent just to make sure that we kept putting into our savings".
Even so, the couple said they would have been unable to afford the deposit or secure a loan without borrowing around 40 per cent of the value of the home from her partner's family.
"It means we'll be using most of our savings," she said. "We will be paying it back; it's just instead of paying a mortgage and interest, you're paying your family. That means sacrificing for the next few years, on a lot of things."
Without similar support, Miriam said many of her friends assume they will "have to rent" for the rest of their lives.
Chambers notes that "the whole aged care system is really built on an assumption that people will have their own home" by the time they retire.
Renting in retirement is "actually pretty grim," Anglicare modelling shows, with more people expected to enter aged care earlier as they simply run out of money.
"It actually is a bit of a tsunami that's going to hit the country if we don't address it in some way," she said.
Breunig, however, argues that while homeownership is down "a little bit" among younger Australians, people are still buying homes later in life. That demographic will also have benefited from having had superannuation for longer, so are likely to be better off in retirement, he said.
'Something' must be done
The bigger driver of wealth inequality is a tax system that doesn't account for the vast rise in property prices over the last 20 years, Breunig argued.
"[Growing inequality is a result of] our failure to tax the major vehicle in which people hold their wealth," he said.
Data varies, but around 40 per cent of total wealth in Australia is in owner-occupied housing. Breunig argues that, at some point, something will need to be done about it.
While he said a "death tax" is likely politically too toxic, he advocates for a broad-based land tax to "really tax the wealth people are holding in property".
The ACT is halfway through its 20-year plan to transition the territory toward this arrangement, although the federal government has repeatedly rejected calls for a national land tax.
Making the economic changes necessary to avoid runaway inequality is deeply unpopular, Chambers said, arguing a "loss of trust in governments and institutions" means people want more of their income.
"If we don't do something ... we're going to end up in a place that's not really very great for anyone," she said. "And it's not that far away; it'll be in a couple of generations."

US accuses Chinese AI firms of ‘malicious’ copying of AI technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:30:42 UTC
04:30:42 KST

US accuses Chinese AI firms of ‘malicious’ copying of AI technology
- The US accuses six Chinese AI firms of maliciously copying American AI technology using a method called distillation to speed up their AI development.
- US officials claim these activities likely have Chinese government awareness and could enhance China’s military and cyberattack capabilities.
- China denies the accusations, calling their AI progress a result of scientific self-reliance and urges cooperation between the two countries on AI safety.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The US government on Sept 8 accused Chinese artificial intelligence companies of maliciously copying technology from American artificial intelligence (AI) firms, potentially complicating relations ahead of a planned meeting between leaders of the world’s two biggest economies later in September.
The Chinese companies copied US AI labs’ intellectual property through a technique known as distillation, according to a statement from US law enforcement and intelligence officials.
Distillation is the process of training smaller AI models using output from larger, more expensive ones as part of an effort to lower the costs of training a new AI tool.
US officials accused six Chinese companies, including DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and Alibaba, of tapping variants of American-made AI models to train their AI products more quickly.
The companies did so “likely with Chinese government awareness,” according to the statement from US officials, who added that the Chinese companies targeted AI models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Alphabet’s Google and SpaceX.
“China-based AI companies are engaging in aggressive, malicious and targeted distillation activities at an industrial scale,” the officials said.
US officials made the allegations as the administration of President Donald Trump prepares for Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US in late September.
The US and China are also gearing up to discuss AI safety risks during a dialogue planned for mid-September, Reuters previously reported.
In response, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said on Sept 9 that China’s AI advances were the result of “achieving high-level science and technological self-reliance.”
“We hope the US will earnestly implement the important consensus reached by the leaders of both countries and refrain from making false accusations and smearing China,” Mao said.
“As major powers in artificial intelligence, China and the US should strengthen cooperation.”
The US made a similar accusation in April ahead of Trump’s visit to Beijing.
The Sept 8 statement alleged that the distillation not only reduces research and development costs for Chinese AI firms, but also enhances China’s “military and cyberattack capabilities that could be used against the US and our allies.”
Reuters reported on July 31 that Chinese military researchers have used outputs from leading US AI models to train domestic Chinese AI systems and advance China’s defence capabilities. REUTERS

Lavrov says US accepts Ukraine 'realities,' rejects NATO bid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:28:00 UTC
04:28:00 KST

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Tuesday that Washington's approach to ending the war in Ukraine recognizes what Moscow calls the "realities on the ground" and rules out efforts to bring Kyiv into NATO.
Speaking in an interview with Channel One’s Bolshaya Igra show, Lavrov said these principles formed the basis of discussions during recent contacts between Russian and U.S. representatives, including a meeting between U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
"I can safely tell you that the substance of what was discussed is based on the position that President Trump set out on Ukraine immediately after returning to the Oval Office,” Lavrov said.
He said the first element of the U.S. position was that efforts to bring Ukraine into NATO should be abandoned.
"He (Trump) said, first of all, that they should even forget about trying to bring Ukraine into the North Atlantic Alliance,” Lavrov said, adding that Trump had described the issue as "settled.”
The second element, according to Lavrov, was the U.S. recognition of what "realities on the ground.” He stressed that Moscow understood the term as referring not simply to territory but to the people living in the areas concerned and their political preferences.
"The realities on the ground that President Trump and his team recognize, as far as we can judge, and continue to recognize ... are connected with people,” he said.
Lavrov dismissed speculation about what Witkoff and Kushner may have discussed in Moscow and Kyiv, saying the US side had not publicly disclosed details of its next diplomatic steps.
"A lady, a member of the Verkhovnaya Rada (Ukraine's parliament) has already said that what they (Witkoff and Kushner) brought was far worse than what Ukraine had previously rejected,” he said.
He also rejected reports that direct Russia-U.S.-Ukraine talks would necessarily resume after Russia’s Sept. 20 parliamentary elections, saying such statements had come from the French side rather than Washington.
Turning to the EU position, Lavrov said European countries had several opportunities to play a constructive role in efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict but to no avail.
"Europeans had a huge number of opportunities to play a constructive role. They believe that without them there can be no negotiations, that they must be at the negotiating table,” he said.
Lavrov pointed to the negotiations that led to the Minsk agreements in 2015 as one such opportunity. He also cited the Russia-Ukraine talks in Istanbul in 2022, saying Russian negotiators had accepted proposals put forward by the Ukrainian side.
The minister criticized former German Chancellor Angela Merkel, former French President Francois Hollande and former Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko over their later statements about the Minsk process, saying they had acknowledged that the agreements were used to give Ukraine time to strengthen its army.
Lavrov also disputed former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s account of his role in the collapse of the 2022 negotiations.
The minister cited comments by David Arakhamia, then and now the parliamentary leader of Ukraine’s ruling Servant of the People faction, claiming Johnson had urged Ukrainian officials not to sign an agreement with Russia.
"The Europeans had other opportunities to take the same reasonable and responsible position as the Trump administration - to look at the real facts, the situation on the ground, including the people who live there and their views,” he said.
Instead, he said, European governments continued to call for Russia to suffer a "strategic defeat” and insisted that Ukraine was defending European values.
Lavrov sharply criticized that argument, saying Ukraine is practicing discrimination based on language, nationality and religion.
Asked to clarify his warnings about the possibility of a new war in Europe, Lavrov said they were prompted by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s repeated statements that Russia poses the main threat to Europe and that Germany should become the continent’s leading military power.
Lavrov said Merz had repeatedly spoken of the need for Germany to be prepared for a possible war against what he described as the Russian threat.
"He really believes this,” Lavrov said, adding that he did not consider Merz’s statements a "Freudian slip.”
Asked about a possibility of a meeting between Putin, Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in China in November, Lavrov said the Russian leader would not reject such an encounter.

IRS under Trump unlawfully shared taxpayer info with immigration authorities, court rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:27:13 UTC
04:27:13 KST

IRS under Trump unlawfully shared taxpayer info with immigration authorities, court rules
- A US appeals court ruled that the IRS unlawfully shared about 47,000 taxpayer addresses with immigration authorities under a Trump-era policy.
- The policy allowed ICE to obtain taxpayer information without proper legal requirements, violating post-Watergate privacy laws.
- The court blocked the policy, emphasising the need to protect taxpayer privacy and prevent government overreach in information sharing.
AI generated
BOSTON - A US appeals court on Sept 8 upheld an injunction blocking an Internal Revenue Service policy that allowed it to share thousands of taxpayers’ addresses with immigration authorities, saying the Trump administration’s practice violated federal law.
A three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit ruled that the IRS in 2025 disclosed roughly 47,000 taxpayer addresses to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement under a procedure adopted as part of the administration’s efforts to expand immigration enforcement.
The IRS did not respond to a request for comment.
A spokesperson for the US Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, in a statement said it disagrees with the ruling and “will continue using every lawful tool available to locate and remove illegal aliens with final orders of removal.”
Under an agreement between the agencies, the IRS in July 2025 began processing ICE requests for the last known addresses of as many as 1.28 million people suspected of unlawfully residing in the United States.
The IRS adopted a procedure that allowed ICE to obtain information on taxpayers if it provided a five- or nine-digit number in an address field, even if that number was not an actual ZIP code.
Groups including the Centre for Taxpayer Rights and the Main Street Alliance sued, arguing the practice was unlawful.
A lower-court judge agreed and blocked the policy, by which time the IRS had already shared 47,289 records with ICE.
President Donald Trump’s administration on appeal contended the ruling hindered federal law enforcement.
“But that’s a gripe with Congress, not the court,” US Circuit Judge Cornelia Pillard said in the appeals court’s ruling.
Pillard, like the rest of the three-judge panel, was appointed by Democratic President Barack Obama.
After the Watergate scandal during President Richard Nixon’s era exposed abuses of US taxpayers’ information, Congress barred the IRS sharing information with other government agencies unless they complied with stringent conditions.
Pillard said the procedures the IRS under Trump adopted violated federal law in numerous ways, including “most egregiously” by not even requiring ICE to provide an actual address for a taxpayer as legally required.
The practice, Pillard said, “automates the review of millions of records without any individual review or any other means of ensuring compliance with the legal prerequisites to releasing each individual taxpayer’s information.”
Skye Perryman, whose liberal legal group Democracy Forward represented the plaintiffs, in a statement said she was pleased the court “acted to stop this unlawful behaviour.”
“The privacy laws enacted in the post-Watergate era exist to prevent abuses of power just like this,” she said. REUTERS

Palestine welcomes trade restrictions by 12 countries on illegal Israeli settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:22:35 UTC
04:22:35 KST

Qais Abu Samra and Mohammad Sio
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
Palestine on Tuesday welcomed a joint statement by 12 countries reaffirming their commitment to the two-state solution and announcing restrictions on trade in goods produced in illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories.
 
Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh said the measures were a “step in the right direction,” but called for binding international action to halt illegal settlement expansion and the de facto annexation of the West Bank.
 
The statement was issued by the foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden and the UK.
 
The ministers announced restrictions on trade in illegal settlement goods amid Israeli government measures, unprecedented levels of occupier violence and continued settlement expansion.
 
Al-Sheikh said the international community must move beyond condemnation and political statements to “binding and decisive measures” to stop illegal settlement expansion and annexation.
 
He called for respect for international law, UN Security Council resolutions and accountability for those responsible for settler violence.
 
E1 project threatens territorial continuity
 
Al-Sheikh warned that Israel’s continued illegal settlement plans, particularly the E1 project, threaten to fragment Palestinian territory, separate the northern and southern West Bank and undermine the possibility of a contiguous, viable Palestinian state.
 
The E1 project covers an area between Jerusalem and the Maale Adumim settlement east of the city. Palestinian and international officials warn that its implementation would divide parts of the West Bank and severely damage prospects for a geographically contiguous Palestinian state.
 
“Protecting the two-state solution is not limited to reaffirming political commitment to it,” al-Sheikh said, stressing the need to protect Palestinian land from annexation, settlement expansion and occupier violence, end the occupation and translate international law into action.
 
He said practical measures to halt settlement activity and hold those responsible for violations accountable would help preserve prospects for peace and promote regional and international security.
 
The measures come amid escalating Israeli army and occupier attacks in the occupied West Bank since the start of the Gaza genocide in October 2023. Palestinian authorities have documented killings, arrests, home demolitions, attacks on mosques and vehicles, destruction of agricultural land, restrictions on farmers’ access to their property and forced displacement.
 
According to Palestinian figures, around 750,000 Israeli occupiers live in 156 illegal settlements and 360 outposts across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem.
 
Palestinians warn that Israeli military operations and occupier violence are paving the way for formal annexation of the West Bank, which would undermine the establishment of a Palestinian state under relevant UN resolutions.

MOD details fate of nine removed Chinook helicopters
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
20:22:02 BST
04:22:02 KST

The Ministry of Defence has detailed what happened to nine Chinook helicopters removed from the reported UK fleet between 2024 and 2026, with aircraft retained for training, heritage and spare parts while five are being disposed of.
The breakdown was provided in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked about the reduction identified in the UK Armed Forces equipment and formations statistics published on 20 August.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard said: “Nine Chinook helicopters were removed from the reported fleet between 2024 and 2026.”
Of those aircraft, three have been retained by Defence for training and heritage purposes, while five are being disposed of under existing Defence procedures.
Pollard said: “Of these nine aircraft, three have been retained for training and heritage purposes, five are being disposed of in accordance with Defence disposal policy, and one aircraft is being retained to provide structural spares in support of the remaining in-service Chinook fleet.”
The answer accounts for the full reduction of nine aircraft recorded between the 2024 and 2026 equipment figures. Five are therefore leaving the Defence inventory through disposal, while four continue to have a role supporting training, heritage or the operational fleet. The aircraft retained for structural spares will be used to support the remaining in-service Chinook force, allowing components from the airframe to contribute to sustaining other helicopters.
Obese-Jecty’s question followed publication of the latest annual UK Armed Forces equipment and formations statistics, which showed that the reported Chinook fleet had fallen by nine aircraft compared with 2024. Chinook helicopters provide heavy-lift support to the Armed Forces, moving personnel, equipment and supplies and supporting a range of military tasks. Maintaining structural spares from a withdrawn airframe provides another source of components for aircraft remaining in service.

August in the Financial Markets: Fed Signals, a Global Rise in Bond Yields, and New Records in the Semiconductor Market  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:21:11 UTC
04:21:11 KST

Six months into the Hormuz war, August added borrowing costs at multi decade highs and a Fed preparing to hike. The 30-year Treasury yield hit its highest since 2007 mid-month before the Treasury doubled buybacks of 10- to 30-year debt, steadying the long end of the curve but stoking debasement talk and carrying gold to a three-month high near USD 4,700/oz. Then came Jackson Hole. Kevin Warsh, in his first symposium as Chair, warned that better summer CPI and PCE prints “do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved” and that the Fed still has work to do, language that lifted September hike odds from 36% to roughly 60% in a session.
The S&P 500 gained roughly 2.6% and the Nasdaq Composite 3.9%, both snapping two month losing streaks, while the Dow's 1.3% secured a fifth consecutive winning month. Seoul, the epicenter of July's rout, delivered the mirror image - KOSPI rebounded some 22% in ten trading days off its 30 July low, helped by SK hynix's KRW 40t buyback.
STOXX 600 added 0.3% for a fifth straight positive month, while Bitcoin rallied 25% to about BTC/USD 78k. Brent dipped below USD 80/bbl early in the month before closing near USD 90.50/bbl, up only ~3% after July's surge, as Washington and Tehran exchanged fire on the final weekend of August for the first time in a month and Trump threatened Iran's Kharg Island export hub.
Everyone's a bond vigilante now
July's long-end selloff was largely American, but in August it stopped being so. The August 18 session that carried the 30-year Treasury to 5.34% also lifted 10- and 30-year Bunds to their highest since 2011, Canada's 30-year to a 2010 high and the UK's 50-year gilt to a record 5.39%. Japan moved furthest, the 10-year JGB reaching 2.945%, its highest since 1996.
The response came from issuers rather than central banks as Washington doubled long-end buybacks, Japan's Ministry of Finance cut super-long issuance to a 17-year low, and the UK Debt Management Office shifted its GBP 252b remit shorter. France remains the most exposed in the EU, the 10-year OAT above 4.1% for the first time since November 2008 and the Bund spread near 83bp against a deficit of 5.1% of GDP.
Two summits for two global orders
The last 48 hours of August produced two competing views of the global order. In Asheville, the G20 finance track, 85% of global GDP met under the US presidency against an IMF briefing showing five-year growth projections near their weakest since 2009. Bessent's message was that “the world is awash in debt and only growth gets it out”, though the joint statement set no targets. The more consequential item was “Economic D-Day”: secondary sanctions on enablers of Iranian oil exports, with EU backing secured, and “all options on the table” on China's Iranian crude purchases. The bloc on the receiving end marked its own 25-year anniversary in Bishkek.
The SCO's ten members, part of a 27-country grouping with combined GDP near USD 30t, signed a declaration condemning unilateral sanctions and demanding more developing country weight in the IMF, alongside 27 documents, a 2026-2030 ports roadmap and progress on the USD 4.7b China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway. Putin cited USD 400b of trade and 98% local currency settlement with the rest of the SCO. Yet the proposed creation of a Development Bank agreed a year ago still has no charter, capital or timetable, and the chair passed to Pakistan with the financial architecture no further along.
Memory chips now cost more than gold
Nvidia's 26 August result was the beat the market wanted: revenue of USD 96.2b against USD 92.1b expected, a next quarter guide of USD 108b against consensus near USD 104b, and an 8.7% move in the shares. Management put CapEx at the five largest hyperscalers at USD 1.3t next year, up from roughly USD 800b in 2026, and AWS committed to 2m GPUs. The more consequential number came from Korea.
DRAM export prices averaged USD 92,183/kg over the first twenty days of August, up 401% YoY, with export values up 505%. Since January 2023 memory has risen twelve and a half times against gold's two and a half, and Germany's DDR5 retail index reached 486% of its mid-2025 level. Analysts now expect higher memory costs to cut global PC and smartphone shipments this year on physical constraint, with fabs years away and the DRAM deficit projected to widen into 2027.
Nothing from the greenback, but plenty from commodities
The Dollar Index failed to hold above 100 mark and has moved back into its established range, while EUR/USD briefly traded above 1.1700 before the dollar found buyers late in the month. We see 1.1400-1.1800 as the key range and a decisive break either way could mark the start of a more durable trend. Our dollar outlook remains neutral to modestly negative.
With inflation expectations rebuilding, precious metals have recovered from their recent correction. We continue to favor silver and platinum over gold, while our newer idea, agricultural commodities, was one of the standout performers of the month.

Signet Bank is Latvia’s leading investment bank. Founded in 1991, it is one of the first banks established following the restoration of Latvia’s independence. Signet Bank provides sustainable financing and investment solutions to local entrepreneurs and businesses. Since 2021, Signet Bank has helped more than 50 Latvian companies raise over EUR 1 billion through bond and equity issuances, while providing an additional EUR 500 million in new lending transactions. In 2025, assets under management reached EUR 1.7 billion. Signet Bank is the leading arranger of corporate bond and equity issuances in Latvia and one of the leading stockbrokers in the Baltic region. The Bank’s shareholders include 47 Latvian and international private investors. The largest shareholders are Signet Acquisition III (20.4%), wholly owned by U.S. investor Alexander Solovey; SIA Reglink (9.6%), founded by banking professional Irīna Pīgozne; and AS RIT Group (9.4%), a Latvian company owned by the Rapoport family

NRD Cyber Security: AI is accelerating the cyber race for attackers and defenders  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:21:08 UTC
04:21:08 KST

Russia’s war against Ukraine and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence are reshaping the cybersecurity environment, forcing governments and businesses to think about resilience well beyond traditional IT defences, according to Vilius Benetis, Director of Lithuania-based NRD Cyber Security.
The company reported €14.2mn in revenue in 2025, up 24 percent on year, and carried out projects in 34 countries.
“For the Baltic states, sitting on NATO and the EU’s eastern flank, the experience of Ukraine has provided particularly important lessons about protecting critical infrastructure and preparing organisations to continue operating during sustained attacks. Ukraine’s critical infrastructure, particularly its energy and public sectors, have been subject to numerous attacks. Representatives from Ukraine’s critical infrastructure often attend cybersecurity conferences, where they share insights on these attacks. In a sense, we are in a fortunate position to be able to consider events and possibilities such as cyber provocations, and to discuss how we are going to react, behave, mobilise and organise ourselves. In such a way we are building our additional resilience – mental, cooperative, and technical,” Benetis told The Baltic Times.
He says all three Baltic countries have invested heavily in strengthening national and sectoral cyber resilience, although their regulatory structures and approaches differ. Each has also developed an ecosystem combining domestic and international cybersecurity companies, regulators and academia.
Critical infrastructure remains an obvious target. Rather than describing particular industries as the most vulnerable, however, Benetis prefers to focus on those facing the greatest pressure.
“Perhaps a more accurate formulation could be ‘most targeted’. According to ENISA (European Cybersecurity Agency) cyber threat landscape report, financial, logistics and healthcare are the sectors where most cyber-attacks have been reported. We observe public and energy/utility sectors among the most targeted ones,” he says.
According to him, AI is now adding another dimension. Automation allows attackers to probe systems faster and at much greater scale.
“The attacks are changing both in scale and size – it becomes easier to organize an automated attack which is not only exploiting the known vulnerability, but explores other vulnerabilities at the same time, relentlessly.”
Defenders are adopting the same technology to strengthen security, meaning the contest is increasingly about speed.
“In the meantime, defenders are using more and more AI-powered tools to ensure preemptive security posture, identify, understand and fix weaknesses, and even handle impactful incidents.”
NRD Cyber Security has evolved alongside these threats. Founded in 2013 as a cybersecurity consultancy, it began developing proprietary products in 2017 and has expanded its managed security service provider business since 2019. The company says its client-centred approach has helped it expand internationally.
“We consider ourselves part of our clients – we like to take responsibility for their success in cybersecurity, and we evaluate how much we have contributed to actual improvements in cybersecurity. Such an attitude of sincerely caring about a client’s success does not seem to be too common yet,” Benetis said.
Its proprietary technologies include Natrix, an IT security threat, incident and network monitoring platform used by security teams and organisations including SOCs and CSIRTs. NRD Cyber Security is increasingly offering the technology to organisations seeking to establish monitoring capabilities in Europe and elsewhere.
Looking five years ahead, Benetis expects the company to combine international consultancy, managed services and proprietary technology.
“We are helping even more countries, sectors, and organisations to secure their digital environments. Our aim is to strengthen our consultancy business, while continuing to provide quality managed security services and offer key cybersecurity technologies. We focus on areas where main enterprise cybersecurity solution vendors are not creating value effectively or not at the right price point for the local market,” Benetis shared the vision.

In Ukraine, children of veterans will receive compensation for the cost of contract-based education in the 2026/2027 academic year
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
22:21:06 EEST
04:21:06 KST

In Ukraine, children of veterans will receive compensation for the cost of contract-based education in the 2026/2027 academic year
Kyiv • UNN
The government has extended the program for full compensation of contract-based education for children of veterans in 2026/2027. More than UAH 320 million will be allocated for the support.
The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine has extended the implementation of a project providing state assistance to cover the cost of education for the children of male and female veterans. It concerns students studying at professional pre-higher or higher education institutions at their own expense. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi reported this, UNN writes.
The children of male and female veterans will be able to receive full compensation for the cost of contract-based education in the 2026/2027 academic year. The government has extended the relevant program. The compensation is available to students of professional pre-higher and higher education institutions
He noted that to do so, applicants must contact their educational institution with the necessary documents. After that, a certificate will become available in Diia, and it must be confirmed within 20 calendar days.
The Ministry of Veterans Affairs will transfer the funds directly to the educational institution. If a student has already paid for all or part of their education independently, the institution will refund the amount paid. Despite the difficult financial situation, support for male and female veterans and their children remains one of the state's main priorities
Additional information
In March last year, the Cabinet of Ministers launched a pilot project to provide state assistance for the education of children of certain categories of people who defended Ukraine's independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity for a period of one and a half years.
Under the project, eligible participants are children who have the status of family members of a fallen (deceased) defender of Ukraine; children of persons with war-related disabilities; children of combatants; children of persons who have the status of war veteran and are considered missing under special circumstances; children of persons who have the status of war veteran and for whom the fact of captivity has been established; and children of persons recognized as victims of the Revolution of Dignity.
As reported by the Ministry of Veterans Affairs, this concerns students studying at professional pre-higher or higher education institutions at their own expense.
"Therefore, students who will study in the 2026/2027 academic year will also be able to receive financial support from the state—a reimbursement of the cost of education under the relevant contract for one academic year. The government will allocate more than UAH 320 million for this," the ministry reported.
The ministry noted that, to receive state assistance, a child who is a student must contact the educational institution with documents confirming their status.
An educational institution participating in the project is required to enter the provided information into the
Unified State Electronic Database on Education (USEDE) within three working days.
The student will receive a certificate through the Diia application, which must be confirmed within 20 calendar days of receipt. After the certificate is confirmed, the funds will be credited to the educational institution's special account.
The ministry also emphasized that the Cabinet of Ministers improved the mechanism for implementing this project, in particular:
-  the procedure for providing state assistance to the children of fallen defenders of Ukraine has been simplified—the verification of  information about the birth of such children has been abolished; 
-  greater emphasis has been placed on the responsibility of educational institutions for the accuracy and timely updating of information in the USEDE; 
-  the possibility of correcting errors in the data and canceling certificates containing inaccurate information; 
-  the possibility of generating a certificate again if a student was unable to confirm it on time due to a technical failure; 
-  the obligation of the educational institution to return excessively received funds to the Ministry of Veterans Affairs within seven working days.

From Arenas to Apps: How Sports Are Expanding the Baltic Entertainment Economy  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:20:42 UTC
04:20:42 KST

A major match changes the city around it. A big game changes the streets around it. Hotels and restaurants get busier, while fans keep discussing the game on their phones after leaving the arena.
The phone has joined the crowd
A fan in the stands may watch the court while checking player statistics, foul counts or results from another game. Someone at home can follow the same numbers beside a live broadcast.
During a long break, some adult viewers move from match statistics to other online entertainment. Casino games are available through Verdekazino.net, while fantasy picks and prediction games offer different ways to follow the sporting action. Once the players return, the live score usually becomes the main screen again.
- The official score and game clock.
- Individual player statistics.
- Tournament standings and upcoming fixtures.
- Short clips shared during breaks.
- Supporter reactions on social media.
- Post-match interviews and analysis.
мThis does not mean every screen deserves equal attention. During a close fourth quarter, the broadcast usually matters more than a stream of notifications, especially when every possession can change the result.
The extra data becomes useful during time-outs or half-time. A box score can reveal that a team leads despite poor shooting because it controls rebounds and avoids turnovers. It also shows which players are carrying most of the workload.
Riga saw the wider bill
Riga felt the tournament well beyond the arena. EuroBasket 2025 drew up to 180,000 spectators to Riga. Bellevue Park Hotel Riga sold out, while Lido served 10,000 to 15,000 more customers than a year earlier. The estimated economic impact on hotels and restaurants reached about €60 million. Fredis Bikovs, director of the Riga Investment and Tourism Agency, later said the figure matched what the city had seen during the event.
Tickets formed only one part of the spending. Supporters also needed flights, rooms, meals, taxis and places to meet before and after games.
One football match can fill a city
The 2018 UEFA Super Cup brought about 10,000 fans and 500 journalists to Tallinn. Hotels filled, restaurants took more bookings, and buses toward the stadium carried far more passengers than usual.
Enterprise Estonia put the extra sports tourism spending at about €5 million. Many visitors arrived by air, stayed in Tallinn and spent money beyond the stadium.
The match also travelled through television coverage, club accounts and posts from players. A host city received attention from people who never entered the stadium.
The event continues after everyone leaves
Sports organisations now plan for two audiences. One buys a seat, while the other follows scores, clips and commentary from elsewhere.
Media rights, sponsorships and digital subscriptions can extend the commercial life of a tournament. A two-hour game may produce several days of interviews, tactical breakdowns and short video clips.
Local businesses gain another chance to reach visitors during that period. A restaurant near the venue can promote a match menu, while a hotel may package accommodation with transport information and late check-out.
Baltic cities do not need weekly global finals to benefit. A well-run international event can fill rooms, bring new customers into local venues and give fans reasons to keep spending after the arena lights go out.
Merchandise moves beyond the venue
Team shirts and event souvenirs no longer depend entirely on stadium shops. Fans often browse official collections before travelling, then order items later after seeing them worn in the stands. Limited tournament designs can keep selling after the final game, especially when photographs and highlights continue circulating online.
Sponsors use the same extended window. The sponsor’s name may appear on the warm-up kit, beside a replay, or behind the player answering questions after the match. A local partner may reach visitors during the event, then stay visible through match recaps shared days later. For organisers, that longer exposure can make sponsorship more valuable than a logo seen only inside the arena.

Surfshark CTO: AI is making cyberattacks more convincing and harder to detect  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
19:20:40 UTC
04:20:40 KST

As artificial intelligence becomes an everyday technology, it is also giving cybercriminals increasingly powerful tools. Donatas Budvytis, Chief Technology Officer (CTO) at Surfshark, a cybersecurity company headquartered in Vilnius, says digital resilience will increasingly depend not only on technology, but also on people’s ability to recognise sophisticated scams and protect their digital identities.
“Both individuals and organizations are facing a sharp increase in AI-powered social engineering cyberattacks, which often lead to account takeovers, data breaches, and exposed sensitive data,” Budvytis told The Baltic Times.
Yet, according to him, the human factor is becoming particularly important. Companies face attacks on vulnerabilities in their supply chains, often involving human error, while individuals are increasingly confronted with convincing scams across email, social media, messaging applications and mobile phones.
“Lithuania is no exception. Fraudulent SMS messages sent to Lithuanian residents increased nearly fourfold in early 2026 compared with the same period of 2025. Such cyberthreats are spreading quickly and becoming more convincing because of AI. This is happening across all channels, including email, social media, and messaging apps,” he says.
AI has fundamentally changed the scale at which fraud can be conducted. Criminals can now produce personalised phishing messages, cloned voices and deepfake material with relatively little effort.
“Artificial intelligence has empowered bad actors, enabling them to increase the sophistication of their attacks with minimal effort,” Budvytis says.
The financial consequences are already substantial. Deepfake-related fraud had caused an estimated $3.7 billion in losses worldwide by mid-2026, according to Surfshark research.
For Surfshark, resilience therefore means reducing the opportunities criminals have to exploit people and their personal information.
“Digital resilience means empowering individuals to safeguard themselves against cyberthreats such as scams and fraud,” Budvytis says. “It involves minimizing online exposure to keep sensitive information secure, thereby preventing data leaks, financial loss, and reputational damage.”
Surfshark has sought to broaden its products accordingly. Alongside its VPN services, the company has introduced a web content blocker, email scam checker and scam text protection. Its technological developments include 100 Gbps servers, FastTrack technology and Everlink.
Another milestone was Dausos, Surfshark’s proprietary VPN protocol and the company’s first consumer-focused VPN protocol developed from scratch.
Yet technology alone cannot eliminate cyber risk. Budvytis stresses that individuals must remain informed and keep their systems updated.
“No individual is immune to the threat of cyberattacks, and Lithuanians are no exception,” he says.
The challenge is likely to become more acute over the next five years. As AI tools become cheaper and easier to operate, criminals are expected to rely increasingly on impersonation and manipulation rather than purely technical attacks on computer systems.
“Automated voice cloning and personalized targeted phishing campaigns will soon become standard tactics, making vigilance and ongoing security awareness essential to mitigate organizational and individual risk,” Budvytis says.
Surfshark, meanwhile, plans to continue expanding its security tools as the threat environment changes.
“Our mission is to build the most beloved security product for everyone,” Budvytis says. “Surfshark will keep developing and enhancing key security solutions against complex online scams and cyberthreats.”
In an environment where AI can make fraud faster, cheaper and more convincing, resilience increasingly means combining technological protection with informed and vigilant users.
                    2026 © The Baltic Times /Cookies Policy Privacy Policy
