Want to Fall Asleep Faster? Write a To-Do List Before Bed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
17:11:06 UTC
02:11:06 KST

Nothing deters sleep like a nighttime mental ambush. Just as your head hits the pillow, tomorrow’s to-do list crawls out from under the bed. You’re suddenly answering emails in your mind, crafting meeting agendas, and ruminating over the appointment you still need to schedule. Try this instead: Write down tomorrow’s to-do list tonight.
“One of the most common things I hear from patients with insomnia is, ‘I’m tired and exhausted, but my mind won’t shut off,’” says Dr. M. Taruj Ali, medical director of sleep medicine at Mary Washington Healthcare in Fredericksburg, Va. His patients often describe “a running mental inventory of unfinished tasks and what needs to happen tomorrow.” Spending a few minutes putting those thoughts on paper can give your brain permission to set them aside for the night.
The timing matters, however: Don’t save the exercise for the moment you climb into bed. Experts recommend spending five to 10 minutes on it in the evening when you wrap up your structured tasks, like finishing work, chores, or whatever occupies the bulk of your time. “Getting those things out of your head and onto paper can reduce the pressure to keep thinking about them,” says Sari Chait, a clinical psychologist in Dedham, Mass. If a forgotten task pops into your head later, jot it on a notepad by your bed without turning it into a full-blown planning session.
Here’s how to create a list that quiets your mind rather than revving it up.
Why does writing a to-do list help?
There’s some evidence that the habit can improve sleep. In a small 2018 study, researchers randomly assigned 57 adults ages 18 to 30 to spend five minutes at bedtime either writing about tasks they needed to complete over the next few days or listing what they had accomplished during the previous few days. The to-do-list group fell asleep an average of nine minutes faster—and the more specific their lists were, the faster they drifted off.
That doesn’t mean a nightly list cures insomnia (or that reflecting on your accomplishments is a waste of time). The study included only healthy young adults who spent just one night in a sleep lab, and the researchers noted that they didn’t know whether the results would extend to people with insomnia. Still, it supports the idea that writing down unfinished tasks helps put them to rest.
This strategy is a form of cognitive offloading: using an external tool—in this case, a physical to-do list—to reduce how much information your brain has to keep track of. Stephanie High, a psychology doctoral candidate in Spokane, Wash., thinks of every unresolved task as a browser tab running in the background of your brain. “You have all these tabs, you have all these apps open, and there’s always some activity in the background,” she says. Even when you’re not actively looking at one, it’s using a little battery and memory. Writing the task down allows you to acknowledge that it requires your attention—and then set it aside. “I know that I need to put my attention on this,” she says. “But I don’t need to do it right this second.”
The benefits extend beyond bedtime. Planning tomorrow before you wrap up today creates a clear dividing line between work and the rest of your life, says Alexis Haselberger, a time-management and productivity coach in San Francisco. “It helps you disconnect, mentally, from work at the end of the day,” she says, rather than running through your responsibilities while you’re trying to talk to your kids, catch up with your partner, or watch TV.
There’s a morning payoff, too: “You have a list, so instead of spending 30 minutes getting into your day, you can just start.”
Start with a brain dump
If your current organizational system could most accurately be described as “chaos,” Chait suggests starting with one big brain dump: “Get it all out on paper, and then you can organize it from there,” she says. Once you’ve made that initial list, the daily exercise can be much smaller. At the end of each workday, choose three priorities for tomorrow.
Next, compare those priorities with your calendar. “If you have five meetings tomorrow, you’re probably not going to be able to make much headway on that big project,” Haselberger says. Move anything that won’t fit to another day. The goal is to make a plan you can reasonably stick to—not compile an unrealistic wish list.
Specificity matters, too. “‘Prep for meeting’ leaves the loop half-open because your mind still has to hold on to what ‘prep’ means,” High says. “‘Pull Q3 numbers, email the deck’ closes the loop, because there’s nothing it has to remember.” The same goes for the difference between “call Mom” and “call Mom about Thursday’s appointment.” Include enough detail that when you wake up, you’ll know exactly what you meant.
You don’t, however, need to produce a display-worthy masterpiece. “It doesn’t have to be perfect,” Chait says. “It doesn’t have to be pretty.” The sleep study used pen and paper, but it didn’t test whether handwriting works better than typing. Chait says a notebook or a notes app on your phone will do the trick; the best method is the one you’ll actually use.
Don’t turn it into another obligation
For some people, writing a to-do list can increase anxiety, especially if it morphs into a tedious planning session or an inventory of everything you failed to accomplish. If the page starts filling up with every unresolved problem in your life, it can feel less like a plan and more like self-flagellation. “You’ve just handed your nervous system a threat list right when you’re trying to wind down,” High says.
Keep the exercise brief, and focus on what you’ll do next rather than dwelling on what went wrong that day. The goal isn’t to plan out your entire life. It’s to spend five or 10 minutes capturing what needs to be remembered—and then disengage from planning until the next day.
If another task pops into your head later, write it down—but stop there. Chait keeps a pen and paper next to the bed for exactly that reason. You don’t want to spend time processing your feelings or actually acting on the thoughts, like writing an email,” she says. “You simply want to write down what the thought or to-do is.” Then put the paper away.
Finally, treat the habit like an experiment, not a new obligation. “It only works if it works for you,” High says. Try it for a few days, notice whether you feel calmer at night and more focused in the morning, and adjust how much detail you include. Otherwise, she points out, you risk opening “another tab of how I need to close more tabs”—when the whole point is to give your brain less to do.

Renoir theft 'shows museums should check security'
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
18:10:28 BST
02:10:28 KST

Renoir theft 'shows museums should check security'
- Published
A Guernsey art gallery says smaller museums should have tighter security measures after paintings by 19th Century painter Renoir were stolen in France.
Two thieves broke into the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer on Tuesday and walked out with four items worth more than 9m euros (£7.7m) each, before two were abandoned and recovered by authorities.
David Ummels, from Art for Guernsey, who was instrumental in bringing an exhibition of the impressionist's work to the island in 2023, also said attitudes towards art had changed.
He said: "It's sad people are seeing artwork for their price rather than for the value that they've managed to create, and the way they have inspired communities."
Pierre-Auguste Renoir visited Guernsey in 1883 and during his month-long visit is thought to have created 15 paintings.
Some of those works were displayed on the island in 2023 thanks to provisions by private collectors and galleries across the world.
Protecting legacy
Ummels said that, unlike bigger territories, Guernsey's security was "ideally positioned" to protect artwork.
But he added it had become very difficult to balance security with letting people enjoy the paintings.
"My philosophy when we have people visiting a show is always to keep security measures to a minimum, but you have to protect the artworks against a moment of craziness.
"But this [theft] shows perfectly that smaller museums are really struggling because they have treasures and legacy, but they have less budget than the big museums.
"So they have to live with like suboptimal security systems.
"And so there is probably a big rethinking that needs to be done in the big countries on how they manage the security of the smaller museums."
Ummels arrived on the island 11 years ago and said he "fell in love" with Guernsey's "incredible integrity", and viewed it as something worth preserving.
"It's important to pass on the heritage and legacy, but also to inspire the youth, and to give them bravery.
"We have community spirit, the kindness, and it is very fortunate that things like [the theft] tend not to happen in Guernsey."

A Ukrainian strike drone that quietly hit 450-plus Russian targets steps out of the shadows

A Ukrainian strike drone that quietly hit hundreds of Russian targets, with air-defense systems among them, has come out of the shadows. Ukrspecsystems publicly unveiled the RAM-2X, an X-winged loitering munition long used at the front but kept classified, at the MSPO defense expo in Poland, dev.ua reports.
Its relay capability allows the strike drone to operate in tandem with reconnaissance platforms such as the SHARK-M. In this configuration, the reconnaissance aircraft provides target designation, enabling the strike drone to more effectively counter Russian electronic warfare (EW) systems.
A proven drone steps into the open
To mark the reveal, the company opened an "X-Archive" of declassified combat video, starting with strikes on Russian surface-to-air missile systems and radars — the hardest targets a strike drone faces, since they are built to shoot drones down.
RAM-series loitering munitions are now credited with more than 450 target engagements, over 400 of them against air defenses, according to the manufacturer, which cleared the footage with the units involved before releasing it.
A scout and a striker hunt together
The pairing is the point of what Ukrspecsystems calls its "system of systems."
"Those who operate our reconnaissance equipment can add a strike component that works on the same antennas and stations," the company said.
This closes the reconnaissance-strike loop with its own forces. Built on shared components, a common ground station, and a single software, the RAM-2X supports several radio bands and Starlink terminals, so a jammer that blocks one link does not blind the drone.
The specs reach deep behind the front
The RAM-2X operates at the operational-tactical level, remains airborne for more than two hours, and carries a high degree of automation, with the option to run AI assistants on board. Its warhead is an explosively formed penetrator weighing 2.7 or 3.5 kilograms.

US targets Iran’s airlines with sweeping new sanctions

The US on Tuesday issued 36 fresh Iran-related sanctions targeting Iran’s aviation sector and other companies as part of a broad push to escalate economic pressure on Tehran as the war in the Middle East entered a seventh month.
The US Treasury Department said the action was aimed at grounding Iran’s Mahan Air, already sanctioned by the US and the European Union, and all other Iranian airlines.
The sanctions also took aim at covert front companies, foreign intermediaries and deceptive transshipment routes that Washington says Iran relies on to obtain US-origin aircraft and sensitive technology.
The Treasury also issued an alert asking financial institutions to report any procurement networks supporting Iran’s aviation industry, while designating firms based in Turkey and the United Arab Emirates that it said helped Tehran procure US-origin aircraft and sensitive technology.
Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control also suspended three Iran-related aviation authorisations that allowed overflights and permitted non-US airlines to fly US-origin or US-controlled commercial aircraft into Iran.
Tuesday’s actions marked a sharp escalation of the Trump administration’s renewed push to squeeze Iran’s economy and pressure Tehran to loosen its chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz.

Beyond presence: Iran’s opportunity for Judicial diplomacy in BRICS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
17:07:04 UTC
02:07:04 KST

Beyond presence: Iran’s opportunity for Judicial diplomacy in BRICS
The world is moving through a profound geopolitical transition. The international order that emerged in the aftermath of the Second World War continues to shape global institutions, but the distribution of economic, political and strategic power has changed dramatically. Emerging powers and countries of the Global South are increasingly seeking a greater role in shaping the rules that govern international relations.
In such a moment, participation in multilateral institutions cannot be reduced to attendance at official meetings or diplomatic ceremonies. The real question is whether countries can move beyond presence toward influence—from being rule-takers to becoming participants in rule-making.
It is against this broader backdrop that the visit of Iran’s Judiciary Chief, Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Ejei, to India and his participation in the BRICS judicial meetings should be viewed.
At the invitation of India’s senior judicial authorities, Mohseni-Ejei is visiting New Delhi at the head of a high-level Iranian delegation. The agenda includes participation in specialized panels and working groups, bilateral meetings with judicial officials from BRICS countries, and discussions on issues connected with global trade and international legal cooperation.
The significance of this visit, however, extends well beyond judicial relations.
It represents an opportunity to place law and justice at the center of the debate over the emerging international order.
BRICS and the emergence of a new multilateral landscape
BRICS was initially understood primarily through the lens of economic cooperation, trade and financial coordination. Yet its evolution over recent years suggests a broader ambition: to provide a platform for cooperation among emerging powers and countries of the Global South on a growing range of economic, political and institutional issues.
Its expanding membership and increasingly diverse geographical and economic composition have brought issues such as trade, investment, energy, technology, development finance and global governance into its broader agenda.
This does not mean that the existing international order is about to disappear or that BRICS represents an immediate replacement for established global institutions. The reality is more complex.
The international system is undergoing a period of transition in which established institutions remain influential while simultaneously facing questions over representation, legitimacy, double standards and their capacity to respond effectively to major global crises.
This transition creates an important strategic choice for countries such as Iran.
They can either remain observers of the emerging changes or seek to participate actively in shaping them.
The distinction is crucial: participation is not the same as influence, and influence ultimately depends on the ability to contribute to institution-building and rule-making.
National power has a legal dimension
Iran’s participation in BRICS therefore should not be viewed solely through the prism of economic or political opportunities.
There is also a legal dimension.
No sustainable economic order can exist without a reliable legal infrastructure. International trade requires legal certainty. Investment requires enforceable contractual rights. Cross-border business requires effective mechanisms for resolving disputes.
An investor entering a foreign market is concerned not only with tariffs, infrastructure and market size. The investor also needs to know what happens if a contract is breached, which authority has jurisdiction, how disputes will be resolved, whether judgments or arbitral awards can be enforced, and how effectively the legal system protects legitimate commercial interests.
For this reason, judicial security is an essential component of economic security.
The development of trade among BRICS members will inevitably increase the need for stronger mechanisms of judicial cooperation, arbitration, mediation, mutual legal assistance and enforcement of judgments.
This is where judicial institutions can contribute to the economic objectives of BRICS.
Judicial diplomacy as an instrument of economic cooperation
Courts and judicial institutions are often perceived as actors that enter the picture only after a dispute has occurred.
In the contemporary international economy, this understanding is too narrow.
A predictable and efficient judicial system can reduce transaction costs and legal uncertainty before disputes arise. Cooperation among judicial authorities can facilitate cross-border commerce, strengthen confidence among businesses and improve the enforceability of rights.
Judicial diplomacy can therefore serve as a bridge connecting law, economic cooperation and foreign policy.
For BRICS, this dimension deserves greater attention.
As economic relations among its members expand, judicial cooperation can become part of the institutional infrastructure supporting those relations. Areas such as mutual legal assistance, extradition, transfer of sentenced persons, enforcement of judgments, mediation, commercial arbitration, combating transnational organized crime, cybercrime, corruption and money laundering are no longer exclusively domestic concerns.
They are increasingly transnational challenges requiring transnational solutions.
Iran can make a meaningful contribution to this process.
From domestic judicial transformation to international engagement
Iran’s judicial transformation should also be considered within this wider international context.
Judicial reform is not limited to improving domestic procedures, reducing delays, expanding digital services or increasing access to justice. These reforms are essential, but they represent only one dimension of a modern judiciary.
The nature of contemporary crime and commerce has changed.
Organized crime networks operate across borders. Financial crimes involve multiple jurisdictions. Assets can be transferred almost instantly between countries. Cybercrime disregards territorial boundaries. Commercial disputes increasingly involve parties, contracts and assets located in different legal systems.
A modern judiciary must therefore be capable not only of operating efficiently at home but also of cooperating effectively abroad.
This is the essence of judicial diplomacy.
Judicial diplomacy does not mean that courts should interfere in foreign-policy decision-making. Rather, it means using the capacity of legal institutions to protect national interests, strengthen international cooperation, exchange judicial experience and defend the rights of citizens and the state within the framework of international law.
Direct dialogue between judicial authorities, cooperation between courts and legal institutions, mutual legal assistance agreements and participation in international mechanisms for dispute resolution are increasingly becoming important elements of modern statecraft.
Giving Iran’s voice a legal dimension
The current circumstances also give the Iranian delegation’s participation in BRICS an important international-law dimension.
Mohseni-Ejei has stated that one of the objectives of the visit is to explain Iran’s position regarding the attacks and acts of aggression it attributes to the United States and Israel, and to convey the concerns of the Iranian people to the international community.
In international affairs, however, there is an important distinction between a political statement and a legal argument.
Political messages may attract attention, but legal arguments can be documented, examined and preserved within international institutions and legal processes.
Questions concerning sovereignty, territorial integrity, the prohibition of the use of force, state responsibility and the lawful exercise of self-defense are not merely political slogans. They are subjects governed by international law and must therefore be articulated through evidence, legal reasoning and reference to applicable international norms.
This is particularly important in a world in which the credibility of international law is increasingly being tested by armed conflicts and geopolitical rivalries.
If Iran seeks to make its voice heard effectively, presenting a documented and legally grounded narrative can complement political and diplomatic efforts.
The language of law can give greater institutional durability to a country's position because legal arguments can be reflected in official documents, expert discussions, diplomatic negotiations and international legal proceedings.
This is an area in which judicial diplomacy and traditional diplomacy can complement one another.
India: more than a host
India’s role as host also adds an important bilateral dimension to the visit.
Iran and India share deep historical and civilizational ties, while their contemporary relations encompass economic, political, regional and strategic interests.
The judicial dimension of this relationship should not be underestimated.
Stronger cooperation between the legal and judicial institutions of the two countries could contribute to greater legal certainty in bilateral economic relations and provide additional support for trade, investment and regional connectivity.
As commercial and transport links between the two countries develop, legal cooperation becomes increasingly important.
Economic corridors require legal corridors as well.
From participation to rule-making
Ultimately, the importance of Iran’s participation in BRICS should be understood within the larger transformation of the international system.
The rules of the next phase of global governance have not yet been fully written.
This creates both uncertainty and opportunity.
Countries seeking a meaningful role in the emerging order cannot rely solely on their economic weight, geopolitical position or political alliances. They must also possess the institutional and legal capacity to contribute to the creation of new mechanisms and norms of international cooperation.
For Iran, BRICS can become one of the platforms through which such capacity is exercised.
Its judicial institutions can contribute to the development of practical mechanisms for legal cooperation among member states, support secure and predictable economic relations, promote alternative dispute resolution and strengthen collective responses to transnational crime.
At the same time, Iran can use such platforms to present its legal positions on international disputes and violations of international law through a documented and reasoned framework.
National power in the twenty-first century is therefore not measured only by military capability or economic strength.
It also includes the ability of a state to defend its legal rights, protect its citizens and businesses, cooperate effectively with foreign judicial institutions and contribute to the evolution of international rules.
This is why the Iranian Judiciary Chief’s participation in BRICS should be viewed as more than a diplomatic visit.
It is an opportunity to connect Iran’s domestic judicial transformation with the changing architecture of global governance.
The real test, however, lies beyond participation itself.
If Iran can transform its BRICS engagement into sustained institutional cooperation, legal initiatives and an active program of judicial diplomacy, it can move from simply being present in the emerging order to having a voice in shaping it.
The future international order is still being written.
For countries of the Global South, the strategic question is no longer simply where they will stand in that order.
It is whether they will have a role in writing its rules.
BRICS is becoming one of the important arenas in which that process is unfolding.
For Iran, judicial diplomacy can be one of the instruments through which its participation becomes influence—and through which law and justice become not merely the subjects of international cooperation, but part of the architecture of a more balanced global order.
 
 
 Hassan Babaei is assistant Professor of International Law, Science and Research Branch, Islamic Azad University

Bailey said: “As outlined in the Strategic Defence Review (SDR), it is critical the national health ecosystem—Defence, the NHS, and the private sector—has the capacity and capability to meet the Nation’s needs in peacetime and during conflict.”
The MOD did not provide a numerical assessment of how many rehabilitation personnel would be required in such a scenario, nor did it state that existing staffing levels were sufficient. Russia Develops FSB-Approved Browser With Domestic Encryption as Alternative to Google Chrome
Russia is developing a new internet browser designed to support domestic encryption algorithms approved by the Federal Security Service (FSB), The Moscow Times reported on September 8, citing Russian newspaper Kommersant
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The product, called CryptoPro Browser, is being developed by CryptoPro, a Russian provider of cryptographic information protection systems that is under US sanctions. According to the outlet, the browser will be incorporated into version 6.0 of the company’s CryptoPro CSP cryptographic software and will support integration with its plugin.
“It will make it possible to provide secure access to websites using Russian cryptographic algorithms, which is also necessary in all use cases requiring cryptographic protection in accordance with the requirements of Russia’s FSB,” CryptoPro CEO Stanislav Smyshlyaev said.
According to the company’s notice, the FSB has approved the project to develop the browser, although no timeline for its completion or release has been disclosed.
The development follows Google’s removal of the CryptoPro plugin from the Chrome Web Store in February 2025. The plugin had allowed web browsers to work with Russian electronic signatures, and the new browser is expected to provide a domestic alternative to the US-developed Chrome browser.
Russian IT industry representatives interviewed by Kommersant suggested that CryptoPro Browser could eventually become mandatory for government institutions. An unnamed information security executive at Axiom JDK said the browser could immediately satisfy a significant share of requirements imposed by Russia’s Federal Service for Technical and Export Control and the FSB.
The executive estimated that use of the browser could become mandatory within one to two years after it receives the necessary certifications.
The project comes amid Russia’s broader push to reduce its reliance on foreign technology and develop domestic alternatives.
Russia’s largest oil producer, Rosneft, headed by Igor Sechin, a close associate of Russian leader Vladimir Putin, has raised doubts about plans to develop “sovereign” and “national” artificial intelligence models under draft legislation prepared by Russia’s Ministry of Digital Development.
In its response to the proposal, Rosneft argued that developing and deploying AI models in isolation from the global technology ecosystem would not be technically feasible.

Russia’s Cultural Network Keeps Shrinking as Germany Shuts Its Largest Overseas House

Russia’s Cultural Network Keeps Shrinking as Germany Shuts Its Largest Overseas House
At least 13 Russian Houses have closed worldwide since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
This was reported by Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU) on its official website on September 8. The service framed the shuttered network—overseas branches of the state agency Rossotrudnichestvo—as “fronts for espionage and propaganda dressed up as culture.”
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Roughly 15 such centers operated across the European Union before the full-scale war, according to the SZRU.
The rollback has unfolded across four years:
- In September 2026, Germany took significant action by ordering the closure of the Russian House, the largest Russian diplomatic mission abroad. This move resulted in an estimated annual cost of $10 million for Moscow. Additionally, Germany decided to close Russia’s consulate in Bonn. German media reported that this consulate may have served as a crucial intelligence hub, coordinating Russian operations across Western Europe. Between 15 and 20 diplomats at the post may have been active intelligence operatives who cooperated with Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), the FSB, and the GRU.
- Azerbaijan, 2025: the Baku center closed after a crisis in relations tied to an Azerbaijan Airlines plane incident, prompting a rare Moscow apology rather than mirror-image expulsions.
- Moldova, 2025–2026: Chisinau terminated its cultural cooperation agreement in November 2025, and the local center ceased operations entirely on July 4, 2026; officials cited subversive activity against the country's sovereignty conducted under the guise of cultural activities.
- The Balkans, 2023: the agency's head, Yevgeny Primakov, acknowledged that centers in Slovakia, Croatia, North Macedonia, and Montenegro had ceased operations.
- Romania, February 2023: shuttered the Bucharest branch over what officials there described as the distortion of historical truth and subversive activity.
- Slovenia, April 2022: the first EU country to demand a closure, expelling the Ljubljana center.
- Poland, Denmark: activity collapsed amid mass expulsions of Russian diplomats and refusals to issue new visas.
Pressure on the Berlin center had been building for weeks before its closure. In mid-August, German lawmakers from three parties demanded that the Russian House be shut, describing it as a suspected hub for espionage and the recruitment of agents.
By then, Germany had expelled roughly 400 Russian citizens since 2022, more than 80 of them diplomats assessed to be intelligence officers working under diplomatic cover.

From 22 weeks: how premature babies are cared for
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
20:01:18 EEST
02:01:18 KST

From 22 weeks: how premature babies are cared for
Kyiv • UNN
At the Kyiv Perinatal Center, babies born at 22 weeks and later are cared for. Treatment can last 4–5 months.
The birth rate in the country is falling, while the number of complications and premature births is increasing. Although there are no publicly available nationwide statistics on such cases, doctors confirm this. Caring for “hurry-up babies” is a complex and usually lengthy process. Valeriia Tyshkevych, head of the pediatric intensive care unit at the Kyiv Perinatal Center, explained how it works in a comment to UNN.
The capital’s Perinatal Center is the facility to which women in labor with complications and those giving birth prematurely are referred. This is because it is specifically equipped to provide care for babies requiring special attention.
"We start caring for babies from 22 weeks’ gestation and weighing 500 grams or more, but sometimes they can be born at 22 weeks weighing 480 or even 370 grams. It is very difficult, but if the baby is born alive, we provide assistance and do everything possible to help the baby survive," Tyshkevych says.
After the baby is born, assistance is usually provided immediately in the delivery room. Such babies require medication, but as a rule, medications are not administered in the delivery room unless full resuscitation is being performed. According to Tyshkevych, babies born weighing less than 1,500 grams less often require such immediate resuscitation. If it is necessary, the baby is given adrenaline and saline solution.
"The baby is then taken to the intensive care unit. A polyethylene bag is then placed over the baby to prevent heat loss," the doctor said.
The bodies of prematurely born babies retain heat and moisture poorly, and polyethylene prevents their loss. This prevents the development of neonatal hypothermia, which can increase the risk of infections and other complications. Polyethylene is transparent, so doctors can see the baby’s skin color and perform the necessary procedures.
The baby is placed in an open resuscitation system, and a temperature sensor and pulse oximeter are connected.
"In the open resuscitation system, the baby receives the necessary assistance and is subsequently placed in a transport incubator. Even before being transferred to the intensive care unit, the baby is connected to a mechanical ventilator, because these babies have breathing problems," Tyshkevych explains.
Once in the intensive care unit, the baby is given surfactant—a lipid-protein complex that prevents the lungs from sticking together during exhalation. Such medication can be administered up to three times over a 72-hour period.
According to Tyshkevych, surfactants are expensive, and today the facility is forced to purchase them independently.
"And in accordance with national protocols, we обязательно administer surfactant to all babies under 32 weeks who require intubation and oxygen. The dose of surfactant is calculated according to weight. For example, if the baby weighs less than 1,000 grams, the dose is 200 milligrams per kilogram, while one vial contains 120 milligrams—so that is already one and a half vials," the doctor explains.
A central venous catheter is also inserted for prolonged parenteral nutrition.
"Then come antibacterial drugs and complete parenteral nutrition—there is a standardized mixture, or glucose, protein preparations, and a fat emulsion. We purchase all of this as well," Tyshkevych said.
Such babies often also require other medications, including caffeine citrate, antibacterial and anticonvulsant drugs, blood products, and more.
"Treatment for a baby born at 22–25 weeks’ gestation lasts 4–5 months, three of which are highly intensive," the doctor says.
Tyshkevych explains that the care of such babies is not fully covered by payments from the National Health Service, partly because the institution calculates tariffs based on an average level of expenses.
"At a facility where, as in ours, such babies are concentrated, the expenses are not fully covered," Tyshkevych says.
Today, up to 10% of babies born at the Perinatal Center are born prematurely.
"Our facility specializes in caring for them. Here, children can receive a full range of services up to the age of three. From the intensive care unit, the child is transferred to post-intensive care, followed by medical rehabilitation. After being discharged home, the child can continue receiving rehabilitation and follow-up care at our facility until the age of three," the doctor explains.
Such babies often require open-heart surgery or intestinal surgery because they are unable to feed independently. Neurosurgical procedures are also not uncommon.
Immaturity of the gastrointestinal tract, electrolyte or metabolic disorders, respiratory dysfunction, hemorrhages, and cardiac problems are issues that, unfortunately, "preemies" face.
"Unfortunately, treatment is not fully covered by the state," Tyshkevych says.
According to calculations that Perinatal Center Director Dmytro Hovsyeiev announced at a Kyiv City State Administration commission meeting, on average, caring for such a child costs the facility approximately 35,000 hryvnias: depending on the infant's condition, the figure ranges from 20,000 to more than 100,000. A significant share of the expenses goes toward medications for treating respiratory disorders in such children, which are expensive.

Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong’s first chief executive, dies aged 89

Tung Chee-hwa, who served as Hong Kong’s first chief executive and oversaw the 1997 return of the city to Chinese rule, has died.

Tung was surrounded by loved ones when he died, his office said. It is understood that he died at Hong Kong Sanatorium & Hospital.
He was last seen in public in July 2021 when he attended the premiere of a film to mark the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Communist Party.

A choir of katydid ancestors filled the Jurassic rainforest with song
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

A choir of katydid ancestors filled the Jurassic rainforest with song
Fossils reveal an extinct soundscape made by the motion of insect wings
A symphony of insect songs rang through the Jurassic rainforest, and scientists have now found the traces of this ancient soundscape.
Based on an analysis of fossilized katydid ancestors, the notes these insects played by strumming their wings can be reproduced, researchers report August 25 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
“Most fossils tell us about anatomy — shape, size, structure,” says Jun-Jie Gu, an evolutionary biologist at Sichuan Agricultural University in Chengdu, China. “But these fossils preserve something far more ephemeral: sound.”
The rocks holding the remains of these ancient insects come from rural Daohugou, China. This landscape of hills and grasslands was a hot, humid forest with giant ferns and ancient conifers during the Jurassic Period, 200 million to 145 million years ago. It hosted a stunning array of insects, Gu says, including ensiferans, the group that includes katydids, crickets and grigs.
The fossils reveal the wing structures used to make mating calls. They’re like “nature’s violin,” says biophysicist Fernando Montealegre-Zapata, of the University of Lincoln in England. One wing sports a row of microscopic teeth. As the wings close, a scraper on the other wing hits the teeth, making vibrations that are amplified by the rest of the wing. This forms what the team calls a syllable, the basic unit of sound. The song emerges as the creatures rhythmically open and close their wings.
For 20 fossils representing nine extinct species, the team simulated wing acoustics based on the teeth spacing, wing size and wings’ vibrating area. The researchers also used an evolutionary family tree to home in on each species’ call frequency, or its pitch. They checked their process by reproducing the calls of living katydids, crickets and grigs based on photos of these insects’ wings. This confirmed that the measurements needed to figure out the animals’ sounds can be obtained from the kinds of 2-D images of wings made from photos of fossils.
The cadence, or repetition, of those syllables isn’t clear from the fossils, Montealegre-Zapata says. So the team looked to living ensiferans, whose repertoire is related to body shape and size and changes with temperature. The team trained a machine learning model with those characteristics and used the temperature of the Jurassic rainforest to simulate ancient insect calls. The result was a chorus of katydid ancestor calls.
The work is “very exciting,” says Roy Plotnick, a paleobiologist at the University of Illinois Chicago who was not involved with the study. The team is “able to show that each particular species had a distinctive sound,” or characteristic frequency, which could be used for mate recognition, he says.
Scans of these ancient insects’ ears, which are located on their forelegs, support the notion that these insects hear those of their own kind.
A Jurassic soundscape
How can a fossil tell us what an insect sounded like 165 million years ago? Scientists used details preserved in the wings of Jurassic insects to reconstruct their calls. Listen to each call while seeing the fossil used to re-create the sound.
The Jurassic insects’ sounds are clear and musical, unlike buzzing or hissing sounds, which contain many frequencies. The source of musical tones can be difficult for mammalian predators to identify based on the physiology of their ears. So these single note tones could have helped the creatures stay somewhat inconspicuous to predators while sending communiques to potential mates, says Daniel Robert, a biophysicist at the University of Bristol in England.
One of the nine ancient species produced calls in the ultrasound, above the range of human hearing. This creature evolved nearly 100 million years before bats evolved with their ears attuned to ultrasonic frequencies.
Meanwhile, other groups have found fossils of early mammals from the same formation in China. Their work on a shrewlike critter’s preserved inner ears suggests that their hearing range could capture the calls of some katydid forerunners. These insects may have been evolving to escape the hearing range of hungry mammals, which in turn may have evolved to hear higher pitches, Montealegre-Zapata says.
“That’s a very stimulating thought — a very interesting hypothesis — but it needs to be tested,” says Zhe-Xi Luo, a paleobiologist at the University of Chicago who wasn’t involved with the study. Luo’s team is working to better understand the hearing capability of early mammals by comparing their hearing structures with those of modern mammals. But it’s likely, he says, that insects were just abundant in the Jurassic and early mammals evolved capabilities to exploit the glut of food.
There’s still much to learn about the soundscape of the Jurassic and that of even earlier periods, Plotnick says. Researchers could search other fossils for insect body parts that make sound by rubbing together.
“We often think of fossils as silent stones,” Gu says, “but our work shows that we can actually hear what 165-million-year-old animals were saying.”

““Objectivity” in the first sense was a property of theories which, having been…”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:58:01 UTC
01:58:01 KST

““Objectivity” in the first sense was a property of theories which, having been thoroughly discussed, are chosen by a consensus of rational discussants. By contrast, a “subjective” consideration is one which has been, or would be, or should be, set aside by rational discussants — one which is seen to be, or should be seen to be, irrelevant to the subject matter of the theory. […] For a consideration to be subjective, in this sense, is simply for it to be unfamiliar. So judging subjectivity is as hazardous as judging relevance. In a more traditional sense of “subjective,” on the other hand, “subjective” contrasts with “corresponding to what is out there,” and thus means something like “a product only of what is in here” […] In this sense “subjective” is associated with “emotional” or “fantastical,” for our hearts and our imaginations are idiosyncratic, while our intellects are, at their best, identical mirrors of the self-same external objects. […] The various ambiguities of “objective” and “subjective” illustrate the way in which the confusion can develop. If it were not for the traditional linkage of these distinctions, a historian of inquiry who emphasized similarities between the controversies of scientists and those of literary critics would not have been construed as endangering our minds by upgrading our hearts.”
– Richard Rorty, Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature

The sixth Astute-class attack submarine, HMS Agamemnon, is still completing the final stages of its in-water commissioning before being handed over to the Royal Navy for sea trials, the Ministry of Defence has said.
The update was provided by Defence Minister Luke Pollard in response to a written parliamentary question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked whether delays identified in the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority’s Major Projects Annual Report had affected the in-water phase for Boat 6.
Pollard did not state directly whether the delays had changed the planned duration of the in-water phase, but confirmed the submarine’s current position in the programme.
He said: “In September 2025, the sixth Astute Class submarine, HMS AGAMEMNON was commissioned into the Royal Navy and is undertaking the final stages of her in-water commissioning, before a handover to the Royal Navy to undertake sea trials.”
Agamemnon was commissioned into the Royal Navy in September last year but has remained with the build and commissioning programme while work continues ahead of sea trials. In-water commissioning covers the period in which systems are progressively tested and prepared after the submarine has left the construction hall and entered the water.
Pollard also provided an update on Achilles, the seventh and final Astute-class submarine, which remains under construction at BAE Systems’ Barrow-in-Furness site. He said: “Achilles, the seventh and last boat of the class, remains at an advanced stage of build in Barrow-in-Furness and work to recover from the impact of the fire in the Devonshire Dock Hall is progressing well.”
The fire in the Devonshire Dock Hall affected the site where the final Astute-class submarine is being completed, requiring recovery work while construction continues.
Achilles will complete the seven-boat Astute programme, following HMS Astute, Ambush, Artful, Audacious, Anson and Agamemnon. The nuclear-powered attack submarines are designed for anti-submarine warfare, anti-surface warfare, intelligence gathering and land-attack missions. Asked in effect whether the programme’s schedule had shifted, the MOD again declined to disclose the planned in-service dates of the submarines.
Pollard said: “The planned in-service dates for Royal Navy submarines are withheld as disclosure would, or would be likely to, prejudice the capability, effectiveness, or security of the Armed Forces.”

'Turning blind eye' to AfD win further angers voters, political scientist warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:54:41 UTC
01:54:41 KST

Chancellor Merz's government must recognise the far-right AfD's victory in Saxony-Anhalt and voter discontent that led to the win, or further cement its downfall, an expert on East German politics warned.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his coalition government's response to the historic victory of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in the Saxony-Anhalt state election will be pivotal in deciding the future of the federal government, political scientist Nicolas Spohn told Euronews.
Final results following last Sunday's election in the eastern German state showed AfD received 43.8% of the vote, more than double its showing five years ago in the region of 2.1 million people. Merz's party, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), slumped to 17.2%.
"First of all, it really is a historic victory for the AfD, and it is an earthquake for the rest of the parties," Spohn, an expert on East German state politics, said.
The pro-Kremlin, anti-immigration party's win marks the first time a far-right party is within reach of power at the state level since WWII.
Questions have been raised about what this means for national politics in Germany. Thorsten Frei, the leader of the CDU in Germany's federal parliament, or Bundestag, denied that the result suffered by the CDU in Saxony-Anhalt would have consequences on the national level.
"But this is what frustrates people," Spohn said, adding that "turning a blind eye to the warnings of elections like in Saxony-Anhalt could give the AfD more votes."
Voter discontent
Failure to deliver on promises made ahead of the 2025 elections — notably his vow to revive Germany’s stagnant economy — saw Merz's popularity sink. A recent YouGov poll showed just 16% of Germans have a favourable opinion of Merz.
"The election here shows that the CDU must, on the national level, correct their political course," the political scientist explained. "A lot of people are frustrated with the work of the CDU. They promised different things than what they achieved after the elections. The economy is doing worse than before the last election on the national level."
He recognised that some factors are not under the control of the CDU, such as the ongoing wars in Ukraine and Iran. "These are issues that Chancellor Merz can't do a lot about, but still, Germans feel this economically."
This discontent is particularly visible in Saxony-Anhalt, where Merz's popularity sank to just over 9%. Spohn believes this was more of a decisive factor in the election than support for the AfD's policies was.
"It is not genuine support for the AfD's agenda, but rather for the [idea associated with the party] of doing everything differently."
Saxony-Anhalt, whose territory was formerly part of the German Democratic Republic (East Germany), has experienced the largest population decline of any German state over the past 35 years, losing a quarter of its inhabitants since German reunification in 1990. This is particularly visible in rural areas and among young people, who bear the brunt through teacher shortages and poor career prospects.
"What I'm trying to say is that 40% of the voters do not vote for the AfD because of its far-right policies, but rather despite such policies. People in eastern Germany are not more right-wing; they are simply more frustrated."
The party now has strong momentum heading into regional elections in Berlin and another eastern German state, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, in just under two weeks. The AfD is leading in voter intent polls in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, with about 35%.
To turn the tide, Spohn argued, Merz's CDU party will have to provide a positive outlook for voters. "At the moment, we don't have this positive vision, and the AfD is the only party giving voters some kind of positive outlook, which was, 'everything is possible'. So, everything can also be different."

Eleven European countries – France, the UK, Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, and Sweden – plus Canada on Tuesday announced their intention to impose national restrictions on settlement trade and/or support European restrictions.

Staticus to invest €31.5M in advanced façade manufacturing hub in Lithuania  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:52:20 UTC
01:52:20 KST

Façade systems manufacturer Staticus Group is investing €31.5 million to build an automated aluminium and glass façade plant with an integrated testing laboratory in Vilnius, creating at least 24 highly qualified jobs. The project, “Campus Staticus,” has been granted large-scale investment project status by Lithuania’s Ministry of the Economy and Innovation.
“This project reflects the broader transformation of Lithuania’s manufacturing industry towards automation, digitalisation and sustainability. Staticus is not only expanding its production capacity but also bringing to Lithuania the manufacturing of products that have so far been sourced from subcontractors. Such investments strengthen the country’s export potential and create highly qualified jobs,” says Edvinas Grikšas, Minister of the Economy and Innovation.
“Campus Staticus” spans several complementary areas: a new production complex with an integrated façade testing laboratory, an automated production facility, process robotisation solutions, and an integrated enterprise resource planning (ERP) system. The new capacity will be dedicated to manufacturing aluminium and glass structures, including windows, doors, glazed opening elements, and sliding structures.
The project also introduces a product Staticus has never manufactured before: new next-generation hybrid unitised timber-aluminium façade (HUF) elements. Pairing timber with aluminium can cut embodied carbon by up to 70%, meeting increasingly strict sustainability requirements for low-carbon façades.
Every product will be tested on site in the new laboratory against the international CWCT, EN, and AAMA standards, which assess a façade’s resistance to air, water, wind load, kinetic impact, and seismic activity. This will ensure that every product meets the highest quality standards demanded by international markets. The 24 new roles will all be for highly qualified professionals: specialists and engineers in façade testing, structural modelling, automation and robotics, R&D, digital twins, BIM, and IT.
“Demand is growing rapidly for large-scale façades with high safety and technical requirements – the kind used on hospitals, data centres, and critical infrastructure buildings. We see significant growth potential here. Our engineering expertise and our ability to deliver technically complex façade projects are already recognised internationally, so we are now strengthening that capability by expanding production in Lithuania. The new investment will let us manufacture a larger share of our output in Lithuania and export it to foreign markets, while also allowing us to take on more complex, higher-value orders,” says Staticus Group CEO Aušra Vankevičiūtė.
Staticus is one of Europe’s largest façade contractors, designing, manufacturing, installing, and maintaining unitised façades for complex, large-scale buildings. With more than 20 years of experience, the group has offices in seven countries and currently employs more than 600 people.
The group’s companies have delivered more than 100 projects across the UK, Scandinavia, and Central Europe. Current projects include the Vista quarter in London’s South Bank (the UK’s first closed-cavity façade), Oslo Spektrum, and The Whale visitor centre in northern Norway. One of the group’s most recent projects in Lithuania is the Hero business centre in Vilnius – the first building in the Baltic states to pursue WELL Gold and BREEAM Excellent certification.
The new facility will rise in Vilnius’ Metalo Street district, where Staticus already has its headquarters and production base. The company chose the site for its synergy with existing operations, the availability of engineering, IT, and R&D talent, and convenient access to Vilnius Airport, important for serving laboratory clients and delivering mock-ups. The architectural vision for “Campus Staticus” was developed by the Danish architecture firm Schmidt Hammer Lassen Architects.
The project is scheduled to be completed in 2031. At least 90% of production is expected to be exported, with the company’s main clients operating in the UK, Scandinavian, and Central European construction markets.
“Lithuania can take pride in its strong, export-oriented engineering companies like Staticus, which is putting Lithuanian engineering on prestigious architectural landmarks across Europe. With this project, the company will start manufacturing in Lithuania the products it has until now bought from subcontractors abroad. That means not only new highly qualified jobs, but also a greater share of added value staying in the country. Every time a Lithuanian-owned company takes this path, the whole industrial base grows more resilient,” says Elijus Čivilis, General Manager of Invest Lithuania.

EU, UK express dismay over Mladic funeral in Serbia
September 8, 2026
Both the EU and UK on Tuesday expressed dismay over the funeral in Belgrade, Serbia of late war criminal Ratko Mladic a day prior.
Thousands of people, including at least six Serbian ministers, attended the event on Monday which was seen as glorifying Mladic. He received military honors at the funeral, with the head of Serbia's Orthodox Church presiding over the ceremony.
The Bosnian Serb commander died last month at The Hague, where he had been imprisoned for life. Mladic was convicted in 2017 of genocide, having orchestrated the July 1995 Srebrenica massacre, where 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed.
Mladic, called the "Butcher of Bosnia" by some international press, is a revered as a war hero by many Serbian nationalists in both Serbia and Bosnia.
EU leader call Mladic state funeral 'deeply regrettable'
EU leaders condemned the funeral, with the bloc weighing an official response to the event.
"The elements of official support and the presence of some senior Serbian officials at the funeral are deeply regrettable," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa said in statements posted on X.
"They demonstrate a failure to confront a dark chapter in Europe's recent history and contradict the values underpinning Serbia's path towards the European Union," they added.
A European Commission spokeperson, in comments to German news agency DPA, said next steps were being evaluated.
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas added: "Serbia's path into the European Union requires an unequivocal commitment in fundamental European values and historical truth."
Serbia first applied for EU membership in 2009. Serbia's EU candidacy was confirmed by the European Council in 2012.
UK summons Serbian envoy
The UK, meanwhile, summoned Serbia's charge d'affaires in response to the funeral.
"As a military commander, Mladic presided over crimes that are among the worst committed in Europe since the Second World War," the British Foreign Office said in a statement.
"The thoughts of the UK Government are with Mladic's victims and their families. They deserve respect, compassion and accountability, not efforts to rewrite proven history," the statement added.
The UK said that the "glorification of a convicted war criminal directly undermines trust, fuels division, and is incompatible with the process of reconciliation within Bosnia and Herzegovina and the region."
Bosnia expels Serbian diplomats, says Belgrade crossed 'red line'
In its reaction to the funeral, neighboring Bosnia expelled two Serbian diplomats, saying Serbia crossed a "red line" in its display of reverence for Mladic.
"They crossed every red line with what they did yesterday, the day before, and in the days leading up to the reception," Bosnian Foreign Minister Elmedin Konakovic told a Sarajevo press event.
Konakovic had also said he would withdraw most staff from the Bosnian Embassy in Belgrade in an effort to reduce ties to "the lowest possible level"
Serbian President Aleksander Vucic was not present at Mladic's funeral, although his son Danilo, did attend the event. Vucic rejected allegations that Mladic was being glorified at the funeral and said the event was put together by Mladic's family rather than the state.
The controversial funeral comes ahead of snap elections next month. Serbia has faced a political crisis in the past two years triggered by the collapse of a concrete canopy at a railway station in Novi Sad.

George Monbiot condemns Andy Burnham for his alleged subservience to the interests of the wealthy (Andy Burnham has already made a mistake that will cost him his premiership: he lost his nerve over political donations, 2 September). If true, I agree. But the same could be said of any interest holding sway in our politics. Lobbying groups, activists, unions, thinktanks, people who obsess about this, that or the other. It is surely not OK for our democracy – at local or national level – to have its priorities dictated by those with the shrillest voices, as well as those with the deepest pockets.
Speaking from Scotland, I think that our public realm is a case in point. It seems special interest groups are, to all intents and purposes, the main driver of government policy now. And all too often, said influence is framed by an ideological mission that does not necessarily align with that boring, broad swathe of folks who don’t follow politics closely, and don’t see government as a means to progress personal hobbyhorses or single-issue causes.
The latter are, in their own insidious way, as injurious to democracy as the whispers of the wealthy in the ears of politicians. So too is turning a blind eye to such undue influence because its aims chime with your own beliefs. Leaders of any party must endeavour to serve not some, but all – without fear or favour – including those who didn’t vote for them. Not easy. No guarantee of success. But abandoning that principle makes our politics all the poorer.
Colin Montgomery
Edinburgh
I was surprised to see George Monbiot paying feasance to that liberal shibboleth, “the general interest”. If a society is fractured by inequalities of class, race, gender, sexuality, etc, then there can be no “general interest” until these are overcome. Ensuring trade union influence over Labour policy through the continuation of union donations acts as leverage against policy being captured by the likes of Lord Alli and Lord Sainsbury.
When Monbiot goes on to say that “Labour governments know they can safely bash benefit recipients, who aren’t unionised, while they tread very carefully – far too carefully in my view – around the interests of oil workers”, he misses the obvious point that the way, then, to protect benefit claimants is to organise them. Unite, for instance, already has a community membership for students, claimants and pensioners, and has organised days of action against benefit cuts and sanctions. Monbiot’s proposal would not strengthen the power of benefit claimants, it would simply weaken the power of trade unions.
Nick Moss
London

Next year we will breach the 1.5C limit stipulated in the Paris agreement, and this will be followed by the disappearance of coral reefs and the eventual disintegration of the Western Antarctic ice sheet – irreversible events that will undermine the marine food chain and raise sea levels by six metres. Andy Burnham’s lukewarm approach won’t look so pragmatic to our descendants when coastal cities worldwide are under water.

Thousands across Germany protest against AfD after election victory
Unknown

01:46:50 KST

By dpa correspondents.
Berlin (dpa) – Thousands of people across Germany protested against the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) on Monday following its landslide victory in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt.
In Berlin, police estimated a crowd of around 5,000 had gathered at Brandenburg Gate and said the demonstration passed without incident. Organizers put the number of participants at around 14,000.
The rally was called at short notice by campaign organization Campact and the Fridays for Future climate movement.
Among those taking part were prominent German climate activist Luisa Neubauer and the lead candidates of the Greens and The Left in Berlin’s state election on September 20.
Protesters carried banners with slogans including “Fascism is not an alternative” and “Stop AfD Nazis! End racism and social cuts,” while crowds chanted: “All together against fascism!”
The party won Sunday’s election by a wide margin but fell short of an absolute majority, leaving open the possibility of Germany’s first AfD-led state government.
The domestic intelligence agency has classified the AfD’s state branch as “confirmed right-wing extremist.”
Protests were also called in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, where a new state parliament will be elected later this month and the AfD is leading in the polls.
In Schwerin, according to police reports, several hundred demonstrators gathered, while in Rostock, more than 500 people came together for a communal sing-along.
In Essen, about 1,200 people gathered, according to police. Carrying rainbow flags and cardboard signs with messages such as “Ban the AfD now” and “No place for Nazis,” the participants marched through the city centre.
Hundreds of people also gathered in Potsdam to protest against the AfD, as did others in Hesse. Around 80 people protested in Kassel.
Police said about 2,500 people demonstrated in Frankfurt on Sunday, calling for a review of the possibility of banning the AfD.

OpenAI Just Claimed a Huge Math Discovery. Some Academics Are Crying Foul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:42:05 UTC
01:42:05 KST

OpenAI said today that it has found an AI-generated solution to one of the biggest problems in mathematics—a 200-year-old equation that describes the natural behavior of fluids like water and air.
The announcement appears to demonstrate the stunning power for AI to advance mathematics. But it has been marred by claims from another mathematician, Tristan Buckmaster, who says that OpenAI rushed ahead to solve the problem after learning of the work of Buckmaster and a colleague—Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge. Buckmaster claims OpenAI also tried to influence who got credit for the work.
The proof concerns the Navier-Stokes equation, one of the unsolved problems in the Clay Millennium prizes, which are each worth $1 million.
Sebastien Bubeck, a mathematician and AI researcher at OpenAI, said in a press briefing that the company began training a new AI model with advanced mathematical capabilities on August 28.
After reading rumors that Anthropic was making progress toward solving Navier-Stokes, Bubeck said the company decided to dedicate more resources to tackling the problem. The company had more than 1,000 agents tackle the problem over more than 50 hours; eventually, as many as 10,000 agents were hard at work before the company discovered that it had come up with a solution.
“I thought there must be a mistake somewhere,” Bubeck said. “And on Sunday morning we had the final solution, Lean-formalized and everything.” (Lean is a programming language that can be used to formalize mathematical proofs.)
OpenAI noted that solving this problem required using considerably more computing power than it had previously spent on solving mathematical problems. The amount required cost “in the millions of dollars,” said Mark Chen, head of research at OpenAI.
On Monday, Alpöge and Buckmaster, a mathematician at NYU, posted documents claiming key advances in an area relevant to the Navier-Stokes problem. The pair says they used several AI models, including Claude and Codex, to complete their work.
Buckmaster also posted a statement claiming that, last week, he learned that OpenAI had become aware of his and Alpöge’s work and had started putting significant resources toward the problem. Buckmaster claims that he asked OpenAI leaders about whether the company had accessed the pair’s Codex logs. He says he was told the model “didn’t look up user data” but claims the company didn’t respond to questions about training. He then says that OpenAI offered several “proposals,” including one in which Buckmaster could publish a paper announcing the Navier-Stokes problem had been solved by an internal OpenAI model but without Alpöge’s name included.
In a post on social media, Bubeck pushed back on the idea that the company had suggested removing Alpöge’s name. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also stepped into the fight, and defended the team's work.
Buckmaster, Alpöge, and Anthropic did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
In the briefing, Bubeck and other OpenAI executives denied that the company had ever inspected the pair’s Codex prompts in order to inform their work. “We, whether it’s the researchers or the agents, did not see any of their work until it was released publicly last night,” he said.
In a blog post detailing the work, the company wrote, “while unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models.”
“I want to be extremely clear that we recognize the priority of Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster’s work on unforced Euler, and we have nothing but congratulations to them on this monumental achievement that they have made. To be clear, we did not use their prompt or proof to prompt our models or direct our agents,” said Bubeck.
Ven Chandrasekaran, a mathematician at the company, also emphasized that their solution was significantly different in nature from the one produced by OpenAI’s model.
The spat over who gets credit for solving one of the biggest problems in math may rumble on for a while. As AI takes on more of the work involved with finding proofs, such fights could perhaps become more common.

The arrival of the ‘ber months’ signals start of Christmas in the Philippines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:50 UTC
01:41:50 KST

At a city block-sized market in the Philippine capital, a platoon of plastic Santa Claus figures parachute from the ceiling of a shop already stacked high with Christmas decor, despite the holiday being fully four months away.
The site is a familiar one in the Philippines, where Sept. 1 means radio stations playing Christmas carols, homeowners putting up lights, and the country’s giant shopping malls unleashing their most impressive displays.
Welcome to the “ber months” — September, October, November, December — a months-long countdown to the most anticipated holiday on the calendar in the deeply Catholic country.
Photo: AFP
“We can smell it coming,” sales clerk Cora Lansangan, 73, said during a reporter’s visit to a Christmas shop that began stacking its shelves on July 31.
The store was already packed with shoppers buzzing around displays of Christmas trees, ornaments, plastic reindeer, mangers and festive lanterns.
“Even though life is hard, the mere sight of a Christmas tree brings us relief,” Manila real-estate agent Kathlene Santidad, 33, said, as she hunted for tinsel and baubles for her own tree, armed with a 10,000-peso (US$160) budget.
She said she shopped for decorations early because “I hate crowds” and wanted to take her time picking specific items from shops crammed with everything from tiny 300-peso tinsel to an 8,000-peso Christmas tree.
Coming toward the end of a rainy season typically marred by destructive typhoons and floods, the Christmas countdown is a marker of better things ahead, said Mark Godwin Villareal, a sociologist at Manila’s University of Santo Tomas.
“It provides a kind of continuity and stability in our social life, despite these economic, political, or even personal challenges that we are facing as a community or society,” he said.
The “ber months” had a rhythm, Villareal said.
September was for decorating, while October was time to start saving money for gifts and food for reunions with friends and relatives and the all-important midnight meal on Christmas Eve.
More than 100,000 of the country’s crucial overseas workforce, dubbed OFWs (overseas Filipino workers), can typically be counted on to rush home in time for the main event.
The extended season drives foot traffic and sales for the country’s giant shopping malls, many of which AFP journalists saw were already heavily decked out.
“For Filipinos, Christmas symbolizes belonging, faith, hope and joy,” said Christian Mathay, senior assistant vice president for SM Supermalls, a chain of 90 shopping malls that began setting up Christmas ornaments in August.
“Starting early gives shoppers more time to enjoy that experience,” he said.
In Pampanga province, north of Manila, weeks of flooding that stranded thousands of commuters failed to dampen the enthusiasm of manufacturers of star-shaped holiday lanterns known as parol, the single must-have Christmas decoration in a Filipino home.
“Water seeped into the showroom, so we had to clean up instead of working ... the thing with lanterns is, they’re waterproof,” said fifth-generation lantern-maker Angelica David, 26.
“We all need to recover from the floods. After that, people should start buying lanterns,” she said.
The decorations will only come down on Jan. 6, marked in the Philippines as the day when the magi brought gifts for the infant Jesus.
School superintendent Ricky Angeles, on a Christmas shopping trip to Manila, said he preferred to leave his lantern hanging all year round in a window of his home in the northern city of Cabanatuan, along with blinking strings of lights in his garden.
“We need a lengthy display period” to justify their cost, the 51-year-old said with a smile.
Then he ducked into a store to buy some more.
Singapore’s air quality hit an unhealthy level yesterday, as haze from forest fires raging in Indonesia continued to spread across swathes of Southeast Asia. The city-state is currently one of the 10 most-polluted major cities in the world, coming in at third in IQAir’s ranking. Kuching, in the Malaysian part of the island of Borneo, was No. 1. A government taskforce has “activated haze response plans” for schools, workplaces and community centers, Singaporean Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu (傅海) said in a video message on Facebook. Most people could continue essential daily activities, but the elderly or vulnerable should

Server shipments to soar 15.1 percent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:41:50 UTC
01:41:50 KST

Global server shipments this year are expected to grow 15.1 percent year-on-year to 16.6 million units, while artificial intelligence (AI) server shipments are forecast to rise 20.7 percent to 4.6 million units, the Market Intelligence and Consulting Institute (MIC) said yesterday.
Next year, global server shipments are estimated to grow 12.4 percent year-on-year to 18.6 million units and AI server shipments are predicted to rise about 18 percent to 5.4 million units, MIC deputy director-general Edward Lin (林柏齊) told a news conference in Taipei.
Growth next year would be driven by AI infrastructure investment by major cloud service providers and AI model developers, as well as neocloud providers’ accelerated deployment of computing capacity to meet global inference demand, he said.
Photo: Meryl Kao, Taipei Times
Robust AI infrastructure momentum is expected to continue through 2028 and is unlikely to fade before 2030, Lin said.
Private-sector investment is continuing to grow as cloud service providers, technology companies and data center operators increase spending on servers, networking equipment, memory, power and cooling systems, he said.
Initiatives such as the Stargate Project in the US, the EU’s planned AI Gigafactories and China’s computing network strategy are moving toward the procurement and funding stage, creating new opportunities for Taiwanese and global AI supply chains, he said.
Taiwanese server makers — including Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海), Quanta Computer Inc (廣達), Inventec Corp (英業達), Wistron Corp (緯創), Wiwynn Corp (緯穎), Pegatron Corp (和碩) and Giga Computing Technology Corp (技鋼) — have accelerated their diversification of production to meet customer demand, Lin said.
Their production sites span Taiwan, China, the US, Southeast Asia and Mexico, he said.
Plants in Thailand and Malaysia are being tasked with higher-end system assembly, while those in Vietnam mainly focus on “Level 6 (L6)” compute-tray assembly, Lin said.
The companies also use Mexico and the US as interconnected manufacturing hubs, with Mexican plants mainly handling Level 10 (L10) assembly, while US plants, being closer to major cloud service providers, focus on Level 11 (L11) assembly, rack configuration and delivery, he said.
The diversification of Taiwanese server production to the US, Mexico and Southeast Asia would be a continuing trend, driven by customer demand for local manufacturing and geopolitical risk management, Lin told the Taipei Times on the sidelines of the forum.
“These manufacturers’ overseas capacity is expected to increase, but Taiwan would remain their main production base for AI servers,” he said.
Taiwan’s server industry would not be hollowed out, as global server demand is still expanding and the value of local production could continue to grow despite some capacity moving abroad, he said.
In the near term, Taiwan is likely to retain production of graphics processing units, next-generation server platform design, prototype development and validation, given its concentration of semiconductor and component suppliers, Lin said.
High-value, compact modules could be shipped overseas for further assembly, he said.
Large systems and rack-scale integration from L10 to L11 are more likely to move closer to overseas customers first, where local assembly can reduce transport and logistics costs, he said.
As manufacturing experience improves later, overseas plants could gradually take on more manufacturing stages, including L6 assembly, he said.
The extent of the shift would depend on whether upstream suppliers establish local operations alongside system makers, he added.
