Germany says it will transfer PAC-2 missiles from its stocks to Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
18:06:00 EEST
00:06:00 KST

Germany says it will transfer PAC-2 missiles from its stocks to Ukraine
Germany will transfer PAC-2 interceptor missiles to Ukraine from its own stocks and is calling on other states to follow suit.
Source: German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius, speaking ahead of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group (also known as the Ramstein format) meeting on 8 September in a video conference format, as reported by a European Pravda correspondent
Details: Pistorius announced that PAC-2 missiles will be supplied to Ukraine from Bundeswehr (Germany's Armed Forces) stockpiles.
Quote: "I've decided... to deliver urgently needed PAC-2 interceptor missiles from Bundeswehr stocks to Ukraine. I appeal to all members of the UDCG to look into their own stocks and make similar deliveries."
More details: Pistorius pointed out that air defence is Ukraine's most urgent requirement.
He did not specify exactly how many missiles will be transferred.
Quote: "Since Russia is only advancing very slowly on the front line, it is trying to destroy Ukraine's economic base and critical infrastructure by way of air raids on port installations, power plants and other civilian targets. Unfortunately, we can expect Russian air raids to increase again once temperatures drop, and then the damage will be even greater."
More details: Pistorius called on all allies to "take the right measures to increase Ukraine's resilience".
Quote: "I'm aware that it is not easy to strike a balance between one's own security requirements and urgently needed support to Ukraine. But please, if in doubt, decide in favour of Ukraine. From NATO's perspective, further substantial deliveries of Patriot interceptor missiles by allies are acceptable."
Background:
- It was reported earlier that the EU has agreed to purchase Patriot missiles for Ukraine worth €3.2 billion.
- Kaja Kallas, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, also said that during the informal meeting of EU foreign ministers in Wicklow, Ireland, on 2 September, several EU member states made new commitments to provide Ukraine with interceptor missiles.
- On 8 September, it was reported that the United Kingdom is providing £100 million (US$135 million) for an air defence package for Ukraine ahead of winter, including Patriot missiles. The weapons will be supplied through the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) programme.

Endangered Sumatran tigers born in Greece as zoos build safety net
Three two-month-old Sumatran tiger cubs receive identification microchips and their first vaccinations at a zoo near Athens
The world’s most endangered tigers have started a family in Greece, offering hope for a predator rapidly vanishing from the wild.
Three two-month-old Sumatran tiger cubs received identification microchips and their first vaccinations on Tuesday at a zoo near Athens, as part of a global effort to build a backup population.
The Sumatran tiger, classified as critically endangered, is found only on the Indonesian island of Sumatra, which is slightly larger than Sweden.
As few as 400 are believed to remain in the wild, mainly because of aggressive forest clearing. It joins the South China tiger and the Malayan tiger in the category of severe risk.
“The Sumatran tiger is one of the most threatened tiger species in the world, and among felines in general,” said Theodoros Babilis, head keeper of cats and monkeys at Attica Zoological Park.

11 European nations and Canada announce trade sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:03:38 UTC
00:03:38 KST

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband accused "settler terrorists" of "ethnic cleansing" in areas of the West Bank and said the UK was bringing in an "import ban on goods from illegal settlements." Israel closed the British consulate in Jerusalem in response.
The UK and France were among 12 countries to announce new trade sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank on Tuesday, amid what they called a "rapidly deteriorating" situation marked by increasing settler attacks on Palestinians.
Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden joined the UK and France in confirming plans to introduce restrictions on trade with settlements, according to a joint statement from the countries' foreign ministers.
"The Government of Israel’s actions in the West Bank are undermining the possibility of a two-State solution," the statement reads, adding that there have been "unprecedented levels of settler violence and settlement expansion."
"Together, we are resolute: the two-state solution must be protected, and we will take action in pursuit of a just and lasting peace," it continued.
It comes after the Israeli government last month opened up tenders for the construction of around 1,200 housing units in the West Bank, drawing widespread condemnation from the international community and human rights groups.
The units, destined for the E1 settlement area, would further isolate East Jerusalem from the rest of the territory.
In their statement on Tuesday, the 12 foreign ministers called the decision to publish tenders "unacceptable."
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney "have agreed on the need to take action to prevent further damage," the statement added.
'Ethnic cleansing'
Speaking to parliament on Tuesday, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband accused "settler terrorists" of "ethnic cleansing" in areas of the West Bank, saying that the Israeli government had often "turned a blind eye to this."
He announced that the UK would also be bringing in an "import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories."
"I do not believe the British people want us supporting the occupation by accepting products from settlements in our shops and supermarkets," he told MPs.
In a post on X, Miliband's French counterpart, Jean-Noël Barrot, said Paris had taken the decision to enforce the sanctions as the West Bank was "on the brink of explosion."
"Unchecked expansion of settlements in violation of international law, a surge in violence committed by extremist settlers against Palestinians, and acts of terror condemned by the Israeli authorities themselves," he wrote.
Burnham later issued his own statement on Tuesday evening, calling the newly announced measures "carefully judged, targeted steps that are not aimed at the Israeli people, but at the unacceptable policies of the current Israeli government."
"Before I became Prime Minister, I said our country’s response had been too slow and simply not good enough. That’s why I committed to changing the government’s approach," the UK leader added.
Israel responds
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar on Tuesday ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem in response to the moves taken by Westminster, as he hit out at Miliband's statement.
"The accusations made today by the foreign secretary in the British Parliament were outrageous lies," Sa'ar said.
Israel has also announced that it will henceforth refuse entry to 12 British nationals.
The list reportedly includes former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, his Your Party cofounder and MP for Coventry South Zarah Sultana, and Diane Abbott, the MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington.
The West Bank
The West Bank has been occupied by Israel since 1967 and has seen a surge in violence since the start of the war in Gaza, which broke out following the Hamas militant group's attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023.
According to a report from the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, there were around 737,000 Israeli settlers in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, as of October 2024.
Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.

China, UK should boost cooperation: Xi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:03:04 UTC
00:03:04 KST

President Xi Jinping on Tuesday said China and Britain are comprehensive strategic partners and share more common interests than differences in a phone conversation with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Xi urged the two countries to respect and trust each other, seek common ground and expand mutually beneficial cooperation, according to Xinhua News Agency.
The president also called on the UK to fully protect the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese investors.
Pointing out that China and Britain are both major countries in science and technology with rich resources in education, culture, sports and other fields, Xi called on the two sides to maintain an open and forward-looking mentality and strengthen exchanges and cooperation in various fields.
He added that the two countries should strengthen communication and coordination within frameworks such as the United Nations, the Group of 20 and the World Trade Organization, and promote an equal and orderly multipolar world and a universally beneficial and inclusive economic globalisation.
A readout from Burnham's office said they discussed the "importance of pragmatic cooperation", including on economic growth and raising living standards for people in both their countries.
“The prime minister said that he would engage frankly and constructively on issues that matter for both countries, and raised domestic security, Russia's war in Ukraine, Hong Kong, human rights and consular cases of particular importance," a Downing Street spokesperson said.
It was the first publicised conversation between the two leaders since Burnham took office in July. (Xinhua and agencies)

Moscow Used US Envoys to Deliver Tougher Peace Demands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:02:41 UTC
00:02:41 KST

A Trump administration attempt to jump-start stalled Russo-Ukrainian peace talks not only failed to bring the warring sides closer together, but wound up delivering to Kyiv even tougher Kremlin terms, opposition Ukrainian parliament member Anna Skorokhod said on Monday.
The main message brought to Ukraine by a senior US diplomatic delegation led by Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner and New York real estate billionaire Steve Witkoff was that Russia remains unwilling to compromise or offer concessions. Moreover, the Kremlin used the American envoys to deliver a new set of demands to Kyiv.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“It was not only not a diplomatic breakthrough, they [Witkoff and Kushner] arrived with even worse conditions than we had before. We see that on both sides there is no desire to communicate directly rather than through envoys, or to sit down at the negotiating table together,” Skorokhod said in part.
Skorokhod is a Kyiv region parliament member who broke with the ruling Servant of the People (SoP) party in 2019, citing what she described as corruption and favoritism toward big business in the party’s land reform agenda. She is now a minority faction member usually critical of the SoP, with reform and closer Ukrainian integration to Europe at the top of her agenda.
“All these attempts [to restart the peace process], as we can see, aren’t successful,” she said. “And the result has been that the Russian Federation now is setting forth even worse conditions… unfortunately, we have another complete failure in negotiations.”Skorokhod’s comments, made to a widely watched news and political program, contrasted sharply with upbeat remarks by Witkoff on Sunday, when he told Kyiv reporters that the negotiating process was moving forward.
US Destroys Five Iranian Oil Tankers as Tehran Threatens Vessels Off Kuwait, Bahrain
“I think we made significant progress in Moscow. We heard new ideas,” Witkoff said. “Jared [Kushner] and my job is to bring the sides together, reduce the differences between them, and establish effective channels of communication. Hopefully, we have started this constructively over the last 48 hours. We are confident that a successful solution can be found.”
According to Skorokhod, the Russian negotiating team headed by President Vladimir Putin, not only presented the Americans with a tougher set of demands for Ukraine but also made it clear to Witkoff and Kushner that the Kremlin would accept peace only on the terms dictated by Moscow. “If earlier [Russia] did not demand changes in the Ukrainian constitution conceding territories in the past, now they are,” Skorokhod said.
Russia’s most recent formal declaration of the peace terms it would accept from Ukraine, issued in June 2025, contained 31 demands amounting to Ukrainian capitulation. Among other conditions, the terms would require Ukraine to surrender roughly 20% of its territory to Russia, leaving an estimated 7 to 8 million Ukrainians as citizens of the Russian Federation.
Critically, Russia’s territorial demands call for Ukrainian forces to retreat from a New Jersey-sized area still under Kyiv’s control, clearing the way for Russian troops to occupy the territory and establish Kremlin rule.
Under Russian terms, Ukraine would also be required to declare neutrality, permanently abandon its bid for NATO membership and participation in other military alliances, ban foreign military forces from its territory, reaffirm its renunciation of nuclear weapons, cut its armed forces by approximately 80%, waive all claims for war damages against Russia, and remove all sanctions and tariffs on Russian goods and services.
Russian must also be made an official state language in Ukraine, the Kremlin-controlled Russian Orthodox Church must be allowed to operate freely, and the Ukrainian government must hold national elections and remove all officials, elected and otherwise, deemed by Russia to be “Nazis,” according to the Kremlin’s policy statement.
Ukrainian official and public rejection of those terms is nearly unanimous. Ukraine’s longstanding red line, that it will never agree to the transfer of Ukrainian territory, property, or people into formal Russian Federation control because doing so would legitimize Russia’s unprovoked invasion, meant that Witkoff and Kushner’s trip to Ukraine and Russia “was just political theater,” Skorokhod said.
Skorokhod said she was aware of other new, harsher Russian peace terms delivered by Kushner and Witkoff to Kyiv from the Kremlin, but said she did not want to make them public because she had received the information by unofficial means.
In a Monday article titled “New Ideas, Old Deadlock,” the leading Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda (UP) argued that the main objective of the Kushner-Witkoff mission was to revive negotiations by introducing “new ideas” regarding the status of Ukrainian territories occupied by Russia. However, the publication concluded that the US initiative was effectively stillborn and wasteful because the Russian and Ukrainian positions remain too far apart.
“It is already clear that a peace agreement is still far away. And although Trump’s envoys came with new ideas, their content and Russia’s willingness to agree to them remain unknown,” UP said.
The Ukrainian television news channel 24 Kanal, in a Monday report titled “No Promises, No Forgiveness: What Did the Witkoff and Kushner Visit Bring Ukraine?,” similarly predicted that the US initiative would yield no meaningful results. The report pointed to a three-and-a-half-hour “working lunch” between the American envoys and their Russian counterparts at Moscow’s upscale Avrora restaurant, known for its seafood cuisine, as possible evidence that the US negotiating team was not acting as a neutral intermediary.
Russian state television channel Rossiya 1, which aired its own footage and reporting from the restaurant, said the Russian and US delegations held their lunch meeting in a secured third-floor room. The broadcast also showed Kushner and Witkoff walking past a pair of signs above the restaurant entrance bearing the slogan “Everything for Victory!”
“Everything for Victory!” is familiar to millions of Russian schoolchildren and virtually all Russian citizens as a famous Soviet World War II slogan urging the population to make sacrifices in support of the fight against the German invasion. Today, the phrase is widely used by Russian state media to encourage Russians to accept lower living standards and economic hardship in support of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Most Russian state media reports highlighted that the American delegation refreshed itself at a Moscow restaurant whose facade prominently displayed the well-known wartime slogan “Everything for Victory!” However, the coverage did not address whether Kushner and Witkoff were aware that they had been escorted to lunch beneath signage now used by the Russian state to rally public support for the war against Ukraine, nor whether they knew they were being photographed and filmed by state-controlled media as they entered the venue.
Avrora owner Anton Pinsky later published a video suggesting that the visit by the American delegation was a testament to the restaurant’s quality. As a mark of what he called the “honor” of hosting the talks, Pinsky said he would rename the third-floor private dining room the “Hall of Peaceful Negotiations.”
“We very much hope that this and future meetings there [in the Avrora private dining room] will bring a result to our country. A result, that will be in the interests of Russia,” Pinsky said in a comment attached to the video.
At a Monday press conference in Kyiv, Witkoff was asked by a local reporter how, as an American businessman, he could sit down for negotiations with Putin, the leader who launched Europe’s largest war since World War II and who is the subject of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over the unlawful deportation and transfer of thousands of Ukrainian children from occupied areas of Ukraine to Russia. “We have always been received with respect by President Putin and his team. Relationships are crucial to resolving such conflicts,” Witkoff said.
During televised remarks to Putin on Sept. 5, Witkoff said: “First of all, President Putin, thank you so much for having us. We were sitting outside just now, me, Jared [Kushner], and [Russian chief negotiator] Kirill Dmitriev, and then [Putin senior aide] Yuri Ushakov joined us, and we were all talking about when we retire, we’ll have all these incredible stories and incredible memories, and yours [Putin’s] will be right at the top of it all.”

Saudi Arabia strikes back after Houthis hit oil sites in heaviest attack in years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:02:30 UTC
00:02:30 KST

Houthi missiles struck Abha International Airport, King Khalid Air Base and Aramco facilities, injuring 73 and forcing temporary shutdowns at oil sites. Saudi Arabia launched strikes on Taiz and Marib provinces, as analysts said Riyadh now faced a "spiral of escalation".
Saudi Arabia hit back with a series of strikes on Tuesday after the Iran-backed Houthis targeted oil facilities and other sites across the border in their heaviest attack in years.
The rapid exchange of fire follows the unravelling of a four-year truce in July, months into the war between the United States and Iran.
Saudi strikes hit Taiz province, where deadly fighting has raged for days, and Marib province, the Houthis' Almasirah TV station said. There was no immediate comment from Riyadh.
Overnight, Houthi attacks caused "temporary" shutdowns at oil sites and left 73 injured, authorities said. Saudi officials had vowed to respond.
The latest strikes add to a rapidly deteriorating situation in Yemen, where hundreds have died in recent days as the Houthis try to capture land at the mouth of the Red Sea from the forces of the internationally-recognised government.
The Houthis, who control about one-third of Yemen's territory — albeit the most densely populated parts — are vying to seize the narrow Bab al-Mandeb strait, an increasingly important route for oil after Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz, slowing Gulf exports to a trickle.
Houthi attacks on oil infrastructure and Saudi tankers have further contributed to a spike in oil prices, which leapt towards $100 a barrel on Tuesday.
Houthis claim revenge
The group accused Riyadh on Monday of an attack on a prison that killed 11 people and left 20 inmates missing, according to the Houthi-controlled Almasirah TV channel.
The Houthis said they fired dozens of ballistic missiles, hitting Abha International Airport, King Khalid air base and facilities belonging to Saudi state oil giant Aramco in Abha and Jizan.
An energy ministry source told the Saudi Press Agency that "several energy sector facilities and installations" in the south were targeted.
"The attacks caused fires at several locations, leading to a temporary halt in some operations" as well as several injuries, the source said.
Jizan, on the Red Sea coast just north of Saudi's Yemen border, has one of the country's biggest oil refineries with a capacity of 400,000 barrels per day.
According to maritime tracking company Kpler, it was out of action for several weeks until at least 20 August following earlier Houthi attacks.
Saudi Arabia's Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan said the door to diplomacy was still open, but Riyadh was ready to defend itself.
"The Kingdom will always support peace and diplomatic solutions," he said during a press conference in Moscow.
"However, (Saudi Arabia) will not hesitate to defend itself, protect its interests, and support measures that secure the interests, security, and stability of brotherly Yemen."
'Spiral of escalation'
The Houthis triggered a return to hostilities in Yemen's civil war in July, when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace. Riyadh retaliated by striking the airport.
The Saudi-led coalition, which has been fighting the Houthis on the internationally recognised government's behalf since 2015, said it would "take all necessary measures and actions to respond to the sources of the threat and neutralise its danger".
Andreas Krieg, a Gulf expert from King's College London, said the Houthi attacks create an "extremely uncomfortable dilemma" for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the de facto Saudi ruler.
After years of trying to withdraw from the Yemen war, "restraint now carries the risk of allowing the Houthis to dictate the spiral of escalation," he said.
"Saudi Arabia's immediate response is likely to remain measured, involving airstrikes, intelligence support, and the reinforcement of Yemeni government forces," Krieg added.
"Should attacks on Saudi cities persist, maintaining this restraint will become increasingly difficult. In effect, the Houthis are testing exactly where Riyadh's true red line now lies."
Formally known as Ansar Allah, the Houthis came to power in late 2014 after storming Sana'a and seizing the presidential palace and key military sites, forcing Yemen's government into exile.
The group is part of Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance — a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.
While the Houthis do not control the part of Yemen’s coastline along Bab el-Mandeb, they hold territory less than 100 kilometres away.
The strait, whose name in Arabic means "Gate of Tears," connects the southern Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, and carries roughly 12% of global maritime trade.
The Houthis disrupted it severely with their campaign against Israel-linked shipping during the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza, claiming it was a show of support for Palestinians.

Israel hits back at UK sanctions, closes Jerusalem consulate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:02:11 UTC
00:02:11 KST

Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar announced a series of retaliatory measures against Britain on Tuesday evening after London unveiled economic sanctions targeting Israeli settlements in the West Bank, escalating a diplomatic dispute over settlement policy and the future of a two-state solution.
The measures include closing the British Consulate in Jerusalem, removing British representatives from the Gaza multinational coordination headquarters in the southern city of Kiryat Gat, ending British involvement in training Palestinian Authority security forces in Ramallah and barring 12 British elected officials from entering Israel.
Sa’ar said the 12 officials had been involved in what he described as antisemitic and anti-Israel activity and had denied Israel’s right to exist. They were later identified as lawmakers Jeremy Corbyn, Zarah Sultana, Naz Shah, Diane Abbott, Hannah Spencer, Carla Denyer, Sian Berry, Ellie Chowns, John McDonnell, Richard Burgon and Adrian Ramsay, as well as Fahad Ansari, director of Riverway to the Sea.
“Britain initiated and led the current move — it planned it long in advance,” Sa'ar said. He added that Israel could take measures against other countries involved in the initiative at its discretion.
“The message to every government that harms us is this: Whoever acts against Israel, Israel will act against them, and they will lose their influence and relevance,” Sa'ar said. “Steps against Israel will not go unanswered.”
Britain announced Tuesday that it would impose economic sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank as part of what Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband described as a policy aimed at preserving the possibility of a two-state solution. Britain said it would restrict settlement goods and target companies providing services including construction, financing and real estate to settlements. London said the measures were directed at settlements rather than Israel itself and that broader trade with Israel would continue.
Britain also said it would maintain its suspension of 30 arms export licenses related to Israeli military operations in Gaza and refuse licenses for weapons sales that it determines contribute to settlement activity in the West Bank.
The announcement came alongside a joint statement from Britain, Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden saying they intended to impose trade restrictions on settlements they consider illegal under international law. The countries accused the Israeli government of undermining prospects for a two-state solution and called on it to halt settlement expansion and address settler violence.
Most of the international community considers Israeli settlements in the West Bank illegal under international law, a position Israel disputes.
Sa'ar accused Britain’s Labour government of acting for domestic political reasons ahead of the party’s conference later this month.
“The British move is morally distorted and constitutes blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state,” Sa'ar said. “The Jewish people have a right to live throughout the Land of Israel no less than the British have a right to live in Britain or the French in France.”
Sa'ar also invoked the 1917 Balfour Declaration, in which Britain expressed support for the establishment of a “national home for the Jewish people” in Palestine. He argued that Jewish rights in what is now the West Bank were encompassed by the subsequent British Mandate for Palestine.
“A boycott of products from Judea and Samaria is a despicable practice that harms a productive, law-abiding population,” Sa'ar said, using the biblical names commonly used in Israel for the West Bank. “Sanctions on services are abhorrent.”
Sa'ar also accused the British government of interfering in Israel’s election campaign, saying London was attempting to influence Israeli voters and pressure Israel into accepting a Palestinian state.
“The Labour government’s decision constitutes blatant interference in the election campaign of a sovereign state,” he said. “It is a crude and unacceptable attempt by a foreign country to influence the election.”
Sa'ar asserted that the Israeli public overwhelmingly opposes Palestinian statehood, pointing to the Oslo peace process of the 1990s, the establishment of the Palestinian Authority, Israel’s unilateral withdrawal from Gaza in 2005, the second Palestinian intifada and the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel.
“After everything we have seen,” Sa'ar said, Israelis reject what he described as the establishment of “a jihadist terrorist state in the heart of the Land of Israel.”
Britain says its measures are intended to achieve the opposite objective. Miliband said the two-state solution was the guiding principle of British policy and accused settlement expansion of undermining the possibility of creating a Palestinian state alongside Israel. British officials stressed that the measures were not intended as a boycott of Israel as a whole.
Sa'ar rejected the argument that international pressure could bring the sides closer to resolving the conflict.
“The Israeli-Palestinian conflict is an age-old conflict,” he said. “Unfortunately, the Palestinians have always rejected proposals for a solution and have never moved away from terrorism and incitement.”
“This conflict will not be resolved by declarations from London and Paris,” he added. “An anti-Israel approach only moves us further away from a solution instead of bringing it closer.”
A senior British official told ynet that the decision to impose sanctions on settlements in the West Bank followed growing concern over settler violence.
“The extremists have completely lost it. The violence is severe,” the official said. “More than 2,200 Palestinians have been displaced from their homes since January. From the British government’s perspective, it’s impossible to ignore this. They felt they had to do something.”
The official said Israel had not informed Britain of any planned retaliation. “If there are steps, you enter into a tit-for-tat, and that doesn’t benefit anyone,” the official said, adding that “UK-Israel relations are strong.”
The confrontation follows warnings earlier Tuesday from President Isaac Herzog, who called the sanctions a “grave miscalculation” and also characterized them as interference in Israel’s elections. Herzog urged foreign governments to abandon sanctions in favor of dialogue and argued that restrictions could also hurt Palestinians employed by settlement businesses.
The Labour government had previously sanctioned individual Israeli settlers and unauthorized outposts over alleged violence against Palestinians and unauthorized development. The new measures significantly broaden that approach by targeting trade in goods and potentially services connected to West Bank settlements.

Flushing the toilet can release a ‘plume’ of breathable pathogens – and closing the lid won’t stop their escape
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:00:43 UTC
00:00:43 KST

Flushing toilets release particles into the “breathing zone” of adults and can remain suspended in the air for at least 20 seconds, a new study has found.
And closing the lid might not be enough to avoid a “plume” of potential pathogens.
Meanwhile, previous research has shown public toilets are an inescapable hotbed of microbes.
Flinders University researchers reviewed 22 studies of toilet-generated aerosols, publishing the results in the Science of the Total Environment journal.
They found microbes from the water used for flushing or from contamination of the bowl ended up as aerosols, with more “turbulent” flushing releasing more particles.
That included bioaerosols – aerosols that contain biological material and can transmit pathogens including legionella, influenza and norovirus. There are differing reports about whether Covid spreads through toilet aerosols.
The researchers found higher levels of aerosols in the water and higher levels of turbulence during the flush increased the volume of particles suspended in the air, but the effects of bathroom ventilation and whether the lid was up or down were unclear.
Despite that, lead author and PhD student Lira Adiyani said she would still recommend putting the lid down after using the toilet.
“Toilet flushing creates turbulence that can release aerosols into the surrounding air,” she said.
“Some studies detected these aerosols at adult breathing height, indicating a potential pathway for inhalation exposure.
“The more microbes present in the toilet, the more bioaerosols may be released. Therefore, larger flush volumes generally produce more aerosols.”
Adiyani said “based on the available evidence” she would still recommend closing the lid as a precautionary measure, “while recognising that it does not completely prevent aerosols from escaping”.
In the report, the researchers wrote that the effects of indoor aerosols had been “understudied” despite the risk of infection. This had “important implications for risk assessment, building design, and infection control in an era of water security pressures and emerging infectious diseases”, they wrote.
“Indoor aerosols influence air quality and human health as their small size allows them to penetrate deep into the respiratory tract when inhaled, providing a direct exposure pathway.”
Co-author, environmental health professor Harriet Whiley, said people didn’t have to be worried in their own homes, unless someone in the house was immunocompromised.
She said the team was working on “protecting the most vulnerable through good design” in places such as hospitals and aged care environments.
They are increasingly concerned about “opportunistic pathogens” that can be present in water, particularly recycled or rainwater. “They don’t affect healthy people,” she said. “But if you’re immunocompromised you can get very sick, and it can be fatal.”
So it’s about getting “an effective flush with less volume and less turbulence”, she said.
Dr Lotti Tajouri, an associate professor in molecular genetics at Bond and Murdoch universities wasn’t involved in the research but warned bathroom dangers go well beyond the toilet.
His own research is particularly focused on public toilets and mobile phone use in toilets.
“As soon as you enter a toilet, consider everything contaminated,” he said.
The door will have microbes on it, as will the floor – so you should never put anything on it, he said. Then you might touch the lid, after which you flush with the lid up or down.
If it’s up, you get the “plume” effect, an “explosion or aerosols … you are literally sprayed [with]”.
Flushing with the lid down might limit your exposure to the plume, but depending on the cleanliness of the toilet, previous users have left microorganisms on every surface anyway. “The roof, the walls, the floor,” he said.
Then, you touch the toilet door again, before (hopefully) washing your hands. But you will probably touch the taps again, blow microorganisms around with the hairdryer, touch the exit door and then touch your phone.
“Studies show between 50% and 80% of people use mobile phones in the toilet. For younger generations it’s almost 100%,” he said. “They will contaminate their phones and fingers with fecal microorganisms – salmonella, campylobacter, all sorts of bacteria and viruses.
“The less contact you have, the better it is.”

Organised crime driving illicit cigarette factory boom ‘in almost every EU state’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:00:42 UTC
00:00:42 KST

The illegal trade in tobacco is booming in the EU, according to a report by the bloc’s financial watchdog, with almost one in 10 cigarettes produced illicitly or smuggled, causing an estimated €13bn loss in tax revenue each year.
The European Court of Auditors (ECA) said in a report on Tuesday that the trade had “changed significantly” in recent years as smuggling, while still “a problem”, was overtaken by illicit manufacturing, which has increased dramatically in the bloc.
Organised crime gangs are moving production inside the EU “to shorten supply chains and get closer to consumers”, said the ECA’s Petri Sarvamaa. “Illegal production sites have now been detected in almost every EU member state.”
The ECA cited the example of a large-scale illicit cigarette factory in Belgium dismantled by police last year. It operated around the clock, with 50 workers running four production lines, each able to produce 1m cigarettes every hour.
During a raid on the largest illegal facility so far uncovered, in Spain, police seized 3m packs of cigarettes valued at €15m, five tonnes of raw tobacco worth €5m, and made 20 arrests. The factory’s products had been distributed across six EU countries.
“The scale is quite remarkable,” Sarvamaa said. “Last month French authorities dismantled a cross-border operation that had been supplying the city of Lille only since last December but had already made 120 deliveries of 7,500 packs each.”
The ECA report said such illicit cigarette factories, which usually operate for two- to four months, were using sophisticated equipment and employing experienced technicians to set up and maintain their machinery.
The organised crime groups that run them split production across multiple facilities and often locate them in border regions, tailoring their operations by producing specific brands for individual markets and even developing new tobacco products.
The damage goes beyond lost tax revenue. The trade “undermines public health policies by making tobacco products cheaper and more accessible, especially to young people”, Sarvamaa said. It also feeds organised crime and finances other illegal activities.
While, overall, tobacco consumption has continued to fall across the EU, the quantity of illicit tobacco products has risen steadily, reaching about 8.8 % of total cigarette consumption in 2023 (the latest figures available), the report said – although information about the size, structure or economic impact of the trade remains “incomplete and unreliable”.
The report said the EU and many member states had taken steps to combat the trade, but were hampered because European law in the area was not harmonised and member states’ efforts were uneven, leaving enforcement gaps.
National control systems and enforcement have different definitions of offences and of penalties, encouraging criminals to move to the more lax jurisdictions, and information exchanges in the bloc were inconsistent.
“Criminals involved in the illicit tobacco trade are succeeding not because Europe lacks legislation but because gaps remain in coordination, information and enforcement,” Sarvamaa said. “Organised crime has a strategy. We need one too.”

US laser weapon maker gets its first foreign buyer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:00:21 UTC
00:00:21 KST

- AeroVironment secured its first international order for the LOCUST laser weapon system, worth more than $50 million, the company said September 8.
- The buyer, unit quantity and delivery timeline were not disclosed, and the order follows the company's $464.8 million U.S. Army E-HEL contract.
AeroVironment has received its first international order for the LOCUST laser weapon system, a purchase worth more than $50 million, the company announced September 8.
The direct commercial sale covers an initial batch of LOCUST systems and support services. AeroVironment did not disclose the buying country, the number of units included, or a delivery date.
The order comes two months after AeroVironment won a $464.8 million contract from the U.S. Army for its Enduring-High Energy Laser program, known as E-HEL. AeroVironment has described that contract as the first production award for high-energy laser weapons in U.S. history. The company did not specify how many LOCUST units the Army contract covers.
“This first international order signals increasing global recognition that high-energy laser weapon systems are essential to modern air defense,” said Wahid Nawabi, president, chairman and chief executive officer at AeroVironment.
“The threat from low-cost drones is global and has fundamentally changed the economics of warfare,” Nawabi said. “LOCUST gives our customers an affordable, scalable way to defeat drone threats at scale without relying solely on expensive interceptors.”
LOCUST is a high-energy laser system built to track and destroy Group 1 through Group 3 drones, a category that covers small quadcopters up to fixed-wing aircraft weighing up to 600 kg (1,320 pounds). The system can be mounted at a fixed site, moved on a pallet, or installed on a vehicle, and it can link to other radars and command networks already in use by a customer.
AeroVironment says each LOCUST shot costs less than $10, a fraction of the price of a missile interceptor. The company has cited that cost advantage as the main selling point for militaries facing repeated drone attacks, where traditional air defense missiles can cost tens of thousands of dollars per shot.
“This first international order for LOCUST is a pivotal milestone in our directed energy roadmap,” said Mary Clum, president of space, cyber and directed energy at AeroVironment. “We are not only accelerating the fielding of an operationally proven laser weapon system, we are also establishing a foundation for sustained and expanded international adoption to provide layered innovation in counter-drone defense.”
LOCUST has already been used in U.S. military testing and operations. AeroVironment says the system carried out the U.S. military’s first acknowledged laser kills along the southern border and shot down multiple drones during a demonstration aboard the USS George H. W. Bush. The company has also integrated LOCUST onto Infantry Squad Vehicles and Joint Light Tactical Vehicles under the Army’s AMP-HEL program, and has run live-fire tests at White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth operated the system during one of those tests, according to AeroVironment.
The Federal Aviation Administration and the Department of War have signed a safety agreement that creates a pathway for LOCUST to operate in U.S. airspace, following an FAA review of the system.
To meet rising orders, AeroVironment is spending more than $30 million to expand its manufacturing campus in Albuquerque, New Mexico. The company says the expansion will add more than 450 jobs and generate over $670 million in economic impact, and will serve as a production hub for directed energy, space and other defense systems.

Antidepressants show wide variation in physical side effects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:00:10 UTC
00:00:10 KST

Different antidepressants can have drastically different effects on a patient’s physical health, according to a recent review of medical research. Some medications cause substantial weight gain and increased blood pressure, while others lead to weight loss and lowered heart rates. The findings were published in The Lancet.
Millions of people rely on prescription medications to manage mental health conditions. Up to 17 percent of adults in Europe and North America currently take antidepressants. While these drugs are effective at treating mood disorders, they can also cause unintended bodily changes. These physical side effects are a common reason why people stop taking their prescribed treatments.
Medical guidelines recommend that doctors discuss potential physical changes with patients before starting a prescription. However, it can be difficult for physicians to provide precise comparisons between specific drugs.
Toby Pillinger and Atheeshaan Arumuham of King’s College London led the research team to address this knowledge gap. They worked alongside other international experts, including Orestis Efthimiou of the University of Bern, Oliver D. Howes of King’s College London, and Andrea Cipriani of the University of Oxford. The team wanted to determine exactly how different medications compare in terms of physical side effects. They also wanted to see if factors like age or starting weight influenced these bodily reactions.
To answer these questions, the researchers conducted a network meta-analysis. This type of statistical study pools data from multiple independent trials. It allows researchers to compare treatments that might never have been tested directly against each other in the same room. By linking trials through a common comparator, researchers can estimate how two different drugs would perform head-to-head.
The team gathered data from 151 randomized controlled trials and 17 government regulatory reports. The resulting large study included 58,534 participants. The researchers evaluated 30 different antidepressants prescribed for acute psychiatric treatment, which typically lasted about eight weeks.
The analysis revealed major differences in how these drugs affect body weight. People taking agomelatine experienced the most weight loss, losing an average of about 2.4 kilograms compared to those taking a placebo, an inactive control pill. On the other end of the spectrum, maprotiline and amitriptyline caused the most weight gain, adding up to 1.8 kilograms on average. This created a roughly four-kilogram gap between the highest and lowest weight-altering medications.
The researchers estimated that almost half of the people taking maprotiline or amitriptyline would gain a noticeable amount of weight. Medications that caused the most weight gain were generally those known to block specific histamine and serotonin receptors, which act as chemical docking stations in the brain. Over time, extra weight can elevate a person’s risk for metabolic issues and joint stress.
Cardiovascular changes also varied widely depending on the specific medication. Nortriptyline increased patients’ heart rates by an average of nearly 14 beats per minute. By contrast, fluvoxamine lowered heart rates by about eight beats per minute. This difference amounts to a 21-beat-per-minute gap between the two drugs.
Blood pressure effects showed a similar split among the evaluated medications. Amitriptyline raised systolic blood pressure, which measures the pressure in your arteries when your heart beats, by almost five millimeters of mercury. Nortriptyline lowered the same metric by over six millimeters of mercury. The researchers noted that these cardiovascular shifts could influence a patient’s long-term risk for heart disease, especially if the changes persist over several years.
The medications that increased blood pressure were largely serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors, or tricyclic antidepressants. These drug classes share a mechanism that affects the neurotransmitter noradrenaline. This chemical messenger plays a well-documented role in blood pressure regulation.
The researchers also tracked metabolic markers like cholesterol and blood sugar. Paroxetine, duloxetine, desvenlafaxine, and venlafaxine were associated with measurable increases in total cholesterol. Duloxetine was also linked to increased blood glucose levels. These metabolic increases occurred even though the medications themselves generally caused patients to lose body weight.
Some medications also affected liver function tests. Duloxetine, desvenlafaxine, and levomilnacipran caused increases in the concentration of certain liver enzymes. These enzymes are proteins that help the organ filter blood and break down medications. While these enzyme elevations were substantial enough to measure, the researchers noted that the amounts were not high enough to pose an immediate medical threat to most patients.
The team did not find that any of the evaluated antidepressants altered heart rhythm intervals to a problematic degree. The medications also did not have a strong effect on sodium levels, potassium levels, or kidney function markers during the trial periods.
In a separate analysis, the researchers examined how patient characteristics influenced these side effects. They used a statistical technique called meta-regression to look for trends across the different study populations. They found that groups of patients with higher starting body weights experienced larger medication-induced increases in blood pressure and liver enzymes. Populations with a higher average age saw larger medication-induced increases in blood sugar.
Finally, the team wanted to know if experiencing physical side effects was linked to mental health improvements. In patients with severe psychiatric conditions like schizophrenia, past research has shown a correlation between metabolic disturbances and improved symptoms. To test this concept in depression, the researchers looked specifically at trials involving patients with major depressive disorder.
The researchers compared the change in depressive symptoms against changes in weight, cholesterol, and blood sugar across the studies. They did not find a correlation between improved mental health and metabolic side effects. This suggests that patients do not need to experience physical changes to get the mental health benefits of the medication.
A primary limitation of this research is the short duration of the included trials. Most studies lasted only eight weeks, meaning the long-term physical effects of these medications remain unconfirmed by this specific analysis. Some cardiovascular shifts might fade over time, while other metabolic changes could worsen over a period of years.
The trials also mostly included younger, relatively healthy individuals taking only one medication. This focus might obscure side effects that occur more frequently in older adults or people taking multiple drugs at once. Real-world observational data suggests that certain antidepressants might increase the risk of low sodium or heart rhythm problems in older populations. The researchers suggest that doctors should consider both clinical trial data and real-world observations when prescribing medications to older or medically vulnerable patients.
The study, “The effects of antidepressants on cardiometabolic and other physiological parameters: a systematic review and network meta-analysis,” was authored by Toby Pillinger, Atheeshaan Arumuham, Robert A McCutcheon, Enrico D’Ambrosio, Georgios Basdanis, Marco Branco, Richard Carr, Valeria Finelli, Toshi A Furukawa, Siobhan Gee, Adrian Heald, Sameer Jauhar, Zihan Ma, Valentina Mancini, Calum Moulton, Georgia Salanti, David M Taylor, Anneka Tomlinson, Allan H Young, Orestis Efthimiou, Oliver D Howes, and Andrea Cipriani.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is arriving in Colombia, the first stop on a Latin American tour designed to bolster pro-US leaders and cement influence over the region.
The recent election of Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, a hard-right lawyer, has been a game-changer for Washington, which had combative relations with left-wing former president Gustavo Petro.
De la Espriella, a flamboyant 48-year-old millionaire, was elected in June on an anti-establishment and pro-Trump platform.
Rubio is to meet the new Colombian president in his stronghold of Barranquilla, a Caribbean port city more famous for being pop star Shakira's hometown than as a venue for geopolitics.
The Colombian president defeated a left-wing candidate in June's runoff election on the promise of ending peace talks with drug-running armed groups and tackling crime.
Since then, Colombia has stepped up air assaults on these groups and authorised joint military operations with the United States.
Colombia has also joined the "Shield of the Americas," a coalition of countries led by Trump to combat drug trafficking in the region.
The stated objective of this trip is "enhanced cooperation in the shared fight against narcoterrorism," according to the State Department.
Colombia's Foreign Minister Omar Bula said the trip would start "rebuilding a strategic alliance with the United States."
He said it would focus on security, trade and "a commitment to Western values."
In Barranquilla, Rubio will also discuss reconstruction after an August 10 earthquake that struck the country's coffee-growing region, killing more than 330 people, according to State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott.
The quake destroyed schools, hospitals and scores of residential buildings across several towns and cities.
The new president has requested US assistance and, in particular, a suspension of customs duties to support reconstruction.
Donroe Doctrine
The tour by America's top diplomat in Colombia, Ecuador and Peru from Tuesday to Thursday comes after a string of right-wing electoral victories across Latin America.
Since President Donald Trump's return to the White House in January 2025, several Latin American countries, including Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador and Honduras, have initiated or confirmed a conservative turn.
The US has openly expressed its desire for control over the South American continent under the "Donroe Doctrine".
The term blends President Donald Trump’s first name with that of the fifth US president, James Monroe, who declared Latin America an exclusive American sphere of influence over two centuries ago under the "Monroe Doctrine".
This strategy is spelled out in the new US National Security Strategy, and Rubio, himself of Cuban heritage, is its chief architect.
After Colombia, the US Secretary of State will travel to Ecuador, where he will meet President Daniel Noboa.
Washington and Quito are carrying out operations against boats they say are linked to the criminal group Los Choneros, which is involved in drug trafficking in Ecuador.
A year ago, the US government launched a campaign of air strikes against vessels suspected of being used for drug trafficking in the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific. The attacks have left more than 200 people dead.
The administration has failed to provide evidence against these vessels, drawing accusations that the attacks amount to extrajudicial killings.
The final stop is Peru, which has been led since late July by right-wing President Keiko Fujimori, who is also aligned with the US president's policies.

Criminal gangs are using artificial intelligence to help them find locations in Europe to build illicit cigarette factories with less chance of getting caught, an EU auditor warned on Tuesday.

Now, with AI, it’s easier to find places to operate that are closer to their markets, he said, in rural locations and villages. “This reduces the risk in the supply chain for the criminals,” added Esther Torrente Heras, senior auditor.
Advertisement
It’s just one of the many challenges facing EU and member countries as they grapple to clamp down on illicit tobacco networks, which cause at least €13 billion in lost revenue in the bloc annually. In 2023, almost one in 10 cigarettes in Europe was illegally produced or smuggled in.
The report also lands as EU countries' attempts to find agreement on raising minimum tobacco and vape taxation levels have slowed after snus-loving Sweden — which is holding a general election next week — rebuffed a levy on nicotine pouches. The aim of the law is to harmonize prices across the bloc, strengthening the single market while nudging smokers to quit.
A lack of coordination and intelligence sharing between EU agencies and member countries’ authorities is hindering the bloc’s response to new cigarette factories, meaning “most alarmingly” the true size, structure and economic impact is unknown, Sarvamaa said.
To clamp down on this illegal activity, “it all starts with the Commission,” Sarvamaa said. “Better intelligence sharing between all relevant actors is essential.”
And the Commission needs to take a greater role in coordinating a strategic response of these actors, he added, including: the European Anti-Fraud Oﬃce OLAF, Europol, Eurojust and the European Public Prosecutor's Oﬃce, EPPO.
The Commission broadly accepted ECA’s recommendations, bar areas it said were beyond its role. It pushed back on defining strategies for the various EU authorities, noting that OLAF and others are responsible for setting their own strategic priorities. And it said it was not possible to provide a robust approach to assessing the size and economic impact of illicit trade, since no single method could do this.
“The union cannot afford to lose this fight,” Sarvamaa warned, saying that public health, safeguarding the integrity of the single market and preventing organized crime were all at risk.
But he stopped short of recommending how Europe should proceed with its overhaul of tobacco products and excise legislation, saying this was a role for policy and lawmakers.

Below is the audio recording of Lisa Tessman’s presidential address, “Holding Ourselves Responsible: When What Rightly Matters Doesn’t Really Matter,” given at the 2024 Eastern Division Meeting. The full text is available on the APA website (member sign-in is required).
The audio of the lecture is available here:
“Holding Ourselves Responsible: When What Rightly Matters Doesn’t Really Matter” by Lisa Tessman
Lisa Tessman is Professor of Philosophy at Binghamton University and a senior researcher at the University of Oslo, where she is currently doing collaborative work on the topic of moral residue. She has a B.A. in philosophy from Carleton College and an M.A. and a Ph.D. in philosophy from the University of Massachusetts Amherst. Her area of specialization is ethics, including normative ethics, metaethics, moral psychology, and feminist ethics. Her publications include When Doing the Right Thing Is Impossible (Oxford University Press, 2017), Moral Failure: On the Impossible Demands of Morality (Oxford University Press, 2015), Burdened Virtues: Virtues Ethics for Liberatory Struggles (Oxford University Press, 2005), as well as a number of articles in journals such as the Journal of Ethics, Philosophical Topics, The Journal of Value Inquiry, and Hypatia. She served as president of the APA Pacific Division in 2023–2024.
About this series: The Blog of the APA is pleased to publish the presidential addresses and John Dewey Lectures given at the Eastern, Central, and Pacific APA Division Meetings, which communicate the ideas and experiences that the renowned philosophers who delivered them felt are most important for people in the field to know. The blog wishes to thank the APA leadership and Jeremy Cushing for their support and assistance in making these recordings available.

Democrats have hit back against Donald Trump’s suggestion that the state of New Mexico should be renamed “New America”, accusing the US president of trying to distract from his war on Iran and rising prices.
The administration moved to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America” hours after Trump’s return to office in January 2025. In August, as trade tensions escalated between the US and Canada, it moved to do the same with Lake Ontario, moving to rename it as “Lake America”.
The president spent Labor Day posting memes on social media platform in support of changing the name of the state of New Mexico to “New America” as tense trade negotiations with Mexico ramp up.
On Sunday Trump claimed that he had received suggestions to change the name of the state and that he liked the idea. “So much more prestigious and beautiful for the people of that potentially incredible State,” he wrote on his Truth Social platform. “Wow, I Love It!!!”
The US federal government has no authority to change a state’s name. Any renaming would require New Mexico voters to approve an amendment to the state constitution through a ballot measure. The state is currently governed by Michelle Lujan Grisham, a Democrat. She has been in the job since 1 January 2019, and was re-elected in 2022.
The governor said in a post on X: “New Mexico’s name isn’t up for debate – it’s been ours since before the United States existed.”
“While the President tries to distract Americans from his disastrous war in Iran, gas prices keep soaring,” she wrote. “Americans are also spending more at the grocery store, losing access to health care and wondering if they’ll ever be able to afford a home.”
New Mexico’s senior senator, Martin Heinrich, blasted the president’s recent efforts to rename bodies of water via executive order. “Three things I will always call by their actual names,” Heinrich wrote. “The Gulf of Mexico, Lake Ontario, New Mexico.”
His colleague in the Senate, Ben Ray Luján, echoed the sentiment.
“It’s New Mexico, always has been and always will be,” he said, adding that Trump will “always be a sinvergüenza” – a spanish word for scoundrel – and “corrupt”.
Melanie Stansbury, one New Mexico’s Democratic US House representatives, was also resolute. “WE ARE NOT CHANGING OUR NAME!” she said in a video, standing on the banks of the Rio Grande, which runs through the state. “New Mexico is New Mexico. We are fiercely proud of our name, our people, and our places, including this river.”
Even Greg Hull, the Republican nominee running to replace Grisham, who is term-limited, denounced the president’s suggestion. “New Mexico does not need a new name. This state carries the history of Native nations and Spanish explorers who named this land nearly five hundred years ago, and generations of families who built New Mexico into what it is today. That identity is not up for negotiation,” Hull said in a statement to Santa Fe Public Radio.

Global trade accounted for 35% of the EU's carbon footprint in 2023, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:58:12 UTC
23:58:12 KST

A report argues that cooperation and shared climate standards – particularly with China – could be more effective than simply policing imports at the EU's borders.
The European Union is making a full-on effort to cut emissions at home, but 35% of its carbon footprint was generated abroad in 2023, according to data from the European Climate Foundation (ECF) and climate consultancy Matière.
The new figures, which show that more than one-fifth of global greenhouse gas emissions are now linked to global trade, create a political problem for Brussels, which is heavily investing in the decarbonisation of factories, power plants and cars even as the bloc still consumes goods whose production generates substantial emissions abroad.
The new Traded Emissions Tracker reveals that in Ireland, Sweden, Austria, Cyprus, Malta and Spain, imports accounted for more than 40% of the national carbon footprint in 2023, excluding intra-EU trade.
The tracker, which covers 45 major economies from 2010 to 2023, shows that trade-related emissions have grown faster than global emissions overall, widening by 10 percentage points between 1995 and 2023.
The China problem
The ECF and Matière report suggests that cooperation with trading partners, such as China, could deliver the largest emissions reductions, particularly through common product standards.
The EU-China relationship is not just about Europe's dependence on Chinese solar panels, batteries, electric vehicles, machinery or critical raw materials. It is also about the carbon embedded in the supply chains that support European consumption.
Aligning EU and Chinese climate requirements for products could influence trade flows equivalent to about 7% of global emissions and almost one-third of emissions linked to international trade, the report reveals.
"International cooperation is likely to offer the greatest potential for reducing emissions linked to trade. The EU can support its trading partners in decarbonising their production and work with other major economies to establish common environmental standards," the ECF and Matière stated.
According to the European Commission, Beijing accounted for 27.2% of global consumption-linked greenhouse-gas emissions in 2023, compared with 7.8% for the EU.
The bloc's massive demand for Chinese products has driven the trade deficit between the two blocs to €1 billion per day, according to the Commission. EU officials are currently trying to weaken EU demand and Chinese dumping with ongoing discussions and an official visit to Beijing scheduled for October to discuss trade imbalances.
Such climate alignment could make common standards more powerful than policing the carbon content of individual imports at the border. Alternatively, the climate tracker suggests, EU lawmakers should facilitate bringing production back to Europe.
However, the report stresses that reshoring is not automatically a climate win. If European production is itself carbon-intensive, relocating factories could simply shift emissions geographically rather than eliminate them.
The EU has already started curbing emissions from abroad through tools such as the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which puts a carbon price on certain imports.
Through the bloc's anti-deforestation law, set to enter into force on 30 December 2027, Brussels is banning imports of commodities such as cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya, and wood if their extraction has contributed to deforestation or forest degradation.
"While CBAM and the European Union Deforestation Regulation can help integrate carbon content into trade, the tracker’s creators argue for larger cooperation with trading partners to make meaningful progress," said ECF and Matière.
So far, no country has formally set a target to cut imported emissions. France, Denmark and the Netherlands are beginning to move in that direction, potentially opening a new front in national climate policy.

British family speaks out over nine-year ordeal after husband is abducted by Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:55:08 UTC
23:55:08 KST

A British woman has spoken out for the first time about the alleged abduction, torture and coercion of her husband at the hands of Saudi authorities, after nine years of “failed” quiet diplomacy.
The businessman Rami Naimi was first abducted in Dubai in 2017 on his return from a trip to Australia with his father. After being tortured, he was released the following year.
The father of three, who is the son of Ali Al-Naimi, a former Saudi oil minister and head of the state oil company Aramco, was detained again in 2022 and held for two years. Last year he was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment after a secret trial.
He was initially detained alongside 400 of the kingdom’s most powerful people in an infamous round-up at the the Ritz-Carlton hotel in Riyadh, which became the biggest and most contentious purge in the modern kingdom’s history.
Speaking out for the first time after years of what they described as a failed diplomatic process, his family has alleged abduction, disappearance, torture and coercion at the hands of Saudi authorities.
Naimi now faces a second trial for allegedly following certain accounts on X critical of Saudi Arabia and for attempting to leave the country without permission – both of which he denies.
“The first thing I wanted to do was speak out, but I was told no,” said his wife, Mira Lozi, speaking alongside her son at a campaign launch to bring Naimi home in London on Tuesday.
Lozi, currently fighting cancer, fought back tears as she said she had been encouraged to keep silent since 2017 to help secure his release.
“For nine years my children and I have lived through a nightmare,” she said. “Saying the truth today is like a liberation, enough is enough and we’re just hoping that we can end this nightmare and all the governments will be able to help us.”
Naimi left Saudi Arabia aged 13 and travelled for years between the UK, US and Middle East as a businessman. His family claim he was abducted in Dubai in 2017 after returning home from a book tour trip from Australia with his father.
They say he was blindfolded and forcibly taken by car to Abu Dhabi and then by private jet to Saudi Arabia. He was surprised to find himself with the others who had been rounded up, his family said, as he is not a journalist, activist or politician.
His abduction in 2017 came as the kingdom’s elite were detained at a five-star hotel in Riyadh during a purge in which princes, tycoons and ministers were stripped of their fortunes. Accounts later surfaced detailing torture and coercion, and the event preceded the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi, whose assassination at the Saudi consulate in Istanbul in 2018 sparked revulsion around the world.
Naimi was held at the hotel and tortured, electrocuted, waterboarded and psychologically abused for three months, his family said. He was told, falsely, that his father was being tortured next door. He was released in January 2018 after signing a “settlement agreement”.
He was subsequently forced to sign a document pledging to surrender 5bn Saudi riyals, later “discounted” to 1bn riyals (£200m) – which the family says neither he nor they possess. Naimi was placed under electronic surveillance and banned from leaving the kingdom.
His family said he was disappeared again for nearly two years in 2022, and subjected to further torture, and emotional and psychological abuse. They said they had no idea if he was alive or dead, and learned only through the help of his legal team and diplomats that he was being held in Saudi’s notorious Al Ha’ir prison.
It was after his release in March 2025, with an electronic tag and subject to a travel ban, that he learned of charges against him claiming he had “exploited” his father’s official influence. Naimi faced allegations he acted as an agent for a US company in Saudi Arabia and helped Aramco to secure a contract to provide technology to prevent diesel smuggling.
After seven years without charges, Naimi, an EU citizen, was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment after a secret trial. Now he is unable to leave Saudi Arabia and his communications with his family remain monitored. He has no idea, the family said, of their decision to go public with his case.
“Until today we have no idea why Rami was targeted,” said Lozi, who is too frightened to return to Saudi Arabia or travel to the United Arab Emirates.
“It really is something out of a movie. It’s shocking and we just want to end this nightmare,” said his 21-year-old son, Ali, who was 12 when his father was abducted.
In recent years the UK’s relationship with Saudi Arabia has come under scrutiny over the flow of arms between the two countries, Riyadh’s use of public executions and targeting of exiled activists and dissidents.
“Any family making a decision like this needs to be supported by the government,” said human rights lawyer Caoilfhionn Gallagher KC, who is leading the case.
As the family hopes to meet the new prime minister and foreign secretary, Gallagher said the recent appointment of a special envoy for Britons detained overseas did not go as far as campaigners, experts and parliamentarians had called for.
Gallagher described it as: “Tea and sympathy for a very limited group of people.”
Last month the Guardian reported that X had become the latest US social media company to block the accounts of Saudi dissidents so they are no longer visible inside the kingdom, following orders from Saudi authorities.
The UK Foreign Office declined to comment. The Saudi embassy in London has been approached for comment.

Far-right broadcaster ON switched off over licensing breaches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:53:47 UTC
23:53:47 KST

Far-right broadcaster ON switched off over licensing breaches
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Culture minister Rianne Letschert has confirmed that she intends to take far-right broadcaster Ongehoord Nederland off the airwaves after the media regulator asked her to withdraw its licence.
Letschert said the decision was the “most serious means at my disposal” and followed a series of breaches of broadcasting rules since ON started showing programmes on the Dutch public networks in 2022.
“There are clear rules for broadcasters that want to make programmes with public money,” the minister said. ”And if you repeatedly fail to abide by them, there comes a point where it has to stop.”
The breaking point was a panel discussion posted on ON’s YouTube channel in July that featured a clip from a speech by Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler in which he fulminated against the ”rootless international clique”, referring to the Jews.
Panellists, including editor-in-chief Joost Niemöller, agreed with a proposition that the “cosmopolitan elite” was “essentially hostile” to ordinary people, though they also rejected Hitler’s anti-Semitism.
Vlemmix called the decision a “very worrying day for Dutch public broadcasting” and said he would fight for “the interests of everyone who welcomes our views, but also public broadcasting and the views of the right in general.”
Regulator call
Letschert had previously rejected demands to take ON off the air, arguing that as a government minister she could not interfere in its editorial line.
Her legal position changed when the media regulator CvdM wrote to her last week telling her that ON was not fulfilling its obligations under Dutch broadcasting law.
The NPO, which is responsible for the three Dutch public TV channels, also asked the minister to intervene because ON was not prepared to work as a partner organisation.
The broadcasting ombudsman has reprimanded the channel several times for disseminating untrue information and mixing fact with opinion.
ON has also been fined twice in the last year by the media regulator, once for breaching conflict of interest rules and once for breaching its own editorial code.
Letschert said those three reasons were enough for her to pull ON’s licence, though the broadcaster will not be taken off the air immediately because it has the right to appeal against her decision.
Rules of freedom
“The Netherlands is a democratic state that observes the rule of law. That obliges us to take great care with the decisions we make,” she said. “Ongehoord Nederland will therefore have the opportunity to respond to my proposal and I will consider that response carefully before I make a final decision.
“A free public broadcasting system should have space for difference, debate and for views that clash and sometimes cause offence. But that freedom is only strong if everyone observes the rules that protect it.”

New Google DeepMind atlas could transform our understanding of genetic diseases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:53:22 UTC
23:53:22 KST

Atlases have long helped humans navigate unfamiliar terrain. And now a new atlas from Google DeepMind aims to better map the terrain of our biology: the human genome.
On Tuesday the company released AlphaGenome Atlas, a database that charts predictions of the possible effects of nine billion single variants in the human genome.
The database is based on the AlphaGenome, a DeepMind artificial intelligence model released last year that analyzes stretches of noncoding DNA, which primarily regulates gene activity. The model then predicts how much those variants affect molecular function. With the new atlas, all that analysis has been done ahead of time, and researchers can search for any DNA variant to see its predicted effects down to the level of specific tissues.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“This represents the first time that any researcher in the world can access a comprehensive map of the human genome and its variations by simply opening a browser,” said Pushmeet Kohli, vice president of science at Google DeepMind, in a press briefing.
Researchers have been puzzled by the intricacies of the genome, especially noncoding DNA—the 98 percent of DNA that doesn’t code for specific proteins but still plays a major role in the body’s function. AlphaMissense, another DeepMind tool, makes predictions for coding DNA, or the genes that make proteins. The new atlas covers everything else and contains a whopping petabyte of data—a quadrillion bytes.
Single variants in coding DNA can cause diseases such as Tay-Sachs and sickle cell anemia. Noncoding DNA variants have also been linked to some types of cancer. To trace these mutations, researchers typically must painstakingly search through billions of data points to search for signals, but AlphaGenome Atlas could offload a lot of that work. Jonathan Sebat, a psychiatric geneticist at the University of California, San Diego, says it could help speed up such research.
“Our own workflows in the lab can be streamlined quite a bit because we don’t actually have to compute anything,” Sebat says. “We literally can just look up everything.”
In some ways, the atlas acts as a successor to the database for AlphaFold, an earlier DeepMind project that effectively solved the protein prediction problem, winning then DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis a share of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. It has since been used by scientists worldwide for disease research and drug discovery. AlphaGenome Atlas, by contrast, focuses on DNA—the instructions to make proteins and regulate their function—not proteins themselves. The new atlas is also 30 times larger than AlphaFold’s database, although it is far less accurate.
Rather the new database is meant to serve as a starting point, says Žiga Avsec, genomics lead at Google DeepMind. It may be especially useful for research questions that involve more than one variant across the genome, for example, he says.
While AlphaFold’s database was free to use—which was reportedly the cause of some recent shake-ups at DeepMind, including Hassabis’s move to Alphabet, Google’s parent company—commercial users such as drugmakers will have to license AlphaGenome Atlas.
The new atlas also gives genetic variants a so-called AlphaGenome Variant Impact (AVI) score. The measure combines the AlphaGenome and AlphaMissense predictions and ranks each variant by how much it affects function.
The database looks at single-letter changes in the genome, meaning a single change in the base pair—if you imagine that a double helix of DNA is a twisting ladder, a base pair is a rung on that ladder. These tiny changes won’t be able to give the full picture of all genetic diseases on their own, but they can provide clues.
“If somebody is studying a disease, and they don’t have any idea about what cell types to look for or what molecular processes are impacted, then starting with an AVI score, which is a single score, is a great starting point to help you prioritize variants and try to find that needle in the haystack,” Avsec says.

Germany to send more Patriot missiles to Ukraine, warns of stepped-up Russian winter attacks

Speaking at a videoconference of nations supporting Ukraine, Pistorius said he had decided to "deliver urgently" additional PAC-2 interceptor missiles.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte also pressed allies to increase support, saying civilian casualties from the war were at their highest level since May 2022.
"Nations must dig deeper. We do not have a choice," he said.
