SWISS plans to donate last Airbus A340 to transport museum
Swiss International Air Lines (SWISS) and the Swiss Museum of Transport have announced a joint museum project for the last Airbus A340-300 in the SWISS fleet. The aircraft is due to be incorporated into the aviation exhibition in Lucerne in early 2028.
However, as SWISS and the Swiss Museum of Transport announced on Tuesday, a number of significant technical, financial and regulatory issues still need to be resolved before the plan can be implemented.
The aircraft, which weighs around 125 tonnes and which SWISS intends to donate to the Swiss Museum of Transport, must be transported from Zurich Airport to Lucerne and positioned on the museum grounds. The costs for the transfer, structural modifications and the interior design are estimated to run into the high single-digit millions.
The Swiss Museum of Transport must raise these funds by the end of 2026, primarily through third-party funding from foundations, patrons and companies. The final decision on the project will only be made once transport, permits and funding have been secured.
More
Pass the Swiss sick bag
With the Airbus A340-300 being taken out of service at the end of 2027, the era of four-engine passenger aircraft will come to an end at SWISS. For many years, this aircraft type was a defining feature of the Swiss airline’s long-haul fleet and connected the country with destinations all over the world.
At the Swiss Museum of Transport, the aircraft is to be displayed in the outdoor area in front of the Aerospace Hall. The interior of the aircraft is to be showcased in a variety of ways, according to the press release. The Convair 990 “Coronado”, a former four-engine long-haul aircraft from Swissair, is already part of the exhibition.

Veterans strategy linked to future Armed Forces recruitment
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:07:22 BST
23:07:22 KST

The Government says its 10-year Veterans Strategy is intended not only to support former service personnel but also to strengthen the appeal of military service to future recruits, Veterans and People Minister Calvin Bailey has said.
The position was set out in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Stuart Anderson, who asked what progress the Office for Veterans’ Affairs had made in helping veterans succeed after service while supporting wider efforts to connect Defence with society and recruit the next generation.
Bailey said: “The Strategic Defence Review recognised the role of the Office for Veterans’ Affairs in helping veterans thrive after service and ensuring their skills, experience and contributions are valued across society.”
He added: “Through the UK-wide Veterans Strategy, the Government is working with employers, local communities and delivery partners to support successful transitions to civilian life and improve opportunities for veterans.”
The new 10-year Veterans Strategy was published in November 2025 and is intended to provide a UK-wide framework for government, employers, charities and wider society.
Bailey said: “Published in November 2025, the new 10-year Veterans Strategy sets out a fresh narrative that recognises veterans as one of the UK’s greatest strategic assets.”
He continued: “It aims to improve public understanding of veterans, celebrate their contribution to society, and challenge misconceptions about military service and life beyond the Armed Forces. The Strategy applies across the UK and provides a framework for government, business, charities and wider society to support veterans.”
The strategy is organised around three themes: Celebrate, Contribute and Support. The first focuses on recognising service and sacrifice, the second on the skills and experience veterans bring to society, the economy and national security, and the third on access to assistance when it is required.
Bailey said: “It is structured around three themes: Celebrate, by recognising the service and sacrifice of veterans; Contribute, by valuing the skills, experience and expertise they bring to society, the economy and national security; and Support, by ensuring veterans can access timely and effective assistance when needed.”
The MOD also explicitly linked the treatment and public perception of veterans with the attractiveness of joining the Armed Forces in the future. Bailey said: “By helping veterans succeed after service and promoting greater recognition of their positive contribution, the Strategy strengthens the connection between the Armed Forces community and society, while supporting the attractiveness of military service to future generations considering a career in the Armed Forces.”
The answer does not provide specific recruitment figures attributable to the Veterans Strategy, but sets out the Government’s position that better outcomes and public recognition for veterans form part of the wider effort to strengthen the relationship between the Armed Forces and society.

Dubai launches Agentic AI training drive for 14,000 businesses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:04:46 UTC
23:04:46 KST

Dubai is training more than 14,000 businesses to use AI that doesn't just answer – it acts without being asked.
The initiative, launched by Dubai Chambers, is training private-sector companies to move beyond AI tools that simply respond to prompts and towards systems that can carry out tasks and make decisions with limited human input.
Aimed at member companies of Dubai Chambers’ Business Groups and Business Councils, the initiative will be delivered through the newly launched Dubai Chambers Academy, an integrated e-learning platform offering specialised Agentic AI training tracks alongside other programmes for the private sector.
It forms part of Dubai’s wider push to transition businesses towards Agentic AI under the directives of Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence of the UAE, and Chairman of The Executive Council of Dubai.
The Dubai Chambers Academy was launched on 1 September in the presence of H.E. Eng. Sultan bin Saeed Al Mansoori, Chairman of Dubai Chambers, H.E. Mohammad Ali Rashed Lootah, President and CEO of Dubai Chambers, and 90 chairpersons of Business Groups and Business Councils.
“The programme to transition the private sector towards Agentic AI reflects Dubai’s commitment to advancing the vision of its leadership by preparing the business community to adopt advanced technologies and use them effectively to create sustainable value,” says Al Mansoori.
“This will strengthen companies’ competitiveness and their ability to innovate and grow in the economy of the future.”
Turning AI potential into practice
Participants will explore the latest Agentic AI tools and solutions, learning how to use them to streamline operations, boost productivity and efficiency, and support quicker, smarter decision-making.
The training will also examine practical approaches to adoption, helping companies identify where the technology could have the greatest impact across their operations.
“Agentic AI is opening up new possibilities for the way companies operate. It can help manage complex tasks, enable more effective decision-making, enhance productivity and create new opportunities for growth,” adds Al Mansoori.
“Through these specialised training tracks, we aim to equip the private sector with the capabilities and expertise needed to understand Agentic AI and translate its potential into practical applications.”
Building a bigger Agentic AI ecosystem
The training tracks form part of a wider programme to transition Dubai’s private sector towards Agentic AI.
Other initiatives include establishing incubators for Agentic AI companies that support Dubai’s transition, supporting companies specialising in the development and deployment of Agentic AI solutions, and promoting knowledge-sharing and capacity-building within Dubai Chambers.
Together, these efforts are designed to strengthen private-sector competitiveness and reinforce Dubai’s leadership in adopting future technologies.
The launch follows Dubai Chambers’ formation of the Executive Committee for Agentic AI.
The committee was established to accelerate the adoption of Agentic AI across the private sector, prepare the business community for global technological shifts, enable companies to benefit from advanced AI solutions, and reinforce Dubai’s position as a global hub for the digital economy and future industries.
Business Groups and Business Councils play an important role in supporting Dubai’s commercial and economic growth by ensuring that different sectors are represented and providing a platform for constructive dialogue between the business community and relevant government entities.
They also contribute to efforts to enhance the business environment and promote sustainable economic growth in the emirate.

Saudi Arabia has threatened to hit back after a wave of missiles from Yemen's Houthis set Aramco oil facilities ablaze, the group’s heaviest attack in years, pushing Brent crude prices to their highest in six weeks, nearing $100 a barrel.
The attacks that hit facilities belonging to state oil giant Aramco in Abha and Jizan on Tuesday caused "temporary" shutdowns and left 73 wounded, Saudi authorities said.
The Houthi attacks on energy facilities pushed up oil prices, which have spiked since the US-Iran war.
Meanwhile, Houthis later reported a series of retaliatory Saudi strikes, with no confirmation from Riyadh yet.
Just after the Houthi strikes, Saudi Arabia’s foreign ministry said, "Riyadh will take all necessary measures to defend its sovereignty," demanding a halt to the Houthi strikes and their attacks on Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea.
‘Large-scale attacks’
The Houthis fired dozens of ballistic missiles, their military spokesperson said.
In a statement, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group carried out a “large-scale” military operation using dozens of ballistic missiles and drones.
He also said the attacks targeted Aramco facilities in Abha, Najran and Jizan, as well as Khamis Mushait Air Base.
Saree claimed the strikes were “precise and direct” and caused extensive damage to the targeted facilities.
The Houthi spokesperson said the operation was in response to Saudi air strikes in Yemen, claiming that Saudi Arabia had carried out 121 strikes over the past three days in Marib, Al-Bayda, Al-Hudaydah, Taiz and Al-Jawf provinces.
‘Dangerous escalation’
The Saudi energy ministry also reported strikes at energy facilities in the kingdom’s southern region and said some operations at the targeted sites were temporarily halted.
Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki called the attacks a “dangerous escalation” and said the coalition would take all necessary operational measures to deter the Houthis and neutralise sources of threats.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognised Yemeni government.
Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces has reignited after a four-year truce collapsed in July, months into the Middle East war between the United States and Iran.
In recent days, hundreds have died in clashes around the Bab al Mandeb strait, the mouth of the vital Red Sea shipping route.
The Houthis imposed a naval blockade in July against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea in response to what they described as a Saudi siege on Yemen, an allegation Riyadh has denied.
Diesel prices have also hit record highs and nearly doubled since the start of the US-Iran conflict, as have gasoline prices.

Macron summit to seek boost for European space despite no-shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:02:30 UTC
23:02:30 KST

Macron summit to seek boost for European space despite no-shows
PARIS, Sept 8 - France is pressing ahead with a space summit shunned by the U.S. tech giants and hampered by a lower-than-expected turnout from European leaders as President Emmanuel Macron seeks a stronger role for Europe in the competitive maelstrom of space.
Organisers had billed the International Space Summit in Paris on September 9 and 10 as a forum for decision-makers, corporations and scientists from 120 nations including rival space powers U.S. and China to find ways to cooperate and improve regulation.
But White House concerns about what it perceives as a pro-European agenda prompted four U.S. space firms including Elon Musk's SpaceX and Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin to pull out, scrapping a handful of announcements, sources said last week.
Germany, which is officially co-chairing the summit but has increasingly looked at odds with the French hosts on space policy, said on Friday that Chancellor Friedrich Merz would not attend because of other commitments. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni will also not attend, her office told Reuters.
France has been leading calls for Europe to increase its autonomy in space while Germany appears less willing to close the door on SpaceX, which dominates the modern launch market.
Paris and Berlin have also struck a contrasting tone on the fragmentation of Europe's efforts to counter the influence of Musk's Starlink, with Macron backing the European Union's IRIS² secure satellite constellation, while Germany planning its own secure network.
Organisers played down gaps in attendance and said the event would still feature U.S. firms among 2,000 delegates expected at the glass-domed Grand Palais, built as a symbol of industrial ambition more than a century ago.
DECLARATIONS, CONTRACTS ON THE AGENDA
The informal political gathering is not expected to produce decisions.
France, however, is trying to secure a number of broad declarations on topics, such as space traffic and access both to space and the scarce frequencies needed to operate there, an issue dividing companies in the United States and Europe.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is scheduled to give a keynote policy speech on Thursday. China is also due to attend, officials said without elaborating.
The meeting is also expected to be a showcase for commercial announcements timed to raise the profile of the event, echoing billions of euros of deals announced at a French summit on AI last year.
France is historically Europe's leading space power dating back to its 1950s ballistics programme but Germany has overtaken its neighbour as top contributor to the European Space Agency.
Europe spends about five times less than the United States on space investments, according to European Space Agency Director General Josef Aschbacher.
He told reporters ahead of the event that ESA is drawing up emblematic proposals for Europe to break its reliance U.S. rockets to launch human astronauts into space.
Other topics include a roll-call of European concerns about space including the growing issue of security, according to Philippe Baptiste, France's higher education minister. REUTERS

Burundians seek papers to leave Kenya despite amnesty
NAIROBI, Sept 8 - Hundreds of Burundians flocked to their embassy in Nairobi on Tuesday to get travel documents to return home, saying they feared violence even after Kenya announced a temporary amnesty for undocumented East Africans in the country.
Many said they had faced threats after Kenyan President William Ruto last week told authorities to close down all small-scale businesses operated by foreign traders as that work should be left to locals only.
The presidency issued a statement on Tuesday saying it would still safeguard the rights of registered foreigners to work there in other sectors - and give unregistered people 90 days to sort out their papers.
'WE FEEL UNWANTED HERE'
Burundians at their embassy told Reuters they still wanted to leave, saying they doubted the amnesty would protect them.
"The president has treated us like we are not human beings," Habonimana Jacques, a Burundian motorcycle taxi driver, told Reuters.
He said amnesty had been announced as an afterthought. "Even if we decide to remain we won't have security because most Kenyans are already harassing us."
Burundi's Foreign Affairs Minister, Edouard Bizimana, did not immediately respond to a call for comment.
"We feel unwanted here ... it's time to go home," Eric Niyonkur, a Burundian second-hand clothes seller, told Reuters. Some of those at the embassy had camped there for two straight days without food, he added.
Ugandans in Kenya were also heading back across the border, Uganda's Daily Monitor newspaper and NTV Uganda television reported. Reuters was not able to verify the report. A spokesperson for Uganda's police did not immediately respond when contacted for comment.
There are about 16,000 Burundian refugees and asylum seekers in Kenya, according to the U.N. refugee agency. Many work in small-scale businesses in Nairobi, selling items such as coffee and used clothes.
Critics of the anti-immigration crackdown have accused Ruto, who is expected to seek re-election in polls due next year, of blaming foreigners for Kenya's economic difficulties.
In Tuesday's statement from the presidency, spokesperson Hussein Mohamed said all undocumented aliens should use the 90-day amnesty to regularise their stay and warned enforcement operations would begin after the three months had elapsed.
He warned against xenophobia and said authorities would not tolerate any discrimination, lawlessness and violence against foreign nationals. REUTERS

France groundwater levels fall as 61% remain below normal amid dry weather
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:01:15 UTC
23:01:15 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
Groundwater levels in France remained below seasonal averages at 61% of monitoring points as of Sept. 1, with levels falling at 90% of points in August, the French Geological Survey (BRGM) said Tuesday.
“The situation of groundwater remains largely degraded due to the lack of effective rainfall in August and continued high water demand for various uses,” said BRGM.
The share of monitoring points with below-average groundwater levels was higher than a year earlier, when 44% were below their monthly averages.
Groundwater levels were stable at 8% of monitoring points in August, while 2% recorded an increase. The decline was more pronounced than in August 2025.
The BRGM attributed the continued decline to a lack of effective rainfall since May, more pronounced drought and high temperatures since June, as well as summer water withdrawals.
By the end of August, 39% of monitoring points had satisfactory groundwater levels, meaning they were slightly above or around their seasonal averages.
The lowest were recorded in the Limousin bedrock aquifers, the Jura limestone aquifers and the northern Alsace plain.
Among more responsive aquifers, levels remained relatively high in the Vistrenque formations, while levels in the Armorican bedrock and Aquitaine Basin had fallen to low levels.
The BRGM said autumn rainfall could help replenish groundwater reserves, but uncertainty remained about its distribution and effectiveness.
It added that lower withdrawals for irrigation and drinking water as summer demand declines would reduce pressure on groundwater resources.

People with narcissistic traits generate more original and malicious ideas for revenge, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:00:47 UTC
23:00:47 KST

People who have previously used their imagination to harm others or who possess highly narcissistic traits tend to generate more original and malicious ideas for revenge. These findings indicate that past actions and personality shape how individuals apply their problem-solving skills during interpersonal conflicts. The research was published in The Journal of Intelligence.
Creativity is typically viewed as a positive force in society, driving art, science, and innovation. But creativity also has a dark side, known as malevolent creativity. This involves the application of original ideas to purposely harm, deceive, or manipulate others. It is essentially creative problem-solving with malicious intent, evident in everything from everyday pranks to complex criminal activities.
To understand why some people use their imagination for harm, psychologists often refer to a framework called the AMORAL model. This model suggests that dark creativity results from a combination of personal traits, such as a natural propensity for creativity or certain personality types, and environmental factors, such as a provoking situation.
Among personality types, the dark triad traits are particularly relevant. These include psychopathy (a lack of empathy and high impulsivity), Machiavellianism (a tendency to be strategic and manipulative), and narcissism (a sense of grandiosity, egocentrism, and a strong need for admiration). People high in narcissism tend to be especially reactive to social slights or threats to their ego. A 2021 meta-analysis found that among these dark traits, narcissism has the most consistent relationship with self-reported general creativity.
“Society generally views creativity as a good thing, but some people use their creativity to harm others,” Natalie Ceballos, a professor of psychology at Texas State University, told PsyPost. “I’m interested in the individual and environmental factors that might influence someone to steer their creativity toward antisocial ends.”
The current research, conducted by Ceballos alongside cognitive neuroscientist Carmen E. Westerberg and pre-med student Ruby N. Sweet, aimed to untangle how a person’s history of malicious behavior influences their current ability to devise revenge plots, above and beyond their everyday problem-solving skills and personality.
“We aimed to determine what factors are most relevant for understanding when creative people may use their skills for nefarious purposes,” Ceballos said. “Studies have shown that the dark triad personality traits predict malevolently creative ideology, but how other factors like history of creative malevolence or reaction to acute provocation might interact with dark triad traits is an area that requires further research.”
The research team recruited 248 undergraduate students for an online survey. The participants were predominantly young women, with an average age of 20. First, the students answered questions about their demographics and rated their own potential for everyday creative problem-solving on a simple five-point scale.
Next, participants completed a questionnaire assessing their past malevolent creativity. They rated how often they had engaged in behaviors like fabricating lies to simplify a problem, thinking up ways to take revenge, or playing tricks on others. They also completed a standard personality test to measure their levels of narcissism, psychopathy, and Machiavellianism.
To measure malicious ideation in real time, the researchers used a task built around a hypothetical conflict. Participants read a vignette in which a neighbor asked for help with apartment renovations and promised to pay them. In the scenario, the participant does the work, but the neighbor later denies that any agreement took place and refuses to pay. The participants were instructed to type out as many original ideas as possible to get back at the neighbor.
“Some of the participants’ ideas were malevolent but not very creative, like simply physically assaulting the neighbor,” Ceballos noted. “Other ideas, like seeding the neighbor’s lawn with invasive plants, were more original and showed an appreciation for the long game.”
After generating their ideas, the students rated how provoked they would feel if the situation happened in real life. Two independent raters then evaluated the participants’ responses. They calculated a fluency index, which was the total number of malicious ideas generated. They also calculated a malevolence index, counting ideas that were rated as at least slightly harmful, and a composite score, which only counted ideas that were both harmful and highly original.
The researchers found that different personal factors predicted different types of creative output. A participant’s self-perception of their everyday problem-solving skills predicted their fluency index. People who viewed themselves as good at solving regular problems came up with a larger quantity of revenge ideas, regardless of how original or harmful those ideas actually were.
When it came to the quality of the revenge ideas, personality and past behavior played a larger role. High levels of narcissism and a history of past malevolent behavior predicted both the malevolence index and the overall composite score. This means that individuals who were highly narcissistic or who had a habit of playing tricks and seeking revenge in the past generated ideas that were more harmful and more unique.
Interestingly, past malevolent behavior contributed to the generation of harmful and original ideas independently of everyday problem-solving skills and narcissistic traits. While feeling provoked by the scenario correlated with generating darker ideas, the level of provocation did not uniquely predict the task outcomes once past behavior and personality were factored into the statistical models. Psychopathy and Machiavellianism also did not emerge as unique predictors in the final analyses.
“We were a bit surprised that provocation level didn’t have a larger effect on malevolent creativity,” Ceballos said. “In our study, it appears that past behaviors and personality traits were more closely tied to malevolently creative ideation.”
The findings align with research covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that dark personality traits and a history of malicious actions relate to generating novel ways to harm others. They also fit with a 2021 study covered by PsyPost indicating that narcissism helps explain variations in malevolent creativity, though the new study specifically measured idea generation in real time rather than just relying on general behavioral tendencies.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relied on a cross-sectional design, meaning the data was collected at a single point in time. Because of this, the researchers cannot determine cause and effect. It is not possible to say that past malicious behavior directly causes a person to generate better revenge ideas today, only that the two are associated.
The participant pool also consisted mostly of female college students in the United States. The results might not generalize to older adults, men, or people from different cultural backgrounds, especially since dark personality traits often vary across age and gender. Additionally, the study relied on self-reports for past bad behavior, which can be skewed if participants want to present themselves in a positive light.
The measure for everyday creativity was also based on a single question, which might not capture the full scope of a person’s creative abilities.
“What leads a person to use their creative abilities to harm others? I think the take-home message is that a complex mixture of personality, lived experiences, and current circumstances all come together to create a perfect storm of malevolent creativity,” Ceballos explained. “Our study included only a small subset of the factors that might contribute to malevolent creativity. A lot of open questions remain for future work, but our results suggest that it’s not a simple explanation.”
For instance, future studies could track people over time to see if a habit of malicious creativity builds on itself through positive reinforcement, eventually creating an automatic cognitive strategy for dealing with conflict.
“My collaborators and I have backgrounds in neuroscience, so our natural next step involves the exploration of potential neurophysiological correlates of malevolent creativity,” Ceballos said. “We’re particularly interested in how different kinds of acute and chronic stress, and even factors like sleep quality, might influence malevolent creativity and which therapeutic strategies might help to reduce negative outcomes.”
The study, “Self-Reports of Past Malevolent Behavior and Narcissism as Predictors of Malevolent Creativity on a Real-World Ideation Task,” was authored by Natalie A. Ceballos, Ruby N. Sweet, and Carmen E. Westerberg.

People in Preston-next-Wingham told of how hundreds of men had started to arrive in the village of just over 920 residents on Friday afternoon and in effect “took over” the village.
At least one person is understood to have sought to pass on details to counter-terrorism police after people heard the far-right activists boasting in the local pub that they intended to go to Dover and “attack Muslims”.
The information was passed on to police but little or no interest was shown in the tipoff, according to the anti-fascist group Hope Not Hate, who spoke to the person. Others reported careless and illegal parking to the police but no action was said to have been taken.
The claims have raised fresh questions about Kent police’s handling of the protest, in which hundreds descended on Dover at 7am and which the force described as “spontaneous”. No arrests were made during the action, which involved hundreds of black-clad masked men standing in the middle of roads and led to access to the port of Dover being blocked for several hours.
Kent police admitted on Tuesday that an initial review of its handling of the protests found that the force had received non-emergency information late on Friday evening that a protest could take place in the town the next day.
“This information was not fully assessed. If it was, it may have allowed the force to consider its resourcing,” it said in a statement.
“However, this information would not have prevented the lawful protest from taking place, nor the disruption experienced by the town, port and wider community.”
Roger Gale, the MP for Herne Bay and Sandwich, who lives in Preston-next-Wingham, said the unrest in Dover on Saturday was clearly not “spontaneous”.
He said that the village in Kent was unusually full of cars on Friday night and that a local car park and the recreation ground was still full of vehicles on Saturday morning, prompting him to call 999.
Gale said: “A local councillor took photographs of the number plates and they should be able to work back from those to establish who owns the cars. I called 999 at around 9.30am on Saturday and two officers came over quite quickly.
“I am going to write to the chief constable to ask what they are going to do with this information. There were roughly 50 cars in the car park and the recreation ground and more on the road. [What happened in Dover] was not spontaneous. It was carefully coordinated. Those participating were transported from the village to Dover, most likely in Luton vans.”
Gale was not aware of calls being made to the police on Friday but he added that he knew that conversations among participants in Saturday’s unrest had been overheard in the village pub on Friday night.
The action was organised by Daniel Thomas, a long-term associate of the far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, known as Tommy Robinson. Thomas, who has established an umbrella grouping called Patriot Platform, was also linked to a blockade in Portsmouth the following day.
One person who lives in Preston-next-Wingham told Hope Not Hate: “There were hundreds of them. They took over the place.
“They were literally parking everywhere. They parked in the recreational ground, in the butcher’s car park, in the primary school, on the roads and even on junctions.”
A fleet of vehicles is understood to have arrived at about 5.30am on Saturday in the village. Video footage later showed men who took part in the protest disembarking from the back of the vehicles in Dover.

"It's very hard to do things on your own," Maman told POLITICO, warning that the militarization of space "is already happening — we just don't realize how much" and that Israel is seeing more interest from allies in "dual-use" technology for both civilian and defense purposes.

A string of recent deals have seen the EU pursue closer military and technological relations with Israel, after several years of effective disengagement as a result of political tensions that have followed the war in Gaza. In 2024, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen backed calls from Polish and Greek Prime Ministers Donald Tusk and Kyriakos Mitsotakis to create an EU-funded air defense shield.

Now though, in a major expansion of its operations in Europe, Israeli firm Rafael Advanced Defense Systems confirmed Monday that it will open a factory producing its Iron Dome air-defense system in a former Volkswagen factory in Germany. One week ago, Greece struck a €3 billion deal with Israel’s Defense Ministry to build a new multilayered air defense network designed to take down drones, hostile jets and rockets.

"We see that convergence of everything, of that multi-layer defense approach," said Maman, pointing to satellite imaging and AI modeling as a key focus for joint development.
"I don't treat only defense as ballistic missiles from Iran ... think about a fire or a flash flood or even a prolonged drought ... we have a proven track record and we do have very good results," she said.

Innocent-looking AI reasoning can make bad behavior harder to catch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

Innocent-looking AI reasoning can make bad behavior harder to catch
One AI can monitor another, but the safeguard may miss signs of trouble
Safety concerns about AI are growing, and now, a common method for catching misbehaving systems could have flaws, new research suggests.
In experiments with AI agents, researchers found that chain-of-thought monitoring, in which one AI checks another’s work, became far less reliable when the monitored AI’s reasoning was the main clue that something was wrong, they report August 1 on arXiv.org. That exposes a weakness in the approach: If suspicious behavior is visible mainly in the reasoning, an innocent-looking chain of thought can make that behavior much harder to catch.
The stakes are growing higher as AI continues to operate more independently. During internal cybersecurity evaluations, OpenAI models circumvented controls designed to isolate them from the internet, compromising parts of OpenAI’s internal research infrastructure and Hugging Face’s systems. Episodes like that have raised interest in ways to catch suspicious behavior before an AI agent can act on it. OpenAI says it is now investing more computing resources in chain-of-thought monitoring.
But machine learning engineer Shikhar Shiromani and AI researcher Leo Richter’s new work suggests that this type of monitoring may have a weakness. In a subset of 251 cases in which reasoning was the only clue to the problem, the monitor’s detection rate fell from 96.2 percent to 3.8 percent after the researchers rewrote the reasoning to make the behavior appear innocent without changing its actions.
“The AI isn’t necessarily lying about its action,” says Shiromani, a research fellow at the nonprofit Pivotal. “It is more or less giving a misleading, innocent-sounding explanation of its intentions.”
Jacob Andreas, a computer scientist at MIT, says that chain-of-thought, or CoT, reasoning can provide clues about what a model is trying to do.
“But we should be skeptical: (a) that any individual CoT provides us insight into model behavior on a specific example, and (b) that absence of evidence of bad behavior in a CoT should be taken as evidence of absence,” he wrote in an email.
Andreas questioned how much Shiromani’s main experiment says about real-world monitoring. Because the researchers rewrote the reasoning after the fact, he says, it is unclear whether a real model could produce the same innocent-sounding reasoning while taking the suspicious action, such as trying to hack another system.
The researchers also tested live AI agents. After adjusting the monitor for each model, it caught every GPT-5.4 hack and all but one DeepSeek hack. Claude Opus was harder to catch, with the monitor missing seven of 20 hacks on one task and 12 of 20 on another.
“And at the end of the day, there is no substitute now for really rigorous behavioral testing, and no substitute for human operators simply declining to run agents in situations where there is potential for substantial harm,” Andreas says.

Richard Kelly on Donnie Darko at 25: ‘It’s a Miracle That Any Movie Gets Made’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

For a diehard fan of Donnie Darko, meeting director and screenwriter Richard Kelly is a thrill in itself. But to first encounter him as a silhouette in a darkened movie theater is to feel almost like a character in one of his films—unmoored by indefinite space and physics, questioning your altered perception.
It’s a hot Friday in mid-August when I sit down with Kelly, 51, at Santa Monica’s Aero Theatre, a beloved repertory venue that makes a key appearance in Donnie Darko, his remarkable debut feature. Released in October 2001 with virtually no marketing due to the tragic events of 9/11 weeks prior (the plot hinges on a plane accident), it couldn’t get a toehold at the box office. But in the months and years that followed, the film became a hit on the home video market and gained a fervent cult fandom thanks to its unique supernatural mystery.
To mark its 25th anniversary, Fathom Entertainment will mount a limited theatrical rerelease of the film in a new 4K presentation, complete with a special introduction by Kelly—he’s just wrapped recording when I walk into the Aero. Screenings begin on October 2, the date that launches mentally disturbed suburban teenager Donnie Darko (Jake Gyllenhaal) on a surreal journey that may or may not lead to the end of the world. Snippets of the movie play without sound as Kelly and I settle into a back row to talk.
“My memories of this film run the entire spectrum from fear to love,” Kelly jokes, alluding to the corny pop psychology peddled by Patrick Swayze’s self-help guru in the film. This occasion, Kelly says, is all about the “love,” as he couldn’t be more grateful to “all the people who have continued to support” his work.
That camp should be pleased to hear that on December 15, Kelly will publish his mammoth first novel, The Philosophy of Time Travel, available for preorder now. The 800-page volume picks up right where the movie left off and is intended to set the stage for a film sequel as well. “It’s been very inspiring for me to remain focused on continuing the journey that began 25 years ago, on my own creative terms,” Kelly says. “This film has defined my entire career, but at the same time, it’s set a benchmark in the sense of the movies that I want to continue to make.”
Here, the auteur revisits the unforgettable dreamscape that put him on the map, and considers the artistic possibilities still ahead.
On when he realized Donnie Darko was becoming a cult hit:
There was one specific moment, I think in March of 2002, when I was in New York City. I was walking through the East Village, and I walked past a pizza restaurant called Two Boots, and my poster for Donnie Darko was hanging in their window. I saw the poster and I was like, “What’s going on? This is bizarre. Why does a pizza restaurant have a movie poster?” I went inside and I asked the manager, and he said, “Well, we have a little theater in the back, the Pioneer, and we’re playing your movie every Saturday night at midnight—and it’s selling out.”
I showed up the next Saturday night at about two in the morning, when the movie was finishing. I expected there’d be maybe 10 people there, and he wasn't joking, it was sold out, and there were people with camcorders and lights in my face, and Michael Musto from the Village Voice was there. I was just completely bowled over by the fact that there were people who cared, who were really, really connecting with the movie. That was the moment I knew that it wasn’t over, that the movie was going to have a second wind.
On how Drew Barrymore and Jason Schwartzman saved the screenplay from Hollywood purgatory:
It all started with Jason Schwartzman. He attached to play Donnie, and by virtue of his attachment, the script got sent around to a whole new round of people. It had been circulating for about a year, and the story was, “Oh, the writer won’t sell it. He wants to direct. It's his first movie, it’s too ambitious. It’s just a writing sample, he’s never gonna get that movie made. He won’t let anyone else take it away from him.”
Then the script got sent to Nancy Juvonen, who’s partners with Drew Barrymore [at Flower Films]. She read it and flipped out and wanted to meet me, so we went down to the set of Charlie’s Angels. We went into Drew Barrymore’s trailer, and she was finishing the script, and we just immediately hit it off. I’m like, “Drew, would you like to play the English teacher, Mrs. Pomeroy?” And she’s like, “Will you let my company, Flower Films, produce the movie with you? And I’m like, “Of course.” She had a one week window in August of 2000 before she was going to do a Penny Marshall film called Riding in Cars with Boys. We had to meet that deadline and get Drew to shoot her out in one week.
Jason Schwartzman had a scheduling conflict, and then in walks Jake Gyllenhaal. So it all happened really quickly. Nancy and Drew really deserve an enormous share of the credit in getting this whole thing off the ground—and Jason Schwartzman, too. Had he not attached, I would not have a career.
On having real-life siblings Jake and Maggie Gyllenhaal anchor a fictional on-screen family.
I heard from Joseph Middleton and Michelle Morris Gertz, our wonderful casting directors—they told me that Jake has an older sister, her name is Maggie Gyllenhaal, and she’s a brilliant actress. She had only appeared in one movie thus far, Cecil B. Demented, a John Waters film. I think she had a tiny cameo, but she had done a lot of theater and was obviously an enormous talent, like her brother, and once I realized there was a possibility of getting her, I was just like, “We have to get Maggie. It will anchor the family with real siblings, and Maggie will be this great foundation for Jake, and for the whole cast, and she was just so essential.” Sometimes the cards are dealt in your favor in terms of who’s available, who is interested, and so much of filmmaking is just the timing. It’s a miracle that any movie gets made.
On giving Seth Rogen his first film role (as a high school bully):
He had done Freaks and Geeks, and he was a standup comedian, performing in comedy clubs. Seth was one of these prodigy kids, really wise beyond his years and ahead of the game. He was maybe 19 years old when we shot the movie, the same age as Jake—incredibly observant, very articulate and funny young actor and writer and comedian, he was already pursuing all these different avenues. I felt like we had access to all the cool LA kid actors, because we shot in Los Angeles, it was the summer of 2000, and there was a commercial [actors] strike where all of the commercials were dark.
On creating the 1980s setting of Donnie Darko.
When we were doing the ‘80s, it was the year 2000, and we were capturing 1988, which is completely insane. That’s 12 years. So you subtract 12 years from 2026 and we are in 2014, which seems completely insane to do a period piece about 2014, because things don’t look that different than they did in 2014—but the disparity between 2000 and 1988 aesthetically was pretty significant. The cars looked completely different, the TVs looked different, the clothing looked different.
In terms of the ’80s aesthetic, we wanted it to feel subtle, we didn’t want a lot of big ’80s hair, and we didn’t want someone wearing a “Beat It” Michael Jackson jacket. We didn’t want it to be kitschy. April Ferry, our incredible, Oscar-nominated costume designer, who we lost a few years ago, was so wonderful in bringing the ’80s fashion for Mary McDonnell and Beth Grant—you see them with the shoulder pads and the different ’80s suburban costuming.
On the movie reference from his original script that didn’t make it to the screen:
In the original script, Donnie and Gretchen went to go see C.H.U.D., just because I thought it was a funny ’80s horror movie. Linda McDonough, who was an executive at Flower Films, was trying to track down the licensing permission for the movie C.H.U.D. as we were approaching the shoot date here at the Aero Theatre, and she was getting nowhere. It was one of the big studios, and there was some woman in charge of licensing at that studio who was just like, “You’re never getting this.”
You would think we were trying to license Lawrence of Arabia or Citizen Kane. They wanted so much money, and we were three days from shooting the scene, and we didn’t have a movie to show. Linda, to her enormous credit, said, “Richard, I am friends with the producers at the studio that owns The Evil Dead, they own the negative. Sam Raimi is a great guy, and they will let us have the poster to show at the front in the lobby of the theater. They’ll let you show any clip from The Evil Dead you want, the music, you can have it basically for free.” It was like a deus ex machina in the form of Sam Raimi. That led to the whole Evil Dead sequence in the movie, that was so perfect. Then we were able to do the marquee with The Last Temptation of Christ—we weren’t showing a clip from the Scorsese film or the poster, just showing the title. That’s an easier ask.
On the influential soundtrack of post-punk and new wave music:
I wasn’t thinking that deep. I was just like, “I love this song.” Like, “Head Over Heels” [by Tears for Fears] was written into the script because I knew that when Donnie and his friends jump out of the school bus, when Donnie’s feet hit the pavement, that first big piano note of “Head Over Heels” starts. When the camera flies through the window and you see all the kids sitting down and Drew Barrymore gathering the class together … “Time flies.” I had to get from the feet hitting the pavement to when they said, “Time flies,” and I had to edit the song down. It was just me doing a music video and loving that song and the vibe and the energy of it.
I have to give an enormous amount of credit to Manish Raval and Tom Wolfe, my music supervisors, who really expanded the canvas of the music in the movie to include Joy Division and Echo and the Bunnymen. It really did form a cohesive musical narrative. We were very fortunate, because no one was really trying to license a lot of that music in the year 2000.
The one song that we could not get—if you go back and watch the dailies, the Sparkle Motion dance scene was choreographed to Pet Shop Boys, but that was a no-go, we could not afford it, so we replaced it with Duran Duran.
On the dialogue that has had a surprising impact—such as the line “Sometimes I doubt your commitment to Sparkle Motion,” as delivered by actor Beth Grant:
It’s so ridiculous. You never know it’s gonna connect. Literally that’s gonna be in my obituary, that line of dialogue, the only thing people remember that I wrote. Beth Grant is the best.
On what the social media reaction would be like if Donnie Darko came out today:
I can’t even wrap my head around it. Online discourse is terrifying, and you kind of try to stay away from it. Any filmmaker that gets too caught up in online discourse, that can only have a negative impact on one’s art. You have to be cognizant of what’s going on in the world, but I think you need to curate your own art as the artist. We need more of that, art that is purely what the artist wants to say.
But I’m emboldened and excited about the younger generation going back to the theaters and reading books. Launching a book, the enormous amount of work that’s gone into writing a novel—it’s very gratifying to get to the finish line on something like that because you realize how a novel can help be the engine for something that is very difficult to get made because of the budget.
On the newer films and filmmakers to catch his eye:
Like everyone else, I saw Obsession. I thought it was terrific. Incredibly well done for such a small budget. The performances were great. I love Ari Aster’s work. I love Jane Schoenbrun’s work. I’ve not seen [Sex and Death at] Camp Miasma, that’s next on my list.
On the movie he most wants to make (besides a sequel to Donnie Darko):
There are so many scripts I’ve written and projects that have hit roadblocks for various reasons. I would love to get my Rod Serling biopic made. That is a very ambitious project that tells the life story of Rod Serling using a fantasy and science-fiction language, in conjunction with his daughter Anne Serling and her memoir about her father. It’s an expensive movie to make, given the fantasy elements and the period elements and the scope. If there are big influences, they would be Defending Your Life, the Albert Brooks film, A Matter of Life and Death by Powell and Pressberger, and All That Jazz by Bob Fosse.

Ambassador Cuculi Opens the School Year at the State School in Athens
On the high school’s 70th anniversary: ‘A point of reference for the Italian community’
08 September 2026, 15:59
ANSA English Desk
Share
Link copiato
- ALL RIGHTS RESERVED
The Italian Ambassador to Greece, Paolo Cuculi, inaugurated the school year at the Italian Comprehensive State School in Athens, coinciding with the 70th anniversary of its high school.
The school, one of seven public schools abroad, enrolls approximately 300 students and offers an educational program ranging from elementary through high school, in addition to housing an accredited preschool on its premises.
The Ambassador, recalling the recent visit to the school by Minister of Education and Merit Valditara, wished the students a new year of fruitful learning and emphasized the importance of the school in Athens, a point of reference for the Italian community and for Greek families, and an important bastion for the promotion of Italian culture and the strengthening of relations between Italy and Greece.

No rooms, Rs 2.3 lakh a night: BRICS Summit sends Delhi hotel rates soaring
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:56:57 UTC
22:56:57 KST

NEW DELHI: As India prepares to host the 18th BRICS Leaders’ Summit, luxury hotels in the national capital are facing a sharp squeeze in room availability, with tariffs at some marquee properties climbing beyond Rs 2 lakh a night ahead of the September 12-13 gathering.The summit, which brings leaders of the expanded BRICS grouping to Delhi and marks two decades since the bloc’s founding, is driving concentrated demand for high-end accommodation, with several premium hotels showing limited or no availability and others quoting rates of more than Rs 2 lakh per night, according to news agency PTI.Booking checks showed no room availability at Taj Mahal and The Oberoi in New Delhi for September 11-12, while Taj Palace had no rooms available for September 10-12. The Leela Palace, New Delhi, was also not accepting bookings for stays between September 10 and 12.At ITC Maurya, New Delhi, rooms available for September 10-13 were commanding tariffs starting at more than Rs 2.3 lakh a night.The surge comes as delegates and other visitors are expected to arrive in the capital ahead of the two-day summit and extend their stays, putting pressure on room inventory, particularly in central Delhi.
K B Kachru, president, Hotel Association of India (HAI) and Chairman - South Asia, Radisson Hotel Group, said the summit was highlighting the pressure on India's hospitality infrastructure."India is commanding global attention at a defining moment -- as the nation prepares to host marquee international events and cements its position as a premier MICE destination, the world is watching how we scale to meet our tourism targets."The BRICS Summit alone will put considerable focus on room inventory and that spotlight is exposing a hard truth: our hospitality infrastructure has not kept pace with our tourism ambition," he said, according to PTI.Kachru said India currently has only about 200,000-220,000 branded hotel rooms, which he described as inadequate for the country's tourism ambitions.The demand is also being felt beyond central Delhi. Rahool Macarius, Market Managing Director, Eurasia, Wyndham Hotels & Resorts, said the summit was creating a distinct demand pattern across Delhi-NCR."At Ramada Encore by Wyndham, Dwarka Expressway, this event-led demand is reflected in occupancy for September 12-15, currently tracking at 65 per cent, significantly ahead of the broader market demand," he said.For tourists, business travellers and families visiting Delhi during the period, the squeeze could mean higher accommodation costs or a shift towards hotels outside central areas and lower-priced properties.
However, hotel tariffs and availability remain dynamic and can change with bookings, cancellations and fresh inventory releases. Emails seeking comments from the hotels cited for availability and tariffs remained unanswered till the time of publication, PTI reported.

====================================================================================================

Channel 4 to axe about 300 jobs in biggest layoffs in its history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:56:34 UTC
22:56:34 KST

Channel 4 is poised to cut about 300 jobs – about a quarter of its workforce – in the biggest round of layoffs in its 43-year history, as the broadcaster seeks to dramatically cut costs.
Priya Dogra, who took over from Alex Mahon as chief executive in March, is to address an all-staff meeting on Wednesday on a wide-ranging review of Channel 4’s strategy and structure.
The broadcaster’s head count had risen to 1,276 by 2025, according to its latest annual report, after undergoing an expansion across the UK.
Channel 4 is still working on final numbers for job losses but multiple sources said the level of savings being sought, which will also come from efficiencies in other parts of the business, equates to about 300 to 325 staff roles.
Two years ago, Mahon announced 200 job cuts, then the biggest round of layoffs in more than 15 years, as staff numbers swelled to a record 1,350 amid the worst TV advertising downturn since 2008.
At the time of Mahon’s cost-cutting programme, Channel 4’s wage bill had hit £108m. It has grown significantly in the past two years to £122m.
When the TV advertising market slumped during the 2008 financial crisis, Channel 4 sought to balance its finances by cutting 200 jobs, almost a quarter of its then 875 permanent employees.
Staff are expecting the cuts to be “brutal”, a source said, and London is likely to be a significant focus, given it was only last year when Channel 4 delivered on a promise to increase employee numbers in the nations and regions to 600.
According to the annual report, Channel 4 employs 255 full-time equivalent staff in the commercial department, 423 in creative roles, 542 in operations and 56 at its 4Talent arm.
Dogra is also expected to make changes to the content and commissioning operation, which last year operated with a £640m programming budget, of which £480m was spent on British original content.
It is understood that Dogra wants Channel 4 to cut back on the number of shows it commissions with a focus on finding fewer but more well-funded hits, and increase marketing firepower to promote programmes, a model she operated with while an executive at Sky and Warner Bros Discovery. However, the overall aim of the restructure and strategy is to limit the extent of cuts to the content budget.
A spokesperson for the broadcaster said: “As we have shared publicly, under the leadership of our new chief executive, we have been assessing Channel 4’s strategic direction, including a comprehensive review of the structure, shape and size of our organisation.
“We have committed to keeping Channel 4 staff updated in a timely and transparent way, so any organisational change will be shared with them first and we won’t be commenting on speculation.”
The announcement comes as candidates for the new director of programmes, a role created after chief content officer Ian Katz announced his departure, are understood to be facing first-round interviews with Dogra this week.
Channel 4 reported a pre-tax loss of £10m last year, a third annual deficit in a row after £12m in 2024 and a record £52m in 2023.
Its total revenues fell by 1% to £1.03bn last year, with total advertising revenues falling by 2%, outperforming the wider market.
The broadcaster is dependent on advertising for 90% of total revenues, making it particularly vulnerable as digital platforms such as YouTube continue to hoover up ad budgets.
Enders Analysis published a report in May on Channel 4 titled Time for Reset, which said that a £69m drop in the broadcaster’s cash reserves to £49m at the end of last year marked their lowest level in more than 20 years.
In July, Channel 4 secured an agreement with the government to tap the remaining half of its £150m revolving credit facility. The broadcaster, which is state-owned but commercially funded, is able to access £75m of its credit facility immediately, but needs state approval to access the remaining half.
In its most recent annual report, Channel 4 said it intended to tap the remaining facility to “protect liquidity headroom and manage risks arising from the current geopolitical and economic environment and our on-going business transformation”.

Local think tank Our Hong Kong Foundation said the latest Global Innovation Index, of which the Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou cluster retained the top spot, reaffirmed the comprehensive innovation strength of the Greater Bay Area.

“It reflects not only Hong Kong’s distinctive strengths in basic research, but also the sustained recognition by an authoritative international institution of closer I&T collaboration in recent years between Hong Kong and mainland GBA cities,” the foundation's deputy research director Victor Kwok said.
He said China leads all nations with the most clusters in the ranking for the fourth straight year – showcasing the effectiveness of its policies in science, technology and innovation.
The SAR should lure more global I&T investment to the city and the GBA through the government's HK$10 billion innovation fund and its international capital networks, Kwok added.

She said that moving forward, deepening cooperation between Hong Kong and other GBA cities will boost the nation's overall I&T development.

African countries interested in Kalashnikov’s KUB-10ME long-range munition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:55:30 UTC
22:55:30 KST

MOSCOW, September 8. /TASS/. The long range of Kalashnikov’s newest strike munition, the KUB-10ME, is generating significant interest among African countries, Leonid Rokeakh, the Kalashnikov Group’s international business director, said at the El Alamein International Airshow 2026, which is taking place in Egypt.
"The capability of Kalashnikov Group’s KUB-10ME tactical-class guided munition to deliver precision strikes against stationary and moving targets at ranges exceeding 100 km has sparked heightened interest among our partners in North Africa," the company quoted him as saying.
According to Rokeakh, the range of the KUB-10ME is a gamechanger. "The range of the KUB-10ME is currently a very sought-after feature of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). The capability to engage moving targets at distances exceeding 100 km, along with an excellent optoelectronic system that outperforms similar systems on reconnaissance UAVs, and pinpoint accuracy, makes our UAV an indispensable weapon in modern warfare – a fact clearly demonstrated in the special military operation zone for which the UAV was originally designed," he added.
The group noted that the KUB-10ME with an 11-kilogram high-explosive fragmentation warhead, is capable of engaging a wide range of targets, including unarmored and lightly armored vehicles (such as APCs), personnel wearing body armor, elements of command posts and air defense missile system battalions, air defense, missile defense, electronic warfare, and rear-area facilities, UAV launch positions, as well as enemy aircraft openly parked at airfields.
The company added that the KUB-10ME strike munition is capable of flying at altitudes ranging from 80 to 1,800 meters at a cruising speed of 120 km/h, and also offers greater protection against electronic warfare and air defense systems compared to similar weapons.

Accessibility is a banking standard, not a competitive edge – Oschadbank chair
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:55:13 EEST
22:55:13 KST

Inclusivity has ceased to be a competitive advantage and has become a basic norm and standard for providing services in Ukraine's financial market, Chairman of the Supervisory Board of JSC Oschadbank Volodymyr Lavrenchuk said.
"My point of view and deep conviction is that inclusivity is not a factor related to competitiveness or competition as such. Inclusivity is already a norm or basic standard without which it is difficult, and unnecessary, to imagine banking services or any services in general today, especially in Ukraine," he said at the 3rd annual My Barrier-Free Environment. Lessons Learned forum in Kyiv on Tuesday.
According to him, compliance with barrier-free principles is an obligation of bank management and staff.
Lavrenchuk stressed that for Oschadbank, its long-standing recognition of this norm serves as the foundation for strengthening public trust. He added that the financial institution would continue developing its barrier-free accessibility efforts.
The Interfax-Ukraine news agency is an information partner of the event.
The 3rd annual My Barrier-Free Environment. Lessons Learned forum was initiated and organized by Oschadbank with the support of Visa as part of Ukrainian First Lady Olena Zelenska's Without Barriers initiative. Oschadbank and its partners are working to make barrier-free accessibility an established social norm.

Kalev Stoicescu: Notes for the future defense minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:55:00 UTC
22:55:00 KST

Kalev Stoicescu: Notes for the future defense minister
National defense is not above criticism, but given the geopolitical situation, political unity on strengthening national defense is absolutely essential, writes Kalev Stoicescu.
At long last, there has been a genuine recognition that the systemic shortcomings and problems in the defense sector, which the National Audit Office has pointed out year after year, are very serious. Recognition alone, however, is not enough unless there is a fundamental change in attitude. Without such a change, it will not be possible to successfully resolve either existing problems or those that may arise in the future.
The next defense minister must, of course, have experience in national defense, but must also be able and willing to strengthen civilian control. Without it, things cannot be put right.
The Riigikogu performs its oversight function most effectively through the National Defense Committee, which specializes in national defense issues. The State Budget Control Select Committee, chaired by (opposition Isamaa leader — ed.) Urmas Reinsalu, has taken the reins, but both this and numerous previous examples show that the committee is driven by a clear desire to put on a political show, which tends to create even more confusion and tension rather than resolve issues.
A change in attitude means having the desire and willingness to genuinely cooperate with the National Audit Office to resolve accounting-related problems. The Ministry of Defense must immediately draw up an appropriate plan setting out all the problems identified by the National Audit Office and how they will be resolved. It must also include specific deadlines. There is no point in drawing up a plan without deadlines because that would render the promises made meaningless.
The Ministry of Defense, the agencies under its administration and the National Audit Office must report regularly to the Riigikogu National Defense Committee, for example every three months. This reporting must, of course, cover implementation of the plan until it has been completed. The next defense minister must be able to get this entire process, for which the minister is responsible, underway before the Riigikogu elections.
A calm working environment must be restored. Military personnel do not interfere in politics, just as politicians must not interfere in the Defense Forces' day-to-day military activities. The Ministry of Defense, the Defense Forces, the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) and the National Audit Office must work together professionally and in good faith to eliminate shortcomings of every kind, rather than sweep them under the rug. We are not talking about the interests of government agencies or political parties, but about the vital interests of the country.
The most precious things that must be preserved are faith in our country and its national defense, as well as the will to defend it. These are more valuable than all the artillery shells and drones in the world.
Everyone within the Ministry of Defense's area of administration must understand that (military) national defense does not consist solely of Defense Forces and Defense League units, weapons and ammunition, other military equipment and supplies and military infrastructure — all of which enjoy a high level of satisfaction and trust — but also, in a broader sense, accounting, including procurement, transactions, (advance) payments, asset accounting and much more. This other side must be in impeccable order as well, just like the first.
Professional military personnel obviously do not need to be accountants, but professional accountants, warehouse managers, accounting staff and others must perform their jobs properly and in accordance with the rules and regulations that apply throughout the country. No exceptions have been made for anyone.
Day-to-day politics and political infighting must not be allowed to intrude into national defense from every direction, particularly during an election campaign. The national defense sector is not taboo or above criticism, but given the geopolitical situation, political unity in strengthening national defense — and not merely on spending 5 percent of GDP — is absolutely essential. Constructive, substantive criticism aimed at solving problems, on the other hand, must be accepted.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Ahead of BRICS summit, Brazil’s top diplomat rejects anti-West framing for the group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:55:00 UTC
22:55:00 KST

Ahead of BRICS summit, Brazil’s top diplomat rejects anti-West framing for the group
- Brazil's Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira rejected the idea that BRICS is anti-West or pursuing de-dollarisation or a common currency, emphasising flexible, low-cost bilateral payment systems instead.
- BRICS members have differing views; countries like Brazil and India support economic realism and non-alignment, while some under sanctions lean towards de-dollarisation and anti-West stances.
- Brazil is strengthening ties with ASEAN and Singapore, highlighting trade growth and shared international law views, while calling for urgent reform of global institutions to better include developing countries.
AI generated
SINGAPORE – Days before leaders from around the world gather in New Delhi for the 18th BRICS Summit, Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira has cautioned against characterising the grouping as an anti-Western bloc.
He also refuted claims that BRICS – an 11-member bloc of emerging markets – intends to challenge the US dollar and dismissed speculation that the bloc is pursuing de-dollarisation or attempting to create a joint BRICS currency.
A few BRICS leaders, including Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, had previously entertained such possibilities in their public addresses. But the bloc has made no formal proposals for de-dollarisation or a BRICS currency.
“I think it’s a mistake to say that BRICS is looking for the promotion of de-dollarisation or creating a new currency. It’s not,” Vieira said.
Instead, he highlighted efforts by BRICS countries to establish voluntary, low-cost payment mechanisms allowing member states to settle bilateral trade in a currency of their choice, whether their own currencies, the euro or the US dollar.
“It’s not going away from the dollar; it’s creating new ways to promote trade and to have a fast system, direct system, and, of course, also a cheaper system of bilateral trade among countries,” he added.
Increased transactions in local currencies, however, even if not aimed at de-dollarisation, can create a de facto shift away from the US dollar.
While some BRICS members under Western sanctions, such as Iran and Russia, have leaned towards a more confrontational, anti-Western and de-dollarisation stance, others, including Brazil and India, have championed non-alignment and economic realism.
Lacking the consensus needed for drastic moves like a common currency or forced de-dollarisation, the bloc’s financial strategy appears to be leaning towards the lowest common denominator – building flexible payment channels that lower transaction costs and allow states to trade in preferred currencies that serve their national commercial interests.
Instead of a monetary union, Vieira highlighted the potential of using newer instant payment systems with lower transaction friction and bank fees, such as Brazil’s Pix and India’s UPI.
“We have in Brazil the Pix, which is used by 80 per cent of the Brazilian population. It is very fast, efficient and free. I’m sure that other systems similar to this one will be put in place in the future for payments among countries,” he said.
Vieira spoke to The Straits Times while on an official visit to Singapore, ahead of stops in Bangkok and New Delhi. During his time in the city-state, he met Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan, Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu, and Minister of State for National Development and Foreign Affairs Alvin Tan.
“We had a good discussion on strengthening our longstanding partnership, including growing our economic links in agri-trade, the digital economy and sustainability. The Mercosur-Singapore Free Trade Agreement, which entered into force between Singapore and Brazil on 1 August 2026, will create more opportunities for our businesses and bring our economies closer together,” Balakrishnan wrote in a Facebook post following their meeting.
The Mercosur-Singapore Free Trade Agreement is Singapore’s first trade deal with the founding states of Mercosur, a South American economic and political trade bloc, and Mercosur’s first free trade deal with an ASEAN country. In addition to Brazil, the agreement has already entered into force for Singapore with Paraguay and Uruguay, while ratification procedures are ongoing for Argentina.
“We also discussed Brazil’s growing engagement with ASEAN and how we can advance ASEAN-Brazil cooperation during Singapore’s ASEAN chairmanship next year,” Balakrishnan wrote.
ASEAN was Brazil’s fifth-largest trading partner in 2025, with bilateral trade reaching US$38.2 billion (S$48.3 billion), nearly rivalling Brazil’s US$40 billion in trade with Mercosur.
Vieira told ST that Brazil’s trade volume with ASEAN is nearly equal to that with its neighbours, underscoring the importance of the region and of Singapore to Brazil.
He further noted that the ASEAN countries and Brazil share “similar visions with relation to international affairs, to international law, and the rule of law in international relations”.
While in Singapore, Vieira also delivered the 7th International Institute for Strategic Studies Raffles Lecture on Brazil’s global strategy in a changing world.
In his lecture, he said that while the prevailing international order has yielded some positive outcomes, it needs urgent reform as it does not serve the interests of developing countries in the Global South or provide them with the recognition they deserve.
“Brazil is a developing nation, striving to chart its own path towards development amid a global order in disarray. As a leading voice of the Global South, Brazil has never shied away from criticising the flaws and limitations of the international order,” he said.
“On international finance, the Bretton Woods institutions have served important purposes over decades, but their governance structures have not kept pace with the shifting weight of the global economy. Emerging economies contribute more and more to global growth, yet their voice in these institutions remains disproportionately limited,” he said.
BRICS, now a major bloc of developing economies representing over a third of global gross domestic product, is increasingly seen as a potential counterweight to the wealthy, influential Group of Seven countries.
“The current paralysis of the World Trade Organization (WTO) is no longer tenable. The WTO does need reform, an urgent and profound one. A reform that better reflects the interests of developing nations, restores its dispute settlement branch, and adapts the organization to new economic realities,” he added.
He cited the New Development Bank (NDB) as an example of an institution developed by BRICS countries for equitable governance and inclusive institutional design, which he said older institutions overlooked.
The NDB, formerly known as the BRICS Development Bank, was set up in 2015 to mobilise financial resources for development projects in emerging economies.
The expansion of BRICS in the last two years has occurred amid an increasingly transactional US foreign policy and tariff environment under President Donald Trump, who has also withdrawn the US from various international institutions and treaties.
The grouping was formalised in 2006 with Brazil, Russia, India and China as its founding members. Membership expanded to include South Africa in 2011, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates in 2024 and Indonesia in 2025.
On new members joining BRICS, he said: “It brought a new breath to BRICS and a new vision of the world. I believe that it’s a place to discuss issues of development and inclusion in world affairs of countries who are looking for a place to make their voices heard.”
