- Days before mail-in ballots arrive statewide, Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton will face off Sept. 30 in California’s high-stakes governor’s race.
- Voters will see sharply contrasting views on taxes, spending and California’s clashes with the Trump administration as the state prepares to choose a successor to termed-out Gov. Gavin Newsom.
- After weeks of Hilton accusing Becerra of ducking debates, the nationally televised, hourlong CNN event — without a studio audience — will give millions of Californians a side-by-side comparison.
Days before California voters receive their mail-in ballots, gubernatorial candidates Xavier Becerra, a Democrat, and Steve Hilton, a Republican, will debate in a nationally televised face-off.
On Sept. 30 at CNN’s Burbank studio, the two candidates hoping to succeed termed-out Gov. Gavin Newson are expected to spar over sharply divergent visions for the future of the state. California’s next leader is expected to face pressing fiscal issues, as well as a continued battle with the Trump administration.
Given California’s deep Democratic tilt, there was a question whether the two men would debate.
On Aug. 19, Becerra promised multiple debates with Hilton ahead of the general election.
“We will have debates, and between now and Nov. 3, we will continue to go out there and meet with folks to make sure they have an opportunity to see the candidates,” Becerra told reporters after greeting business owners, community leaders and voters during a walking tour of Little Tokyo in downtown Los Angeles. “Voters need to have good information. We’ll make sure they have it, and there will be debates.”
The following day, Hilton said he was skeptical of Becerra’s promise.
“I don’t believe him unless he commits to an actual debate. Invitations are on the table for dates and places,” Hilton said. “Why can’t he just accept them? I think he’s lying. I don’t think he wants to do debates because he doesn’t want to debate his record.”
Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton are competing in the race for California governor. Here’s what you need to know about the candidates.
September’s hourlong debate, taking place shortly before county elections officials begin mailing ballots to all the state’s registered voters, will be moderated by the cable network’s anchors Dana Bash and Jake Tapper.
It is the most attention a California gubernatorial contest has drawn since 2010, when “Today” show host Matt Lauer and NBC News Political Director Chuck Todd moderated nationally televised clashes.
That is perhaps unsurprising given how sharply the California electorate has swung left, with no Republican winning a statewide contest since 2006. Two did that year.
While there will not be a studio audience, the debate will air on CNN, CNN International, CNN en Español, CNN.com and related TV and mobile apps for subscribers.

Made in Uzbekistan: Local brands look to new markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:00:59 UTC
22:00:59 KST

From fashion and traditional crafts to electronics and manufactured goods, Uzbek companies are increasingly looking beyond production to build brands that can compete at home and reach consumers abroad.
The “Made in Uzbekistan” label is appearing across an increasingly diverse range of products, as local companies expand production and entrepreneurs look to turn locally made goods into recognisable brands.
The shift can be seen across industries, from textiles, clothing and traditional crafts to electronics, home appliances, food and other manufactured products. It comes amid broader growth in Uzbekistan's manufacturing and exports: industrial production increased by 6.8% in 2025, while exports rose by 24% to about €29 billion, according to the National Statistics Committee.
Changing attitudes towards local products
That change has been particularly visible in Uzbekistan's creative sector.
Teplo Store started organising markets for local designers in 2018 before expanding into a permanent store, festivals and, more recently, an online platform. Today, its store represents around 100 designers, while its festivals can bring together up to 150 participants. Overall, more than 200 designers have worked through the platform.
Co-founder Charos Kamalova says attitudes towards locally made products have changed considerably during that time.
When the project began, she said, products made in Uzbekistan were often associated either with traditional crafts or affordable mass-market goods. Independent designers have since helped create another category based around distinctive ideas, presentation and quality.
“Today it became kind of cool to support local brands,” Kamalova said. “People are coming here, buying this stuff and showing others that, look, I'm supporting local brands.”
Traditional craftsmanship remains an important part of that identity, but designers are increasingly adapting it to contemporary products.
Designer Gulnoza Jo‘rayeva has worked with traditional Uzbek adras, a silk-and-cotton textile, and natural silk for more than 12 years. Her business started at home before gradually expanding and is now represented in seven locations across Uzbekistan.
The production involves young designers, seamstresses and artists, while much of the process remains based on manual work and traditional techniques. Demand has also extended beyond Uzbekistan: the company ships worldwide and has received requests from customers to expand into other cities.
For Teplo co-founder Timur Kamolov, this heritage gives Uzbek designers an advantage — but only if it can be adapted to the needs of modern consumers.
“The key competitive advantage for our brands would be the craftsmanship that we have,” he said.
Kamolov argues that traditional techniques need to be reinterpreted in contemporary and practical products if designers want to compete internationally. At the same time, companies need stronger business processes to turn creative projects into scalable businesses.
Moving beyond the domestic market
Some local brands are already testing demand abroad.
Teplo operated a six-month pop-up store in London's Soho and participated in the London Design Biennale, taking products from Uzbek independent designers directly to international consumers.
Kamalova said the project attracted visitors from different countries and demonstrated interest in Uzbek design beyond the domestic market.
“We saw people from around the world, not only locals in London, that showed huge interest,” she said. “We think that our designers have great potential there.”
Digital sales are providing another route. Teplo has since developed an online platform allowing customers outside Uzbekistan to buy products from local designers, while e-commerce marketplaces are creating additional channels for producers across different sectors to reach consumers abroad.
But moving from local production to international sales brings practical challenges.
For Teplo's London project, the company handled logistics, customs procedures and documentation for participating designers. Kamolov said these processes can be particularly difficult for independent creators, whose expertise often lies in design and production rather than international trade.
The challenge extends beyond the creative industries. According to figures presented by President Shavkat Mirziyoyev following a recent study of exporters, 40% reported difficulties finding foreign customers, while 36% struggled to adapt products to international standards and certification requirements. Another 37% pointed to insufficient financial instruments for exports, and 33% reported gaps in market information, marketing and branding skills.
Building brands for export
New measures announced in August during President Shavkat Mirziyoyev’s open dialogue with entrepreneurs aim to address some of those barriers as Uzbekistan seeks to increase exports and develop national brands.
An “Export Navigator” system is planned to support companies entering foreign markets. Authorities also intend to identify 100 products with export potential and provide guidance on overseas competitors, tariffs, certification requirements and logistics.
The measures specifically target branding and market access. Businesses will be eligible for subsidies of up to €43,000 to promote national brands abroad and adapt them to international requirements. Half the cost of bringing in foreign branding specialists is expected to be covered, as well as half of certain warehousing and sales expenses associated with marketplaces.
The government has also announced support covering 80% of consulting costs for participation in international tenders as part of a wider €860 million export-support system.
For Uzbekistan's businesses, these measures come as the idea of what constitutes a locally made product is broadening. Traditional materials and craftsmanship increasingly sit alongside modern manufacturing, independent design and new consumer businesses.
The next test is whether more producers can turn those locally made products into brands that consumers recognise beyond Uzbekistan.

From corals to saiga: Inside the recovery of threatened wildlife
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:00:46 UTC
22:00:46 KST

From heat-resilient corals in the Gulf of Oman to saiga antelopes on the Ustyurt Plateau, scientists and conservationists are using research, technology and hands-on protection to safeguard threatened wildlife.
Studying the ocean of the future
On the UAE’s east coast, scientists at the Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre are studying marine ecosystems and recreating conditions that could become more common in the oceans of the future.
Some of the centre’s tanks simulate warmer, more acidic waters with lower oxygen levels. Professor Stephen Widdicombe, the centre’s director, says they offer an insight into how marine life could respond as ocean conditions change.
“The oceans are incredibly important, they represent 90% of the habitable space for life on this planet,” Widdicombe said. But he warned, they face pressures ranging from climate change and pollution to other human activities.
One area of research focuses on sea turtles. Every turtle has a unique pattern of scales on its face, much like a human fingerprint. Marine biologist Dr Jon Lapeyra photographs turtles along roughly one kilometre of coastline each week and uses artificial intelligence to help recognise individual animals.
“AI for us, and for this project in particular, has been a game changer,” Lapeyra said.
When the same turtle reappears, researchers can build a record of where it spends time and how it moves. Over six months, 95% of the turtles Lapeyra personally photographed were juveniles, which he described as an encouraging sign for the population.
Coral reefs are another focus. Corals in the Gulf of Oman already experience temperatures that would put many reefs elsewhere under severe stress, making them valuable for research into how reefs may respond to warmer oceans.
“The studies we do on coral reefs here can, of course, tell us something about future scenarios in other places of the world,” said Professor Henrik Stahl, the centre’s head of research and innovation.
Researchers are also working on restoration. Small coral fragments are placed on nursery tables anchored to the seabed, where they can grow into larger colonies under suitable conditions. Protecting threatened species often depends on understanding not only the animals themselves, but the habitats and resources they need to survive.
Protecting wildlife across vast landscapes
On Uzbekistan’s Ustyurt Plateau, the more than 600,000-hectare Saygachiy Complex Landscape Sanctuary protects part of the range of the saiga, a migratory antelope found across Central Asia.
“When we first arrived, we would see only two or three saiga antelopes,” said chief inspector Ortiqbek Saydullayev. “Today, we have managed to establish a resident population.”
Maintaining suitable conditions requires work throughout the year. Staff provide grain and other fodder when snow covers vegetation in winter, while water is pumped to watering points during the dry summer months. Saydullayev says 83 wells are spread across the sanctuary.
Saiga can also travel across national borders in search of food and milder weather. Their movements mean conservation depends not only on conditions within the sanctuary but also on the landscapes through which they migrate.
When protected habitats lose water
Further west, in Karakalpakstan, the Sudochye lake system shows another challenge facing protected wildlife.
Once connected to the Aral Sea, Sudochye became an independent lake system as the sea retreated and remains an important stopover for migratory birds.
“Water levels in the lakes have been declining year after year,” said Aymuradov Tokhtamurad, chief specialist at the Sudochye-Akpetki State Wildlife Sanctuary. “As inflows decrease, salinity increases. This affects wildlife and can force animals to leave the area.”
The changes can be seen along the shoreline, where vegetation remains green in areas still reached by water while reeds and plants further away have dried.
Sanctuary officials say Sudochye is the only nesting site for flamingos in Uzbekistan. If water levels continue to fall, they warn, the lakes could eventually stop functioning as a breeding site anced become primarily a passage point during migration.
Protected status can reduce some pressures, but it cannot replace the water on which an ecosystem depends.
Tracking recovery in the mountains
In southern Uzbekistan’s Kugitang mountains, Surkhan State Nature Reserve protects the markhor, a wild goat known for its corkscrew-shaped horns, and the Bukhara urial, a wild sheep.
The reserve was established in 1986 after populations of both species had fallen sharply. Wildlife censuses are now conducted twice a year.
“In November 2025, we counted nine hundred and eighty-one markhor and one hundred and thirty-seven Bukhara urial,” said deputy director Muhiddin Mamatqulov.
Researchers supplement those counts with 32 camera traps operating across the reserve. Senior researcher Umidjon Murtazayev says the devices record wildlife around the clock and help scientists study rare species, their behaviour, population dynamics and migration.
Technology has not replaced fieldwork. Ranger Bobur Eshoniyev says teams often remain in the mountains into the evening, when many animals become more active.
Reserve officials say the markhor population is growing, although threats including poaching, livestock pressure and fragmented habitat remain.
Across these projects, conservation increasingly combines long-term fieldwork with technologies ranging from artificial intelligence to remote cameras. The next test is whether recovering populations can continue to grow while the habitats they depend on face changing environmental pressures.

Study maps the strategies women use to defend against sexual violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:00:29 UTC
22:00:29 KST

Women identified more than 9,000 possible ways of preventing or responding to sexual violence, with the strategies they suggested varying according to who posed the threat and whether an assault had already occurred. This research was published in Evolutionary Psychological Science.
Sexual violence can produce serious physical, psychological, reproductive, and social consequences. Although considerable research has examined why sexual violence occurs, substantially less has investigated the full range of actions women may use to prevent an assault, resist one in progress, or reduce its consequences afterward. Previous studies have also tended to examine a predetermined set of behaviours, such as avoiding isolated places, travelling with others, or carrying a weapon, rather than allowing women to generate strategies themselves.
This earlier research has often focused on assaults by strangers, even though sexual violence is frequently perpetrated by acquaintances, dates, and romantic partners. Strategies that might be useful against a stranger could carry different practical or social consequences when the potential perpetrator is someone the woman knows.
Rebecka K. Hahnel-Peeters and David M. Buss sought to develop a broader, context-sensitive taxonomy of women’s potential defenses. Drawing on sexual conflict theory, they proposed that women may have learned, developed, or evolved a varied set of responses that are sensitive both to their relationship with a potential perpetrator and to whether they are trying to prevent an assault or manage its aftermath.
Study 1 included 262 women between the ages of 18 and 75, with an average age of 22. Participants were recruited between August 2021 and May 2022 through the University of Texas at Austin psychology participant pool, social media posts, and snowball sampling. They considered five scenarios presented in random order: travelling through a dangerous area, attending a party where an acquaintance accused of sexual assault might be present, meeting a man from a dating app, dealing with a sexually aggressive romantic partner, and a general opportunity to suggest additional protective behaviours.
For each scenario, participants listed three to six things they might do, producing 4,467 nominations. They subsequently provided demographic information and completed measures of sociosexual orientation, perceived mate value, fear of crime, and perceived physical formidability. Responses were organized into an initial coding scheme using both categories suggested by previous theory and categories that emerged from the participants’ answers, after which research assistants who were unaware of the study’s hypotheses independently coded the nominations.
Study 2 included 301 women recruited through the University of Texas at Austin participant pool between August 2023 and May 2024. They were between 18 and 26 years old and were randomly assigned either to suggest ways of preventing an impending sexual assault or to suggest ways of protecting oneself from the consequences of a completed assault. The prevention condition included 148 participants and the aftermath condition included 153.
After reading an explicit definition of sexual assault, participants responded to four randomly ordered prompts involving a stranger, acquaintance, date, or current romantic partner, listing three to six strategies for each. They also reported their biological sex, gender, ethnicity, age, and history of sexual violence. Participants generated 2,268 prevention strategies and 2,350 aftermath strategies, which were independently coded by pairs of research assistants.
In Study 1, the most frequently suggested strategies involved using social allies as “bodyguards.” Women described telling trusted people where they were going, arranging check-ins, bringing someone with them, or pretending that someone else knew their whereabouts. These strategies accounted for nearly 29% of all responses. Preparing to use a weapon or pepper spray accounted for approximately 14%, while other common responses included avoiding isolated places, unwanted attention, nighttime travel, or the situation altogether.
Participants also generated strategies that had received comparatively little attention in previous research, including remaining sober, ending a relationship, researching a potential date, changing clothing or body language, wearing shoes suitable for running, and warning other women through informal “whisper networks.” The strategies varied substantially across scenarios. Remaining sober was overwhelmingly associated with the acquaintance-party scenario, gathering information was especially common before an online date, and ending the relationship or verbally asserting refusal was concentrated in the romantic-partner scenario.
Study 2 showed that women generated similar overall numbers of strategies for prevention and aftermath, but the kinds of strategies differed. For preventing an assault, aggressive defenses, such as carrying a weapon, learning self-defense, or fighting back, were most common, accounting for 33.2% of nominations.
Verbal defenses accounted for 19.0%, using social allies for 16.6%, vigilance for 9.8%, and avoidance for 8.5%. Aggressive defenses were suggested more often against strangers, while avoidance was suggested far less often against romantic partners than against other potential perpetrators. In the aftermath condition, seeking medical or psychological support was the most common response, accounting for 29.4% of nominations.
Participants also suggested turning to social allies, preparing to defend themselves against future assaults, withdrawing socially, engaging in activism or expression, controlling who learned about the assault, pursuing legal action, practising self-care, and warning others. Aftermath strategies were generally less dependent on the perpetrator’s identity, although women were more likely to suggest managing information following an assault by an acquaintance, verbally asserting boundaries with romantic partners, and withdrawing socially following assaults by partners rather than strangers.
Combining both studies produced a preliminary taxonomy of more than 19 broad categories and 48 specific tactics.
The authors emphasize that the taxonomy documents strategies women could imagine using; it does not establish whether participants would use them in real situations or which strategies are most effective.
The research, “Women’s Defenses Against Sexual Violence,” was authored by Rebecka K. Hahnel-Peeters and David M. Buss.

Could China sanction US for illegal international seabed mining? A study says yes

Even the whole GDP won't cover spending: Ukraine has received US$200bn from its partners, but that isn't enough
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:00:00 EEST
22:00:00 KST

Even the whole GDP won't cover spending: Ukraine has received US$200bn from its partners, but that isn't enough
The amount of international financing Ukraine has received from its partners since 24 February 2022 has reached the equivalent of the country's 2021 pre-war GDP. In total, Ukraine has raised almost US$200 billion during this period to fund civilian government spending and, more recently, weapons purchases.
Including financing expected by the end of 2026, the total support provided since the start of the full-scale war will significantly exceed Ukraine's pre-war GDP. Yet even this will not be enough to cover all of the state's financial needs.
Ekonomichna Pravda previously reported that the Ukrainian government needs to secure at least UAH 326 billion (about US$7.4 billion) in additional funding for defence spending, although the Ministry of Defence has requested UAH 1.1 trillion (US$24.9 billion) for the final four months of the year. The most likely option is to bring forward part of next year's funding to cover current defence needs.
Ever-increasing aid volumes
The full-scale war dealt a body blow to Ukraine's economy and public finances. From day one of the invasion, spending soared and budget revenues plummeted.
This resulted in an unforeseen deficit in the state budget. To cover it, the authorities made spending cuts, reducing non-priority expenditure, and increased domestic borrowing. But these measures weren't enough, so the government turned to other countries and international organisations for assistance.
Russia's invasion in 2022 came as a surprise not only to Ukraine but also to its Western partners. Some of them, despite having intelligence about preparations for the attack, did not expect Ukraine to hold out for so long. None had budgeted for financing Ukraine's needs.
By the end of 2022, Ukraine had received US$31.1 billion from its partners. The remaining funding gap had to be covered by borrowing from the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU). During the first year of the full-scale war, the NBU issued UAH 400 billion (US$9 billion) to meet the government's financing needs. This enabled the government to fund defence spending, but significantly weakened the hryvnia's purchasing power and accelerated inflation.
In 2023, Kyiv's international partners became more actively involved in financing Ukraine's needs. By then it had become clear that Ukraine needed long-term, multi-billion-dollar support programmes rather than ad hoc solutions. The key programmes are outlined below.
IMF Extended Fund Facility (EFF) – US$15.6 billion. This was the first major lending programme agreed upon during the full-scale war to provide financing over four years. It followed lengthy negotiations and several tranches of emergency financing provided in 2022.
	
The EFF for Ukraine was the first loan in the IMF's history to be granted to a country engaged in a full-scale war and experiencing extreme macroeconomic uncertainty.
Ukraine ended the programme early in 2025 because its assumptions no longer matched the realities on the ground. During the initial negotiations, the IMF had expected the full-scale war to last 18 months to two years, followed by a recovery phase. Consequently, from 2025 onwards, the programme's financing volumes and structural benchmarks no longer aligned with Ukraine's macroeconomic situation.
Despite its substantial size – almost US$16 billion – the EFF programme largely covered Ukraine's scheduled repayments to the IMF on previous loans. However, it also served as a kind of seal of approval which enabled Ukraine to secure financing from other partners.
In early 2026, the IMF approved a new four-year EFF programme for Ukraine worth US$8.1 billion. As with its predecessor, the amount broadly corresponds to Ukraine's repayments on previous IMF loans.
Ukraine Facility – €50 billion. A four-year EU programme agreed upon at the end of 2023. Of the total, €39 billion is allocated as direct budget support, with the remainder going towards business support and interest payments.
The programme has become one of the EU's key mechanisms for providing financial support to Ukraine and a roadmap for the country's further integration into the EU. Access to financing is tied to a reform plan aimed at advancing EU integration, creating not only a political but also a financial incentive for the authorities to adopt necessary and often unpopular measures.
Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration (ERA) Loans – US$50 billion. The first financial instrument backed by windfall profits from Russian assets frozen in the West. Ukraine began receiving funds under the programme in late 2024.
Funding under the programme has been provided to Ukraine over the last two years by the G7 countries and the EU, in whose jurisdictions around US$300 billion in Russian assets have been frozen. Interestingly, even now no one knows the exact value of these assets. What is known is that the bulk of the funds – more than US$200 billion – is held in accounts at the Belgian securities depository Euroclear.
Financing under the ERA Loans Initiative has been provided by the United States (US$20 billion), the EU (US$20 billion) and other G7 countries (US$10 billion). A distinctive feature of the loan is that Ukraine is not required to repay it unless Russia agrees to pay reparations after the war ends.
Ukraine Support Loan (USL) – €90 billion. The second financial mechanism linked to frozen Russian assets. The loan covers 2026-2027, with €60 billion earmarked for weapons procurement. As with the ERA Loans, Ukraine will not have to repay the USL, as it is backed by the proceeds of frozen Russian assets.
The loan was the subject of long and difficult negotiations during which Ukraine and most EU countries pushed for frozen Russian assets to be used to support Kyiv. Belgium, where Russian central bank assets are immobilised, strongly opposed the move, citing concerns about the "legal consequences".
Using these Russian assets to back the loan was a compromise solution of sorts that enabled Ukraine to cover a significant share of its external financing needs for 2026-2027.
Meanwhile, Ukraine has not abandoned the idea of directly seizing Russian assets and recently sought to reopen discussions on the issue within the EU.
The problem is that after accounting for the funds provided under the ERA Loans and the USL, the amount of frozen Russian assets still available for a new mechanism is rapidly shrinking. If all these assets were transferred to Ukraine, just over half of the amount frozen in the West since the full-scale war began would ultimately reach the Ukrainian budget. The remainder would go to international creditors.
A club of friends
During the early years of the full-scale war, the US played the most significant role in providing financial support to Ukraine. Unlike the programmes offered by the EU, IMF and Kyiv's other partners, US assistance came in the form of grants, meaning it did not have to be repaid.
In 2022-2023 the US provided Ukraine with almost US$22 billion, compared with US$21 billion from the EU. From 2024 onwards, however, America's financial and defence aid to Ukraine became a contentious issue in the presidential election campaign as Donald Trump castigated the White House for its continued financial support for Ukraine.
Since Trump's re-election, the US has not provided Ukraine with direct budget support. However, the EU has adopted large-scale programmes over the last few years to support Ukraine's financial stability.
In addition to the US and the EU, Japan has contributed unexpectedly substantial budget support to Ukraine – almost US$10 billion. Canada, the UK and Germany have provided a further combined total of almost US$11 billion. Germany also plays a pivotal role in financing Ukraine through EU mechanisms, as it is the European Union's largest economy.
The debt trap
Not all the international financing Ukraine has received since the start of the full-scale war has been provided as grants. Most has taken the form of loans, albeit on concessional terms.
That means that this financial support has increased Ukraine's public debt, which according to the Ministry of Finance has more than doubled to US$214.18 billion.
The structure of Ukraine's public debt has also deteriorated significantly during the full-scale war. At the end of 2021, 41.6% of the total was domestic debt and 58.4% was external. Today, the share of domestic debt has fallen to 21.7%, while 78.3% is owed to external creditors.
This structure makes public debt more sensitive to fluctuations in the hryvnia exchange rate and political developments in partner countries, posing additional risks to Ukraine's financial stability.
In the summer of 2024, the government reached an agreement with commercial creditors to restructure its eurobond debt. At the end of 2025, it also restructured its GDP warrants, payouts from which were linked to economic growth. Although the burden on the state budget has been significantly reduced by these measures, it remains substantial.
For example, debt repayment and servicing costs in 2027 will exceed UAH 1 trillion (US$22.6 billion). The government is likely to seek to cover some of these payments through further borrowing. As a result, servicing and repaying wartime debt will remain one of the largest items in the state budget for years, if not decades, to come.

Murder For Hire: Details Emerge About Alleged Cross-Border Plot to Kill Twin Brothers in Cyprus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Reported by
On the evening of August 10, a person using the handle “Sponge Jobb” posted a call for a hitman to a group on the Signal messaging app.
The group member, who used an avatar of the cartoon character SpongeBob SquarePants, said weapons and transport were available. The person ultimately offered $60,000 in cryptocurrency for the murder.
Days after the advertisement for a contract killer appeared, a Danish man answered. But the would-be hitman was actually an undercover officer. His work triggered an international police operation leading to an attempted murder case now unfolding in Cyprus, where the hit was allegedly intended to take place.
Those are some of the details gathered by OCCRP member center CIReN from the Cypriot court, where authorities have submitted information from their investigation into the alleged murder plot.
Many questions remain, and authorities are keeping tight-lipped as the investigation is ongoing. The targets were described in the Cyprus court only as twin brothers vacationing on the island. The possible motive for their murder has not been revealed.
The brothers left Cyprus as the plot was unfolding, and authorities are now searching for them with the help of Interpol, the international policing agency.
Eight alleged participants of the plot have been arrested, including an Irish national, two Norwegians and five Swedes. OCCRP’s media partners in Norway and Sweden have found information about the criminal histories of some of the suspects.
The five Swedes were already known to authorities, according to Teodor Smedius, Superintendent at the Swedish Police Authority’s National Operations Department.
“This is a fairly typical violence-as-a-service setup,” he told Sweden’s SVT.
Smedius declined to comment on where the order for the murder may have originated, but said: “It is absolutely clear that our domestic criminal networks cooperate with other organised criminal networks across Europe.”
The two Norwegians had criminal convictions in their home country, according to court records obtained by Norway’s VG.
One man was convicted of assault and fraud, and was sentenced to a year and five months in prison, records show. The other man’s history includes a five-month sentence for storing narcotics. The Norwegian records show no indication that the sentences were appealed.
Alexandros Clerides, the lawyer appointed in Cyprus to defend one of the Norwegians, said his client “categorically denies any involvement in, or connection with, the matters being investigated by the Cypriot police.”
“My client was in Cyprus on holiday,” Clerides told VG.
Omar Tashakori, the attorney for the other Norwegian suspect, said he had no comment on the case.
After the arrest of two Norwegians and an Irish national, the international police operation netted five Swedes. Reporters were not able to reach their lawyer for the Swedes or the Irish citizen before publication.
In court in Cyprus, the two Norwegian suspects exercised their right to silence.
According to information from Interpol’s Ireland office, which has been brought forward in Cypriot court, the Irish suspect has no criminal history and is known to police in his home country only for traffic offences.
The Irish suspect testified that he was not involved in any murder plot, and had been on vacation in Cyprus where he met one of the Norwegians and began hanging out with him. He said the Norwegian had paid him 200 euros to deliver an envelope containing 1,000 euros to a location in the Cypriot resort town of Ayia Napa. He stated that the Norwegian had told him he owed the money to a friend.
But that payment was allegedly intended for the contract killer, according to information that has emerged in court.
The Danish undercover officer posing as the hitman collected the money from a cardboard box behind rubbish bins near Ayia Napa Primary School, while two alleged participants in the plot watched from nearby.
By then, he had also been provided with images of his targets. Two photographs were sent to his phone: the twins he was allegedly hired to kill.
The weapons were supposed to come next. The Danish officer was discussing with a Signal contact the delivery of two pistols and magazines, allegedly brought in from Turkey.
But before the weapons could reach the undercover officer, the twins left Cyprus. With the alleged targets gone, police moved against the men they had been watching.

Ukraine has received US$200bn from its partners, but that isn't enough
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
16:00:00 EEST
22:00:00 KST

Even the whole GDP won't cover spending: Ukraine has received US$200bn from its partners, but that isn't enough
The amount of international financing Ukraine has received from its partners since 24 February 2022 has reached the equivalent of the country's 2021 pre-war GDP. In total, Ukraine has raised almost US$200 billion during this period to fund civilian government spending and, more recently, weapons purchases.
Including financing expected by the end of 2026, the total support provided since the start of the full-scale war will significantly exceed Ukraine's pre-war GDP. Yet even this will not be enough to cover all of the state's financial needs.
Ekonomichna Pravda previously reported that the Ukrainian government needs to secure at least UAH 326 billion (about US$7.4 billion) in additional funding for defence spending, although the Ministry of Defence has requested UAH 1.1 trillion (US$24.9 billion) for the final four months of the year. The most likely option is to bring forward part of next year's funding to cover current defence needs.
Ever-increasing aid volumes
The full-scale war dealt a body blow to Ukraine's economy and public finances. From day one of the invasion, spending soared and budget revenues plummeted.
This resulted in an unforeseen deficit in the state budget. To cover it, the authorities made spending cuts, reducing non-priority expenditure, and increased domestic borrowing. But these measures weren't enough, so the government turned to other countries and international organisations for assistance.
Russia's invasion in 2022 came as a surprise not only to Ukraine but also to its Western partners. Some of them, despite having intelligence about preparations for the attack, did not expect Ukraine to hold out for so long. None had budgeted for financing Ukraine's needs.
By the end of 2022, Ukraine had received US$31.1 billion from its partners. The remaining funding gap had to be covered by borrowing from the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU). During the first year of the full-scale war, the NBU issued UAH 400 billion (US$9 billion) to meet the government's financing needs. This enabled the government to fund defence spending, but significantly weakened the hryvnia's purchasing power and accelerated inflation.

Russians restrict use of military equipment in Oleksandrivka sector due to Ukrainian FPV drones – press officer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Russians restrict use of military equipment in Oleksandrivka sector due to Ukrainian FPV drones – press officer
This was stated in an interview with Ukrinform by Serhii Kolesnychenko, an officer with the communications section of the 148th Separate Zhytomyr Artillery Brigade of the Ukrainian Air Assault Forces.
“The enemy has enough weapons to conduct intensive offensive operations. They have artillery, armored vehicles and a large number of unmanned systems. At the same time, they face difficulties in using these weapons effectively. Because the battlefield is saturated with Ukrainian FPV drones, the enemy is forced to limit the use of equipment that cannot reach the line of contact within 15 kilometers,” Kolesnychenko said.
According to him, once Russian military equipment enters the kill zone, it is immediately targeted and destroyed by FPV drones operated by Ukrainian forces. As a result, Russian forces are being forced to disperse their equipment and rely increasingly on long-range strike capabilities, including unmanned systems.
“That is why the Security and Defense Forces of Ukraine must do more than simply destroy enemy weapons. They must systematically undermine the enemy’s ability to deploy them in the right place and at the right time,” the officer emphasized.
Kolesnychenko noted that artillery is also being used extensively in the Oleksandrivka sector, although its role has changed significantly compared with 2024.
“As for heavy equipment, the high density of UAVs on the battlefield makes it virtually impossible to conceal it – sooner or later, it will be destroyed. Artillery is also being used more cautiously and often from greater distances. Today, the most effective approach is not relying on any single type of weapon, but combining them. Reconnaissance identifies the target, unmanned systems carry out the strike and adjust fire, while artillery provides the necessary fire support,” the serviceman said.
According to Kolesnychenko, what matters on the modern battlefield is not who has more of a particular type of weapon, but who can detect a target faster, make a decision and strike first. The speed of this cycle is a major factor in determining how effectively weapons can be used, he stressed.
As reported by Ukrinform, Kolesnychenko previously said that the main result of the Defense Forces’ operation in the Oleksandrivka sector was not the liberation of more than 745 square kilometers of territory and 26 settlements, but the fact that Russian forces had been unable to carry out their plan at the pace they had intended.

Russia to emerge from Ukraine conflict even stronger militarily — RUSI report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:59:46 UTC
21:59:46 KST

LONDON, September 8. /TASS/. Russia will be in a much stronger military position following the special military operation in Ukraine than it was before, in terms of its possession of high-precision weapons capable of striking enemy targets, says a report by the London-based Royal United Services Institute for Defence and Security (RUSI), obtained by TASS.
The report, authored by RUSI Senior Research Fellow Sidharth Kaushal and Sam Cranny-Evans, an Associate Fellow at RUSI, editor-in-chief of the online military technology publication Calibre Defense, notes that during the conflict, the Russian Armed Forces supplemented their customary tactics of suppressing the enemy with massive artillery fire by making more extensive use of precision-guided weapons. "Since 2022, the war has led Russia to significantly expand its precision strike capabilities in terms of quantity, quality, scale and integration," the report states.
"At the tactical level, Russia retains the ability to conduct massed artillery fires. Precision targeting, drones and reconnaissance-strike complexes have not replaced artillery but rather complement Russia’s enduring preference for overwhelming firepower along key axes of advance," the experts noted.
"Russian forces have also developed a substantial cadre of reconnaissance personnel with extensive experience locating small, mobile targets under combat conditions. If this expertise is retained after the war, it likely that Russia will enter future conflicts in a far stronger position than it had in 2022," the report emphasizes.
Doctrinal changes
The authors also noted that "in parallel, the distinction between reconnaissance-fire and reconnaissance-strike complexes has increasingly blurred. Precision strike capabilities are now routinely employed for counter-battery missions and attritional strikes." At the same time, "drones operate as part of an integrated system that also includes guided missiles and glide bombs. The shift from the massive use of munitions to the use of precision-guided weapons may be more significant than the specific types of systems deployed in the conflict in Ukraine," the experts added.
Kaushal and Cranny-Evans noted that "the operational and doctrinal adaptations observed during the conflict in Ukraine--such as a reinforced single chain of command, streamlined target acquisition, and the integration of low-cost and high-tech strike systems--will define future Russian military operations."
"Russia has shifted from relying on mass firepower to mass precision strikes. In turn, these adaptations are likely to shape future Russian doctrine and force structure, producing forces that are more lethal and effective at targeting adversaries once ISTAR superiority is established," the report states.
At the same time, the experts state, "This evolution should not, however, be conflated with UAVs alone: this paper’s central argument is that UAVs are one component of an evolving precision strike complex, alongside more accurate artillery and air-launched standoff munitions. Russia’s methods of employing certain capabilities will probably prove more enduring than the munitions themselves," the experts concluded.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan International Ports Corporation said Monday that it has secured more berths for Coast Guard ships to dock between operations.

Taiwan International Ports Corporation said it has consistently supported Coast Guard maritime operations since 2021. It provides the administration with about 26 available berths across seven international and two domestic commercial ports.
The company said it will continue improving flexible use of existing berths at Keelung, Taipei, Suao, Taichung, Kaohsiung, and Hualien. New dedicated Coast Guard wharf projects are also planned at Taipei, Taichung, Kaohsiung, Anping, and Penghu’s Longmen port area, adding an estimated 14 berths.

After Greece signs deal to buy Achilles Shield, Israel’s control of source code sparks controversy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:59:34 UTC
21:59:34 KST

Ayhan Mehmet
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
Just a week after Athens agreed to buy an air and missile defense system from Israel, revelations that Greece will not have access to the Achilles Shield's source code have drawn criticism from opposition parties and the Greek media.
The controversy intensified after Moshe Patel, director of the Israel Missile Defense Organization, told Greek daily Kathimerini that Greece would not be granted access to the source code.
The opposition Panhellenic Socialist Movement (PASOK) called on the government to clarify the issue.
Mihalis Katrinis, PASOK’s lawmaker responsible for defense affairs, said Defense Minister Nikos Dendias said in a July 23 speech that the procurement of systems for the Greek Armed Forces would not proceed unless Greece secures access to the source code.
Katrinis noted, however, that the Israeli Defense Ministry said on Aug. 31 that the new national command-and-control infrastructure would be developed by Israeli company Rafael.
“Will the source code of the Achilles Shield ultimately belong to Greece?” he asked.
He said PASOK had brought the issue before parliament on Sept. 1 and is awaiting a written response from the Defense Ministry.
Katrinis called for the agreement’s technical and legal provisions to be made public, stressing that access to the source code is crucial for safeguarding Greece’s national interests in a deal worth billions of euros.
The Greek Left Alliance, founded by former Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras, said the lack of access raised serious questions about the management of the system and “the protection of national interests.”
The party said the government had been “left exposed” and warned that Greece could become dependent on another country unless it secures full control of the system.
Greek daily Efimerida ton Syntakton reported that Israel’s latest statements referred to technology transfer and the joint use of software and technology with the Greek Armed Forces, but did not explicitly say the source code would be handed over.
Asked by Kathimerini whether Greece would have access to the source code linked to the system’s command-and-control capabilities, Patel replied: “No, because the source code was not included in the agreement’s user license.”
Efimerida ton Syntakton alleged that the question-and-answer section was removed from Kathimerini’s website before the report was updated with references to “technology transfer” and the “joint use of software and technology.”
To Vima said Patel’s statement had raised serious questions in Athens and appeared to contradict previous statements by Greek officials.
 
€3B defense agreement
Israel and Greece signed the approximately €3 billion ($3.5 billion) Achilles Shield agreement in Tel Aviv on Aug. 31.
Under the deal, Israel will establish a multilayered air-defense network in Greece made up of Rafael’s David’s Sling and Spyder systems, Israel Aerospace Industries’ Barak MX system, and MMR multimission radars.
The agreement also includes a new national command-and-control system to be developed under Rafael’s leadership.
Opposition parties have argued that the deal would increase Greece’s defense dependence on Israel, burden taxpayers, and tie Athens’ regional policy more closely to Israel.
Former Finance Minister Yanis Varoufakis called the agreement “shameful.”
“Although the vast majority of Greeks oppose the genocidal apartheid state, we have allowed our ruling class to stain Greece with this disgraceful agreement,” he said.

Sadiq Khan rounds on Westminster council for keeping ‘vertical drinking’ curbs on pubs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:59:26 UTC
21:59:26 KST

Sadiq Khan has criticised the “breathtaking arrogance” of Westminster council, which has kept restrictions on vertical drinking in Soho and an effective ban on new bars and pubs in the area.
The mayor of London has accused the Conservative-led council of “ignoring” the responses to a consultation into its new licensing policy. The vast majority of respondents, 81%, disagreed with the council’s “cumulative impact zone” which decrees that applications for bars and pubs in the West End of London, one of Europe’s most famous nightlife districts, will be refused unless in exceptional circumstances. Eighty-four per cent said the licensing policy would be bad for business.
Respondents also criticised the council’s position on “vertical drinking”, which is standing up to have a beverage, a common practice in British pubs. The council proposed, to widespread outcry, that new licences for pubs and bars should be granted to those venues which have table service instead of ordering at the bar, and those in which people are seated rather than standing.
The mayor had responded to a consultation held this summer by the council and ordered them to scrap the cumulative impact zone and allow pubs and bars to have space for vertical drinking. Andy Burnham, the prime minister, also waded into the row, saying vertical drinking is “British life”.
Despite this, the council is continuing with both the vertical drinking policy and the cumulative impact zone, and said that those who wrote to complain did so because they did not understand the terminology in its licensing document.
Khan told the Guardian: “The arrogance of Westminster council is breathtaking. By ignoring all those who oppose their plans and viewing hospitality in the heart of our capital city as a problem, they are letting down businesses, residents and our economy. They would rather see nightlife die than thrive.”
Tim Barnes, Westminster city council’s deputy leader, said the issue was a policing one and called for more resources for the area. He added: “Beyond disagreements over policy jargon there are serious issues acting as a drag on our hospitality industry.
“A lack of investment in policing has left the Met objecting to many licensing applications over public safety concerns.”
But the final licensing policy keeps restrictions on vertical drinking. It reads: “When considering new licence applications, discourage excessive drunkenness and encourage the provision of more seating in premises that serve alcohol for people to sit and enjoy a drink and order food by table service in place of open bar space that caters for high volume vertical drinking.”
In the revised policy, the council says it did approve a new pub in the cumulative impact zone recently – The Lady in Covent Garden. However, most of the space in this pub is for a sit-down restaurant. The document states that the bar on the bottom floor of the pub would not usually be allowed, but in this case it is because it will “only operate in association with the restaurant use”.
The government is due to grant new powers to Khan, allowing him to “call in” local council decisions he opposes.
He said: “London’s famous hospitality and nightlife sectors are vital for our economy, and one of the reasons our capital is so special.
“Running our world-famous nightlife district with a nimby village-hall mindset is simply not sustainable. This is why the government was right to give me new powers to help ensure our fantastic hospitality and nightlife can flourish, helping create more jobs and ensure we stay a vibrant global city.”
Data shows that only 3.5% of applications that went to a licensing subcommittee in Westminster were approved exactly as applied for between 2023 and 2026. Pub and wine bar applications were down 80% in 2022-24.
The Soho Society, a group established in 1972 aimed at “preserving the character of Soho”, voted in its AGM earlier this summer for a new licensing mandate, meaning it will challenge all new applications for bars and restaurants in the area, including reviews of existing licences. It will also object to any venue that wishes to open beyond “core hours”, which Westminster council decrees end between 10.30pm and midnight, depending on the business and day of the week.

Ozempic and Wegovy may have an unexpected mental health benefit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:59:00 UTC
21:59:00 KST

Ozempic and Wegovy may have an unexpected mental health benefit
Semaglutide, better known through Ozempic and Wegovy, was linked to a 21% lower risk of psychiatric hospitalization in people with bipolar disorder.
- Date:
- September 8, 2026
- Source:
- Griffith University
- Summary:
- Semaglutide, the drug behind Ozempic and Wegovy, may have benefits that extend well beyond weight loss and diabetes. In a large Swedish study of nearly 15,000 people with bipolar disorder, its use was linked to a 21% lower risk of psychiatric hospitalization. Researchers think effects on inflammation and brain-related biological pathways could help stabilize mood, though other GLP-1 drugs did not show the same association.
- Share:
Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), widely used to treat diabetes and support weight loss, may also have benefits for mental health, particularly among people with bipolar disorder, according to new research from Griffith University.
Diabetes, obesity, and bipolar disorder frequently occur together and may share some underlying biological mechanisms. According to the latest World Health Organization estimates, about one in 200 people worldwide, or roughly 37 million people, live with bipolar disorder.
GLP-1 medications are already established treatments for diabetes and obesity, but their possible effects on bipolar disorder have remained unclear.
Large Study Examines GLP-1 Drugs and Bipolar Disorder
To investigate the connection, researchers led by Professor Mark Taylor from Griffith's School of Medicine and Dentistry analyzed nationwide Swedish data from nearly 15,000 people with bipolar disorder who had been prescribed GLP-1 medications over a 15-year period.
"People with bipolar disorder who were taking semaglutide (otherwise known as Ozempic or Wegovy), a type of GLP-1 medication, had significantly lower rates of psychiatric hospitalization compared with periods when they were not taking GLP-1 medicines," Professor Taylor said.
"The findings add to growing evidence that GLP-1 receptor agonists may have benefits beyond diabetes and obesity treatment, and could represent a promising new avenue for bipolar research."
The researchers found that semaglutide use was associated with a 21 percent lower risk of psychiatric hospitalization.
Semaglutide May Affect Brain-Related Processes
The findings suggest that GLP-1 signaling could help protect the brain by reducing inflammation, cellular stress, and other biological processes associated with bipolar disorder.
These effects could potentially contribute to greater mood stability and a lower risk of relapse.
However, the same pattern was not seen with every GLP-1 medication. Liraglutide and dulaglutide were not associated with a reduced risk of psychiatric hospitalization, indicating that any potential mental health benefit may not extend across the entire drug class.
Professor Taylor said he hopes the findings will now be examined in a randomized controlled trial, which would provide stronger evidence about whether semaglutide itself can improve psychiatric outcomes in people with bipolar disorder.
The paper 'Use of glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists and the associated risk of hospitalisation in bipolar disorder, from a nationwide cohort, 2009-2024' has been published in Acta Psychiatrica Scandinavica.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Griffith University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Heidi Taipale, Mark Taylor, Markku Lähteenvuo, Ellenor Mittendorfer‐Rutz, Antti Tanskanen, Jari Tiihonen. Use of Glucagon‐Like Peptide 1 Receptor Agonists and the Associated Risk of Hospitalisation in Bipolar Disorder, From a Nationwide Cohort, 2009–2024. Acta Psychiatrica Scandinavica, 2026; 154 (4): 305 DOI: 10.1111/acps.70120

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) said Monday that Taiwan will deepen cooperation with like-minded countries to protect its democracy.
Hsiao made the remarks while meeting scholars from the Taiwan in the Indo-Pacific Region program at Stanford University’s Hoover Institution, per CNA. She discussed Taiwan’s cross-strait relations and thanked the delegation for its long-standing interest in Taiwan-US ties.
On defense, Hsiao said the government is increasing defense spending while strengthening combat capabilities. She pointed to the recent Han Kuang exercises, which for the first time included an urban resilience exercise linking military drills with civil defense preparations.

On cross-strait relations, Hsiao said the situation remains difficult because China’s leadership has refused dialogue with Taiwan’s democratically elected government. She said Taiwan will not provoke conflict but will not compromise its freedom and democracy.
Hoover Institution Senior Fellow Larry Diamond called Taiwan a model of democratic resilience and urged its political parties to take a pragmatic approach to domestic divisions.

Ukraine unveils Koral air defense system launcher for first time
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
15:58:46 EEST
21:58:46 KST

Ukraine has developed its own surface-to-air missile system for intercepting ballistic targets, with a missile weighing 450 kg, including a 36-kg warhead, Militarnyi reports.
Ukraine displayed the Koral air defense missile launcher publicly for the first time at the MSPO defense exhibition in Poland, according to Militarnyi. An image released by Ukroboronprom shows a missile being launched from a self-propelled launcher mounted on a Czech Tatra truck chassis.
The missile is designed to intercept air and ballistic targets and is intended for use as part of an air defense system, though the developer notes it can also, in exceptional cases, be used against ground or surface radar-contrast targets.
The missile weighs 450 kg, including a 36-kg warhead. Its guidance system combines an inertial navigation system, radio correction and an active radar homing head. The missile has a diameter of 230/300 mm and a length of 4.8 meters, with a wingspan of 835 mm and a control fin span of 685 mm. By comparison, the Patriot system's PAC-3 missile weighs 316 kg, with a 24-kg warhead.
Work on the Koral project began back in 2016, when the missile appeared in documents as a component of a ship-based air defense missile system, according to Militarnyi.
Koral first came into wider public discussion in 2021, when the Luch Design Bureau presented a full-scale mockup of the missile at the Arms and Security 2021 exhibition.

Netanyahu races to unify Israel's right wing in bid to avert election defeat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:57:12 UTC
21:57:12 KST

Netanyahu races to unify Israel's right wing in bid to avert election defeat
JERUSALEM, Sept 8 - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is seeking to consolidate Israel's fractious right-wing parties ahead of a Tuesday deadline in order to avoid an election loss forecast by opinion polls.
Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, is seeking a record seventh term in the October 27 election, but he has faced pressure over the Hamas-led 2023 attack on Israel and subsequent wars in Gaza, Iran and Lebanon, and surveys have for months been pointing to a defeat for his nationalist-religious coalition.
Netanyahu has therefore been pressing allies to merge their candidate lists and raise their chances of gaining parliament seats, so far with only partial success.
Their deadline, when running parties must submit their final lists of candidates, expires on Tuesday night.
"When we unite, we win. When we splinter, we lose," Netanyahu said in an August 30 interview on Channel 14, a pro-Netanyahu television station. "I am doing all I can, as I did in the previous election, to unite these parties."
RIGHT-WING NEWCOMER WORRIES NETANYAHU
No single party has ever won an outright majority in the 120-seat Knesset, Israel's parliament, making coalition governments the norm and sometimes giving as many as a dozen parties a chance of winning seats.
To do so, they must pass a 3.25% vote threshold, equal to four seats, meaning smaller parties risk drawing votes without gaining a seat.
Polls suggest Netanyahu's Likud party stands to lose a third of its parliamentary power. Though it may still remain the largest party, winning 20-23 seats, Netanyahu would likely need his coalition allies including the far-right Jewish Power and Religious Zionism parties to remain in office.
Religious Zionism, headed by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, has been polling between zero and six seats, down from seven currently. With Netanyahu's blessing — and his help, according to two political sources — it merged its list on September 1 with that of Zehut, a small party headed by former far-right libertarian and Likud member, Moshe Feiglin.
But National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has rebuffed Netanyahu's calls for his Jewish Power party, which currently holds six seats, to run with Religious Zionism, as it did at his behest in the last election. Ben-Gvir has argued that the parties would be stronger running separately.
Feiglin's views on the Palestinians are similar to those of Ben-Gvir and Smotrich, whose calls to annex the occupied West Bank and depopulate Gaza have drawn international ire.
Though such foreign criticism may have little impact on the vote, another worry for Netanyahu is political newcomer Ofer Winter, a right-wing former brigadier general whose views are largely aligned with those of Smotrich.
But Winter has rejected calls to merge his party, saying he will not run with anyone who may be responsible for the security failure that allowed for the 2023 Hamas-led attack.
Winter has cast the election as a protest vote and says he will draw right-wingers who are seeking a fresh start. Latest polls show him at four seats or none.
"He chose to go separately and we are now in danger," Netanyahu told Channel 14, arguing that he risks "wasting" crucial right-wing votes if he does not win enough seats to enter the Knesset.
HAWKISH IMAGE SHATTERED
The parliamentary system delivered a decisive victory for Netanyahu in the previous 2022 election, when a splintered centre-left was knocked out by a unified right-wing alliance.
Now, however, Israel's most dominant politician of his generation is in a far weaker starting position.
Netanyahu's hawkish image was shattered by the security failing of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack, with critics angered by his refusal to take responsibility, and by wars in Gaza, Iran and Lebanon that brought military successes but no lasting victories.
"He's never faced anything like what he faces now. Everyone in Israel shares a sense of historical crisis, and his name is all over it. And he knows this," said Amotz Asa-El, a political analyst with the Shalom Hartman Institute in Jerusalem.
With Israel's military death toll at its highest in decades, Netanyahu's concessions toward ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies who want many of their men exempt from conscript military service have further alienated his traditional supporters.
Netanyahu's strongest rival at the moment is Gadi Eisenkot, Israel's former military chief, who lost a son in Gaza. His Yashar party has been on a steady rise for months, matching and sometimes overtaking Likud in the polls, though his path to power is still unclear.
Netanyahu's age is a factor too, said Asa-El.
"When he first ran in '96, he was the Israeli Kennedy. Now he's running as the Israeli Biden." REUTERS

Kyiv airports ready to host foreign delegations if Russia guarantees safe corridor, Zelensky says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:56:43 UTC
21:56:43 KST

Kyiv airports ready to host foreign delegations if Russia guarantees safe corridor, Zelensky says
Airports in Kyiv and the surrounding region are technically ready to receive aircraft carrying foreign delegations, but their use depends on Russia agreeing to provide a safe corridor, President Volodymyr Zelensky told journalists on Sept. 8.
Airports across Ukraine have been closed since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion amid continued Russian attacks, making trains the primary mode of travel for foreign delegations and other official visitors.
According to the president, Ukraine had been prepared to receive a U.S. aircraft carrying President Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner during their Sept. 6 visit to Kyiv.
A day before the delegation arrived, Zelensky said Russia had deliberately targeted the runways at Kyiv's Zhuliany airport and Boryspil International Airport after discussions emerged about the possibility of Witkoff and Kushner flying directly into Ukraine.
The airport strikes were part of a broader Russian overnight attack involving ballistic missiles and 167 drones, which killed at least seven people and injured at least 51 others across Ukraine.
The president said another option considered for the U.S. delegation was to fly to Gomel, Belarus, and then travel to Ukraine by road.
"From Gomel, it's a little over three hours by road. We worked through that option as well, and formally our security service was ready to meet Steve and Jared," Zelensky said.
Witkoff and Kushner ultimately chose to travel to Ukraine by train.
"They chose the train route. We told them it would be a safe and comfortable way to arrive in Ukraine," Zelensky said. "The entire American delegation really liked the train. We agreed that they would come again."
Despite railways becoming one of the main means of transportation within Ukraine and abroad following the suspension of air travel, Russian forces regularly target Ukraine’s railway infrastructure, including civilian trains.
The latest such attack took place on Sept. 8, when Russian drones struck a Kyiv-Sumy passenger train. No one was injured after the train was stopped during an air raid alert and around 90 passengers, along with crew members, were evacuated under new safety rules.
In 2024, the Ukrainian government considered reopening some airports in major cities such as Kyiv and Lviv, saying it was "95%" ready to reopen the country's airspace. Still, officials said discussions about resuming flights without sufficient air defenses would be "impractical" as long as the war continues.
In March 2025, the general director of Lviv's Danylo Halytskyi International Airport said flights could resume as early as April or May under an optimistic scenario being considered by the government. At the same time, the airport held talks with Wizz Air, airBaltic, Turkish Airlines, SkyUp, Austrian Airlines, Lufthansa, and LOT about a possible resumption of flights.
As of 2026, all Ukrainian airports remain closed to commercial flights.

Beaten, starved and chained — in Dnipro, a couple is accused of torturing six children

Unknown Publisher

Beaten, starved and chained — in Dnipro, a couple is accused of torturing six children
Kyiv • UNN
Foster parents are accused of subjecting six children to years of beatings, starvation and cruel punishments. The case has been referred to court.
In Dnipro, two foster parents at a family-type orphanage have been accused of systematically torturing six children aged between 3 and 10. According to the investigation, from 2019 to 2024, the children were beaten, starved, humiliated and subjected to cruel punishments. This was reported by the Prosecutor General’s Office, UNN writes.
Juvenile prosecutors of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office have sent an indictment to court against two foster parents at a family-type orphanage. They are accused of systematically torturing six children aged between 3 and 10 (Part 1 of Article 28, Parts 1 and 2 of Article 127 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine). According to the investigation, from 2019 to 2024, the children were systematically beaten, humiliated, deprived of food and subjected to cruel punishments
It is noted that the children were not addressed by name; instead, offensive and obscene nicknames were used. The girls’ heads were shaved, and they were beaten with rose stems. One of them was struck in the face with a twig because she had lost a needle she was trying to use to mend her clothes.
For “disobedience,” the children could be forced for weeks to sleep on a wooden bench without bedding and fed only bread and water. They were punished even for taking food without permission.
For the slightest offense, the children were beaten with a belt with a metal buckle, twigs, sticks and a carpet beater—sometimes with such force that it broke. One of the children said that a foster parent had run up and kicked him in the head, then continued beating him with his fists.
The children were also forced to kneel on buckwheat and walk on stones until they bled.
Among the most brutal episodes established by the investigation were punishments during which the children were put on a chain and forced to imitate animals’ behavior. Food was thrown onto the ground, and if a child did not pick it up, their face was pushed into the bread. After a walk with a dog, one of the boys was put in a collar.
In addition, the children were used as unpaid labor during repair work at the foster parents’ country house.
It became known only after the oldest of the children entered an educational institution and dared to talk about what he had experienced that this was what had been happening for years at the family-type orphanage
The foster parents were served with notices of suspicion in February this year. The pre-trial investigation has been completed, and the indictment has been submitted to court.
The family-type orphanage ceased operating. All the children were placed with new foster families.

China
Unknown Publisher

21:56:01 KST

ZHENGZHOU, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- Jin Xiangjun, former governor of north China's Shanxi Province, was sentenced to death, with a two-year reprieve, for taking bribes.
The sentence was handed down by a court in Xinyang, central China's Henan Province, on Tuesday.
Jin was also deprived of his political rights for life. All of his personal property shall be confiscated, and his illegal gains shall be recovered and turned over to the state treasury, according to the court sentence.
The court found that Jin had abused his power at various posts, including those in Guangxi, Tianjin and Shanxi, to provide assistance to companies and individuals in matters such as business operations, project contracting and personnel promotion. In return, he illegally accepted money and valuables worth over 148 million yuan (about 21.8 million U.S. dollars).
The court noted that Jin's offenses had caused particularly serious losses to the interests of the state and the people. However, because his offenses involved attempted acts, he cooperated with the investigation, and some of his illegal gains were recovered, the court decided to impose a lighter sentence.
A public hearing on the case was held on June 11.
Jin was expelled from the Communist Party of China and dismissed from public office in October last year. ■

Malaysian PM says ASEAN haze mechanism in need of review
China

2026-09-08

21:55:59 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- ASEAN needs to review and strengthen its mechanism for tackling transboundary haze, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Tuesday as poor air quality persists in the region.
The grouping must take the recurring haze problem seriously because it directly affects public health and people's lives and ensure that its existing mechanisms are translated into more effective action against the sources of transboundary haze, Anwar told a press briefing.
"There is room for improvement. I think the ASEAN ministers must seriously look at it, because this is affecting lives, particularly of children and babies, and if we have seen in Serian, it is really concerning," he said, referring to a district in the northern Borneo state of Sarawak where an emergency had been declared after air quality hit hazardous levels.
Following the end of the emergency declaration on Monday, Serian's air quality returned to the hazardous level, with the district recording an Air Pollutant Index (API) reading of 302 early on Tuesday.
According to the country's air quality rating, an API reading of zero to 50 is "good," 51 to 100 "moderate," 101 to 200 "unhealthy," 201 to 300 "very unhealthy," and 301 and above is "hazardous."
Anwar added that any allegations of open burning in Indonesia by Malaysian companies must first be thoroughly investigated to establish the actual cause of fires before action is taken against those responsible.
He said Malaysia would respect any enforcement action taken by the Indonesian authorities and would not intervene to protect companies found to have contributed to the haze. ■

The fixture follows an agreement between the NFA and the Russian Football Union, which also confirmed the match on Tuesday.

Benjamin said his players needed such matches regularly to build experience and competitiveness, "making them ready to face their peers at continental level in the CAF/Africa Cup of Nations."
Russia is ranked 35th in the latest FIFA men's world rankings, while Namibia sits 121st.
The friendly will follow Namibia's opening two matches in the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers.
According to the Confederation of African Football's schedule, Namibia will face the Republic of the Congo on September 24 and Comoros on September 29 in Group G, which also includes Cameroon. ■

China steps up crackdown on emerging forms of organized crime
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
20:55:50 CST
21:55:50 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 8 (Xinhua) -- China is stepping up its fight against organized crime, with a particular focus on emerging offenses involving online platforms and non-violent forms of coercion, as part of broader efforts to maintain public security and build a safer society.
In July, a one-year nationwide campaign was launched to crack down on emerging forms of organized crime, including those involving online platforms and less visible forms of coercion.
As part of the campaign, the Supreme People's Procuratorate said Tuesday that procuratorial authorities have targeted offenses that range from online predatory lending and coercive debt collection to extortion through online public opinion, forced consumption and sex-related blackmail. They also target "soft violence" such as stalking, harassment and intimidation.
Prosecutors nationwide have approved the arrests of 342 suspects in 104 organized crime cases and prosecuted 900 people in 151 cases, the top procuratorate said in a statement.
Procuratorial agencies are also investigating officials suspected of facilitating or shielding organized crime. Seven judicial personnel in six cases have been placed under investigation for suspected duty-related crimes, as authorities vow to work with other law enforcement and disciplinary agencies to target networks providing protection to criminal groups.
Prosecutors will sustain pressure on organized crime while strictly applying legal standards, neither over-classifying ordinary offenses as organized crime nor downgrading cases that meet the legal threshold, according to the statement.
The nationwide campaign comes against a backdrop of declining crime and a growing sense of security among the public in China. Official figures show that criminal cases in the country fell 12.8 percent year on year in 2025, reaching their lowest level since 2000.
Over the past years, China has advanced its "Peaceful China" initiative, with efforts ranging from combating serious violent crime and telecom fraud to strengthening grassroots governance.
At a July meeting on the campaign, a senior Chinese official in charge of political and legal affairs called for closer study of emerging forms of organized crime and stronger preventive measures in key industries and regions, so as to prevent such crime from taking root and further enhance people's sense of security. ■

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said that a US return to its commitments under the Islamabad memorandum of understanding could help ease regional tensions.
Araghchi made the remarks on Monday during a phone call with Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi, according to Iran’s foreign ministry.
Araghchi blamed the current tensions on what he described as Washington’s failure to honour its commitments under the memorandum, saying US compliance would pave the way for a return to “normal conditions”.
The two ministers also discussed bilateral relations and the latest regional and international developments.
Araghchi briefed Motegi on negotiations between Iran and Oman over the Strait of Hormuz, saying the two countries had made “significant progress” towards establishing a temporary transit route through the strategic waterway.
He said consultations would continue on mechanisms for managing the route in the future.
Tokyo calls for restraint
Motegi expressed “deep concern” over the resumption of attacks between the US and Iran and called for an early de-escalation and the resumption of talks.
He urged Tehran to show “maximum flexibility” and restraint, particularly over attacks on civilian vessels.
Japan also called for the restoration of free and safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz without additional costs.
Moteqi said the waterway’s future should be discussed under international law by the international community, including littoral states, users of the waterway and the International Maritime Organization.
Motegi also urged Iran to encourage the Houthis in Yemen to exercise restraint and stressed the importance of stability in the Bab el Mandeb Strait.
The Islamabad memorandum was signed in June following mediation by Pakistan and Qatar, establishing a framework for ending hostilities and negotiations between Tehran and Washington.
Iran has accused the US of failing to implement provisions related to sanctions and a naval blockade, while Washington and Gulf states have called for unrestricted navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran and Oman have since held talks on a temporary transit route, with Tehran saying the arrangement would remain temporary while discussions continue on a permanent mechanism.

Thailand's consumer confidence hits 6-month high in August
