Hungary expels Russian diplomats for the first time since 2018
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:51:09 UTC
21:51:09 KST

Hungary is set to expel 10 Russian diplomats from the country, Budapest's Foreign Minister Anita Orbán wrote on social media earlier today. According to Orbán, several Russian diplomatic mission staff members “had engaged in activities in Hungary that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention.” She stressed, however, that the decision “does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia.”
Since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, hundreds of Russian diplomats have been expelled from EU member states. Hungary, however, whose government was previously led by the Kremlin-friendly Viktor Orbán, did not participate in these measures. The last time a Russian diplomatic mission employee was officially declared persona non grata in Hungary was in 2018.
Current foreign minister Orbán said she had instructed a subordinate to inform Russian Ambassador to Hungary Yevgeny Stanislavov that “10 members of the Russian mission had engaged in activities in Hungary that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention.” As she stressed:
“The Hungarian side has therefore called on the individuals in question to leave Hungary. This decision protects Hungary’s security and sovereignty. It does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia. Hungary intends to continue the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules.”
As reported by the independent news outlet Vot Tak, between February 2022 and October 2025, nearly 700 Russian diplomats were expelled from European countries (those of the EU, plus Montenegro, Norway, North Macedonia, and the UK). Hungary was the only EU member that did not join such measures. Before today, the last time Budapest had declared a Russian diplomat to be persona non grata was in March 2018, when Hungary joined a mass expulsion of Russian diplomats by Western countries over the poisoning of former GRU Colonel Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia in the city of Salisbury, England.
Earlier this year, the Hungarian government also expelled an undercover Russian agent. On May 8, 2026, investigative outlet VSquare reported on the expulsion of Russian spy Artur Sushkov, who had been working in Hungary under diplomatic cover. He was forced to leave the country with his wife on May 4, five days before the government officially changed hands following Viktor Orbán's electoral defeat.
VSquare noted that Hungarian counterintelligence had been pushing for Sushkov’s expulsion since February 2026, but the Orbán government had blocked the proposal. According to the outlet, the authorities did not want to risk worsening relations with Moscow ahead of Hungary’s elections. Sushkov’s ultimate expulsion took place quietly, without any official announcements.
Budapest’s rhetoric changed after Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz party lost the April elections and Péter Magyar became prime minister. The new Hungarian government said it viewed Russia’s actions as a threat to Hungary itself, as well as to Europe and the to the wider “global order.”

Placement & AOS

Placement & AOS
Which areas of specialization have been correlated with higher placement into “permanent” (typically tenure-track or tenured) positions over the past few years?
“The broad finding is that those in Value Theory and History & Traditions (n=1125) have a higher proportion in permanent academic placement… than those in LEMM or Science, Logic, & Math (n=864),” according to Carolyn Dicey Jennings (UC Merced), who analyzed data gathered by Academic Philosophy Data and Analysis (APDA) on graduates from 2021 through 2026 and shared the results in a post at the APDA Blog.
Jennings breaks down the areas of specialization into “big” (more than 100 graduates over the past five years), “mid-sized” (between 20 and 100 graduates), and “small” (fewer than 20 graduates). Within each of those size categorizations, she lists the percentage of graduates with particular AOS’s who have found permanent placement.
Her findings are below. AOS’s listed in bold have a higher than average placement rate (the average across all areas is 32%).
Big
- Social/Political (37%; n=254)
- Ancient (37%; n=101)
- Ethics (36%; n=274)
- Epistemology (33%; n=165)
- Philosophy of Science (29%; n=102)
- Metaphysics (28%; n=112)
- Philosophy of Mind (25%; n=151)
Mid-Sized
- Law (60%; n=25)
- Medieval/Renaissance (52%; n=23)
- Gender/Race/Sexuality/Disability Studies (48%; n=56)
- Philosophy of Physics (40%; n=25)
- Logic (33%; n=39)
- German Philosophy/Kant (31%; n=68)
- Applied Ethics (31%; n=85)
- Modern Philosophy (31%; n=36)
- Historical Philosophy (29%; n=28)
- Continental Philosophy/Phenomenology (29%; n=56)
- Metaethics (26%; n=34)
- Philosophy of Religion (25%; n=20)
- Philosophy of Language (24%; n=70)
- Value Theory (22%; n=27)
- Cognitive Science/Psychology/Neuroscience/Linguistics (22%; n=73)
- Philosophy of Technology (20%, n=40)
Small
- Education (100%; n=2)
- American/Latin American Philosophy (100%; n=2)
- African Philosophy (67%; n=3)
- Philosophy of Action (67%; n=3)
- Philosophy of Biology/Environmental Philosophy (45%; n=11)
- 19th/20th Century Philosophy (44%; n=16)
- Metaphilosophy/Experimental (40%; n=5)
- Asian Philosophy (38%, n=8)
- Decision Theory (31%; n=16)
- Philosophy of Economics (23%; n=13)
- History of Analytic Philosophy (22%; n=9)
- Aesthetics (18%; n=11)
- Philosophy of Math (17%; n=18)
- Comparative Philosophy (15%; n=7)
- Other (0%; n=2)
Jennings adds: “A final point worth considering is that hiring trends come and go, and this analysis is not future-facing/predictive. Yet, the headline success of those in Value Theory and History & Traditions appears to be consistent across past analyses.”

France and Canada join UK in issuing trade sanctions on Israeli settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08

21:49:46 KST

LONDON — France and Canada will join the U.K. in imposing new trade sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in a major diplomatic boost for Britain as it toughens its stance on Israel.
In the House of Commons Tuesday, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband confirmed Britain, France and Canada will impose a ban on the trade of goods and some services from Israeli settlements, having last month condemned Israel’s plans for 1,200 new homes in the E1 area east of Jerusalem.
In response, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar said the British consulate in Jerusalem will be closed, and warned “countermeasures” could be taken against other countries acting “against Israel.”
Advertisement
The U.K., France and Canada are among 12 countries which issued a joint statement Tuesday warning the Israeli government’s actions in the West Bank are threatening the two-state solution.
Miliband told MPs the British government “agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank,” adding that “all too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this.”
He said the U.K. will take action against specific companies and individuals who provide services such as construction, infrastructure, financing, or real estate for settlement expansion.
U.K. sanctions legislation will take between six and nine months to implement, meaning the effects will not be felt immediately.
Britain will “act in concert with others in a broad international coalition,” he said, adding that France and Canada will also ban the import of goods from illegal settlements.
Confirming France’s involvement in a post on X, the country’s foreign affairs minister Jean-Noël Barrot said: “France cannot, through its trade, support a situation that threatens the security of both Israelis and Palestinians.”
Advertisement
Anita Anand, the Canadian foreign affairs minister, said her country will introduce restrictions “in the coming months.”
The coordinated announcement follows a major diplomatic effort by the British government over the summer, which culminated in a visit to Downing Street by French President Emmanuel Macron last week.
Writing on X, EU top diplomat Kaja Kallas noted the announcement and said: “All EU Member States agree that Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law. The Israeli Government’s settlement expansions in the West Bank are undermining the prospects for a viable two-State solution.”
Change of tone
Miliband’s announcement marks a sharp shift in Britain’s stance on Israeli settlements under new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
The U.K. foreign secretary told MPs Britain “should have acted earlier,” and it had taken a change of prime minister “to come in and recognize the gravity of the situation.”
In a press statement to camera, Sa’ar accused Miliband of telling “outrageous lies” in the British parliament and acting for “domestic political reasons” ahead of the ruling Labour Party’s annual conference this month.
Advertisement
Israel also said will deny 12 MPs and British nationals entry to Israel, including veteran Labour MP Diane Abbott and the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, who has since been expelled from the party.
The relationship between Israel and France — historically one of its close allies and home to more Jews than any other country in Europe — has also become strained in light of the war in Gaza.
Macron last year said Europe must “harden” its collective position on Israel given the dire humanitarian situation in the coastal enclave, and he found some success in convincing other Western democracies to join France in recognizing a Palestinian state last year.
Barrot said last week that the recent effort to sanction EU-wide trade with illegal West Bank settlements has been met resistance in Brussels.
Jean-Noël Barrot leaves the Elysée Palace in Paris after a meeting on Aug. 31, 2026. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images
Although several EU countries have pledged to ban trade with the settlements, the move is legally murky under EU law, because trade is an exclusive EU competence. Member countries can do it on the grounds of either national security or violation of human rights and democracy, but any measures at national level are assessed for compatibility with EU law.
UNGA looming
It comes just two weeks before world leaders meet in New York for the U.N. General Assembly — and ahead of Burnham’s expected first in-person meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump since becoming British prime minister.
Advertisement
Miliband said the U.K. will use the gathering to “shine the clearest and harshest spotlight on what is happening and what must change.”
In advance of the sanctions statement Tuesday, U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee suggested the U.S. could retaliate against the U.K. over the move.
Huckabee, who over the weekend condemned the government’s “Jew hate” despite Miliband being Jewish, told the BBC that the decision would be a “discrimination against the Jewish people.” He also suggested that individual U.S. states — specifically Florida — might take trade action against the U.K.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. was made aware of the decision, but are “not going to do what the U.K. did.”
While Trump has yet to respond to the sanctions, political differences have previously influenced his decisions on trade.
In January, the president threatened to impose 10 percent tariffs on eight countries, including the U.K., for opposing his demands to use military force to take control of Greenland.

Why is Israel rallying behind Argentina in disputing Britain’s claims over Falkland Islands?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:49:18 UTC
21:49:18 KST

Far-right Israeli ministers are using the Falkland Islands dispute to hit back at the UK by framing the South Atlantic archipelago as “occupied Argentine territory”.
The latest barrage of criticism follows expected restrictions by the British government on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Israel’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir posted on X in Spanish that it was time for Israel to “publicly recognise that the Malvinas Islands (otherwise known as Falkland Islands) are Argentine territory under occupation, which the British violently steal from the Argentine people”.
He accused Britain of oil drilling that “steals money from the Argentine people” and called on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to recognise Argentine sovereignty and impose sanctions “as long as the occupation continues”.
Israel’s Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich also demanded the British ambassador’s expulsion, declaring the British Mandate over “the Land of Israel is over”.
The sharply critical remarks by top ministers further weaken Tel Aviv’s already deteriorating relationship with London as far-right politicians look for maximum domestic political mileage in the run-up to the general election next month.
Why is Falkland suddenly in the news?
Argentina recently demanded that Britain hand over the islands to the Latin American country, a similar move to London transferring Hong Kong to China in 1997.
But what triggered the critical statements by the Israeli ministers was the prospect of a ban by Britain on trade in goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The planned restrictions will be in line with a 2024 International Court of Justice advisory opinion, which requires that governments worldwide must not help Israel with its occupation of Palestinian territories.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is also expected to “reassert” support for a two-state solution, which has ruffled feathers among right-wing Israeli politicians.
Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have already been sanctioned by the UK, Australia, Canada, New Zealand and Norway in 2025 for repeated incitement of violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and elsewhere.
The same ministers have aimed their guns at Britain on the so-called occupation of the Falkland Islands, even though Israel keeps expanding its own settlements in the occupied West Bank in clear violation of international law.
Analysts say that far-right politicians in Israel are competing for electoral support from voters who want to shift the international focus away from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
There is also a commercial angle. An Israeli-linked company, Navitas Petroleum, holds 65 percent shares in the Sea Lion oil project north of the islands. Argentine President Javier Milei has announced sanctions targeting firms, shareholders and suppliers involved in the project.
What is at stake?
Falklands consist of two main islands: East Falkland and West Falkland, apart from the archipelago of more than 700 smaller islands.
These are located about 480 kilometres east of the Argentine mainland.
Britain has administered them since 1833. Argentina says it inherited the islands from Spain after independence and that Britain occupied them by force.
But Britain insists that the islanders have the right to self-determination.
In 1982, Argentina moved into the islands. A fight ensued when Britain intervened, resulting in the deaths of 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three islanders in the next 74 days.
Even though Argentina surrendered, it never dropped its claim to the territory.
A 2013 referendum showed 99.8 percent of islanders wanted the archipelago to remain a British Overseas Territory.
Argentina dismissed the vote, arguing the population was implanted after 1833, the year Britain assumed control of the area.
The islands are important for many reasons. For example, the Sea Lion oilfield is estimated to hold 1.7 billion barrels of oil, with first production targeted for 2028.
Is Israel diplomatically alone on this issue?
Most governments around the world either stay silent or recognise the islands as British-administered while calling for negotiations.
The UN lists the Falklands as a non-self-governing territory and does not recognise either claim as definitive.
But Latin American states usually back Argentina’s claim at the UN.
The US, however, has traditionally recognised British administration of the islands. But that neutrality is now in question.
According to a leaked Pentagon email, the US may be reviewing its support for Britain’s claim to the Falkland Islands. The possible change in the US stance is apparently in reaction to Britain’s lack of support for Trump’s war against Iran.
Analysts say any change in the US stance on the Falkland Islands will be a psychological blow to Britain’s sovereignty claim over the territories.
Britain midwifed Israel’s birth
The irony in Israel calling out Britain for “occupying” the Falkland Islands is sharp. After all, it was Britain that issued the 1917 Balfour Declaration that called for a “national home for the Jewish people” in Palestine.
The League of Nations later granted Britain the Mandate for Palestine. Afterwards, Jewish immigration increased to Palestine despite Palestinian Arab opposition.
Britain eventually withdrew in 1948 when Israel declared independence, amid an ongoing Arab-Israeli war and the mass displacement of Palestinians from their ancestral lands.
For decades, Britain has remained one of Israel’s most consistent Western supporters. But that relationship has somewhat frayed over Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, illegal settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank and the recognition of a Palestinian state.
How Britain, others have reacted
London’s position on the Falkland Islands remains “unwavering”.
So far, there has been no direct official rebuke of Ben-Gvir’s latest post. However, the two ministers are already persona non grata in Britain for their involvement in incitement of violence towards Palestinians.
US President Donald Trump has said he is reviewing “every position”, reflecting his dissatisfaction with Britain’s hesitation to join the recent US-led war against Iran.
Foreign policy analysts view the statements by the Israeli ministers as transactional rather than principled. They say that sovereignty disputes offer politicians an easy “rally-around-the-flag” opportunity.

UK buys 890 parachutes for high-readiness airborne force
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:49:12 BST
21:49:12 KST

The Ministry of Defence has procured 890 additional parachutes as it works to align the Army’s airborne capability with plans for 16 Air Assault Brigade to lead very-high-readiness land crisis response, Armed Forces Minister Louise Sandher-Jones has said.
The figures were disclosed in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked what progress had been made towards Recommendation 45 of the 2025 Strategic Defence Review. That recommendation calls for global crisis response at very high readiness in the land domain to be led by 16 Air Assault Brigade.
Sandher-Jones said: “Airborne capability is delivered through a combination of parachute equipment, trained personnel and supporting air delivery platforms, and Defence continues to manage these elements to meet current operational requirements.”
She added: “Defence is working to ensure airborne parachute capability and capacity are aligned with Recommendation 45 of the Strategic Defence Review.”
As part of that work, the MOD has purchased 665 additional Low-Level Parachutes and 225 Low Level Reserve Parachutes, giving a combined total of 890 additional parachutes. Sandher-Jones said: “This has included the procurement of 665 additional Low-Level Parachutes and 225 Low level Reserve Parachutes to sustain current fleet levels.”
Sandher-Jones added: “Further work is underway to consider parachute equipment requirements and investment decisions, alongside wider Defence priorities, to ensure Defence retains the capabilities required for future operational tasks.”
16 Air Assault Brigade is the British Army formation associated with high-readiness airborne operations and includes forces trained for rapid deployment by parachute and air assault. Under the Strategic Defence Review, the brigade is intended to sit at the centre of the Army’s ability to respond rapidly to crises overseas.

====================================================================================================

Here in Liverpool, buses are back under public control – and that’s great for the only people who really matter | Steve Rotheram
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:48:35 UTC
21:48:35 KST

One of the best-known scenes from the TV series The Inbetweeners is the four angst-ridden teenage characters shouting abuse at people queueing at a bus stop. Only losers take the bus, is the point – except they use a much ruder word. There’s also a statement, misattributed to Margaret Thatcher, that any man over the age of 26 using a bus was a loser. This idea is deeply ingrained.
But when I was an MP it became obvious that there wasn’t the same stigma attached to jumping on the bus in London as there often was in other big cities. It often wound me up that the rest of the country was expected to accept a suboptimal public transport system – so much so that it could be joked that only losers would use it – while London retained its excellent bus service, which it ran under public control.
And I remember thinking: why can’t we have something like this at home in Liverpool? Well, last weekend Liverpool city region combined authority began to roll back the Thatcherite belief that private was all good, while public was all bad. For the first time in four decades, buses in the Liverpool city region have begun to be brought back under public control, starting in St Helens in Merseyside before spreading across the rest of the region.
What does this mean? Instead of private operators deciding where and when buses run, we will set the routes, fares and standards. Our franchised buses will still be operated by third parties. But we will set the rules, decide what kind of network our communities need and hold operators accountable for delivering it. It is the biggest change to public transport in our region for generations. Nobody standing at a bus stop at six in the morning cares about the finer points of franchising legislation. But they do care whether the bus turns up; whether they can get to work on time, get their kids to school or college, or make it to a hospital appointment.
Public control means we can start putting passengers first, with more frequent services, more evening and weekend buses, better connections to hospitals and railway stations and simpler fares. And we have kept single bus fares capped at £2, the price they have been for the past four years.
Change will be immediate. A new express service now connects St Helens directly with Liverpool John Lennon airport. For a family heading on holiday, that may mean avoiding airport parking charges. For somebody looking to work at the airport, it could open up a job. These changes will make a massive difference to people’s lives.
And, for me, that gets to the heart of the argument for public control. A bus route that helps somebody take a job, gets a student to college or allows an older person to remain independent has a value that won’t always show up on an operator’s balance sheet. Markets have their place. But public control allows us to ask not simply, “does this route make money?” but “do our people need it?”
That principle doesn’t stop with buses. We have bought a £500m fleet of new trains and are working towards bringing Merseyrail services into public ownership in 2028. In the coming weeks, the Royal Daffodil – our first new ferry ’cross the Mersey in 60 years, built by a loyal local workforce – will make its maiden voyage.
For decades we were told that privatisation and deregulation would inevitably deliver better services and that the government’s job was to get out of the way. The experience of millions of passengers tells a different story.
When he was mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham and I spent years working together to make that case and show what can be achieved when local leaders have the power to shape the services their communities rely on. Now we have a Labour government bringing our railways back into public ownership and giving local leaders more power over the essentials that ordinary people depend on.
After decades in which the state steadily retreated from people’s lives, we have an opportunity to prove that active government can be a force for good again. That is what started in St Helens last weekend.
I want the Liverpool city region to have the best public transport system in the country. I want people to come here, get on one of our buses, trains or ferries, see what we have built and go home asking the same question I used to ask in London: why can’t we have this at home?
- 
  Steve Rotheram is mayor of the Liverpool city region

12 South Koreans arrested in Thailand scam centre crackdown
Police say the alleged scammers entered Thailand from a neighbouring country and rented a luxury house south of Bangkok
Thai authorities arrested 12 South Koreans and a Chinese national accused of running a scam call centre from a high-end rented house south of Bangkok, police said on Tuesday.
The alleged scammers “entered Thailand from a neighbouring country and were hiding in Samut Prakan province, renting a luxury house”, Thai police said in a statement, without naming the country.
Cambodia and Myanmar, which border Thailand, have become hubs for criminal groups operating fake romance, investment and other schemes that defraud victims around the world of billions of dollars each year.
But authorities in both nations have also raided scam compounds in recent months, pushing some scammers to set up elsewhere in the region.
Inside the house in Thailand, authorities found a call centre set-up with 13 workstations equipped with Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) phones and other equipment, including dozens of computers, mobile phones and scripts allegedly used in online scams.
Police also discovered a list of South Korean victims and forged documents falsely claiming to be official letters from the South Korean prosecutor’s office.

Russia Uses Military Registry For First Time To Stop Reservist From Leaving Country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:46:35 UTC
21:46:35 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Uses Military Registry For First Time To Stop Reservist From Leaving Country
Russia has recorded its first known case of a military reservist being prevented from leaving the country under a decision issued by a local military enlistment office, according to Russian rights project Idite Lesom on September 5.
The case involves a 24-year-old resident of Russia’s Rostov region who completed compulsory military service in 2024 and was subsequently transferred to the reserve.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
On September 2, he attempted to fly out of Krasnodar but was pulled aside for additional screening during passport control.
Border officials questioned him for roughly an hour before refusing permission to leave Russia and handing him an official notice stating that his right to travel abroad had been temporarily restricted.
The restriction appears to stem from Russia’s expanding electronic military-registration system.
In November 2025, the reservist had personally reported to his military enlistment office after receiving a summons to update his records. Officials placed a mobilization order inside his military ID.
Despite that, the same summons later appeared in Russia’s electronic registry with the status indicating that the “citizen did not appear.”
According to Idite Lesom, the enlistment office subsequently used that record to impose a temporary travel ban.
The reservist had no indication before his trip that any such restriction existed. Nothing in the registry visible to him showed that he had been prohibited from leaving Russia.
He only discovered the measure at the border.
After being denied departure, the man filed a complaint through Russia’s Gosuslugi government services portal and began seeking an official extract from the military registry containing the number and legal basis of the decision.
Rights advocates say the case is the first known example in which a Russian reservist has been stopped from traveling abroad specifically because of a military enlistment office decision linked to the electronic draft system.
Earlier, more than 113,000 Russians left the country for Georgia through the Verkhny Lars checkpoint in a single week following rumors of a new draft.
On August 20 alone, over 20,000 people crossed through the border point. Russia’s Federal Customs Service stated that this figure significantly exceeds levels from previous years.

Russia’s Homegrown Kinzhal Electronics Fell Short—American Chips Are Back Inside
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:46:18 UTC
21:46:18 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Russia’s Homegrown Kinzhal Electronics Fell Short—American Chips Are Back Inside
Russia has returned to using American processors in its Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missiles after domestically produced substitutes apparently failed to meet requirements, Ukraine’s presidential sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk told Militarnyi on September 8.
Specialists examining the Zarya-61 onboard computer recovered from a Kinzhal intercepted in May found processors manufactured by US semiconductor company Texas Instruments.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The discovery is particularly notable because Russian engineers had already attempted to replace those components with domestically produced microchips in 2023.
In the newer Zarya-61 recovered this year, however, those Russian substitutes were gone. Texas Instruments processors had returned, suggesting the domestic replacements did not provide the performance or reliability required for the missile’s electronics.
The findings provide another example of Russia’s continued dependence on foreign semiconductor technology despite years of efforts to localize production and Western restrictions intended to limit Moscow’s access to advanced electronics.
According to Militarnyi, investigators found an even stranger mix of components inside another Russian missile.
Debris from an Iskander contained an electronic board fitted with AMD chips manufactured as far back as 1996, along with a Texas Instruments processor carrying a 1986 marking.
The age and variety of the components illustrate the increasingly fragmented supply chains Russia appears to rely on to sustain missile production.
“It has to combine its own component base with foreign components, while searching for them across different markets and through different supply chains,” Vlasiuk said.
Earlier, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence identified 155 Russian enterprises linked to producing electronic components and technologies used across Russia’s weapons systems, including Iskander-M ballistic and Zircon hypersonic missiles.
In addition, Vadym Skibitskyi, deputy chief of Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate, recently reported that Russia has increased its ballistic missile output, primarily by halting production of Kh-47 Kinzhal missiles.

Hungary Expels 10 Russian Diplomats Over “Unacceptable” Activities
Hungary has ordered the expulsion of 10 members of the Russian mission in Budapest over activities deemed incompatible with their diplomatic status, Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán announced.
Orbán said that the individuals had engaged in activities in Hungary that were “unacceptable for diplomats” under the Vienna Convention.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
A representative of Hungary’s Foreign Ministry informed the Russian ambassador in Budapest that the individuals had been ordered to leave the country.
Orbán stressed, however, that the expulsions do not amount to a severing of diplomatic relations between Hungary and Russia.
“This decision protects Hungary’s security and sovereignty. It does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia. Hungary intends to continue the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules,” Orbán wrote.
The expulsions come as Hungary’s new government takes a tougher stance toward Moscow. In August, Budapest officially identified Russia as a security threat while reaffirming its support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
The position was outlined in instructions for Hungary’s delegation to the United Nations General Assembly in September. The document, signed by Prime Minister Péter Magyar and published in Hungary’s official gazette on August 26, stated that Russia’s actions pose a threat not only to Hungary but also to Europe and the broader international order, according to Der Spiegel.
“Hungary condemns Russian military aggression and fully supports Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders,” the document states. “Russia’s behavior poses a threat to Hungary, Europe, and the global order.”
The shift in Budapest’s approach has also extended to scrutiny of the previous government’s relations with Moscow. Hungary’s new government opened an investigation into former Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó over alleged ties to Russia.

UK announces trade sanctions on Israeli settlements in occupied West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:46:00 UTC
21:46:00 KST

UK announces trade ban on West Bank Israeli settlements
September 8, 2026
The United Kingdom on Tuesday announced trade restrictions on goods made in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The center-left Labour Party government has previously sanctioned some Israeli settlers and illegal outposts over violence against Palestinians and illegal development in the West Bank.
The announcement came as the foreign ministers of 11 other governments announced they too would be slapping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements.
Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden also plan to limit trade with the settlements, according to a joint statement.
Meanwhile, an EU Foreign Affairs spokesperson said the bloc "adopted three packages of sanctions against extreme settlers and their entities."
What did Miliband say?
"I can announce today that we will introduce an import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced in the House of Commons.
"We will take action against specific companies and individuals who provide services such as construction, infrastructure, financing or real estate for settlement expansion," Miliband said.
The foreign secretary said those financing or facilitating illegal settlement would "face the full force of UK sanctions."
Before announcing the sanctions, Miliband said that "settler terrorism was rampant" and referenced various instances of violence in the West Bank.
Miliband told MPs a "new approach" was necessary because plans for development in the West Bank would render a two-state solution "unviable" as it would be "cutting through the heart of Palestine."
Miliband accused the Israeli government of turning a "blind eye" to what he called "ethnic cleansing" by settlers in the West Bank.
Why is the UK restricting trade?
The measures appear to be setting the tone for relations between Britain's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Israel.
According to a Downing Street readout of a phone call between the British leader and US President Donald Trump on the phone on Monday, Burnham laid out "the UK's commitment to working towards peace and security in the region," and stressed the importance of a two-state solution in Israel and the Palestinian territories.
Burnham, along with French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, said in a joint statement on Tuesday that Canada, France and the UK will "take steps to ban the importation of goods from settlements and enforce targeted measures against settlements and those who facilitate them or profit from them."
The United Kingdom, Canada and France recognized Palestinian statehood last year in an attempt to revive efforts to achieve a two-state solution.
The moves come as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing government forges ahead with settlement construction in the West Bank, raising fears among some Western governments that it threatens any possible two-state solution. Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.
The measures also come amid flaring tensions in the West Bank that have involved violent attacks on Palestinians by Israeli settlers.
The UK has previously condemned the violence while calling for civilians to be protected and for those responsible to be held accountable.
The Palestinian Authority welcomed the announcement of sanctions, calling the measures "an important step" to accountability.
"This as an important practical step toward holding the settlement system accountable and demonstrating non-recognition of the unlawful situation created by the occupation," Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas's office said in a statement.
Israel orders closure of UK consulate in Jerusalem
Ahead of the announcement, Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar already indicated that Israel would respond.
"If Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain," Saar warned.
Saar ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem once the measures became known.
"The accusations made today by the foreign secretary in the British Parliament were outrageous lies," Saar said in response to Miliband accusing Israeli settlers of ethnic cleansing in the occupied Palestinian territory.
Saar also said 11 British MPs, including former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and veteran Labour lawmaker Diane Abbott, would be banned from entry to Israel. Fahad Ansari, a lawyer and director of the anti-Zionist Riverway to Sea organization, will also be hit with an entry ban.
Israel's hard-line public security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, urged Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to publicly recognize the Falkland Islands as "Argentine territory under occupation, which the British violently steal from the Argentine people."
UK decision also met with domestic condemnation
The new UK sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank was also met with condemnation within the UK.
Britain's chief rabbi, Ephraim Mirvis, called it a "dark day for British Jews" while accusing the UK government of engaging in "gesture politics."
"These measures will succeed only in bolstering the very extremism they seek to target," Mirvis wrote in a post on X.
Tom Tugendhat, a British Conservative Party lawmaker who serves as shadow foreign secretary, said that "turning Israel into a pariah will risk sectarian division in our own country and risk a further rise in antisemitic violence on our own streets."
Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

Another small-island ferry strike called for September 18
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:46:00 UTC
21:46:00 KST

Another small-island ferry strike called for September 18
Estonia's small island ferry services are facing another strike following a long‑running negotiation deadlock on pay and conditions.
The strike has been called by the Estonian Seamen's Independent Union (EMSA) and is confirmed to take place Friday, September 18, and will last until an agreement is struck.
Talks between EMSA and ferry operator Kihnu Veeteed over a new collective wage agreement have been deadlocked since March, with a warning strike held in July. In any case, the state plans to take over the operation of the routes next year.
The latest planned strike will take place Friday next week and covers all vessels and routes operated by Kihnu Veeteed, following a breakdown in collective negotiations and the formation of a breakaway rival union.
"It is difficult to understand what exactly the problem is," Kihnu Veeteed CEO Jaak Kaabel told regional daily Lääne Elu, noting that workers' pay had been hiked 12‑20 percent depending on the position. Pay had been one of the major issues in the long‑running dispute.
EMSA chairman Jüri Lember said the pay rise had been one thing, but it had not been as generous as might seem at first sight.
"The pay rise is very welcome, but it is a unilateral decision by the employer," Lember said, adding that the real increase was smaller because bonuses had been reduced at the same time.
The ferry company had instead reached an agreement with the newly established Lääne‑Eesti meremeeste ametiühing (Western Estonian Seamen's Union), a breakaway body which represents six employees at the company at present.
Lember said the rival union's agreement allows for a 91‑hour work week and includes a clause stating that no watchkeeping duties have been performed on the ferries — which he called "nonsense" and unacceptable.
EMSA said since Kihnu Veeteed had not been willing to engage in substantive, reasoned negotiations over the union's repeatedly submitted proposals for a collective agreement, or to conclude such an agreement, a strike was inevitable.
Lember added just over half of Kihnu Veeteed's crew roster are EMSA members.
Tanel Viks, municipal mayor on Vormsi, one of the islands affected by the dispute, expressed his anger with EMSA over the strike planned for September 18. "It's outrageous," Viks told Lääne Elu, describing EMSA's actions as "blackmail."
The action will affect four vessels plying the routes between the mainland and the offshore islands of Kihnu and Manilaid, as well as Vormsi. Kihnu Veeteed also serves a short route linking Saaremaa and Hiiumaa, Estonia's two largest islands, and connecting Priisaar, an island on the freshwater Lake Peipus, with the shore too. These will all be affected by the strike.
Talks between EMSA and Kihnu Veeteed over a new collective wage agreement have been deadlocked since March, with EMSA demanding 20–30 percent pay rises and the company arguing its profit margins are too narrow to meet the demands. A one‑hour warning strike took place on July 26. Meanwhile, the Ministry of Regional Affairs and Agriculture has selected Tuule Liinid OÜ to take over the small‑island ferry routes from Kihnu Veeteed from 2027.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Who else made Netanyahu’s Likud list? PM reveals his reserved candidates hours before the election deadline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:45:16 UTC
21:45:16 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel Elections
- Netanyahu unveils Likud reserved candidates hours before election deadline
Netanyahu unveils Likud reserved candidates hours before election deadline
The slate includes wounded IDF reservist Elisha Medan, commentator Yaakov Bardugo and hostage mother Talik Gwili; businessman Oren Dobronsky relinquishes his place but says he may serve as AI minister
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu began unveiling the candidates selected for reserved positions on the Likud electoral slate on Tuesday morning, just hours before the deadline for parties to submit their final lists.
The names were released after Netanyahu failed to meet an ultimatum calling on him to announce the candidates by Monday.
Elisha Medan — No. 15
The first candidate announced was Elisha Medan, an IDF reservist and one of the founders of the Avigail community in the South Hebron Hills.
Medan was critically wounded during an operation in Beit Hanoun in the northern Gaza Strip, losing both legs. Four of his fellow soldiers were killed in the same incident.
“Elisha’s long rehabilitation has become a symbol of strength, determination and faith in life,” Likud said in a statement. “Despite his severe injuries and the heavy personal price he has paid, Elisha chose to look ahead, remain active, strengthen others and offer hope to many Israelis.
“His story reflects the spirit of Israel’s soldiers and Israeli society’s ability to withstand the greatest challenges, recover and continue building.”
The party described Medan as “a torchbearer for healing and rehabilitation” and noted the awards he has received for his courage and public service.
“He embodies dedication, responsibility, love of the land and comradeship,” the statement added. “His journey from the battlefield to rehabilitation is a living testament to the Israeli spirit.”
Talik Gvili — No. 9
Another reserved position was awarded to Talik Gvili, the mother of Yamam officer Master Sgt. Ran Gvili, who was killed on October 7 and whose body was taken to the Gaza Strip.
Ran was the first hostage taken into Gaza and the last to be returned to Israel. His remains were recovered in Operation Brave Heart, a special mission carried out by the IDF and other security forces.
“Throughout this journey, Talik and the Gvili family demonstrated extraordinary strength, deep faith and unwavering determination, even in the most difficult moments,” Likud said.
“Talik proudly preserved Ran’s memory and shared the story of his bravery, his love for the country and his Zionist values. She touched the hearts of Israelis and people around the world. Talik is a symbol of strength, devotion and commitment to the State of Israel, transforming her personal story into an inspiring public mission.”
Yaakov Bardugo — No. 11
Political commentator Yaakov Bardugo was selected for the 11th position.
Bardugo is a presenter and commentator for Channel 14 and Radio Galei Israel. He previously worked as a political commentator and current-affairs presenter for Army Radio.
A lawyer and businessman, Bardugo has also served as director-general of Israel’s Federation of Local Authorities and as chief executive of the national lottery, Mifal HaPais.
David Peter — No. 16
Attorney David Peter, who has represented Netanyahu and the government in legal proceedings, was awarded the 16th position.
Peter holds bachelor’s and master’s degrees in law from Bar-Ilan University and is currently pursuing a doctorate.
Amir Avivi — No. 35
Brig. Gen. (res.) Amir Avivi, founder of the Israel Defense and Security Forum, known as Habithonistim, received the 35th position.
During his military career, Avivi served in several senior roles, including deputy comptroller of the defense establishment, aide-de-camp to the IDF chief of staff and deputy commander of the Gaza Division.
He also commanded the Sagi Brigade, the 605th Combat Engineering Battalion and the IDF’s Combat Engineering School.
Eli Goldschmidt — No. 26
Former Labor lawmaker Eli Goldschmidt was selected for the 26th position.
Goldschmidt previously chaired the Labor faction in the Knesset. According to Likud, years of living near the Gaza border and the events of October 7 led him to reassess his political views.
“He changed his political and security positions and now supports Netanyahu, Likud and the national camp,” the party said.
Itzik Bonzel — No. 29
Itzik Bonzel , the father of fallen IDF Staff Sgt. Amit Bonzel, received the 29th position.
Amit served as a soldier and commander in the Paratroopers Reconnaissance Unit and was killed in combat in the Gaza Strip.
On the morning after the October 7 attacks, Bonzel's sons Amit and Nadav—both soldiers and commanders in the unit—reported for duty. Amit was killed in battle 60 days later.
Oren Dobronsky - reserved position
Businessman Oren Dobronsky, who joined Likud last month as its first reserved candidate, announced overnight that he was giving up his place on the electoral slate.
“Two months ago, the prime minister asked me to join the Likud team ahead of the election, and that remains the plan,” Dobronsky said.
“The prime minister offered me the position of minister for artificial intelligence affairs and a reserved place among the top 10 candidates. However, I preferred to serve solely as a professional minister, where my experience can make the greatest contribution, rather than serve as a member of the Knesset. That is what we agreed.”
Dobronsky said he intends to work closely with Netanyahu and the Likud team “to ensure that the State of Israel becomes an AI powerhouse.”
Last month, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, Defense Minister Israel Katz and Likud Central Committee Chairman Haim Katz were also reported to have received reserved positions.
Some party officials criticized the decision to reserve a place for Haim Katz, accusing him of pressuring Netanyahu to secure the position. Likud’s internal court subsequently approved his placement.

Sunday school brings Munich’s Bulgarian community together
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:44:58 UTC
21:44:58 KST

Author
Gergana Mancheva
News
Sunday school brings Munich’s Bulgarian community together
Tuesday 8 September 2026 14:31
Tuesday, 8 September 2026, 14:31
PHOTO Facebook/ Dora Gabe Bulgarian Sunday school in Munich
Font size
More than 14,500 Bulgarians live and work in Munich, according to figures from the city’s statistical office released last year. Deputy Mayor Verena Dietl described people with Bulgarian roots as a natural and important part of life in the Bavarian capital.
For many Bulgarian families, the community comes together around Munich’s two Sunday schools. More than 300 children attend Paisii Hilendarski and Dora Gabe, from preschoolers to students in Grade 12. Classes follow programmes approved by Bulgaria’s Ministry of Education and Science.
PHOTO Facebook/ Dora Gabe Bulgarian Sunday school in Munich
At the end of the school year, pupils receive certificates recognising the grade they have completed and their studies in Bulgarian language and literature, history and geography. Should they later continue their education in Bulgaria, the certificates mean they do not have to sit equivalency exams in these subjects.
Yet the schools offer something that goes beyond formal education. “It is a tremendous advantage that all the children and teenagers study together – in the same building. This gives them an opportunity to form interest groups and communities, which is particularly valuable for Bulgarian children growing up abroad,” the board of the Dora Gabe Bulgarian Sunday School in Munich writes.
PHOTO Facebook/ Dora Gabe Bulgarian Sunday school in Munich
The aim is to teach as many children as possible, foster a love of the Bulgarian language and awaken their interest in Bulgaria’s literature, history and geography. For 13 years, Dora Gabe School in Bavaria has pursued this mission, opening more doors to knowledge, skills and contacts for children with Bulgarian roots. Starting with just 10 children in 2013, it is now attended by more than 210 children of Bulgarians aged between 3 and 18.
In fact, the school has also become a valuable meeting place for parents, who themselves seek connections with other Bulgarians who have come to live in the heart of Germany.
PHOTO Facebook/ Dora Gabe Bulgarian Sunday school in Munich
“If we had stayed in Bulgaria, we probably wouldn’t have met as many Bulgarians from all over the country as we have here in Munich,” Elena Atanasova, who has lived in Germany for 25 years and is now a member of the board of Dora Gabe School in Munich, told Radio Bulgaria:
“We call the whole school ‘one big sunny family’, because we all work together for it. We have a team – my colleagues and I on the board – we have a director, and around 30 teachers and extracurricular activity instructors. We have a parents’ council that helps us enormously. We also work with many volunteers who help us in every possible way – organising celebrations and events. So we manage by joining forces."
PHOTO Facebook/ Dora Gabe Bulgarian Sunday school in Munich
“But it isn’t easy to motivate the children, to be honest, and that’s why we’re always looking for new ways to keep them interested in the school. We organise celebrations, invite them to summer camps, hold sports days and so on – things that bring them together and help them get to know each other and become friends.”
PHOTO Facebook/ Dora Gabe Bulgarian Sunday school in Munich
Elena has two children, both born in Germany and attending German schools. They speak Bulgarian very well and regularly attend Sunday school, while she makes a point of raising them with Bulgarian culture and traditions. For Elena Atanasova and her husband, who is also Bulgarian, it is important that their children know where they come from and never lose their connection with Bulgaria. They also want them to be able to speak Bulgarian with their grandparents and other relatives.
“If you don’t know your roots, you can’t really know yourself either,” Elena told us.

Lithuania training civilians to defend against a Russian invasion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:44:39 UTC
21:44:39 KST

Amid fear of Russia's war on Ukraine spreading, Lithuania trains civilians, tells Putin: "We don't fear you"
Vilnius, Lithuania — Russia struck Ukraine's capital Kyiv overnight, bringing an end to a three-day pause in attacks by the two countries on each other's capital cities as President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited the region to try and broker a peace deal.
At least two people were killed in the Russian strikes on Kyiv.
The neighboring Baltic countries, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania — all NATO members — were watching carefully as the U.S. envoys continued their efforts to resolve the four-and-a-half-year war.
But as they watch and hope for peace, Lithuania and its neighbors have also long been preparing for the possibility that continental Europe's first land war in three generations could spread to their doorsteps.
CBS News visited an ordinary high school in Vilnius where, in addition to math class, students were learning military-style survival skills. Along with the rest of their country, they're preparing for the possibility of Russia launching an invasion.
"Today we're working on survival training, and we're going to learn about weapons later," said Neda, a 15-year-old ninth grader.
If there is a crisis, Neda said she would likely put her first-aid knowledge to use and try to become a medic.
Lithuania, which has a population of less than 3 million, slightly smaller than greater Minneapolis, is also training up adult civilians.
History professor Mindaugas Nefas has been learning weapons skills. He told CBS News the whole-of-society approach to national readiness sends an important message.
"I think it's a good example, for Russia not to do anything against Lithuania," because it shows not just the military, but all Lithuanians are "preparing to defend our country," he said.
Taking on board lessons learned in Ukraine, Lithuania's preparations include teaching ordinary people how to use drones — and how to shoot them down.
The nation's small professional military is also embracing the new high-tech tools of war pioneered in Ukraine, including networks of sensors and drones known as the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative that, paired together, are intended to slow any theoretical Russian invasion to a crawl.
But old-school defenses still matter, too, including obstacles meant to stop tanks and command posts buried underground across the tiny nation.
Vilnius, Lithuania's capital city, is less than 20 miles from the border with close Russian ally Belarus, which Vladimir Putin's forces used as a launchpad for their ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
But despite that proximity, and Russia's belligerence toward Ukraine's NATO neighbors, Lithuania's Minister of Defense Robertas Kaunas told CBS News he was confident.
He said his nation's message to Russia was clear: "We don't fear you. We understand who are you, and we don't fear you."
The former Soviet Union's occupation of Lithuania only ended when the communist bloc collapsed in 1991, so it is still fresh in the nation's collective memory.
"We are not afraid, because we remember our history," said Kaunas. "We are in our home and we will protect our home."
Until very recently, NATO planners were doubtful that Lithuania could be defended at all against a full Russian assault, given its size and location sandwiched between Russian and Russian-allied territory.
But the technological innovations of the war in Ukraine — and the resilience of the Ukrainian people — have inspired new hope in the Baltic state.

WZO chief predicts most of world’s Jews will live in Israel within 5 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:44:19 UTC
21:44:19 KST

A majority of the world’s Jews will be living in Israel within five years, World Zionist Organization Chairman Yaakov Hagoel predicted during ynet Global’s Aliyah Live Summit, describing what he sees as a profound shift in Jewish identity and attachment to Israel since October 7.
“We are, God willing, within five years of most Jews living here in Israel,” Hagoel said, calling the prospect a historic demographic turning point.
He attributed the trend to a combination of aliyah, assimilation abroad and Israel’s comparatively high birth rate, noting that Israel became home to the world’s largest Jewish population roughly two decades ago, surpassing the United States.
“In another five years, most Jews will live here in Israel,” he said. “For 2,000 years, there has been nothing like this.”
But for Hagoel, the significance of the period since October 7 goes beyond immigration numbers. He said the attack and the surge in antisemitism that followed have prompted many Jews, particularly younger ones, to reconsider what Jewish identity and Zionism mean to them.
‘A renaissance’ since October 7
“Since October 7, there has been a renaissance,” Hagoel said. “People want to connect to the Jewish people and to the Zionist movement.”
He pointed to what he described as tens of thousands of American Jews who refer to themselves as “October 8 Jews” — people whose Jewish identity became more central after the Hamas attack and the events that followed.
Some, he said, had previously drifted away from Jewish communal life or no longer strongly identified as Jewish.
“This crisis woke them up,” Hagoel said. “It woke them up to come home and be part of our people.”
That renewed engagement can be seen, he said, in synagogues, Jewish schools, Zionist organizations and growing interest in aliyah.
The process has not been easy for young Jews abroad, Hagoel acknowledged. He described October 7 as the beginning of a conflict that extended beyond Israel and into Jewish communities around the world, pointing to the rise in antisemitism and hostility toward Jews.
He said the World Zionist Organization is trying to turn that crisis into an opportunity to strengthen Jewish identity and connections with Israel.
What draws young Jews to Israel
Asked whether the forces connecting young Jews to Israel have changed, Hagoel said traditional elements remain powerful — family, heritage, religion and the sense of Israel as a Jewish home.
But newer factors also play a role.
Young Jews see Israel as a technologically and economically advanced country, he said, while the war has also strengthened some young people’s identification with the Israeli military.
“We see quite a few young Jews who, even if they don’t make aliyah, come here to serve in the army through various programs,” he said. “It warms the heart.”
At the same time, he said, that connection can carry a psychological cost.
Hagoel described young Jews who serve in Israel, including reservists, and then return to careers in countries such as the United States or Britain, where they may feel unable to speak openly about what they experienced.
“You were here for three months in the reserves, you go back there and you can’t tell people where you were,” he said. “You can’t share it with someone in your law firm, in high-tech or wherever you work.”
The World Zionist Organization, he said, is working with professional partners to provide support to those individuals.
Engagement — and alienation
Hagoel acknowledged that the war and intense international criticism of Israel have not brought all young Jews closer.
“There is both,” he said when asked whether young Jews were becoming more engaged or more distant.
Some have become more connected to Israel and Jewish life, while others have responded in the opposite direction.
Still, Hagoel said he believes the first group is considerably larger.
“Anyone who is afraid to be Jewish — eventually his grandson will not be Jewish,” he said, arguing that the current moment creates an opportunity to strengthen Jewish identity among younger generations.
The WZO, he said, is trying to reach those young Jews through programs both in Israel and abroad.
Aliyah ‘is not hocus-pocus’
Hagoel stressed that stronger Jewish identity does not automatically translate into immigration.
“Aliyah is not hocus-pocus. Aliyah is a process,” he said.
Before someone decides to move to Israel, he argued, they usually need to strengthen their connection to Jewish identity, the Jewish people and Israel itself.
To build that connection, the World Zionist Organization currently sends around 280 Israeli teachers to Jewish communities abroad for periods of two or three years, Hagoel said. It also works with Jewish youth movements and student organizations on university campuses.
The objective is to create a chain of engagement that can begin with education or a campus experience and eventually lead to a much larger decision.
Israelis, he said, sometimes underestimate just how difficult that decision can be.
“We Israelis live in a kind of la-la land and say, ‘How can they not make aliyah? How can they not all be here?’” Hagoel said.
But Jews abroad may have been born in those countries to parents who were also born there. Making aliyah can mean leaving behind a language, family, livelihood and familiar surroundings.
“It’s not simple,” he said. “It is a major challenge.”
‘Aliyah is the project of the Jewish people’
Hagoel said Israel must also do more to ensure that those who do make the move are successfully absorbed.
“The government needs to do much more,” he said, particularly when it comes to immigrant integration.
He pointed to cooperation between national institutions, the government and local authorities, but argued that absorbing olim cannot be left to institutions alone.
“Aliyah is the project of the Jewish people — you and me,” he said.
Israelis, he argued, need to understand the upheaval involved in immigration and make a deliberate effort to welcome newcomers, whether that means helping them navigate everyday life or simply showing patience with their Hebrew.
“We need to embrace the olim,” Hagoel said. “We need to understand that they are going through a difficult upheaval in coming here.”
For him, that approach is not only about making new immigrants feel welcome. It is central to Israel’s long-term strength.
“Aliyah is the growth engine of the State of Israel,” Hagoel said.

UK accuses Israeli ‘terrorists’ of ethnic cleansing in West Bank with government backing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
12:43:55 UTC
21:43:55 KST

Settler terrorists supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, Ed Miliband has said, in the UK’s starkest condemnation since the foundation of the Israeli state.
Andy Burnham, the prime minister, said he would “not stand by” as horrific suffering continued, writing in the Guardian that for too long the UK had been hesitant to act, “fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel”.
In the Commons, the foreign secretary said the government would now take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety, as he announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements.
The dramatic shift in the UK’s position comes after a summer of intense diplomacy against a backdrop of increasing settler violence in the West Bank, which has resulted in 12 nations – including France and Canada – announcing they would impose sanctions.
In a joint statement Burnham, Emmanuel Macron and Mark Carney said: “The time has come to take further action to uphold our commitment to protect the two-state solution, our interests and to stand up for our values, before it is too late.”
In response, the Israeli foreign minister, Gideon Saar, announced the closure of the UK consulate in Jerusalem and that 12 British MPs and activists – including Jeremy Corbyn and Labour MP Diane Abbott – would be banned from entering Israel.
Saar accused Miliband of “outrageous lies” and said the UK government was “systematically working against the state of Israel”. Washington’s ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, warned that the US could take retaliatory action over trade.
However, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said Washington would “obviously” not follow the UK’s course of action, and did not want to see the West Bank destabilised, but declined to comment further. Burnham had briefed Donald Trump on the plan in advance.
In his statement to parliament, Miliband said the UK government would enact:
- 
  An import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories and a new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”.
- 
  A comprehensive sanctions regime against providing services such as construction or financing for Israeli settlements and a ban on advertising them in the UK.
- 
  Personal sanctions against key individuals accused of promoting settler violence.
- 
  A new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”.
The foreign secretary said the UK’s actions would show that “Britain is not silent in the face of deep injustice, and nor is it powerless”. In an emotional statement, he described the agony he had heard from Palestinians in the West Bank whose homes had been destroyed and from doctors in Gaza who had seen children dying waiting for medical treatment.
The UK’s actions have been made increasingly urgent by Israel’s plans to expand the E1 settlement project east of Jerusalem, which could in effect cut off the north from the south of the West Bank, threatening the viability of any future Palestinian state.
Ministers expect the legislation to enforce the trade ban and sanctions to be in place within nine months, although they could be subject to legal challenge, which would result in a delay.
Miliband stopped short of describing Israel’s actions in Gaza as a genocide, as some on the left have demanded, saying the UK would wait for the determination of the international courts, but that there was evidence of “war crimes”.
Speaking in the Commons, he said: “The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists.
“All too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this and worse, members of it have made statements and taken actions to support the forced displacement of Palestinians.
“I recognise the gravity of saying this, but the truth is the least the people who face such suffering deserve. And it should be the prelude to justice.”
Miliband suggested that Keir Starmer had been reluctant to take action against West Bank settlers during his time as prime minister. “I’ll say very bluntly we should have acted earlier. And it has taken the new prime minister to come in and recognise the gravity of the situation,” he told MPs.
Burnham, who apologised for Labour’s stance on Gaza when he became prime minister, attempting to shore up votes on the party’s progressive flank, also said the previous government had been too slow to act.
Writing in the Guardian , he said: “We have called for years for a two-state solution in the Middle East, but we must recognise that those words are meaningless unless we back them up with action. For too long, we have been hesitant to act, fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel.”
Miliband said he was taking the action as foreign secretary but also as a “proud British Jew” with relatives who had found safety in Israel after the Holocaust. “I am proud of my Jewishness and unwavering in my support for the state of Israel,” he said.
“And there is absolutely no contradiction between this and my support for the state of Palestine. Indeed, quite the opposite. The two-state solution is based on an explicit belief that the only route to security for both peoples is to live side by side in peaceful coexistence with freedom, security and self-determination.”
The foreign secretary said that to respond to threats against Jews around the world, the UK would also impose sanctions on Lebanese Hezbollah’s financing arm, Al-Qard al-Hassan, and reimpose major economic sanctions on Iran in line with the EU and US.
The action marked the beginning of a new approach towards Israel and Palestine, he said, one that not only condemned but took action. “Our argument is not with the people of Israel, with whom the UK has unshakeable bonds. Our argument is with the conduct of its government.”
Burnham wrote that the British Jewish community must not be blamed for the actions of the Israeli government. “[It] is wrong, plain and simple. And it is antisemitism, plain and simple,” he said.
“I met with the representatives of the Jewish community just last week. I know the fear they live with day by day. My government will stop at nothing to ensure they are safe and to stamp out antisemitism in every part of our society.”
The shadow foreign secretary, Tom Tugendhat, said “illegal settlements are wrong” but suggested that Miliband was introducing policies the Foreign Office did not believe would work. Whitehall insiders denied this was the case.
The senior Conservative MP also said there was a risk of harming Palestinians who worked in the West Bank and that “the economies of Palestine and Israel were too interconnected” for a ban on goods for illegal settlements to work.
But the veteran Tory MP Edward Leigh gave full backing to the sanctions. “I am proud to say as the longest serving member of the Conservative Friends of Israel that I absolutely and fully support what he is doing today because it is about standing up for freedom, for morality and justice for all people in this world,” he said.
The move forms part of a broader attempt by Burnham’s government to reset British policy towards Israel, in part to regain the trust among Muslim and progressive voters in the UK they lost in the early days of the conflict.
It was overwhelmingly welcomed by Labour MPs, many of whom have been struggling with the issue in their constituencies, although some sounded a note of caution about the potential impact on local Jewish communities.
Emily Thornberry, the Labour chair of the foreign affairs select committee, said: “At last! I am so very happy to see a British government – a Labour British government – finally doing the right thing and taking a strong stance … no longer a bystander wringing their hands.”

Brazil court crisis deepens as justice orders federal police chief suspended
RIO DE JANEIRO/BRASILIA, Sept 8 - Brazil's Supreme Court crisis deepened on Tuesday as Justice Andre Mendonca ordered the suspension of federal police chief Andrei Rodrigues, a decision backed by the majority of a five-member court panel but challenged by the government.
The suspension represents a new chapter in a conflict that has engulfed the top court, pitting Mendonca against fellow Justice Alexandre de Moraes, and comes as the country heads into a presidential election next month.
Moraes is a powerful figure in Brazil. His pursuit of former President Jair Bolsonaro and allies over a coup plot to reverse Bolsonaro's 2022 election loss led to the former president's conviction last year.
Right-wing opposition leaders have sought to tie leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva to Moraes, while using the court crisis to bolster the presidential campaign of Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the former president's eldest son.
Recent polls indicated Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro are running neck and neck. Opposition supporters took to the streets on Independence Day on Monday to protest against Lula and Moraes and voice support for Mendonca, a Bolsonaro appointee.
COURT CRISIS
Mendonca last week disclosed a report raising questions about alleged contact between Moraes and a banker accused of leading a multibillion-dollar fraud scheme, prompting calls for an investigation of the justice.
Moraes responded by seeking an investigation into Mendonca for alleged abuse of authority, citing federal police intelligence reports that Mendonca has now challenged as illegal.
Mendonca ordered the preventive suspension of Rodrigues, the director-general of the Federal Police, and Leandro Almada, the agency's intelligence chief, over their alleged involvement in the production of the intelligence reports.
The Federal Police did not respond to a request for comment.
A majority of the five-member Supreme Court panel reviewing the case backed Mendonca's decision, with Justices Kassio Nunes Marques, another Bolsonaro appointee, and Luiz Fux joining him.
A top Lula aide criticized Mendonca's move as unwarranted judicial overreach.
"Investigating possible evidence of crimes is correct. But this measure smells electoral to me. That cannot happen," Institutional Relations Minister Jose Guimaraes said on social media.
GOVERNMENT APPEALS
Later on Tuesday, Lula's government said in a statement it had appealed the decision before Supreme Court President Edson Fachin.
The Solicitor General's Office argued that suspending the police chief violates powers constitutionally reserved for the president, while compromising the police's functioning and creating a risk of institutional disarray, the government said in its statement.
In the ruling seen by Reuters, Mendonca said the measure was necessary to preserve the independence of the judiciary and ensure that justices, the solicitor general and police officials could perform their duties free from "illegal constraints."
He said the "exceptional gravity and illegality" surrounding the intelligence reports allegedly involving Rodrigues required immediate action as judicial and police functions risked continuing to be "vilified." REUTERS

Repression in Belarus hasn't eased, activist Bialiatski says before new US talks on prisoners

Repression in Belarus hasn't eased, activist Bialiatski says before new US talks on prisoners
OSLO, Sept 8 - U.S. engagement with Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko has succeeded in freeing hundreds of political prisoners but has not changed the nature of his authoritarian rule, Belarus' most respected human rights figure told Reuters.
Ales Bialiatski, co-winner of the 2022 Nobel Peace Prize, spent 4-1/2 years in prison before being freed and expelled from the country last December in one of a series of deals negotiated by John Coale, President Donald Trump's envoy on Belarus.
Coale has said he hopes for another big batch of releases in a planned visit to Minsk this month, when he expects to meet Lukashenko for the first time since March.
But Bialiatski, while grateful to Washington for its intervention, said the U.S. strategy of easing sanctions on Belarus in return for prisoner releases was not fostering real change in his country.
He described those jailed on politically related charges as "hostages", a term that Trump has also used.
"It's essentially a pure trade. An exchange is taking place — hostages for a change in sanctions — but this doesn't alter the fundamental nature of the Belarusian regime," Bialiatski, 63, said in an interview during a visit to Oslo.
"While I am glad to be free... the machinery of repression keeps running. Every week we see new political prisoners and new methods of repression."
Lukashenko denies holding political prisoners, describing the people concerned as "bandits".
TRUMP DROPS PREVIOUS U.S. STANCE OF SHUNNING LUKASHENKO
Trump's decision last year to re-engage with Lukashenko, a close ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin, marked a sharp change in U.S. policy after years of treating the veteran Belarusian leader as a pariah because of his human rights record and backing for Moscow's war in Ukraine.
However, analysts and opposition figures doubt whether Coale's diplomacy can succeed in peeling Lukashenko away from Putin, given his political and economic dependence on Moscow.
They say that while freeing many prisoners, Belarusian authorities have arrested new ones, in what the opposition describes as a "revolving door".
Coale has claimed credit for the release of 700 to 800 people since mid-2025. But according to Viasna, the human rights group founded by Bialiatski, the net total of political prisoners has only fallen to 888 today from 1,185 at the start of June 2025.
Bialiatski said pressure was also increasing against activists outside Belarus. He himself discovered last month that he had been placed on a "wanted" database by Belarus and Russia, although he did not know why.
BIALIATSKI SAYS EUROPEAN SANCTIONS MUST REMAIN IN FORCE
Bialiatski said the European Union should maintain sanctions on Belarus, including a ban on exports of potash fertiliser, of which Minsk is a major producer.
"As long as the (Ukraine) war continues and Belarus is aiding Russia in it, there are no grounds to discuss a shift in the EU's relationship with Belarus," he said.
Bialiatski predicted that Lukashenko, aged 72 and in power since 1994, would never step aside, for fear of facing criminal charges.
"I think he'll hold onto power until the very end." REUTERS
