Bosses are using AI to spy on employees' productivity—does it work?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:30:06 UTC
20:30:06 KST

Ready for a Whopper with a side of Orwell? Earlier this year, Burger King announced the rollout of Patty, an AI chatbot imbedded in headsets that tracks if cashiers neglect to say please and thank you and chimes in when a soda fountain is running low.
Advances in AI, cameras, sensors and tracking software have given employers unprecedented power to monitor employees. They now observe the physical location of workers, the length and content of phone calls, keystrokes per minute, and even the tone and pitch of conversations with customers.
Now, as companies search for new ways to watch their workforce, researchers are taking a close look at the consequences of constant surveillance.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Employee monitoring has become standard practice in multiple industries and workplaces. Drivers delivering packages or pizzas are increasingly being watched by AI-powered surveillance systems. Many employees in Amazon warehouses are continuously tracked through handheld scanners, badge swipes and workstation software.
Technologies that keep tabs on employees hold a strong appeal for corporate leadership, says Cornelius König, a psychology researcher at Saarland University in Germany. Leaders may believe that close surveillance can help identify top performers, increase efficiency or improve safety, he says.
In practice, though, such benefits are elusive. When König reviewed studies on employee monitoring in the 2025 issue of the Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior, he found little to suggest that electronic surveillance improved performance. “My general take is that [monitoring] isn’t going to matter as much as employers assume,” he says.
Despite the lack of evidence, the global market for employee-monitoring technology is expected to exceed $4 billion in 2026, largely due to major companies in North America. A New York Times investigation in 2022 found that eight out of the 10 largest private US employers, including United Parcel Service, Amazon and UnitedHealth Group, tracked productivity metrics of individual workers, often in real time.
US postal workers are also closely watched. Delivering mail “feels less like public service and more like working inside a quiet surveillance state,” said a Reddit user in 2025. “We’re tracked down to the second. Every scan. Every step. Every stop. They monitor our GPS in real time. They can pull up on us unannounced. We get questioned for things as human as needing the restroom or checking a package twice.”
Any employer of any size can get into the monitoring business. Amazon Web Services sells thousands and thousands of software programs for employee monitoring, says Michele Molè, an employment law researcher at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands. Adding a monitoring app to the workplace can be as easy as downloading Spotify, he says. But instead of music, employers get a stream of data about how each employee is behaving every minute of their day.
Companies that hope to increase their workforce’s performance through monitoring face a basic obstacle in human nature, König says. Workers might briefly up their game, but they tend to revert to their normal routines. “They become habituated,” he says. In his review, he pointed to growing evidence that even body cameras worn by police — an especially high-profile, high-stakes example of surveillance — don’t significantly change the behavior of either the police or the public over the long term.
When workers do respond to monitoring, there can be unintended consequences. A 2020 study found that electronically monitored truck drivers were less likely to exceed daily limits for driving hours, but they also were more likely to crash.
König is far from the only skeptic. “There’s really very little evidence that the mere implementation of monitoring employees is, in itself, going to increase productivity or performance,” says Daniel Ravid, a management researcher at the University of New Mexico.
Ravid conducted a 2022 meta-analysis that combined the results of studies involving more than 23,000 subjects in laboratory experiments and workplace settings, including workers in call centers and offices and police on patrol. Taken together, the studies found no correlation between levels of monitoring and employee performance.
That’s partly because some employees find workarounds to monitoring, even if that means tapping their keyboard periodically while they’re reading a book at lunch. “People are incredibly creative and adaptable, and they’ll find ways to reassert their freedom when it’s threatened or taken away,” Ravid says.
Ravid’s meta-analysis found that any type of monitoring — subtle or obvious, incidental or invasive — tended to increase workplace stress. “I think anything that undermines a sense of dignity is also going to undermine employee attitudes,” he says.
A 2024 study of more than 3,500 workers in Canada underscored the potential downsides of monitoring: Employees who perceived that they were being surveilled on the job reported that they felt more pressure and stress and less autonomy and privacy at work.
In an age of “datafication,” it’s not surprising that companies would look for new metrics to evaluate employees, says Kirstie Ball, a management researcher at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland. “The systematic gathering of data about people and what they’re doing is part and parcel of modernity,” she says. “Surveillance becomes a means of getting things done.”
But not every company knows how to make good use of all those data points, Ball says. “There are many pitfalls along the way. Are you measuring what you think you’re measuring? Are you interpreting the data correctly according to the purpose that you gathered it, or are you looking at it just because you can?”
Employee surveillance without any coherent plan to use the data has become a commonplace scenario in modern companies, König says. Many workplaces end up collecting data simply because they have the technology, not because surveillance supports the company’s overall business strategy. “They end up with terabytes of data on a drive somewhere but don’t know what to do with it.”
“There’s really very little evidence that the mere implementation of monitoring employees is, in itself, going to increase productivity or performance.” —Daniel Ravid, University of New Mexico
Modern surveillance is an inherently electronic exercise, but companies can’t just install an app and expect results, Ravid says. “If managers think that they have a perfect way to measure performance because they have advanced technologies, they’re wrong,” he says. “They still need human insight and conversations to contextualize that data.”
Laws protecting employees from overly invasive surveillance generally haven’t kept pace with technology, says Molè, who wrote the 2026 book Monitored at Work. While the European Union has strong employee privacy laws, with additional legal protections in nations like Italy, Spain, France and Germany, workers in the US have far fewer safeguards and are more likely to be placed under a microscope.
In 2023, three current or former Amazon delivery drivers in Colorado filed a class action lawsuit against Amazon claiming that they were under excessive AI-assisted surveillance and that delivery quotas made it difficult to take necessary breaks. “The drivers were forced to pee in bottles,” Molè says. “This is not happening in Europe.” Amazon called for arbitration, noting that drivers work directly for outside delivery service providers who have contracts with the multitrillion-dollar company, not Amazon itself. The case is ongoing.
Other legal issues can lurk in the fine print that comes with monitoring software. Bosses who download monitoring apps they can’t customize are essentially letting outside companies take control of their employees’ data with little oversight or knowledge of how the data could be used. “We need more labor laws that target providers of technologies,” Molè says. Surveillance companies should be required to work directly with companies and their employees to clearly explain the technologies and tailor each product to meet specific needs and reach specific goals, he says.
Theoretically, monitoring could be a part of a healthy company culture that encourages success, Molè says. “People under monitoring should have a sense of being valued, and the monitoring should be truly meaningful for improving everyone’s working conditions and methods,” he says. “Good monitoring is based on mutual trust.” Companies that thoughtfully build their own system for tracking employee outputs instead of superimposing some “creepy and odd” tool found online are more likely to see actual benefits, he adds.
Success is certainly possible. Headbands that track brainwaves may seem invasive, but an Australian mining company found that such technology helped reduce fatigue-related accidents to almost zero. A 2024 study of remote workers on Upwork found that the productivity of top-performing workers dropped nearly 20 percent after they were allowed to turn off monitoring software without explanation, suggesting that the software had some benefits.
But productivity didn’t fall when that high-performing group was told they had the opportunity to go without supervision because of their impressive output, underscoring the importance of good management — leading the researchers to conclude that spending money on good managers could yield better results than spending it on monitoring software.
Transparency can go a long way to improving workplace culture, Ravid says. His meta-analysis found that, compared with workers who are surveilled without much explanation or consent, workers who have a clear understanding of how they are being monitored and how the data will be used also have a greater sense of fairness and job satisfaction.
New technologies will continue to join the ranks of Burger King’s Patty and other monitoring devices in the modern workforce. But if companies don’t change their basic approach, the results will likely be the be the same: suspicion and confusion for employees and few tangible benefits for employers.

Moscow vows ‘harsh and painful’ response to Hungarian expulsions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:29:09 UTC
20:29:09 KST

Moscow vows ‘harsh and painful’ response to Hungarian expulsions
Moscow will deliver a “harsh and painful” response to Hungary’s expulsion of ten Russian diplomats, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has warned.
The remarks were in response to Budapest’s decision to expel ten members of Russia’s diplomatic mission over alleged activities deemed “unacceptable for diplomats” under the Vienna Convention.
“The response to the Russophobic lobby in Budapest will be harsh and painful,” Zakharova said on Tuesday.
Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban announced the decision on Tuesday. She said the Russian ambassador had been informed that, “according to the assessment of the Hungarian authorities,” the diplomats had engaged in activities incompatible with their status.
Orban did not specify the alleged activities or say how long the diplomats had been given to leave. She said the decision was intended to protect Hungary’s “security and sovereignty,” while stressing that Budapest was not severing diplomatic ties with Moscow and intended to maintain dialogue.
The expulsions come as Prime Minister Peter Magyar’s government has sharply reversed Hungary’s policy toward Russia since taking office in May. In a new foreign policy directive, Budapest designated Russia a “threat to Hungary, Europe, and the global order,” marking a dramatic break with the pragmatic relations pursued under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban.
Hungary had not formally designated Russia as a “threat” at any point since 1945. Under Orban, Budapest repeatedly opposed what the former prime minister called the West’s “war policies,” refused to supply weapons to Kiev, and argued that the conflict could not be settled through a Ukrainian military victory.
Orban also repeatedly delayed or watered down EU sanctions on Moscow and resisted major financial packages for Kiev, while seeking exemptions that allowed Hungary to continue importing Russian oil, gas, and nuclear fuel. He maintained that cutting Europe off from comparatively cheap Russian energy would damage the bloc’s industrial competitiveness.
Magyar’s new position closely mirrors that of the EU, which also advocates “sustainable peace and long-term security guarantees,” but only on terms that recognize Kiev’s maximalist demands – a return to Ukraine’s 1991 borders, freedom to pursue NATO and EU membership, and NATO-like security guarantees provided by European and American forces.
His government has also backed new sanctions on Russia and dropped Budapest’s objections to a €90 billion ($105 billion) EU package for Kiev, reversing policies that had previously set Hungary apart from most other EU members.

Russia’s federal budget spending on the war in Ukraine reached a historic high between January and June 2026. The aggressor state spent 10.687 trillion rubles (106.28 billion euros) on military needs and weapons production, Dialog.ua reports.
The figures were published by Janis Kluge, a researcher at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, following a review of data from the Russian Ministry of Finance.
Compared with the first half of 2025, Russia’s military spending increased by 30%, with an additional 2.46 trillion rubles (24.5 billion euros) spent.
Compared with January–June 2024, expenditure increased by 65%, or 4.211 trillion rubles (42.1 billion euros). Compared with 2023, the increase amounted to 145%, while spending was 285% higher than in the first year of the full-scale war.
Compared with the pre-war year of 2021, Russia’s military spending has increased more than fivefold. On average, Russia’s military machine cost the state budget 1.78 trillion rubles (17.7 billion euros) per month.
That amounts to approximately 59 billion rubles (587 million euros) per day,
or around 2.5 billion rubles (24.9 million euros) per hour.
Almost half of all Russian state budget expenditure is now devoted to military needs. During the first six months of the year, 43.8% of all budget expenditure was spent on the military and weapons production, marking a new all-time high.
Most of Russia’s current military spending is hidden from the public. Around two-thirds of the military budget is classified. In the first six months of 2026, Russia spent 3.546 trillion rubles (35.25 billion euros) on publicly disclosed defence items, while another 7.141 trillion rubles (71 billion euros) was spent under classified budget items.
Classified expenditure is growing particularly rapidly. Compared with last year, such spending has increased by 42% and is now more than seven times higher than before the war.
Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Russian authorities have allocated 57.144 trillion rubles (567.6 billion euros) to military spending and weapons procurement.

Mamdani Expected to Announce Release of 9/11-Related Documents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:26:35 UTC
20:26:35 KST

As the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in New York City approaches, Mayor Zohran Mamdani has launched a portal giving the public access to about 170,000 pages of documents concerning air quality, health hazards, and the government’s response following 9/11.
Its long-sought documents, which had previously been kept out of the public eye, show that New York City leaders were aware of the dangers posed by toxic contamination around Ground Zero following the attacks, even while they continued to tell New Yorkers that the air was safe to breathe.
Some of the pages were reportedly found in 68 boxes stashed in a city office, which advocates argue had been kept away from the public for years. According to a press release from the Mayor's Office, the records "were not located until 2025 despite multiple Freedom of Information Law (FOIL) requests."
Another document included in the records is the so-called Harding memo, an October 2001 document showing that city officials had in the weeks after the attacks already anticipated approximately 10,000 legal claims arising from exposure to toxic air.
The new portal was announced Tuesday morning at a press conference that was also attended by longtime advocate Jon Stewart and others involved in the yearslong legal effort to obtain the records. In June, the mayor allocated $34.2 million from the city’s $125.8 billion fiscal year 2027 budget to create and maintain the portal.
"Now, close to 25 years later, more people have died from 9/11-related illnesses than were killed on the day itself," Mamdani said at the conference announcing the portal. The World Trade Center Health Program, which provides no-cost monitoring and treatment for covered 9/11-related health conditions, said thousands continue to be diagnosed with ailments resulting from their exposure to dust, smoke, debris, and the traumatic events.
The city’s Fire Department released a report on Sept. 1 detailing the lasting effects of the 9/11 tragedy on first responders. More than 12,000 FDNY members have been diagnosed and certified with at least one related physical or mental health condition, including cancers, according to the report.
The mayor’s office has said that additional documents will be added on a rolling basis. "The City expects substantially more documents will be released in the coming year as they are reviewed, and personally identifiable information is removed," the press release said.
“For too long, New Yorkers have had to fight for access to records that should have been available to them in the first place," Mamdani said in the press release. "This portal is part of our administration’s enduring commitment to honor those we lost, care for those living with lasting health consequences and give thousands of New Yorkers the answer they’ve been asking for.”
Mamdani also announced Tuesday that the city had settled two lawsuits brought by 9/11 Health Watch, ending a multiyear legal battle over records concerning post-9/11 air quality and health risks.
What do we know about the content of the documents?
The New York Times obtained early access to the documents and reported that they contain information relating to 15 John Street, near the collapsed World Trade Center, which purportedly detected asbestos—at times exceeding acceptable limits—about a year after the attack.
Among the pages was also an audit from November 2001, submitted to the federal Environmental Protection Agency, which reportedly showed high concentrations of benzene, a cancer-causing substance, in the air near the towers, according to the Times.
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has said that exposure to these contaminants increases the risk of developing health conditions, such as illnesses concerning the airways and digestive systems. The CDC added that after the attacks, around 400,000 people were exposed to these contaminants and other factors that increased their risk for such conditions.
Taking questions at the conference on Tuesday, Mamdani addressed what people can expect to learn from the documents that they might not have already known. "I think that there is going to be a lot to learn from these documents," he said, adding that it's important that "those who faced such sustained pushback for years are finally told by the city of New York: 'You were right.'"
Why Mamdani is under pressure
The release of the documents coincides with Mamdani drawing calls from families of victims of the tragedy and some Republican politicians not to attend the 9/11 remembrance event in New York City on Friday.
In July, 9/11 widower Giovanni Galante began a petition against Mamdani’s attendance, citing concerns over “Mamdani's public positions, associations, and responses to rhetoric that many perceive as hostile.” The petition cites Mamdani’s refusal to condemn those who say “globalize the intifada” as one of the issues. The petition also references Mamdani’s appointment of Ramzi Kassem, who worked for the Biden Administration, as chief counsel to the mayor. Kassem served as legal counsel for Ahmed al-Darbi, who plead guilty to charges stemming from a 2002 al-Qaeda tanker bombing plot and who is the brother-in-law of one of the hijackers in the plane that crashed into the Pentagon.
Former New York Gov. George Pataki told a local CBS affiliate on Thursday that Mamdani should first reject Hasan Piker, who previously earned public ire over a comment that the U.S. “deserved” the attack. Mamdani has already denounced Piker’s comment.
Rudy Giuliani, who was the mayor of New York in 2001, told right-leaning news organization Newsmax that Mamdani should skip the event. “Having lost friends there and being very close to many of the families, it offends me that he's coming,” Giuliani said. The former mayor also attacked Mamdani’s religion, Islam, and baselessly suggested the mayor was supportive of Muslim extremist ideology.
Mamdani, the city’s first Muslim mayor who was nine years old when the attack happened, has long faced Islamophobic comments. Speaking to the Times last year, Mamdani lamented how the 2001 attacks had made anti-Muslim prejudice “a fact of life” for Muslim-Americans, claiming: “It was this horrific day that was also, for many New Yorkers, the moment at which they were marked an ‘other.’”
Before Giuliani’s comments, Mamdani signed city executive orders designating Sept. 11 a New York-wide "Day of Remembrance and Service" and updating emergency preparedness procedures. But the signing caught the ire of some critics after Mamdani handed the 9/11 ceremonial pen to Kassem.
Despite the pushback, Mamdani still plans to attend the commemoration on Friday.
“I’m proud to be the mayor of this city,” Mamdani said. “I love this city. I love this country. And what I want this week to be a focus on is on the families whose loved ones were stolen from them 25 years ago in the horrific act of terror of September 11th, and a focus also on the first responders who gave everything they could to this city and to the people who came together to try and help their fellow New Yorkers.”

Russia looking forward to revival of trilateral Ukraine talks – Kremlin
Moscow appreciates efforts to resume direct negotiations involving Russia, Ukraine, and the US as Washington has stepped up efforts to settle the conflict, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said.
Speaking to Indian media on Tuesday, ahead of the BRICS summit in New Delhi, Peskov said intensive diplomatic work is underway, with American negotiators carrying messages between Moscow and Kiev.
“We hope for a restart of negotiations between three parties – Russia, Ukraine, and America. We do hope for the best. We do hope that sooner or later we will pursue a peaceful solution,” he said.
Peskov added that Russia welcomes mediation efforts by both Washington and New Delhi, and emphasized that Moscow never wanted the Ukraine conflict to happen and launched its offensive in order to end the war started by Kiev in 2014 following the Western-backed Maidan coup.
The spokesman also said Kiev does not appear to be “flexible” or “really willing” to actually end the hostilities, adding that it appears to be “provoked to a great extent by some European countries who cannot get rid of the idea of strategically defeating Russia.”
His comments follow a fresh round of shuttle diplomacy by US President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. The pair met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday for more than three hours before traveling to Kiev for talks with Vladimir Zelensky the following day.
The Kremlin described the Moscow meeting as constructive and “extremely candid,” saying the Americans presented several ideas for ending the conflict while Putin reiterated Russia’s conditions for a lasting settlement.
Witkoff later said progress had been made toward scheduling another three-way meeting, while expressing optimism that diplomacy could produce an agreement.
Zelensky suggested on Tuesday that the next trilateral talks could be held in the UAE, Türkiye, Switzerland, or another country as early as September or October. Moscow and Washington have yet to comment on specific venues or time frames.
The trilateral format was last used in Geneva in February, following two earlier rounds in Abu Dhabi. However, the talks ended without any significant breakthroughs, although Washington said there had been “meaningful progress.”
The negotiations have since stalled as the US shifted its focus to its war against Iran while hostilities between Russia and Ukraine have continued.
Moscow has repeatedly said it remains open to diplomacy but insists any final agreement must address the root causes of the conflict and respect the new realities on the ground. Kiev, however, has resisted Russian demands on territorial and security issues.

Gaza's tents are withering away after three years of genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:25:11 UTC
20:25:11 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza's tents are withering away after three years of heat, rain and endless displacement
Displaced Palestinian people in the war-torn coastal enclave of the Gaza Strip are find it exceedingly hard to afford new tents or maintain their old ones after nearly three years of an Israeli genocide.
Thousands of displaced families remain in tents and makeshift shelters, many of which were intended to provide temporary refuge but have become their only homes.
When Israel's genocidal war began in 2023, Hanaa al-Soltan, 44, left northern Gaza carrying clothes, documents and a few belongings for her children, believing the family would return home within days or weeks. Nearly three years later, she remains displaced in a tent in central Gaza.
"At first, we said it would only be a few days or weeks. Then the first winter came, followed by summer, then another winter, and we're still here," she told The New Arab.
The summer heat is particularly difficult for the family. Under direct sunlight, the tarpaulin heats rapidly, turning the tent into an oven, while limited ventilation offers little relief.
"At midday, the children can't stay inside. We go out looking for shade and return when the sun becomes weaker. Sometimes I feel like we're living in an oven," she said.
But when summer ends, the damage it leaves behind becomes a threat. Months of exposure to heat and wind weaken the tarpaulin, leaving holes and cracks through which rainwater and cold air enter.
"When it rains, we put pots and pans under the holes and lift the mattresses off the ground. We sleep watching the water instead of sleeping," she said.
Unable to afford a new shelter, Hanaa buys used plastic sheets and attaches them to the damaged sections.
"We're no longer looking for a house. We just want a tarpaulin that will last us," she added.
Little protection
Hanaa's experience is shared by thousands of displaced families who have spent years moving from one location to another in search of safety, only to find themselves trapped in increasingly fragile shelters.
Mahmoud al-Arja, 39, moved several times with his wife and six children before settling in a tent in the al-Mawasi area in Khan Younis City in southern Gaza. Since the beginning of the war, he has bought three tents and repaired each of them repeatedly.
"The tarpaulin traps the heat. We open the sides and lift the cover, but the sun comes in from everywhere. The children sweat all the time and can't sleep," he told TNA.
The prolonged exposure to sunlight has weakened the material.
"The sun eats away at the tent. You buy one thinking it will protect you, but after a while, you discover its edges are starting to tear," he said.
When winter arrives, those damaged sections become entry points for rain and wind. Al-Arja uses plastic sheets, blankets and old clothes to seal the gaps before storms arrive.
"In winter, we fear the rain and wind. When water gets into the tent, there's nowhere else to take the children," he said.
The cost of keeping the shelter standing has also become a burden. Families need poles, ropes, plastic sheets and other materials, many of which have become increasingly expensive.
"We're not buying a tent; we're buying extra time," al-Arja added. "Work has stopped, income has stopped, but the expenses for the tent haven't."
Three years of trying to stay dry
Rasha Salama, a 36-year-old mother of three from Gaza City, could not afford a new tent for her four children, so she bought one that had been used by another family.
"I wasn't looking for a nice or new tent. I just wanted anything to give us a roof over our heads," she said.
During the summer, her children sleep drenched in sweat. Opening the tent from both sides provides some ventilation but exposes the family to dust, insects and direct sunlight.
"Some nights, the children want to sleep outside because it's too hot inside," she said.
Winter, however, brings greater anxiety.
"When it rains, the sand under the tent turns to mud, and water seeps in from several places. We lift the mattresses and pile things on top of each other, then wait for the rain to stop," she said.
Rasha keeps scraps of plastic and old fabric inside the tent for emergencies.
"Every piece has a purpose. This one's for patching a hole, this one's for under the mattresses, and this one's for when it rains," she said.
"We've been living like this for three years. The summer suffocates us, the winter terrifies us, and in between, we just try to keep the tent standing," she added.
Market built around survival
The prolonged displacement has created persistent demand for tarpaulins, ropes, wood and other shelter materials. But as families' incomes have collapsed, many can afford only the cheapest or second-hand options.
Abu Salah, a Gaza-based shelter-supplies vendor, told TNA that the market has changed dramatically during the war.
"At first, people would buy complete tents. Now, many just want a tarpaulin because they can't afford a whole set," he said.
Used tarpaulins have become increasingly common, while poles, wood and ropes are salvaged from damaged or abandoned shelters.
"There are families who ask for the cheapest thing available. Even if the tent has a hole, they say they will repair it themselves," he added.
Political analyst Akram Atallah believes the continued reliance on tents nearly three years into the war cannot be separated from the broader political and reconstruction crisis.
"The transformation of the tent from a temporary solution into a dwelling for years reflects the absence of any real prospect for reconstruction and places residents before a new form of daily depletion," Atallah told TNA.
Restrictions on building materials and shelter supplies, he said, delay reconstruction while leaving hundreds of thousands of Palestinians vulnerable to weather, poverty and disease.
"The continuation of these conditions deepens the disintegration of life," he added.

Most Poles use social media but seniors show higher trust, poll finds
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
13:24:45 CEST
20:24:45 KST

Most Poles use social media but seniors show higher trust, poll finds
Nearly three-quarters of Poles (73 percent) use social media networks, driven by a 95 percent adoption rate among young adults, though older generations are far more likely to trust online information and share personal content, a new survey has shown.
The study by the Market and Social Research Institute (IBRiS), commissioned by PAP, found that Facebook remains Poland's most popular service (53 percent), followed by Instagram (31 percent), TikTok (25 percent), and X at 18 percent.
Despite younger generations dominating overall numbers, IBRiS report author Marcin Duma told PAP that older users are far more likely to share their daily lives online and believe the information they find there, whereas younger users exhibit a strong "digital detachment".
Social media adoption stands at 95 percent among adults aged 18–29 but drops to 39 percent for those over 70. Generation Z heavily distrusts online content, viewing it as commercial self-promotion. They form a "silent majority" that rarely posts and strongly guards privacy, Duma said. Older users willingly share personal everyday updates, making them more vulnerable to scams by mistaking commercial content for credible news.
Furthermore, digital confidence shapes threat perceptions. While 85 percent of all Poles have encountered online scams, only 65 percent of young adults view artificial intelligence (AI) fraud as "very dangerous", compared to around 89 percent of older users.
Social media usage also varies sharply by political electorate. Left-wing Razem voters (88 percent) and ultra-nationalist Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) supporters (85 percent) boast the highest presence. The high digital presence of Grzegorz Braun's party is surprising because his voters are mostly lower-income, less-educated, and live in rural areas - groups that usually use the internet less. However, Braun's exclusion from mainstream media forced highly effective, targeted online campaigns.
Supporters of the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) and centre-right Development Plus sit at the bottom with just 56 percent usage due to older voter profiles. Meanwhile, the ruling Civic Coalition (KO) maintains high usage despite an older demographic, driven by higher education and urban residency.
A sweeping 81 percent of all respondents demand stricter state cybersecurity regulations, viewing it as a priority or vital issue. Only 4 percent believe current laws are sufficient. This legislative push is highest among Development Plus (97 percent) and KO (94 percent) loyalists, while far-right Confederation voters remain the most sceptical of state intervention (62 percent).
The data is based on an IBRiS survey conducted between August 29 and 30, 2026, across a representative sample of over 1,000 adult Polish residents. (PAP)

Polish presidential couple join National Reading campaign

He also announced that Joseph Conrad's novel Lord Jim had been selected as next year's National Reading featured text.

This is a major work of Polish literature, and it is one that elevates Mickiewicz to a position among the "great Europeans" such as Dante and Goethe.
The National Reading campaign was launched in 2012 with a joint reading of Pan Tadeusz by Mickiewicz. Past editions featured pieces by other major Polish writers, including Nobel laureate Henryk Sienkiewicz, novelist Boleslaw Prus and playwright Stanislaw Wyspianski. (PAP)

Minister for Backward Classes Welfare V Sampathkumar moved the resolution.
NEW DELHI: The Tamil Nadu Assembly on Tuesday unanimously passed a resolution asking the Centre to use only officially recognised caste names while collecting data on Other Backward Classes during the second phase of the 2027 Census.The resolution covers Backward Classes, Most Backward Classes and Denotified Communities listed by the Tamil Nadu and Union governments. It also calls for these official lists to be built into the census portal so that people can select their caste from a fixed list rather than enter names themselves.The resolution said caste details should be collected for these communities in the same manner as data for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
Why Tamil Nadu wants fixed caste names
Minister for Backward Classes Welfare V Sampathkumar, who moved the resolution, said allowing people to enter different names for the same caste could create confusion, particularly when regional variations are involved.He said such ambiguity could make enumeration difficult and affect the usefulness of the census data."Hence, the exercise must stick to official names alone as per the notifications of the state and union governments to ensure social justice and equal justice," he said.
The minister suggested that the official lists of BCs, MBCs and Denotified Communities should be pre-loaded into the census enumeration portal or application. Enumerators or respondents could then select the relevant caste using a 'drop-down menu'.The resolution also called for the 'open-column method' to be completely avoided while collecting details of these communities.
OBC caste data absent from post-Independence Census
The Assembly said caste-wise data on OBCs has not been included in censuses conducted after Independence. It argued that accurate information is therefore needed based on the official lists notified by the state and Union governments in accordance with the Constitution.“In order to ensure social justice for all sections of society, this Assembly unanimously resolves to urge the union government to collect the caste details of Backward Classes, Most Backward Classes and Denotified Communities during the second phase of the 2027 census of India, in the same manner as followed for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.”
The resolution was passed after legislators, including members of the AIADMK and PMK, spoke in its support.DMK MLAs were not present during the debate and passage of the resolution after they were evicted from the House following a ruckus. Despite their absence, the resolution was passed unanimously.

Germany cannot defend itself without new debt, says finance minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:22:37 UTC
20:22:37 KST

Germany cannot defend itself without new debt, says finance minister
BERLIN, Sept 8 - Germany cannot defend itself without taking on new debt, Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said on Tuesday, justifying rising defence spending amid growing threats.
"It's like flying to the moon without a rocket," Klingbeil said, defending his 2027 draft budget in the lower house of parliament.
Berlin is stepping up spending on defence and security amid pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump on NATO allies to contribute more and as authorities warn of growing cyber and hybrid threats from countries including Russia and Iran.
Germany's cabinet approved the first draft in July, ramping up investment and defence spending to shield its sluggish economy from war-related energy shocks and years of underinvestment.
From 2027 to 2030, Germany plans to borrow a total of €838.2 billion ($973.23 billion).
Opposition to borrowing is deep-rooted in Germany, where the national psyche is still scarred by the experience of hyperinflation in the 1920s, but Klingbeil defended higher investments to make the country fitter for the future.
"We are investing in our future, we are investing in our security, we are creating the freedom to remain capable of acting tomorrow," Klingbeil said.
Total investment will rise to €117.5 billion in 2027 from €78.9 billion in 2025 under the previous government, helped by a €500 billion infrastructure fund and looser borrowing rules for defence.
"Opponents of the special fund criticise this debt. These are the same people whose ideology meant infrastructure was neglected for years," Klingbeil said.
ELECTION DEFEAT
The investment push and economic reforms announced by the ruling coalition of Social Democrats and conservatives failed to win over voters in Sunday's election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) surged into first place.
The election defeat to the anti-immigrant, pro-Russian AfD has reopened divisions in Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition government, as Klingbeil's centre-left SPD calls for planned economic and social reforms to be softened.
"Especially at this time, we must be very clear: We will not accept racism or policies of exclusion. We will not accept the far-right dividing our country into 'us' and 'the others'," Klingbeil said.
"We will not allow the systematic dismantling of our welfare state to be carried out under the banner of reform. The attacks on social rights and achievements must stop."
SECURITY IN FOCUS
Core defence spending will rise to €109 billion in 2027 from €82.2 billion in 2026, according to the draft budget passed in July. The total reaches €130.1 billion including support for Ukraine and other security spending.
Germany was not investing in defence to wage war, said Klingbeil, but rather to ensure that its people do not have to experience one, adding that Russia's war did not stop at the borders of Ukraine.
"We will not be intimidated by (Russian President Vladimir) Putin," Klingbeil said.
The German government said last week that it had concluded that Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport.
He also argued that the funds were helping to return Germany's anaemic economy to growth.
Despite higher prices due to the Iran conflict and uncertainty caused by U.S. tariffs, the German economy has shown resilience and grew by 0.3% in the second quarter.
Several economic institutes have upgraded their economic growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027, saying higher government spending drove a stronger-than-expected recovery in the first half of the year.
"Trust does not arise because politicians tell people to be optimistic. Trust arises when things change," Klingbeil said. REUTERS

PISA study: Swiss pupils falling behind in reading and maths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:22:00 UTC
20:22:00 KST

PISA study: Swiss pupils falling behind in reading and maths
In the 2025 PISA study, Swiss schoolchildren performed significantly worse in reading and mathematics than in previous years. Their performance in science remained stable. Overall, however, their results are above the OECD average.
In the core subject of natural sciences, 15-year-olds in Switzerland scored 501 points. This put them above the average of 482 points for the 38 member states of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the University of Bern said on Tuesday.
Switzerland, however, recorded significant declines in reading and mathematics. Reading proficiency has fallen from 492 to 470 points since 2015. In mathematics, performance dropped from 521 to 499 points over the same period.
For the first time, model-based problem-solving was also tested as a new skill. Here, too, Switzerland achieved an above-average result with 520 points.
More
Why the Swiss school system is so successful
Despite the decline in performance, the study confirmed Switzerland’s strong international standing.
Switzerland also performs particularly well when compared with reference countries. In mathematics and problem-solving, it is surpassed only by Estonia. In reading, Estonia and Canada are ahead of Switzerland, while Finland and Italy are roughly on a par.

As Sweden heads to polls, Israel and Palestine policies are on the ballot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:21:13 UTC
20:21:13 KST

As Sweden heads to polls, Israel and Palestine policies are on the ballot
With the left-wing coalition ahead in polling, the current right-wing government’s policies could soon be up for debate.
Stockholm, Sweden – This Sunday, Sweden will vote in a knife-edge general election that could change the country’s stance on Israel.
In 2014, Sweden became the first European Union member state to recognise Palestine.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘We had an ordinary life’: Iran fisherwoman navigates uncertainty of war
- list 2 of 3As US seeks Gaza donor’s extradition, wife warns of ‘terrifying precedent’
- list 3 of 3Worshippers in West Bank tear-gassed as Israeli attacks on mosques surge
The decision strained relations with Israel, with then Foreign Minister Avigdor Lieberman stating that Sweden did not understand that relations in the Middle East are more complicated than assembling IKEA furniture.
Now, as Swedes head to the polls, the far-right Sweden Democrats, the Nordic nation’s second-largest political party, want that recognition revoked.
But a Novus survey released on Monday suggested 50.3 percent support a left-wing coalition compared with 47.9 percent for the current right-wing government.
The Israel-Palestine conflict has been baked into the political landscape ever since Sweden’s Count Folke Bernadotte, the United Nations’ first mediator for Palestine, was assassinated in 1948 by the Zionist paramilitary group Lehi, widely known as the Stern Gang, in Jerusalem.
Forty years later, Sweden brokered talks in Stockholm between Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat and a delegation of prominent American Jews. Days later, Washington opened dialogue with the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO).
Sweden’s politics run in two blocs.
On the right: The governing Moderates, Christian Democrats and Liberals, plus the Sweden Democrats, who have propped up the government from outside since all four parties signed an agreement in 2022.
Current Prime Minister and Moderate leader Ulf Kristersson and Sweden Democrats leader Jimmie Akesson announced earlier this year that an election victory would see a four-party cabinet, with the Sweden Democrats promised significant portfolios.
On the left: The Social Democrats, the Left Party and the Greens, with the Centre Party a possible fourth.
What could happen if the right-wing bloc wins?
The current right-wing government does not regard Israel’s conduct in Gaza as genocide and has not joined South Africa’s genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
The government suspended Sweden’s funding to UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, after Israel alleged that a number of UNRWA staff took part in the deadly October 7, 2023 attack led by Hamas on southern Israel.
It resumed funding later and then ended core funding in December 2024.
In December 2025, the government allocated about $83m to the humanitarian response in Gaza and the region for 2026, bypassing UNRWA.
When Israeli forces intercepted the Global Sumud Flotilla in international waters in October 2025 and arrested more than 400 people on board, among them Sweden’s Greta Thunberg, the government acknowledged reports of Israeli abuse towards the activists but said it had long advised against travel to Gaza and stated the group had “clear personal responsibility”.
Some MPs in the right-wing bloc appear to be favouring Israel.
Christian Democrat MPs have filed motions calling for Jerusalem to be recognised as Israel’s capital and the Swedish embassy to be moved there, for UNRWA’s responsibilities to be transferred to UNHCR, and ultimately for UNRWA to be wound up entirely.
The party’s leader, Ebba Busch, was photographed about 2009 in front of a military vehicle in the occupied Golan Heights wearing an Israeli army T-shirt.
Alice Teodorescu Mawe, a Christian Democrat member of the European Parliament, argued in October 2024 that people applying for Swedish citizenship should recognise Israel’s right to exist and “embrace the Judeo-Christian values on which Swedish democracy rests”.
In August, she shared a clip published by a pro-Israel media enterprise, The Free Press, that questioned the famine in Gaza. An expert interviewed by SVT, Sweden’s public broadcaster, concluded that the video was misleading.
But the current government is not uniformly pro-Israel. It has pushed for EU sanctions against “extremist” settlers and ministers, and in April proposed extra tariffs and export certificates on settlement products.
However, the Sweden Democrats, a party with neo-Nazi roots, if it were to get into government, would represent the most pro-Israel views in the bloc.
Their motions this session call for moving the Swedish embassy to Jerusalem and ending all Swedish aid to Palestinians.
Akesson also said in January that if it were up to him, recognition would absolutely be withdrawn, and that he would raise it in coalition talks.
In practical terms, recognition is a declaration by a state, and that can be changed, Zina al-Dewany, a political commentator and editorial writer for the Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet, told Al Jazeera.
It is something that could be a possibility given the government has not shown much of a “backbone” in standing up to Sweden Democrats’ wishes, she said.
If the Sweden Democrats join the government, she added, they could theoretically end up in charge of foreign affairs, and “our foreign policy is decided by the government, not the parliament,” which means it would not need a parliamentary vote.
What might happen if the left-wing bloc wins?
The left, currently ahead in polling, is aligned on several key issues, including the resumption of UNRWA funding.
Within the bloc, the Left Party and Green Party have called for Sweden to join South Africa’s genocide case against Israel at the ICJ.
Anfal Mahdi, an opposition councillor in Malmo, told Al Jazeera that her Left Party had been an outlier in its explicit support of Palestine, and that the Social Democrats have been fearful of adopting a clearer stance.
“If the left bloc comes to power, you will see a trade boycott of Israel, more money to UNRWA, and we want more funding to the ICC,” Mahdi said, referring to the International Criminal Court, which issued in 2024 an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over war crimes.
All parties have condemned the October 7 Hamas-led attacks on Israel and state the armed group should hold no role in any future Palestinian government.
The Social Democrats, Sweden’s dominant party for a century and architect of the welfare state that still defines Swedish politics, support elements of these issues, but have erred more on the side of caution, focusing more on targeted sanctions against Israeli officials and “extremist” settlers.

Hungary expels 10 Russian diplomats, Moscow vows ‘painful’ response

Hungary expelled 10 Russian diplomats on Tuesday, saying they had acted in ways incompatible with their diplomatic status, in a stark reminder that the pro-Russian years of former prime minister Viktor Orban are over.
Russia’s foreign ministry said it would retaliate and its response would be painful for Hungary, local media reported.
“The response to the Russophobic lobby in Budapest will be harsh and painful,” said foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova.

After Russia invaded Ukraine, many European countries expelled dozens of Russian diplomats, while Hungary expelled none. Until Tuesday, it had not sent any home publicly since 2018.

Migrants in Germany fear their future after AfD victory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:19:45 UTC
20:19:45 KST

Breadcrumb
They built their lives in Germany. Now the AfD's victory has made them question their future
Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a historic election victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, securing 43.8 percent of the vote and more than doubling its 2021 result.
According to the preliminary result, the party won 39 of the state parliament's 83 seats, leaving it three short of an outright majority.
The Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which had led the state government, fell to 17.2 percent, while turnout reached 77.8 percent, the highest recorded in a Saxony-Anhalt state election since German reunification.
Whether the AfD will be able to form a government remains uncertain. The CDU has ruled out a coalition with it, and the party cannot govern alone without support from other lawmakers.
Yet for many migrants and refugees in Magdeburg, the result already feels consequential.
The AfD's Saxony-Anhalt branch, which the state's domestic intelligence agency has classified as a confirmed right-wing extremist, campaigned on a sweeping programme of tighter immigration controls.
Its manifesto calls for a deportation task force, a dedicated "remigration" unit and commissioner, and the redirection of funds earmarked for integration guides to so-called remigration guides.
It also says an AfD-led state government would use the Bundesrat to seek the abolition of subsidiary protection for people fleeing wars and civil conflicts.
For people who have built jobs, families and futures in the state, the election was therefore about more than who would occupy seats in parliament.
Some could cast a ballot. Others, despite living and working in Saxony-Anhalt, watched a decision with direct consequences for their lives be made by those outside the electorate because they do not hold German citizenship.
Closing today so democracy remains open tomorrow
Eleven days before the election, migrant-run businesses across Magdeburg closed their doors for five hours as part of a protest against racism and exclusion.
Restaurants, grocery stores, barbershops and kiosks joined the action, while demonstrators gathered outside the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament.
Organisers said around 150 businesses had planned to participate.
Among them was Dawoud, a restaurant owner. For him, sacrificing part of a working day was intended as a warning about the years ahead.
"We are closing our businesses today so that the doors to a free democracy are not closed tomorrow," he told The New Arab at the demonstration. "This is not only about today. It is about tomorrow, because we have planned our lives and our future here."
Dawoud said the action was also about the families who live in Magdeburg and across the state, and their desire to remain part of a free and democratic society.
"We want to say clearly and openly that we stand against racism," he said. The strike made visible the economic role of migrant communities in the city.
On election night, however, the question was not only whether their absence from shops could be noticed, but whether their presence in the state was accepted at all.
A vote, but little sense of security
Mohammed Hussein, a Syrian-German childcare worker, has lived in Germany since 2015. He has built a career and family life in the country, and his child attends school in Saxony-Anhalt.
Unlike many of his friends, he was eligible to vote in the state election because of his German citizenship.
On Sunday evening, Mohammed stood with friends in Magdeburg and waited for the results. As the scale of the AfD's victory became clear, he said he felt no optimism about what would come next.
"During the recent election campaign, we saw fear and tension growing among the foreign communities here," he said. "The campaign was consistently negative towards refugees, and that will have a major effect on the city."
Mohammed fears that the political atmosphere could affect not only refugees' sense of safety but also workplaces, businesses and social and cultural activities. He said friends and members of migrant organisations had increasingly discussed leaving Magdeburg or Saxony-Anhalt.
For now, he has made no such decision.
"My family is here, I have my work here, and my child goes to school here," he said. "Leaving would be difficult. I will wait and see how we are treated. If I feel that we are no longer welcome, I will leave. A person cannot live under constant pressure."
After nearly 11 years in Germany, he described the future as newly uncertain. Leaving, he said, would not be a spontaneous act but a decision requiring extensive planning for a family whose life is already rooted in the country.
Living with the result, but without a vote
Hussein Ahmed, a Syrian refugee who works at a grocery store in Magdeburg, lives with protected status but does not hold German citizenship. He therefore had no vote in an election he believes could reshape how migrants are treated.
"I feel frustrated and broken because I do not have the right to vote," Hussein said. "I do not have a voice that I can make heard. If I had the right to vote, there are many things I would want to communicate."
He fears that an AfD-led government would bring sweeping changes to the system and greater pressure on migrants.
Although the party's election victory has not itself changed his residence status, its manifesto includes measures aimed at migrants and refugees, including a proposal to pursue the abolition of subsidiary protection through the Bundesrat.
"We came to Germany to build our future and our lives," Hussein added. "All we want is safety and security, and not to live with racism."
After the result, he said the future no longer appeared secure. If an AfD-led administration resulted in migrants being mistreated or denied their rights, Ahmed said he would leave Germany entirely.
For Ahmed and Mohammed Hussein, Germany had once seemed like the end of a long search for safety. Now, after both men built lives in the country under very different legal statuses, each says the future has become difficult to imagine.
'So now we will have to pack our bags'
The uncertainty is most immediate for a 26-year-old Kurdish Syrian from Kobani who works in a restaurant in Magdeburg. He arrived in Germany in 2024 and asked not to be named because of his precarious legal situation.
After leaving Syria, he said he felt as though he had been given a new life when he reached a country he believed was built on humanitarian and ethical principles.
Since arriving, he has tried to learn German and establish a future in the city while working in a restaurant.
But his asylum application has been rejected, and he has received a deportation warning, he said.
He is also receiving psychological treatment and said that prolonged uncertainty about his legal status has made it difficult to focus on rebuilding his life.
He was in Magdeburg when he learned the election result. His first words were: "So now we will have to pack our bags and leave."
He continued, "Since the result, I have felt even more anxious. I worry about my residence status, my work and whether my life here will become more difficult."
Sometimes, he added, a look or the way someone addresses him can make him feel like a burden on the region and that his presence is unwanted.
He stressed that not everyone treated him that way, but said such encounters felt heavier while he was already under psychological strain.
He has begun considering leaving Magdeburg for another German city where he might feel safer, but does not want to leave the country.
"I want to work and build my future here," he said. "But I also want to live somewhere I feel welcome, rather than seen as a burden on society."
As of Monday, the AfD had not formed a government, and the election result had not automatically altered any of the men's legal rights or residence documents.
But the scale of the party's victory had already changed how they imagined the future of the place they hoped would become home.
"We are not just numbers or asylum files," the young man said. "Behind every file is a human being with feelings, a family and a future."
Somaya Abdelrahman is an Egyptian documentary photographer and journalist based in Germany. Her work focuses on human rights, forced displacement, asylum, migration, and political issues

Canada hits US goods with tariffs of up to 50% as trade dispute escalates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:18:27 UTC
20:18:27 KST

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars’ worth of US products took effect on Tuesday, escalating an 18-month trade dispute between the two North American neighbours.
Canada's counter-tariffs on various US goods take effect on Tuesday, in response to US tariffs on Canadian products imposed after trade talks between the two neighbours collapsed last month.
The counter-tariffs cover C$27.6 billion (€17bn) worth of US goods.
The duties of 15%, 25% and 50% apply to hundreds of products, including steel and aluminium, furniture, clothing, cosmetics, household appliances, electronics, agricultural equipment and dairy goods such as cheese.
Ottawa said the measures match the latest US tariffs “dollar for dollar” and “rate for rate”. Some seafood products were removed from Canada’s initial list.
The counter-tariffs cover around 6% of the goods the United States exported to Canada last year, according to the Associated Press.
Canada has also retaliated beyond tariffs. Eight of its 10 provinces continue to restrict or prohibit sales of US alcohol, according to the AP. The Distilled Spirits Council of the United States said American spirits exports to Canada had fallen by more than 70% year on year since the restrictions were introduced.
RBC Economics said Canada’s measures were unlikely to have a noticeable effect on overall US growth, although some American businesses could be hit considerably harder.
US tariffs pose a modestly negative risk to Canada's overall economy, but analysts note that they have a sharper impact on Central Canada's manufacturing sector.
The tariffs come after US President Donald Trump imposed 50% duties on the same value of Canadian products from 22 August, citing what Washington described as “discriminatory treatment” of the US alcohol, automotive and dairy industries.
The US measures affect products including wine, furniture, dairy goods, cement, clothing, fishing rods and hockey equipment. Together, they cover approximately 5.5% of Canadian exports to the United States.
Trump threatens Bombardier
On Monday, Trump threatened to block sales by Canadian aircraft maker Bombardier in the United States unless it moved manufacturing there.
“No more selling Bombardier in the United States!” Trump posted in capital letters on his Truth Social platform, although he did not explain how such a ban would be introduced.
Thousands of Bombardier aircraft currently operate in US airlines' domestic fleets.
In a statement, the company said it supports “tens of thousands of jobs across the United States”, including direct employment in more than 20 states. It also spends more than $2.5 billion (€2.1 billion) a year with approximately 2,800 US suppliers across 47 states.
“Bombardier values its great partnership with American companies and its US employees,” the company said.
Trade talks remain suspended
Negotiations broke down on 21 August after several days of meetings in Washington.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said he had suspended the talks because the Trump administration’s terms were unacceptable. He said US negotiators had introduced last-minute restrictions on Canada’s ability to make trade agreements with other countries.
The dispute has increasingly extended beyond trade policy. Trump signed an order in August directing the US government to refer to Lake Ontario, which lies on the border between the two countries, as “Lake America”.
Google and Apple subsequently adopted the name for users in the US, although Canada does not recognise the change.
Carney said talks could resume when the Americans “stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough” and start being serious.
The trade disputes began after Trump returned to office and imposed a series of tariffs on Canadian goods despite having negotiated and repeatedly praised the North American trade agreement during his first term. Many of those tariffs violate the pact.
The rupture is especially striking because the countries have long shared one of the world’s closest relationships, with deeply integrated economies, close defence and security cooperation, vast cultural ties and, before relations deteriorated, about 400,000 people crossing the border each day.
Although Carney has strong public support in Canada, the country remains heavily reliant on its neighbour. Nearly 60% of Canada’s imports come from the United States, while about 70% of its exports go to the US market.
To support affected businesses and workers, the Canadian government has announced a C$7.5 billion (€4.6bn) aid package.

Poor condition of Baltic Sea behind flounder population slump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

Poor condition of Baltic Sea behind flounder population slump
Although fishers attribute the low abundance of flounder to the spread of an invasive species, a fisheries scientist says the cause is the Baltic Sea's poor hydrological conditions.
According to Taavi Suitsberg, chairman of the NGO Lääne County Coastal Fisheries Association and a professional fisherman, fishers believe the decline in flounder numbers is due to the invasive round goby, which competes with native fish species for food and reproduces more quickly.
At the same time, Suitsberg said the growing number of gobies is a double-edged sword for fishers. Although they are said to be crowding out flounder species, gobies are themselves edible fish and serve as food for larger fish.
However, Suitsberg acknowledged that he could not say exactly why flounder numbers are declining and that fishers had also learned about the possible impact of the invasive species from scientists.
Redik Eschbaum, head of the coastal fisheries working group at the University of Tartu's Estonian Marine Institute's Department of Fish Biology and Fisheries, said aquatic ecosystems are so complex that it is difficult to pinpoint a single cause for a species' decline.
However, Eschbaum confirmed that a lack of food cannot be the direct cause, as researchers have not found emaciated flounder. Flounder numbers were also already low before the round goby became widespread, all of which points to hydrological conditions as the cause.
According to Eschbaum, cod are in an even worse situation than flounder. Like flounder, their spawning depends on inflows of saltwater. Cod fishing is banned altogether in the Baltic Sea.
One thing flounder and cod have in common is pelagic eggs, meaning their eggs float freely in the water rather than sticking to underwater plants or objects. These species spawn in deeper, saltier layers of water where their eggs also develop.
Eschbaum said there are two possible reasons why spawning has become more difficult for these species. First, decomposing algae on the seabed may be leaving too little oxygen there.
Another possibility is that climate change has altered wind patterns. "Saltwater inflows are no longer as extensive and don't occur at the same time of year as they used to. But the fish have no way of anticipating that," Eschbaum said.
Eschbaum said that historically, two types of flounder were distinguished in the Baltic Sea: deepwater-spawning flounder and coastal-spawning flounder. It was later discovered, however, that they are two entirely separate species.
Although Baltic Sea flounder are a good example of rapid evolution, the two species have adapted differently. Coastal-spawning flounder, for example, are faring somewhat better, although they too would benefit from saltier water.
Although Eschbaum said flounder numbers are not expected to increase in the near future, the species cannot be considered endangered.

Ursula von der Leyen condemns ‘shocking’ Ratko Mladić funeral in Serbia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:13:47 UTC
20:13:47 KST

The Belgrade funeral for war criminal Ratko Mladić contradicts “the values underpinning Serbia’s path towards the European Union,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Tuesday.
Several Serbian ministers and military leaders attended the ceremony honoring Mladić, who died on Aug. 27 while serving a life sentence for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Serbian Orthodox Patriarch Porfirije, a close ally of Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić, led the service and said Mladić’s name “would remain in the memory and prayers of the Serbian people.”
Advertisement
Mladić was the commander of the Bosnian Serb Army during the 1992-95 Bosnian War and was found responsible for the Srebrenica genocide, in which more than 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed in July 1995.
The Serbian government said that it had no hand in organizing the funeral, however Mladić’s body was flown to Serbia on a government plane and his coffin was escorted by members of the Serbian Armed Forces.
“The elements of official support and the presence of some senior Serbian officials at the funeral are deeply regrettable,” von der Leyen said, adding that “they demonstrate a failure to confront a dark chapter in Europe’s recent history.”
“The images from Ratko Mladić’s funeral yesterday in Belgrade were shocking,” wrote European Council President António Costa. “Ratko Mladić was a convicted war criminal. He was responsible for genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity.”
The EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas struck an similarly hard line, calling the public glorification of Mladić “an affront to the memory of the victims” and warning that “true reconciliation cannot be built on revisionism, the denial of genocide or the honouring of perpetrators.”
Serbia, which is an EU candidate country, has not opened a new negotiating chapter with the bloc since December 2021. The process is blocked by eight member countries over its rule-of-law record and its refusal to sanction Russia for its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
This story has been updated with comments from Kaja Kallas. Milena Wälde contributed to this report.

A motorist drives past Iranian flags installed along a street, a day before the funeral procession of Iran's slain supreme leader Ali Khamenei in the holy Iraqi city of Karbala. (AFP Photo)
International testing has been frozen in Iran following the latest U.S. sanctions announced in August, part of Washington’s “economic asphyxiation” of the country over the Middle East war.
The suspension has thrown the plans of students hoping to study abroad into disarray, forcing many to seek costly alternatives overseas.
Iranian student Nikki cried for days, as she had planned to study psychology in Italy, but after U.S. sanctions forced the suspension of an English exam required in order to make her dream come true.
Nikki had been due to take the TOEFL English proficiency test, a key qualification required by many foreign universities, in Iran later this month.
Now, like many Iranian students dreaming of a future elsewhere, she is scrambling to find another way to take it, while absorbing the new exam fee and hefty travel costs.
“When I found out that the exam had been cancelled... I did not leave my room for several days because I was crying,” said the 32-year-old, who works at a pastry shop in the northern city of Lahijan.
“My plans were left hanging midway.”
The U.S.-based Educational Testing Service (ETS), which administers the TOEFL English proficiency test, said the exams were suspended after the U.S. Treasury stopped issuing licenses for them.
On its website, ETS said Iranians could still travel abroad to take the exams.
Alternatives, including the PTE English proficiency test and the increasingly popular Duolingo online exam, have also been suspended, according to Iranian media.

China’s highest court sets out new AI red lines with rules on deepfakes and privacy

China’s highest court sets out new AI red lines with rules on deepfakes and privacy
New guidelines provide a broader legal framework for everything from privacy breaches and sexual content to fraud and consumer protection
Although Beijing has yet to pass a dedicated AI law, the guidelines expand the country’s legal framework governing the technology.
The Supreme People’s Court’s 24-article opinion, released on Monday, instead provides guidance for handling AI-related disputes under existing laws, including the Civil Code, Cybersecurity Law, Copyright Law and Personal Information Protection Law.
The rules were the first of their kind and aimed to “draw clear legal red lines” while supporting innovation and development, the court said, aligning itself with the current national policy.
A major focus of the opinion was the use of AI to create deepfake images and videos, clone people’s voices and digitally “bring the dead back to life”.
The court said this could infringe legal protections covering aspects of a person’s identity and elements such as their image, voice and reputation.

EU court rules in favor of Ikea against Belgian far-right party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-08
11:12:23 UTC
20:12:23 KST

A far-right attempt at political parody was dismantled by a European court like an old Billy bookcase.
Flemish party Vlaams Belang’s anti-immigration campaign spoofing Ikea’s assembly instructions “may cause significant detriment” to the furniture-maker’s reputation, the Court of Justice of the European Union said in a ruling Tuesday.
In 2022, Vlaams Belang presented its “IKEA-Plan”, standing for “Immigratie Kan Echt Anders” or “Immigration can really be different.” Proposals to reform Belgium’s immigration policy were illustrated with the Swedish giant’s blue-and-yellow logo and the smiley characters found in its instruction sheets. “We do not wish our brand to be used to suggest that we support certain positions when we do not,” an Ikea spokesperson said at the time.
Advertisement
The firm sued Vlaams Belang in Belgium in November 2022, alleging trademark law infringement. The Belgian business court then asked the CJEU for its advice on how to strike the balance between freedom of expression and the right of a business to defend its trademark.
“It does not appear that the use of the Ikea trade marks for the sole purpose of taking advantage of their reputation to reinforce a political message … takes precedence over the rights and interests” of the Swedish brand, the CJEU said in its press release about the verdict.
The fact that Vlaams Belang’s campaign was completely unrelated to Ikea’s business — and that people may have believed that the company had endorsed it — weighed into the ruling, said Elena Izyumenko, assistant professor in intellectual property law at Amsterdam’s Institute for Information Law.
“What the court suggests is that a private company can suppress controversial political expression if it can create any impression of a link between the company and the opinion expressed in the parody,” Izyumenko said.
The case will now return to the Belgian court, which will rely on the CJEU’s interpretation of the law to issue its ruling. Looking at the CJEU’s ruling, “It’s almost obvious that it will rule against Vlaams Belang,” Izyumenko said.
“The non-profit organization Vrijheidsfonds of Vlaams Belang takes note of the ruling of the European Court of Justice and will thoroughly examine its scope in the context of further legal proceedings,” a spokesperson for the party said.
“Inter IKEA Systems B.V. … welcome the judgment provided by the Court of Justice of the European Union,” a statement from the Netherlands-based company managing Ikea’s intellectual property said. “Inter IKEA fully believes in – and deeply respects – freedom of expression. At the same time, it cannot accept the use of the IKEA trademarks in ways that damage their reputation or distinctive character,” the statement reads.
This article was updated with a statement from Inter IKEA Systems B.V..
